notes: God good; man becomes like God by free obedience — attribute/providence frame.
latin: Acnitrronem autem accepit homo boni et mali. Bonum est autem obedire Deo, et credere ei, et custodire ejus preeceptum ; et hoe est vita hominis: quemadmodum non obedire Deo, malum ; et hoc est mors ejus. Magnanimitatem igitur prestante Deo, cognovit homo et bonum obedientize et malum inobedientiz, uti oculus mentis utrorumque accipiens experimentum, electionem cum judicio faciat ; et nunquam segnis, neque negligens preecepti fiat Dei, et id quod aufert ab eo vitam, id est non obedire Deo, experimento discens quoniam malum est, neque tentet quidem illud unquam ; quod autem conservatorium vite ejus est, obedire Deo, sciens quoniam bonum est, cum omni intentione custodiat. Propter hoe etiam duplices habuit sensus, utrorumque agnitionem habentes, ut electionem meliorum cum disciplina faciat. Disciplinam autem boni quemadmodum habere potuisset, ignorans quod est contrarium? Firmior est enim et indubitata subjacentium apprehensio, quam ea que est ex susconjectura. Quemadmodum enim lingua per gustum accipit experimentum dulcis et amari, et oculus per visionem discernit quod est nigrum ab albo, et auris per auditum differentias sonorum scit ; sic et mens per utrorumque experimentum disciplinam boni accipiens, firmior ad conservationem ejus efficitur, obediens Deo: inobedientiam quidem primum respuens per poenitentiam, quoniam amarum et malum est; deinde ex comprehensione discens, quale sit quod contrarium est bono et dulcedini, ne tentet quidem unquam inobedientiam gustare Dei. Si autem utrorumque eorum cognitionem, et duplices sensus cognitionis quis defugiat, latenter semetipsum occidit hominem. 2. Quemadmodum igitur erit Deus, qui nondum factus est homo? quomodo autem perfectus, nuper effectus? quomodo autem immortalis, qui in natura mortali non obedivit factori? Oportet enim te primo quidem ordinem hominis custodire, tune deinde participare glorie Dei. Non enim tu Deum facis, sed Deus te facit. Si ergo opera Dei es, manum artificis tui exspecta opportune omnia facientem: opportune autem, quantum ad te attinet, squi efficeris. Preesta ei autem cor tuum molle et tractabile, et custodi figuram qua te figuravit artifex, habens in temetipso humorem, ne induratus amittas vestigia digitorum ejus. Custodiens autem compaginationem ascendes ad perfectum: ab artificio enim Dei absconditur quod est in te lutum. Fabricavit substantiam in manus ejus: liniet te ab intus et a foris auro puro et argento, et in tantum ornabit te, ut et ipse Rex concupiscat speciem tuam, Si vero statim obduratus respuas artem ejus, et ingratus exsistas in eum, quoniam homo factus es, ingratus Deo factus, simul et artem ejus et vitam amisisti. Facere enim proprium est benigisnitatis Dei: fieri autem proprium est hominis nature. Si igitur tradideris ei quod est tuum, id est, fidem in eum et subjectionem, recipies ejus artem, et eris perfectum opus Dei. Si autem non credideris ei, et fugeris manus ejus, erit causa imperfectionis in te qui non obedisti, sed non in illo qui vocavit. Ile enim misit, qui vocarent ad nuptias; qui autem non obedierunt ei, semetipsos priyaverunt regia coena. 3. Non igitur ars deficit Dei; potens est enim de lapidibus suscitare filios Abrahze: sed iile qui non consequitur eam, sibimet suze imperfectionis est causa. Nec enim lumen deficit propter qui semetipsos exceecaverunt: sed illo perseverante quale et est, exceecati per suam culpam in caligine constituuntur. Neque lumen cum magna necessitate subjiciet sibi quemquam: neque Deus coget eum, qui nolit continere ejus artem. Qui igitur abstiterunt a paterno lumine, et transgressi sunt legem libertatis, per suam abstiterunt culpam, liberi arbitrii et suze potestatis facti. Deus autem omnia preesciens, utrisque aptas preparavit habitationes : eis quidem qui inquirunt lumen incorruptibilitatis, et ad id recurrunt, benigne donans hoc quod concupiscunt lumen; aliis vero id contemnentibus, et avertentibus se ab eo et id fugientibus, et quasi semetipsos exceecantibus, congruentes lumini adversantibus preeparavit tenebras, et his qui fugiunt ei esse subjecti, ? convenienti subdidit poenze. Subjectio autem Dei requietio est zeterna: ut hi qui fugiunt lumen, dignum fugze suze habeant locum ; et qui fugiunt eeternam requiem, congruentem fugze suze habeant habitationem. Cum autem apud Deum omnia sint bona, qui ex sua sententia fugiunt Deum, semetipsos ab omnibus fraudant bonis: fraudati autem omnibus erga Deum bonis, consequenter in Dei justum judicium incident. Qui enim fugiunt requiem, juste in poena conversabuntur: et qui fugerunt lumen, juste inhabitabunt tenebras. Quemadmodum autem in hoc temporali lumine, qui fugiunt illud, ipsos se tenebris mancipant; ita ut %et ipsi sibi causa fiant, quod a lumine et inhabitant tenebras, et non lumen causa est eis hujusmodi conversationis, quemadmodum preediximus: sic eeternum Dei qui fugiunt lumen, quod continet in se omnia bona, ipsi sibi causa sunt ut ecternas inhabitent tenebras, destituti omnibus bonis, sibimetipsis causa hujusmodi habitationis facti.

excerpts.author: Irenaeus
english: He recapitulated all things by recapitulating them in Himself, provoking war against our enemy and crushing the one who first led us captive in Adam, bruising his head just as God told the serpent in Genesis: "I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed; he will bruise your head, and you will bruise his heel" (Genesis 3:15). For the One who was to be born of the Virgin according to the likeness of Adam was foretold to bruise the serpent's head — that is, the seed concerning whom the Apostle says in the letter to the Galatians: "The law of works was established until the seed to whom the promise was made should come" (Galatians 3:19). The same letter makes this even clearer: "But when the fullness of time came, God sent His Son, made from a woman." The enemy could not have been justly conquered unless a man born of a woman conquered him, since it was through a woman that dominion over man was first established, the adversary setting himself in opposition to man. That is why the Lord also confesses Himself to be the Son of Man, the first man from whom the creation according to the woman was formed, recapitulating it in Himself so that just as our race descended into death through the conquered man, so also we might ascend into life through the Conqueror; and just as death won the palm against us through a man, so we will win the palm against death through a man.

The Lord would not have recapitulated in Himself that ancient and first enmity against the serpent — fulfilling the Creator's promise and perfecting His command — if He had come from another father. But because He is the one and the same God who formed us at the beginning and sent His Son in the end, the Lord perfected that command by being born of a woman, destroying our adversary and perfecting humanity according to the image and likeness. He did not destroy the enemy by any other means than the words of the Law and the Father's command, using them as instruments for the destruction and overthrow of the apostate angel. First, after forty days of fasting — like Moses and Elijah — He became hungry, so we would know He is a true and steadfast man: it is proper to a fasting man to hunger. This also gave the adversary an opening to attack. In the beginning he seduced a man who was not hungry to transgress God's command through food; in the end he could not persuade the hungry One to turn aside from the food that comes from God. When he said, "If you are the Son of God, command these stones to become bread," the Lord repulsed him by the command of the Law: "It is written: Man shall not live by bread alone" (Deuteronomy 8:3). To the challenge "If you are the Son of God" He was silent, but He confounded the devil by confessing His humanity and, through the Father's word, broke the first assault. The fullness humanity had in Paradise through a double tasting was undone by the need experienced in this world.

Though legally refuted, the devil tried another attack through a command. Taking Him to the pinnacle of the temple, he said, "If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down. For it is written: 'He will command His angels concerning you,' and 'On their hands they will bear you up, lest you strike your foot against a stone'" (Psalm 91:11-12) — hiding a lie in Scripture. The passage spoke of what God commanded His angels concerning the Messiah; it said nothing about throwing Himself down. That was the devil's own persuasion. The Lord legally confounded him: "It is also written: You shall not put the Lord your God to the test," showing what befits a man — that a man must not tempt God. In the man He appeared to be, He did not tempt the Lord His God. The serpent's pride was undone by the humility in this Man; the devil was already twice defeated by Scripture, exposed as one who counsels contrary to God's command and shows himself God's enemy.

Greatly confounded, the devil gathered himself and marshaled all his power into a lie, showing Him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory. As Luke records, he said: "I will give You all these, for they have been delivered to me, and I give them to whomever I wish, if You will fall down and worship me." The Lord answered: "Go, Satan! For it is written: You shall worship the Lord your God, and Him only shall you serve." By that name He unmasked him and revealed who He Himself was — for "Satan" is a Hebrew word meaning "the apostate." Conquering him a third time, He drove him away as one legally defeated. The transgression of God's command that began in Adam was resolved through the command of the Law which the Son of Man kept without transgressing God's command.

Who, then, is the Lord God to whom Christ bears witness — whom no one shall tempt, whom all must adore and serve alone? Without doubt He is the One who gave the Law, God Himself. These things were foretold in the Law, and by the Law's testimony the Lord showed that the Law announces the Word of the Lord from the Father, while the apostate angel of God is destroyed by His voice, overthrown, and conquered by the Son of Man keeping God's command. Because the devil first persuaded man to transgress the Creator's command, he held man in his power — and his power is transgression and apostasy, by which he bound humanity. It was necessary that he be conquered again through a man, bound with the very chains he used to bind man, so that freed humanity might return to its Lord, leaving behind those chains of transgression. The devil's binding became man's liberation, for no one can enter a strong man's house and plunder his goods unless he first binds the strong man. Therefore the Lord, overthrowing him and subjecting him by the command — the command of God being the Law — showed him to be a fugitive, a transgressor of the Law, and an apostate of God. Then the Word firmly bound him as His own fugitive and plundered his goods — the men he held captive and used unjustly. The one who had unjustly led man captive was justly led captive; the man who had been led captive was rescued from the possessor's power by the mercy of God the Father, who pitied His creation and gave it salvation through the Word, that is, through Christ, restoring it — so that humanity might learn by experience that it receives incorruptibility not from itself but from the gift of God. The true Lord and the one God is declared by the Law and manifested by the Gospel through Christ His Son: Him alone we must adore, and from Him alone expect all good, not from Satan.

notes: Recapitulation / victory over devil presupposes true incarnation.
latin: Omnta ergo recapitulans recapitulatus est, et adversus inimicum nostrum bellum provocans, et elidens eum qui, in initio in Adam captivos duxerat nos, et caleans ejus caput, quemadmodum habes in Genesi dixisse serpenti Deum: Et inimicitiam ponam inter te et inter mulierem, et inter semen tuum et semen ejus: tpse tuum lobservabit caput, et tu observabis ejus calcanewm, Ex eo enim qui ex muliere Virgine habebat nasci secundum similitudinem Adam, preeconabatur observans caput serpentis, id est semen, de quo ait Apostolus in epistola que est ad Galatas: Legem + factorum s positam, donec veniret semen cui promissum est. Manifestius autem adhue in eadem ostendit epistola, sic dicens: Cum autem venit plenitudo temporis, misit Deus Filium suum, factum de muliere. Neque enim juste victus fuisset inimicus, nisi ex muliere homo esset, qui vicit eum. Per mulierem enim homini dominatus est ab initio, semetipsum contrarium statuens homini. Propter hoc et Dominus semetipsum Filium Hominis confitetur, principalem hominem illum, ex quo ea que secundum mulierem est plasmatio facta est, in semetipsum recapitulans: uti quemadmodum per hominem victum descendit in mortem genus nostrum, sic iterum per victorem ascendamus in vitam. Et quemadmodum accepit palmam mors per hominem adversus nos, sic iterum nos adversus mortem per hominem accipiamus palmam. 2. Non autem Dominus antiquam illam et primam adversus serpentem inimicitiam in semetipso recapitulatus fuisset, adimplens promissionem Demiurgi, et perficiens preeceptum ejus, si ab alio venisset patre. Sed quoniam unus et idem est, qui ab initio plasmavit nos, et in fine Filium suum misit, preeceptum ejus perfecit Dominus, factus ex muliere, et destruens adversarium nostrum, et perficiens hominem secundum imaginem et similitudinem Et propter hoc non aliunde eum destruxit, nisi ex dictionibus Legis, et Patris preecepto adjutore usus ad destructionem et traductionem apostate angeli. Primo quidem diebus xu. jejunans, similiter ut Moyses et Helias, postea esuriit, ut hominem verum et firmum intelligamus: proprium enim est hominis, jejunantem esurire: deinde autem, ut haberet adversarius ubi congrederetur. Quoniam enim in principio per escam, non esurientem hominem seduxit transgredi preeceptum Dei, in fine esurientem non potuit dissuadere, eam que a Deo esset, sustinere escam. enim eo, et dicente: Si jilius Dei es, dic ut lapides isti panes fant; Dominus autem per preeceptum Legis repulit eum, dicens: Scriptum est, Non in pane tantum vivit homo. Ad illud quidem quod ait, Si filius Dei es, tacuit: exceecayit autem eum hominis confessione, et per paternam dictionem primum ejus impetum evacuavit. Que ergo fuit in Paradiso repletio hominis per duplicem gustationem, dissoluta est per eam, que fuit in hoe mundo, indigentiam. Ille autem legaliter explosus, tentabat et ipse per mandatum rursus legitime facere congressionem. In altissimum enim templi pinnaculum ducens eum, dixit: Si jilius Dei es, mitte te deorsum. Scriptum est enim: Quoniam Angelis swis Deus mandavit de te, et in manibus tollent te, ne forte offendas ad lapidem pedem twum, mendacium abscondens per Scripturam, quod Illud enim, quod Angelis suis mandavit de eo, scriptum erat; Mitte te autem deorsum, * de eo nulla dicebat sed a semetipso hane suasionem Diabolus afferebat. Dominus itaque legitime confutavit eum, dicens: Item seriptum in Lege ostendens id Yuidem quod est secundum hominem, quoniam non debet homo tentare Deum; quantum autem ad illum, in eo homine qui videbatur, non tentaret Dominum Deum suum. Elatio itaque sensus que fuit in serpente, dissoluta est per eam que fuit in homine humilitas: et bis jam victus erat de Scriptura Diabolus, cum est traductus, contraria preecepto Dei suadens, et secundum sententiam suam Dei hostis ostensus. Qui magne confutatus, et quasi semetipsum colligens, universam quam habebat virtutem in mendacium ordinans, tertio ostendit e seculi regna omnia, et gloriam ipsorum, dicens, quemadmodum meminit Lucas: Hee omnia tibi dabo, quoniam mihi tradita sunt, et cui volo do ea, si procidens adoraveris me. Dominus itaque eum qui esset: Vade, inquit, Satana; seriptum est Senim: Dominum Deum tuum adorabis, et illi soli servies. Denudans eum per hoe nomen, et se ostendens qui erat. Satana enim verbum Hebraicum, Apostatam significat. Et tertio itaque vincens eum, in reliquum repulit a semetipso quasi legitime vicet soluta est ea que fuerat in Adam preecepti Dei preevaricatio, per preeceptum legis, quod servavit Filius hominis non transgrediens preeceptum Dei. 8. Quis ergo Dominus Deus, cui Christus testimonium perhibet; quem nemo tentabit, et quem omnes adorare oportet, et soli servire? Omnimodo ille est sine dubio, qui et Legem dedit Deus. Heee enim in Lege preedicta fuerant, et per Legis sententiam ostendit Dominus, quoniam Lex quidem a Patre Verbum Domini annuntiat : apostata autem Dei angelus )per illius destruitur vocem, traductus Nquis esset, et victus a Filio hominis servante Dei preeceptum. Quoniam enim in initio homini suasit transgredi preceptum factoris, ideo eum habuit in sua potestate; potestas autem ejus est transgressio et apostasia, et his colligavit hominem ; per hominem ipsum iterum oportebat victum eum contrario colligari iisdem vinculis, quibus alligavit hominem, ut homo solutus revertatur ad suum Dominum, illa vincula relinquens, per }quze ipse fuerat alligatus, id est transgressionem. Illius enim colligatio, solutio facta est hominis, quoniam non potest ali> quis introire in domum fortis, et vasa ejus diripere, nisi primum ipsum fortem alligaverit. Contraria ergo in sermone ejus, qui omnia fecit Dei, traducens eum Dominus, et subjiciens per preeceptum, preeceptum autem Dei, lex; fugitivum eum Homo ejus et legis transgressorem, et apostatam Dei ostendens, postea jam ®Verbum constanter eum colligavit, quasi suum fugitivum, et diripuit ejus vasa, id est, eos qui ab eo detinebantur homines, quibus ipse injuste utebatur. Et captivus quidem ductus est juste is qui hominem injuste captivum duxerat; qui autem ante captivus ductus fuerat homo, extractus est a possessoris potestate, secundum misericordiam Dei Patris: qui miseratus est plasmati suo, et dedit salutem ei, per Verbum, id est per Christum redintegrans: ut experimento discat homo, quoniam non a semetipso, sed donatione Dei accipit incorruptelam. Dominus verus, et Deus unus a lege declaratur, et Evangelio per Christum ejus Filium manifestatur : quem solum adorare, et ab illo omnia bona exspectare oportet, non a Satana.

excerpts.author: Irenaeus
english: 1. He has therefore, in His work of recapitulation, summed up all things, both waging war against our enemy, and crushing him who had at the beginning led us away captives in Adam, and trampled upon his head, as you can perceive in Genesis that God said to the serpent, And I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed; He shall be on the watch for (observabit ) your head, and you on the watch for His heel. Genesis 3:15 For from that time, He who should be born of a woman, [namely] from the Virgin, after the likeness of Adam, was preached as keeping watch for the head of the serpent. This is the seed of which the apostle says in the Epistle to the Galatians, that the law of works was established until the seed should come to whom the promise was made. Galatians 3:19 This fact is exhibited in a still clearer light in the same Epistle, where he thus speaks: But when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth His Son, made of a woman. Galatians 4:4 For indeed the enemy would not have been fairly vanquished, unless it had been a man [born] of a woman who conquered him. For it was by means of a woman that he got the advantage over man at first, setting himself up as man's opponent. And therefore does the Lord profess Himself to be the Son of man, comprising in Himself that original man out of whom the woman was fashioned (ex quo ea quæ secundum mulierem est plasmatio facta est), in order that, as our species went down to death through a vanquished man, so we may ascend to life again through a victorious one; and as through a man death received the palm [of victory] against us, so again by a man we may receive the palm against death.

2. Now the Lord would not have recapitulated in Himself that ancient and primary enmity against the serpent, fulfilling the promise of the Creator (Demiurgi), and performing His command, if He had come from another Father. But as He is one and the same, who formed us at the beginning, and sent His Son at the end, the Lord did perform His command, being made of a woman, by both destroying our adversary, and perfecting man after the image and likeness of God. And for this reason He did not draw the means of confounding him from any other source than from the words of the law, and made use of the Father's commandment as a help towards the destruction and confusion of the apostate angel. Fasting forty days, like Moses and Elias, He afterwards hungered, first, in order that we may perceive that He was a real and substantial man — for it belongs to a man to suffer hunger when fasting; and secondly, that His opponent might have an opportunity of attacking Him. For as at the beginning it was by means of food that [the enemy] persuaded man, although not suffering hunger, to transgress God's commandments, so in the end he did not succeed in persuading Him that was an hungered to take that food which proceeded from God. For, when tempting Him, he said, If you be the Son of God, command that these stones be made bread. Matthew 4:3 But the Lord repulsed him by the commandment of the law, saying, It is written, Man does not live by bread alone. Deuteronomy 8:3 As to those words [of His enemy,] If you be the Son of God, [the Lord] made no remark; but by thus acknowledging His human nature He baffled His adversary, and exhausted the force of his first attack by means of His Father's word. The corruption of man, therefore, which occurred in paradise by both [of our first parents] eating, was done away with by [the Lord's] want of food in this world. But he, being thus vanquished by the law, endeavoured again to make an assault by himself quoting a commandment of the law. For, bringing Him to the highest pinnacle of the temple, he said to Him, If you are the Son of God, cast yourself down. For it is written, That God shall give His angels charge concerning you, and in their hands they shall bear you up, lest perchance you dash your foot against a stone; thus concealing a falsehood under the guise of Scripture, as is done by all the heretics. For that was indeed written, [namely], That He has given His angels charge concerning Him; but cast yourself down from hence no Scripture said in reference to Him: this kind of persuasion the devil produced from himself. The Lord therefore confuted him out of the law, when He said, It is written again, You shall not tempt the Lord your God; Deuteronomy 6:16 pointing out by the word contained in the law that which is the duty of man, that he should not tempt God; and in regard to Himself, since He appeared in human form, [declaring] that He would not tempt the Lord his God. The pride of reason, therefore, which was in the serpent, was put to nought by the humility found in the man [Christ], and now twice was the devil conquered from Scripture, when he was detected as advising things contrary to God's commandment, and was shown to be the enemy of God by [the expression of] his thoughts. He then, having been thus signally defeated, and then, as it were, concentrating his forces, drawing up in order all his available power for falsehood, in the third place showed Him all the kingdoms of the world, and the glory of them, Luke 4:6-7 saying, as Luke relates, All these will I give you — for they are delivered to me; and to whom I will, I give them — if you will fall down and worship me. The Lord then, exposing him in his true character, says, Depart, Satan; for it is written, You shall worship the Lord your God, and Him only shall you serve. Matthew 4:10 He both revealed him by this name, and showed [at the same time] who He Himself was. For the Hebrew word Satan signifies an apostate. And thus, vanquishing him for the third time, He spurned him from Him finally as being conquered out of the law; and there was done away with that infringement of God's commandment which had occurred in Adam, by means of the precept of the law, which the Son of man observed, who did not transgress the commandment of God.

3. Who, then, is this Lord God to whom Christ bears witness, whom no man shall tempt, whom all should worship, and serve Him alone? It is, beyond all manner of doubt, that God who also gave the law. For these things had been predicted in the law, and by the words (sententiam) of the law the Lord showed that the law does indeed declare the Word of God from the Father; and the apostate angel of God is destroyed by its voice, being exposed in his true colors, and vanquished by the Son of man keeping the commandment of God. For as in the beginning he enticed man to transgress his Maker's law, and thereby got him into his power; yet his power consists in transgression and apostasy, and with these he bound man [to himself]; so again, on the other hand, it was necessary that through man himself he should, when conquered, be bound with the same chains with which he had bound man, in order that man, being set free, might return to his Lord, leaving to him (Satan) those bonds by which he himself had been fettered, that is, sin. For when Satan is bound, man is set free; since none can enter a strong man's house and spoil his goods, unless he first bind the strong man himself. The Lord therefore exposes him as speaking contrary to the word of that God who made all things, and subdues him by means of the commandment. Now the law is the commandment of God. The Man proves him to be a fugitive from and a transgressor of the law, an apostate also from God. After [the Man had done this], the Word bound him securely as a fugitive from Himself, and made spoil of his goods, — namely, those men whom he held in bondage, and whom he unjustly used for his own purposes. And justly indeed is he led captive, who had led men unjustly into bondage; while man, who had been led captive in times past, was rescued from the grasp of his possessor, according to the tender mercy of God the Father, who had compassion on His own handiwork, and gave to it salvation, restoring it by means of the Word — that is, by Christ — in order that men might learn by actual proof that he receives incorruptibility not of himself, but by the free gift of God.

excerpts.author: Irenaeus
english: 1. Inasmuch, then, as in this world (αἰῶνι) some persons go to the light, and by faith unite themselves with God, but others shun the light, and separate themselves from God, the Word of God comes preparing a fit habitation for both. For those indeed who are in the light, that they may derive enjoyment from it, and from the good things contained in it; but for those in darkness, that they may partake in its calamities. And on this account He says, that those upon the right hand are called into the kingdom of heaven, but that those on the left He will send into eternal fire for they have deprived themselves of all good.

2. And for this reason the apostle says: Because they received not the love of God, that they might be saved, therefore God shall also send them the operation of error, that they may believe a lie, that they all may be judged who have not believed the truth, but consented to unrighteousness. 2 Thessalonians 2:10-12 For when he (Antichrist) has come, and of his own accord concentrates in his own person the apostasy, and accomplishes whatever he shall do according to his own will and choice, sitting also in the temple of God, so that his dupes may adore him as the Christ; wherefore also shall he deservedly be cast into the lake of fire: Revelation 19:20 [this will happen according to divine appointment], God by His prescience foreseeing all this, and at the proper time sending such a man, that they may believe a lie, that they all may be judged who did not believe the truth, but consented to unrighteousness; whose coming John has thus described in the Apocalypse: And the beast which I had seen was like a leopard, and his feet as of a bear, and his mouth as the mouth of a lion; and the dragon conferred his own power upon him, and his throne, and great might. And one of his heads was as it were slain to death; and his deadly wound was healed, and all the world wondered after the beast. And they worshipped the dragon because he gave power to the beast; and they worshipped the beast, saying, Who is like this beast, and who is able to make war with him? And there was given to him a mouth speaking great things, and blasphemy and power was given to him during forty and two months. And he opened his mouth for blasphemy against God, to blaspheme His name and His tabernacle, and those who dwell in heaven. And power was given him over every tribe, and people, and tongue, and nation. And all who dwell upon the earth worshipped him, [every one] whose name was not written in the book of the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world. If any one have ears, let him hear. If any one shall lead into captivity, he shall go into captivity. If any shall slay with the sword, he must be slain with the sword. Here is the endurance and the faith of the saints. Revelation 13:2, etc. After this he likewise describes his armour-bearer, whom he also terms a false prophet: He spoke as a dragon, and exercised all the power of the first beast in his sight, and caused the earth, and those that dwell therein, to adore the first beast, whose deadly wound was healed. And he shall perform great wonders, so that he can even cause fire to descend from heaven upon the earth in the sight of men, and he shall lead the inhabitants of the earth astray. Revelation 13:11, etc. Let no one imagine that he performs these wonders by divine power, but by the working of magic. And we must not be surprised if, since the demons and apostate spirits are at his service, he through their means performs wonders, by which he leads the inhabitants of the earth astray. John says further: And he shall order an image of the beast to be made, and he shall give breath to the image, so that the image shall speak; and he shall cause those to be slain who will not adore it. He says also: And he will cause a mark [to be put] in the forehead and in the right hand, that no one may be able to buy or sell, unless he who has the mark of the name of the beast or the number of his name; and the number is six hundred and sixty-six, Revelation 13:14, etc. that is, six times a hundred, six times ten, and six units. [He gives this] as a summing up of the whole of that apostasy which has taken place during six thousand years.

3. For in as many days as this world was made, in so many thousand years shall it be concluded. And for this reason the Scripture says: Thus the heaven and the earth were finished, and all their adornment. And God brought to a conclusion upon the sixth day the works that He had made; and God rested upon the seventh day from all His works. Genesis 2:2 This is an account of the things formerly created, as also it is a prophecy of what is to come. For the day of the Lord is as a thousand years; 2 Peter 3:8 and in six days created things were completed: it is evident, therefore, that they will come to an end at the sixth thousand year.

4. And therefore throughout all time, man, having been moulded at the beginning by the hands of God, that is, of the Son and of the Spirit, is made after the image and likeness of God: the chaff, indeed, which is the apostasy, being cast away; but the wheat, that is, those who bring forth fruit to God in faith, being gathered into the barn. And for this cause tribulation is necessary for those who are saved, that having been after a manner broken up, and rendered fine, and sprinkled over by the patience of the Word of God, and set on fire [for purification], they may be fitted for the royal banquet. As a certain man of ours said, when he was condemned to the wild beasts because of his testimony with respect to God: I am the wheat of Christ, and am ground by the teeth of the wild beasts, that I may be found the pure bread of God.

excerpts.citation: Melito of Sardis — Fragment on the Incarnation (Reliquiae Sacrae)
excerpts.author: Melito of Sardis
greek: Οὐδεμία ἀνάγκη τοῖς νοῦν ἔχουσιν, ἐξ ὧν μετὰ τὸ βάπτισμα ὁ Χριστὸς ἔπραξε, παριστᾶν τὸ ἀληθὲς καὶ ἀφανταστὸν τῆς ψυχῆς αὐτοῦ καὶ τοῦ σώματος, τῆς καθ' ἡμᾶς ἀνθρωπίνης φύσεως. Τὰ γὰρ μετὰ τὸ βάπτισμα ὑπὸ Χριστοῦ πραχθέντα, καὶ μάλιστα τὰ σημεῖα, τὴν αὐτοῦ κεκρυμμένην ἐν σαρκὶ θεότητα ἐδήλουν, καὶ ἐπιστοῦντο τῷ κόσμῳ. Θεὸς γὰρ ὢν ὁμοῦ τε καὶ ἄνθρωπος τέλειος ὁ αὐτὸς τὰς δύο αὐτοῦ οὐσίας ἐπιστώσατο ἡμῖν, τὴν μὲν θεότητα αὐτοῦ διὰ τῶν σημείων ἐν τῇ τριετίᾳ τῇ μετὰ τὸ βάπτισμα, τὴν δὲ ἀνθρωπότητα αὐτοῦ ἐν τοῖς τριάκοντα χρόνοις τοῖς πρὸ τοῦ βαπτίσματος, ἐν οἷς διὰ τὸ ἀτελὲς τὸ κατὰ σάρκα ἀπέκρυβε τὰ σημεῖα τῆς αὐτοῦ θεότητος, καίπερ θεὸς ἀληθὴς προαιώνιος ὑπάρχων.
english: There is no necessity for those who have understanding to prove the true and invisible reality of His soul and body, the human nature as we know it, from what Christ did after His baptism. For the works Christ performed after the baptism, and especially the signs, revealed His deity concealed in flesh and convinced the world. For being God and at the same time also perfect man, He Himself guaranteed to us His two substances: the one indeed His deity through the signs during the three years after the baptism, and the other His humanity during the thirty years before the baptism, in which, because of the imperfection of the flesh, He was hiding the signs of His deity, even though He was true God existing before the ages.

excerpts.author: Novatian
english: The rule of truth demands that first of all we believe in God the Father and Lord Almighty, the most perfect creator of all things. He suspended the heavens in their high sublimity, solidified the earth with a thrown-down mass, poured out the seas with loosened liquid, and arranged and filled all these with their own proper and worthy instruments (Genesis 1:1). In the firmament he kindled the light-bringing sun, filled the moon's shining globe with measured increments of its orbit to comfort the night, and ignited the stars' rays with varied brilliance. He willed them all to circle the whole world's circuit by fixed paths, providing humanity with days, months, years, signs, seasons, and benefits. On earth he lifted the highest mountains to their peaks, sank the valleys to their depths, spread the plains evenly, and usefully ordained herds of animals for human service. He hardened the forests' strength for human use, brought forth crops for food, opened the springs' mouths, and fed the flowing rivers. Afterward, to provide for the eyes' delight, he clothed everything with flowers' varied colors for the spectators' pleasure. In the sea, though already marvelous in size and utility, he fashioned creatures of many kinds -- now moderate, now vast in body -- testifying to the artisan's skill through the variety of his design. Not content with these, lest the waters' roar and surge, at human expense, encroach on a foreign element, he bounded the shores so that when foaming waves and spuming surges came, they would turn back into themselves and not exceed their granted limits, keeping the prescribed laws -- so that humans might keep divine laws all the more, since even the elements obey them. After this he also placed man in the world, made in God's image, giving him mind, reason, and prudence to imitate God. Though his body has earthly origins, a heavenly and divine breath was inspired into his substance. Having given all things into his service, God willed him to be free alone. Lest this freedom fall into danger again, he gave a command: not because evil was present in the tree's fruit, but so that if man chose to despise the law, the warning would be future, and he ought to remain free, lest God's image incongruously serve. The law was added lest unbridled liberty burst forth into contempt for the Giver, so that man would consequently receive fitting rewards and deserved punishments, now possessing the very thing he willed to direct by his mind's motion either way. From this mortality, certainly envy, returned upon him: he could have escaped through obedience, but fell back into it while hastening to be God by perverse counsel. Yet God tempered the punishment indulgently, cursing not the man himself but his labors on the earth. What is required comes not from ignorance but shows the hope of humanity's future in Christ -- both invention and salvation. The prohibition against touching the tree of life comes not from malignant envy, but lest, living forever, man carry his immortal guilt into punishment unless Christ first forgave sins. Although in the realms above -- above the firmament itself, in parts not visible to our eyes today -- he previously instituted angels, arranged spiritual virtues, established thrones and powers, and founded many other immense heavenly spaces and infinite sacramental works, so that this vast world appears almost the last rather than the only work of God's bodily creation. The regions beneath the earth are not empty of ordered and arranged powers. There is a place where the souls of the pious and impious are led, experiencing the future judgment's pre-judgments. Thus the overflowing magnitudes of God's works are not confined within this world's most capacious embrace, as we have said, but extend beneath it, in its depths and heights, so that considering the works' magnitude we may worthily wonder at the Artisan of such great bulk.

latin: Regula exigit ueritatis ut primo omnium credamus in deum patrem et dominum omnipotentem, id est, rerum omnium perfectissimum conditorem, qui caelum alta sublimitate suspenderit, terram deiecta mole solidauerit, maria soluto liquore diffuderit, et haec omnia propriis et condignis instrumentis et ornata et plena digesserit. nam et in solidamento caeli luciferos solis ortus excitauit, lunae candentem globum ad solacium noctis mensurnis incrementis orbis impleuit, astrorum etiam radios uariis fulgoribus micantis lucis accendit: et haec omnia legitimis meatibus circumire totum mundi ambitum uoluit, humano generi dies, menses, annos, signa, tempora, utilitatesque factura. in terris quoque altissimos montes in uerticem sustulit, ualles in ima deiecit, campos aequaliter strauit, animalium greges ad uarias hominum seruitutes utiliter instituit. siluarum quoque robora humanis usibus profutura solidauit, fruges in cibum elicuit, fontium ora reserauit, et lapsuris fluminibus infudit. post quae, ne non etiam ipsis quoque deliciis procurasset oculorum, uariis florum coloribus ad uoluptatem spectantium cuncta uestiuit. in ipso quoque mari, quamuis esset et magnitudine et utilitate mirabile, multimoda animalia, nunc mediocris, nunc uasticorporis fingit, ingenium artificis de institutionis uarietate testantia. quibus non contentus, ne forte fremitus et cursus aquarum, cum dispendio possessoris humani, alienum occuparet elementum, fines litoribus inclusit: quo cum fremens fluctus et ex alto sinu spumans unda uenisset, rursum in se rediret nec terminos concessos excederet, seruans iura praescripta: ut diuinas leges tanto magis homo custodiret, quanto illas etiam elementa seruassent. Post quae hominem quoque mundo praeposuit et quidem ad imaginem dei factum: cui mentem et rationem indidit et prudentiam, ut deum posset imitari: cuius etsi corporis terrena primordia, caelestis tamen et diuini halitus inspirata substantia: quem, cum omnia in seruitutem illi dedisset, solum liberum esse uoluit. et ne in periculum caderet rursum soluta libertas, mandatum posuit, quo tamen non inesse malum fructu arboris doceretur, sed futurum, si forte, ex uoluntate hominis de contemptu datae legis praemonenam et liber esse debuerat, ne incongruenter dei imago seruiret: et lex addenda, ne usque ad contemptum dantis libertas effrenata prorumperet: ut et praemia condigna et merita poenarum consequenter exciperet, suum iam habens illud, quod motu mentis in alterutram partem agitare uoluisset. ex quo mortalitas, inuidia utique, in ipsum redit; qui cum illam de oboedientia posset euadere, in eandem incurrit, dum ex consilio peruerso deus esse festinat. cuius tamen poenam nihilominus indulgenter temperauit, dum non tam ipse, quam labores eius maledicuntur super terra. nam et quod requiritur, non ex ignorantia uenit, sed spem hominis futurae in Christo et inuentionis et salutis ostendit: et quod ne de ligno arboris uitae contingat arcetur, non de inuidiae maligno liuore descendit, sed ne uiuens in aeternum, nisi peccata Christus ante donasset, circumferret secum in poenam sui semper immortale delictum. Quamquam etiam superioribus, id est, super ipsum quoque solidamentum partibus, quae non sunt hodie nostris contemplabiles oculis, angelos prius instituerit, spiritales uirtutes digesserit, thronos potestatesque praefecerit, et alia multa caelorum immensa spatia et sacramentorum infinita opera condiderit, ut immensus hic licet mundus paene nouissimum magis dei corporalium rerum appareat opus esse, quam solum, namque quae infra terram iacent, neque ipsa sunt digestis et ordinatis potestatibus uacua. locus enim est quo piorum animae impiorumque ducuntur, futuri iudicii praeiudicia sentientes: ut operum ipsius in omnibus partibus redundantes magnitudines non intra mundi huius capacissimos licet, ut diximus, sinus conclusas uideremus, sed etiam infra ipsius mundi et profunda et altitudines cogitare possemus; et sic considerata operum magnitudine, tantae molis digne mirari possemus artificem.

excerpts.author: Novatian
english: The rule of truth demands that we believe first of all in God the Father and Lord Almighty, the most perfect Creator of all things (Genesis 1:1). He suspended the heavens in high sublimity, solidified the earth with its thrown-down mass, poured out the seas with loosened liquid, and arranged and filled all these things with their own proper and worthy instruments. In the firmament he lit the light-bringing sun, filled the shining globe of the moon with measured increments of its orbit for the night's solace, and kindled the rays of the stars with varied brilliances of sparkling light. He willed that all these bodies circle the whole circuit of the world in their ordained courses, making days, months, years, signs, seasons, and utilities for the human race. On the earth he lifted the highest mountains to their peaks, cast the valleys down to the depths, spread the plains evenly, and usefully instituted herds of animals for varied human service. He hardened the timber of forests for human use, brought forth crops for food, opened the mouths of springs, and fed the flowing rivers. Lest he fail to provide for the eyes' delight as well, he clothed everything with the varied colors of flowers for the pleasure of beholders. Even in the sea, though it was wondrous in magnitude and utility, he fashioned many kinds of creatures, some of moderate size, some of vast bulk, testifying to the artisan's ingenuity through the variety of their making. Not content with these, lest the roar and rush of the waters — at the loss of the human possessor — should encroach on an alien element, he enclosed the shores with boundaries. Thus when the foaming wave and spuming surge came, they would turn back into themselves and not exceed the granted limits, keeping the prescribed laws, so that humanity might keep the divine laws all the more, since even the elements kept them. After these things he also placed man in the world, made indeed in the image of God (Genesis 1:26). He gave him mind, reason, and prudence, so that he might imitate God. Though his body was of earthly origin, a heavenly and divine breath was breathed into his substance. Having given all things into servitude to him, God willed that he alone should be free. And lest this loosened freedom lead him into danger, he set a command — not to teach that evil was present in the tree's fruit, but that it would come, if perhaps from the will of man, from contempt of the given law, as a warning. Man ought to be free, lest the image of God serve incongruously; and the law was added lest unbridled freedom burst forth into contempt of the Giver. Thus he would receive fitting rewards and deserved punishments, having the power to move his mind in either direction. From this, mortality — certainly envy — returns upon him. When he could have escaped it through obedience, he fell into it instead, hastening to be God by perverted counsel. Yet God tempered his punishment indulgently: not the man himself, but his labors are cursed upon the earth. For what is required comes not from ignorance, but shows the hope of humanity's future in Christ — both discovery and salvation. And the prohibition against touching the wood of the tree of life does not spring from malignant envy, but lest, living eternally, man should carry his immortal delict into punishment unless Christ had first given sins. Although in the realms above — that is, above the firmament itself, in parts not visible to our eyes today — he previously instituted angels, arranged spiritual virtues, established thrones and powers, and founded many other immense spaces of the heavens and infinite works of sacraments, this vast world, though it may seem the latest, rather appears to be the work of God's bodily creation, not alone. For the things beneath the earth are not empty of arranged and ordered powers. There is a place where the souls of the pious and impious are led, feeling the pre-judgments of the future judgment, so that we might not see the overflowing magnitudes of his works only within the most capacious bosom of this world, as we have said, but might also contemplate them beneath this world and in its depths and heights. Thus, considering the magnitude of the works, we may worthily wonder at the Artisan of so great a mass.

excerpts.author: Novatian
english: Containing all things within himself, he leaves nothing empty outside his being, so he has not left room for a superior God, as some imagine. Indeed, he has enclosed the whole universe in the embrace of his perfect magnitude and power. He is ever intent on his work, passing through all things, moving all things, giving life to all things, and seeing all things. He joins the discordant materials of every element into harmony, so that from differing elements one world arises, solidified by this conspiracy, which no force can dissolve unless he who made it commands it to be dissolved, so that he may give us greater things. We read that he contains all things; therefore nothing can exist outside him. Since he has no origin at all, he consequently knows no end either—unless, absurdly, he once began to exist, in which case he would not be above all things but below what preceded him, found lesser in power because he is later in time. For this reason he is always immense, because nothing is greater than he is, and always eternal, because nothing is older than he is. What is without origin cannot be preceded by anything, since it has no time. Therefore he is immortal, not failing at the consummation's end. And because whatever is without origin is without law, he excludes the measure of time, since he recognizes himself as indebted to no one. Consequently, the human mind cannot worthily conceive what he is, how great he is, or what kind he is, nor can human eloquence express a virtue equal to his majesty. In contemplating and speaking of his majesty, all eloquence is rightly mute, and every mind is small. He is greater than mind itself, and cannot be thought as to how great he is, lest if he could be thought he would be less than the human mind that conceives him. He is also greater than all speech, and cannot be expressed, lest if he could be expressed he would be less than human speech, by which, when he is expressed, he can be encompassed and collected. For whatever is thought of him is less than he is, and whatever is spoken of him, compared with him, is less than he is. We can sense him in silence to some extent, but we cannot explain him in speech as he truly is. If you call him light, you have named a creature of his rather than him; you have not expressed him. If you call him virtue, you have named his power rather than him and set it forth. If you call him majesty, you have described his honor rather than him himself. Why should I make a long discussion, running through each thing individually? I will explain the whole matter once: whatever you say of him altogether, you have explained some thing of his, some virtue of his, rather than him. For what can you say or think worthily of him, who is greater than all speeches and all senses? Unless, in one way (and even this, how can we do it, how can we grasp it, how is it permitted to understand it?), we can apprehend what God is with our mind, if we think that he is that which cannot be understood as to its kind and magnitude, and cannot even enter into thought itself. For if the vision of our eyes is dulled by the sight of the sun, so that it cannot look at the orb itself, overcome by the brilliance of its rays, the same thing happens to the vision of the mind in every thought of God; and the more it strains to consider God, the more it is blinded by the light of its own thought. For what can you say worthily of him (to repeat once more), who is more sublime than all sublimity, higher than all height, deeper than all depth, more lucid than all light, clearer than all clarity, more splendid than all splendor, more robust than all robustness, more virile than all virtue, more beautiful than all beauty, truer than all truth, stronger than all strength, more majestic than all majesty, more powerful than all power, richer than all riches, more prudent than all prudence, more benign than all benignity, better than all goodness, more just than all justice, more merciful than all mercy? All kinds of virtues must be less than he who is both God and parent of all virtues, so that it can be truly said that he is God, who is such that nothing can be compared to him. He is above all that can be said. For he is a certain mind that generates and fills all things, which, without any beginning or end of time, moderates the causes of things—naturally linked for the utility of all—with supreme and perfect reason.

latin: Super quae omnia ipse continens cuncta, nihil extra ro se uacuum deserens, nulli deo superiori (ut quidam putant) locum reliquit. quandoquidem ipse uniuersa sinu perfectae magnitudinis et potestatis incluserit, intentus semper operi suo, et uadens per omnia, et mouens cuncta, et uiuificans uniuersa, et conspiciens tota, et in concordiam elementorum omnium discordantes materias sic conectens, ut ex disparibus elementis ita sit unus mundus ista coagmentata conspiratione solidatus, ut nulla ui dissolui possit, nisi cum illum solus ipse qui fecit, ad maiora alia praestanda nobis, solui iusserit. hunc enim legimus omnia continere: et ideo nihil extra ipsum esse potuisse; quippe cum originem omnino non habeat, consequenter nec exitum sentiat: nisi forte, quod absit, aliquando esse coeperit, nec super omnia sit, sed dum post aliquid esse coeperit, infra id sit quod ante ipsum fuerit, minor inuentus potestate, dum posterior denotatur etiam ipso tempore. ob hanc ergo causam semper immensus, quia nihil illo maius est; semper aeternus, quia nihil illo antiquius. id enim quod sine origine est, praecedi a nullo potest, dum non habet tempus. ideo immortalis, non deficiens in consummationis exitu. et quoniam sine lege est quicquid sine origine est, modum temporis excludit, dum se debitorem nemini sentit. De hoc ergo, ac de eis quae sunt ipsius et in eo sunt, nec mens hominis quae sint, quanta sint, et qualia sint, digne concipere potest, nec eloquentia sermonis humani aequabilem maiestati eius uirtutem expromit. ad cogitandam enim et ad eloquendam illius maiestatem et eloquentia omnis merito muta est, et mens omnis exigua est. maior est enim mente ipsa, nec cogitari possit quantus sit, ne si potuerit cogitari, mente humana minor sit, qua concipi possit. maior est quoque omni sermone, nec edici possit: ne si potuerit edici, humano sermone minor sit, quo, cum edicitur, et circumiri et colligi possit. quicquid enim de illo cogitatum fuerit, minus ipso erit: et quicquid enuntiatum fuerit, minus illo comparatum circum ipsum erit. sentire enim illum taciti aliquatenus possumus; ut autem ipse est, sermone explicare non possumus. siue enim illum dixeris lucem, creaturam ipsius magis quam ipsum dixeris; ipsum non expresseris: siue illum dixeris uirtutem, potentiam ipsius magis quam ipsum dixeris et deprompseris: siue dixeris maiestatem, honorem ipsius magis quam illum ipsum descripseris. et quid per singula quaeque percurrens longum facio? semel totum explicabo: quicquid omnino de illo rettuleris, rem aliquam ipsius magis et uirtutem, quam ipsum explicaueris. quid enim de eo condigne aut dicas, aut sentias, qui omnibus et sermonibus et sensibus maior est? nisi quod uno modo (et hoc ipsum quo modo possumus, quo modo capimus, quo modo intellegere licet?) quid sit deus mente capiemus, si cogitauerimus id illum esse, quod quale et quantum sit non possit intellegi, nec in ipsam quidem cogitationem possit uenire. nam si ad solis aspectum oculorum nostrorum acies hebescit, ne orbem ipsum obtutus inspiciat obuiorum sibi superatus fulgore radiorum, hoc idem mentis acies patitur in cogitatione omni de deo; et quanto ad considerandum deum plus intenditur, tanto magis ipsa cogitationis suae luce caecatur. quid enim de eo (ut iterum repetam) condigne dicas, qui est sublimitate omni sublimior, et altitudine omni altior, et profundo omni profundior, et omni luce lucidior, et omni claritate clarior, omni splendore splendidior, omni robore robustior, omni uirtute uirilior, omni pulchritudine pulchrior, ueritate omni uerior, et fortitudine omni fortior, et maiestate omni maior, et omni potentia potentior, et omnibus diuitiis ditior, omni prudentia prudentior, et omni benignitate benignior, omni bonitate melior, omni iustitia iustior, omni clementia clementior? minora enim sint necesse est omnium genera uirtutum eo ipso, qui uirtutum omnium et deus et parens est: ut uere dici possit id deus esse, quod eiusmodi est cui comparari nihil potest. super omne est enim quod dici potest. mens est enim quaedam gignens et complens omnia, quae sine ullo aut initio aut termino temporis causas rerum, naturaliter nexas ad utilitatem omnium summa et perfecta ratione moderetur.

excerpts.author: Novatian
english: We therefore acknowledge and know this God as the Creator of all things, as Lord on account of his power, and as Father on account of his governance. He spoke, and all things came into being; he commanded, and the universe proceeded forth. Scripture says of him, 'You made all things in wisdom' (Psalm 104:24). Moses declares, 'God is in heaven above and on the earth beneath' (Deuteronomy 4:39). According to Isaiah, he measured the heavens with a palm's breadth and the earth with his fist (Isaiah 40:12). He looks at the earth, and it trembles (Psalm 104:32). He holds the circle of the earth, and its inhabitants are like grasshoppers (Isaiah 40:22). He weighs the mountains in a balance and the forests in a scale—that is, by a precise examination of divine ordering. Moreover, lest the earth's vast mass, unevenly spread, collapse into ruin, he balanced it with equal weights and so moderately stabilized this burden of earthly matter. Through the prophet he says, 'I am God, and there is no other besides me' (Isaiah 45:5). Through the same prophet he declares that he will not give his glory to another (Isaiah 42:8); thus he excludes all Gentiles with their fabrications and all heretics, proving that God is not an artifact made by an artisan's hand, nor a fiction invented by a heretic's mind. For that is not God for whom an artisan must be sought in order to exist. He added further through the prophet: 'Heaven is my throne, and the earth is the footstool of my feet; what kind of house will you build for me, and what place will be my rest?' (Isaiah 66:1-2). He says this to show that the temple cannot contain him whom the world cannot contain. He speaks these things not for his own boasting but for our knowledge. He himself does not desire glory of greatness from us; rather, as a Father he wishes to impart to us religious wisdom. Furthermore, desiring to draw our savage minds—swollen with rustic barbarity and roughness—toward gentleness, he says: 'But upon whom will my Spirit rest, if not upon the humble and quiet and those who tremble at my words?' (Isaiah 66:2). He does this so that one may be able to recognize how great God is, while learning to fear him through the Spirit bestowed. Similarly, desiring to come even more fully into our knowledge, and stirring our minds to cultivate him, he was saying: 'I am the Lord, who made light and created darkness' (Isaiah 45:7)—so that we might not suppose some unknown nature to be the artisan of these alternations by which nights and days are governed, but rather recognize God as the Creator, which is the truth. Since we cannot see him with our physical eyes, we learn his greatness, power, and majesty from his works. For, as the apostle Paul says, his invisible attributes—his eternal power and divine nature—have been clearly perceived ever since the creation of the world, understood through the things that have been made (Romans 1:20). Thus the human mind, learning hidden things from manifest ones, may contemplate the greatness of the Artisan from the magnitude of the works it sees. Concerning him the same apostle declares: 'Now to the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God, be honor and glory forever and ever' (1 Timothy 1:17). He has escaped the contemplation of the eyes, having surpassed the magnitude of thought. For, Paul says, all things are from him and through him and in him (Romans 11:36). All things exist by his command, so that they may be from him; all things are ordered by his word, so that they may be through him; and all things fall under his judgment, so that—while they await freedom, having laid aside corruption—they may appear to have been recalled to him.

latin: Hunc igitur agnoscimus et scimus deum, conditorem rerum omnium, dominum, propter potestatem, et parentem propter institutionem: hunc inquam, qui dzx7t, et facta sunt omnia; praecepit, et processerunt uniuersa; de quo scriptum est: omnia in sapientia fecisti; de quo Moyses: deus in caelo sursum et in terra deorsum; qui secundum Isaiam mensus est caelum palmo, terram pugillo: qui aspicit terram, et facit eam tremere: qui continet gyrum terrae, et eos qui habitant in ipso quasi locustae: qui expendit montes in pondere, et nemora in statera, id est certo diuinae dispositionis examine: ac, ne facile in ruinam procumberet magnitudo inaequaliter iacens, si non paribus fuisset librata ponderibus, onus hoc moderanter terrenae molis aequauit. qui dicit per prophetam: ego deus, et non est praeter me. qui per eundem prophetam refert quoniam matestatem meam non dabo alter’; ut omnes cum suis figmentis ethnicos excludat et haereticos, probans deum non esse qui manu artificis factus sit, nec eum qui ingenio haeretici fictus sit. non est enim deus, cui, ut sit, quaerendus est artifex. adhuc adiecit per prophetam: caelum mihi thronus est, terra autem scabellum pedum meorum: qualem mihi aedificabitis domum, aut quis locus requiei meae? ut ostendat quoniam multo magis illum templum non capit, quem mundus non capit. et haec non ad sui iactantiam, sed ad nostri scientiam refert. neque enim ipse a nobis desiderat magnitudinis gloriam, sed nobis uult religiosam, qua pater, conferre sapientiam. quique praeterea ferinos nostros animos et de agresti immanitate tumidos et abruptos ad lenitatem trahere uolens, dicit: ef super quem requiescet spiritus meus, nisi super humilem et quietum, et trementem uerba mea? ut deum aliquatenus quantus sit possit agnoscere, dum illum per spiritum collatum discit timere. qui similiter adhuc magis in notitiam nostri uolens peruenire, ad culturam sui nostros excitans animos, aiebat: ego sum dominus, qui feci lucem et creaui tenebras; ut uicissitudinum istarum quibus noctes diesque moderantur non naturam nescio quam putaremus artificem, sed deum agnosceremus potius (quod erat uerius) conditorem. quem quoniam obtutu oculorum uidere non possumus, de operum magnitudine et uirtute et maiestate condiscimus: uisibilia enim ipsius, inquit apostolus Paulus, a creatura mundi per ea quae facta sunt intellecta conspiciuntur; sempiterna quoque eius uirtus et diuinitas: ut animus humanus ex manifestis occulta condiscens, de operum magnitudine, quae uideret, mentis oculis artificis magnitudinem cogitaret. de quo idem apostolus: reg? autem saeculorum immortali, inuisibili, soli deo honor et gloria, euasit enim oculorum contemplationem, qui cogitationis uicit magnitudinem: guoniam, inquit, ex ipso et per ipsum et in ipso sunt omnia, nam et imperio eius omnia, ut ex ipso sint: et uerbo eius digesta, ut per ipsum sint: et in iudicium eius recidunt uniuersa, ut dum ” ipso exspectant libertatem corruptione deposita, in ipsum uideantur esse reuocata.

english: The Lord declares Him good, and rightly so; the whole world bears witness to His goodness, for He would not have established it if He were not good. Since all things are very good, it follows necessarily that the things He established are also good, and they prove their Establisher to be good; moreover, nothing that comes from a good Establisher can be anything but good. From this truth all evil is excluded. He cannot be the author or craftsman of any evil work, He who claims the name of the Perfect One, the Father, and the Judge, especially because He is the avenger and judge of every evil deed. Evil comes to humanity from no other source than withdrawal from the good God. This withdrawal is evident in humanity, not because it was necessary, but because man himself so willed it. God appeared, and, lest envy be seen in the God from whom evil originated, He shone forth. Therefore He is always like Himself; He never changes or transforms into any form, lest through change He appear mortal. Change is a portion of conversion, and conversion implies a kind of death. Consequently, no addition of any part or honor ever accrues to Him, lest something seem ever to have been lacking to the Perfect One; nor does any loss occur in Him, lest He seem to have accepted the condition of mortality. Rather, what He is, He always is; who He is, He always is; what kind He is, He always is. Increments reveal an origin, and losses prove death and destruction; therefore He says, 'I am God, and I have not changed' (Exodus 3:14-15), holding His state forever, since what is not born cannot be converted. It is necessary that whatever God is, He always be God, preserving Himself by His own virtues. And therefore He says: 'I AM WHO I AM.' A thing has this name because it always retains the same quality. Change removes the name 'He Who Is,' for whatever undergoes change is shown to be mortal by that very fact: it ceases to be what it was and begins to be what it was not. Rightly, then, God's state remains forever, since without loss through change He is always the same and equal to Himself. What is not born cannot change; only things that are made or generated enter conversion, because what once did not exist learns to exist by being born, and so is changed by being born. But those things that have neither birth nor maker have excluded change from themselves, since they lack the origin in which the cause of conversion lies. Therefore He is also declared to be One, because He has no equal; for God, whatever can be God, must be the Highest. And the Highest must be such that it is the Highest, since it is beyond compare. Therefore He must be alone and One, to whom nothing can be compared, because He has no equal. Two infinites cannot exist, as the nature of reality itself dictates. The infinite is that which has neither origin nor end; whatever occupies the whole excludes the beginning of another. If God did not contain all that exists, He would be found within what contains Him, and the container would be found to be less; thus God would cease to be, reduced to the power of another by whose lesser magnitude He would be enclosed, and the container would rather have begun to be God. It follows that even the proper name of God cannot be spoken, because it cannot be conceived. A name contains whatever is comprehended by the condition of its nature; a name is the signification of a thing that can be grasped by that name. But when the subject is such that it cannot even be grasped by our intellects, how can it be pronounced with a worthy title, since it is beyond intellect and therefore beyond the signification of any title? When God adds and prefers His name for certain reasons and occasions, we must understand that He is not so much revealing a legitimate property of the name as establishing a certain signification, to which men run so that they may seem to obtain God's mercy through it. He is therefore immortal and incorruptible, feeling no loss whatsoever and having no end. Because He is incorruptible, He is also immortal; and because He is immortal, He is certainly incorruptible; each quality is intertwined with the other in a mutual, reciprocal bond, and connected to the state of eternity by a vicarious concatenation, with immortality proceeding from incorruption and incorruption coming from immortality.

latin: Quem solum merito bonum pronuntiat dominus: cuius bonitatis totus testis est mundus, quem non instituisset, nisi bonus fuisset. nam si omnia bona ualde, consequenter ac merito et quae instituta sunt bona bonum institutorem probauerunt, et quae a bono institutore sunt, aliud quam bona esse non possunt. ex quo omne malum facessit adeo. nec enim potest fieri ut sit initiator aut artifex ullius mali operis, qui nomen sibi perfecti uindicat et parentis et iudicis, maxime cum omnis mali operis uindex sit et iudex; quoniam et non aliunde occurrit homini malum, nisi a bono deo recessisset. hoc autem ipsum in homine denotatur: non quia necesse fuit, sed quia ipse sic uoluit. apparuit, et, ne inuidia in deo esse uideretur, a quo malum ortum esset, eluxit. Hic ergo semper sui est similis, nec se umquam in aliquas formas uertit aut mutat, ne per immutationem etiam mortalis esse uideatur. immutatio enim conuersionis portio cuiusdam comprehenditur mortis. ideo nec adiectio in illo umquam ullius aut partis aut honoris accedit, ne quid umquam perfecto defuisse uideatur; nec detrimentum in eo aliquod agitur, ne gradus mortalitatis receptus esse uideatur: sed quod est, id semper est, et qui est, semper ipse est, et qualis est, semper talis est. nam et incrementa originem monstrant, et detrimenta mortem atque interitum probant, et ideo: ego, ait, sum deus, et non sum mutatus, statum suum tenens semper, dum id quod natum non est, conuerti non potest. hoc enim in ipso, quicquid illud potest quod est deus, semper sit necesse est, ut semper sit deus, seruans sese uirtutibus suis. et ideo dicit: ego sum qui sum. quod enim est, ideo hoc habet nomen, quoniam eandem semper sui obtinet qualitatem. immutatio enim tollit illud nomen ‘quod est’: quicquid enim aliquando uertitur, mortale ostenditur hoc ipso quod conuertitur: desinit enim esse quod fuerat, et incipit consequenter esse quod non erat. idcirco et merito in deo manet semper status suus, dum sine detrimento commutationis semper sui et similis et aequalis est. quod enim natum non est, nec mutari potest: ea enim sola in conuersionem ueniunt, quaecumque fiunt uel quaecumque gignuntur; dum quae aliquando non fuerant, discunt esse nascendo, atque ideo nascendo conuerti. at enim illa quae nec natiuitatem habent nec artificem, excluserunt a se demutationem, dum in qua conuersionis causa est, non habent originem. Ideo et unus pronuntiatus est, dum parem non habet: deus enim, quicquid esse potest quod deus est, summum sit necesse est. summum autem quicquid est, ita demum summum esse oportet, dum extra comparem est. et ideo solum et unum sit necesse est, cui conferri nihil potest, dum parem non habet. quoniam nec duo infinita esse possunt, ut rerum dictat ipsa natura. infinitum est autem, quicquid nec originem habet omnino, nec finem. excludit enim alterius initium, quicquid occupauerit totum. quoniam si non omne id quod est, quicquid est, continet, dum intra id inuenitur quo continetur, minus inuentum quo continetur, deus esse desierit, in alterius potestatem redactus, cuius magnitudine, qua minor, fuerit inclusus: et ideo quod continuit, deus potius esse iam coeperit. Ex quo effectum est ut nec nomen dei proprium possit edici, quoniam non possit nec concipi. id enim nomine continetur, quicquid etiam ex naturae suae condicione comprehenditur. nomen enim significantia est eius rei, quae comprehendi potuit ex nomine. at quando id de quo agitur tale est, ut condigne nec ipsis intellectibus colligatur, quomodo appellationis digne uocabulo pronuntiabitur, quod, dum extra intellectum est, etiam supra appellationis significantiam sit necesse est? ut merito quando nomen suum deus ex quibusdam rationibus et occasionibus adicit et praefert, non tam legitimam proprietatem appellationis sciamus esse depromptam, quam significantiam quandam constitutam; ad quam dum homines decurrunt, dei misericordiam per ipsam impetrare posse uideantur. Est ergo et immortalis et incorruptibilis, nec detrimenta sentiens omnino, nec finem. nam et quia incorruptibilis, ideo et immortalis; et quia immortalis, utique et incorruptibilis; utroque inuicem sibi et in se conexione mutua perplexo, et ad statum aeternitatis uicaria concatenatione producto, et immortalitate de incorruptione descendente, et incorruptione de immortalitate ueniente.
excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 4

excerpts.author: Novatian
english: The Church knows and venerates this God, setting aside the fables and fabrications of heretics; all creation — invisible and visible alike, the whole of nature at all times — bears witness to him. Angels adore him, the stars marvel, the seas bless him, the lands reverence him, and everything in the netherworld looks up to him. Every human mind perceives him, even if it cannot put that perception into words. By his command all things are set in motion: fountains gush, rivers flow, waves surge, every creature brings forth its young, winds are compelled to blow, rains fall, seas are stirred, and everywhere fertility spreads abroad.

He planted a paradise in the east, a world of eternal life, for the first-formed humans; he set there the tree of life and likewise the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; he gave a command and fixed a penalty for transgression. He saved Noah, the most just, from the flood because of his innocence and faith; he transferred Enoch; he brought Abraham into the fellowship of friendship; he protected Isaac and increased Jacob; he appointed Moses to lead the people; he rescued the groaning sons of Israel from the yoke of slavery; he wrote the Law; he led the fathers' offspring into the promised land; he instructed the prophets by the Spirit; and through them all he promised his Son Christ — and when the time came to give him, he sent him.

Through the Son he willed us to come to knowledge of him, and he poured out the broad bosom of his mercy upon us, conferring a rich Spirit on the needy and the outcast. Because he is generous, bountiful, and good, he did not want the whole world to wither, cut off from the streams of his grace. So he willed that apostles, instructors of our race, be sent into all the world through his Son, that the human condition might recognize its teacher and, if it chose to follow, have someone to call Father in its prayers (Psalm 68:17).

His providence does not merely run through individual lives; it runs through cities and nations, whose destinies the prophets have sung — indeed, through the whole world, whose end, plagues, diminutions, and punishments he has foretold because of its unbelief. Lest anyone imagine this untiring providence fails to reach the smallest details, the Lord says: not one of two sparrows falls without the Father's will, and even the hairs of your head are all numbered. His care did not allow the Israelites' clothing to wear out, nor their sandals — the lowliest things — to deteriorate, nor even the captives' hair to be burned. There is good reason: if he embraces all things and contains all things (for the whole and all things consist of individual parts), then his care inevitably extends to each single thing, since his providence already reaches the whole, whatever it is.

Therefore he sits upon the cherubim — that is, he presides over the variety of his works, with the living creatures subject to his throne holding first place among the rest, and all things covered overhead by the crystal firmament, which is heaven covering all. At God's command this firmament was solidified from the flowing substance of the waters into robust ice, dividing the upper and lower waters so that, its strength reinforced by frost, it could bear the weight of the upper waters. Beneath it turn the wheels — that is, the times — by which all the members of the world are continually revolved; feet are added to them so that these things do not stand forever but pass away. And through every part they are studded with starry eyes, for God's works are to be contemplated with a wakeful gaze. In their midst is the fire of coals: either because this world hastens toward the fiery day of judgment, or because all God's works are fiery, not dark but vigorous, or lest, having arisen from earthly principles, they might naturally grow cold from the rigor of their origin — so the warm nature of the inner Spirit was added to all things to supply equal balances for the use of life to bodies frozen by cold.

This, then, is the chariot of God, according to David: 'The chariot of God is multiplied ten thousand times,' that is, innumerable, infinite, immense. Under the yoke of the natural law given to all, some are drawn back as with reins, others driven forward as with loosened reins. The angels and the stars guide this world, the chariot of God, with all its parts; their varied courses, though bound by fixed laws, we see leading to the goals of an appointed time — so that we too, with the apostle, marveling at the artisan and his work, may rightly exclaim: O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and his ways inscrutable, and all that follows.
