excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 8
latin: Hunc ergo, omissis haereticorum fabulis atque figmentis, deum nouit et ueneratur ecclesia; cui testimonium reddit tam inuisibilium quam etiam uisibilium et semper et tota natura: quem angeli adorant, astra mirantur, maria benedicunt, terrae uerentur, inferna quaeque suspiciunt: quem mens omnis humana sentit, etiam si non exprimit: cuius imperio omnia commouentur, fontes scaturiunt, amnes labuntur, fluctus assurgunt, fetus suos cuncta parturiunt, uenti spirare coguntur, imbres ueniunt, maria commouentur, fecunditates suas cuncta ubique diffundunt. qui peculiarem protoplastis aeternae uitae mundum quendam paradisum in oriente constituit: avdorem uitae plantauit; scientiae boni et mai similiter alteram arborem collocauit; mandatum dedit; sententiam contra delictum statuit; Noe iustissimum de diluui periculis pro merito innocentiae fideique seruauit; Enoch transtulit; in amicitiae societatem Abraham allegit; Isaac protexit; Iacob auxit; Moysen ducem populo praefecit; ingemiscentes filios Israel e iugo seruitutis eripuit; legem scripsit; patrum subolem in terram repromissionis induxit; prophetas spiritu instruxit; et per hos omnes filium suum Christum repromisit; et quando daturum se spoponderat, misit. per quem nobis in notitiam uenire uoluit, et in nos indulgentiae suae sinus largos profudit, egenis et abiectis locupletem spiritum conferendo. et quia ultro et largus et bonus est, ne totus hic orbis auersus gratiae eius fluminibus aresceret, apostolos institutores generis nostri in totum orbem mitti per filium suum uoluit, ut condicio generis humani agnosceret institutorem, et, si sequi maluisset, haberet quem pro deo in suis iam postulationibus patrem diceret. cuius non prouidentia tantummodo singillatim per homines cucurrit aut currit, sed etiam per ipsas urbes et ciuitates, quarum exitus prophetarum uocibus cecinit; immo etiam per ipsum totum orbem, cuius propter incredulitatem exitus, plagas, deminutiones poenasque descripsit. et ne quis non etiam ad minima quaeque dei putaret istam infatigabilem prouidentiam peruenire, ex duobus, inquit dominus, passeribus unus non cadet sine patris uoluntate, sed et capilli capitis uestri omnes numerati sunt; cuius etiam cura et prouidentia Israelitarum non siuit nec uestes consumi, nec uilissima iz pedibus calciamenta deteri, sed nec ipsorum postremum adulescentium captiua sarabara comburi. nec immerito; nam si hic omnia complexus est omnia continens (omnia autem et totum ex singulis constant), pertinget consequenter eius ad usque singula quaeque cura, cuius ad totum, quicquid est, peruenit prouidentia. Hinc est quod et desuper cherubim sedet, id est, praeest super operum suorum uarietatem, subiectis throno eius animalibus prae ceteris principatum tenentibus, cuncta desuper crystallo contegente, id est, caelo omnia operiente: quod in firmamentum de aquarum fluente materia fuerat deo iubente solidatum, ut glacies robusta aquarum terram pridem contegentium diuidens medietatem dorso quodam pondera aquae superioris, corroboratis de gelu uiribus, sustineret. nam et rotae subiacent, tempora scilicet, quibus omnia semper mundi membra uoluuntur talibus pedibus adiectis, quibus non in perpetuum stant ista, sed transeunt. sed et per omnes artus stellata sunt oculis; dei enim opera peruigili obtutu contemplanda sunt. in quorum sinu carbonum medius est ignis; siue quoniam ad igneum diem iudicii mundus iste festinat; siue quoniam omnia opera dei ignea, nec sunt tenebrosa, sed uigent; siue etiam, ne, quia ex terrenis ista fuerant orta principiis, naturaliter de originis suae rigore torperent, addita est omnibus interioris spiritus calida natura, quae frigidis concreta corporibus ad usuram uitae aequalia omnibus libramenta ministraret. hic est igitur currus, secundum Dauid, dei. currus enim, inquit, dei decies milies multtMultiplicatus, id est, innumerus, infinitus, immensus. — sub iugo enim naturalis legis omnibus datae alia quasi frenis reuocata retrahuntur, alia quasi effusis habenis excitata impelluntur. mundum enim istum currum dei cum omnibus et ipsi angeli ducunt et astra; quorum uarios licet meatus, certis tamen legibus uinctos, inspicimus ad metas definiti sibi temporis ducere; ut merito nobis quoque cum apostolo et artificem et opera mirantibus exclamare iam libeat: altitudo diuttiarum sapientiae et scientiae dei, quam inscrutabilia iudicia eius et inuestigabiles uiae eius et reliqua.

excerpts.author: Novatian
english: The same rule of truth teaches us to believe, after the Father, in the Son of God as well — Christ Jesus, our Lord and God, yet still the Son of God. This God is both one and alone, the Creator of all things, as I have already stated above. We read in the Old Testament and see fulfilled in the New Testament that this Jesus Christ — let me say again, the Son of this God — was promised long ago and now appears as the embodied truth that fills every shadow and figure of the sacraments. Abraham and David, no less than the ancient prophecies and the Gospels themselves, bear witness to him. Genesis says, "I will give to your seed" (Genesis); it portrays a man wrestling with Jacob (Genesis); and it declares, "The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor the ruler's staff from between his feet, until he comes to whom it has been promised, and he shall be the expectation of the nations" (Genesis). Moses says, "Provide another whom you will send" (Deuteronomy); and again he testifies, "God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers; hear him as you would me" (Deuteronomy); and again, "You will see your life hanging before you night and day, and you will not believe him" (Deuteronomy). Isaiah announces, "A shoot shall come forth from the stump of Jesse, and a branch shall grow from his roots" (Isaiah); the same prophet says, "Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son" (Isaiah); he places the healings that will come from him: "Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf unstopped; then the lame shall leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute shall sing" (Isaiah); he proclaims the virtues of his patience: "His voice shall not be heard in the streets; a bruised reed he will not break, and a smoldering wick he will not quench" (Isaiah); he describes his Gospels: "I will make with you an everlasting covenant, the steadfast, sure mercies of David" (Isaiah); he prophesies that the nations will believe in him: "Behold, I have given him as a witness to the peoples, a leader and commander for the peoples. Nations that do not know you shall run to you, and peoples that do not know you shall flee to you" (Isaiah). The same prophet cries out concerning his passion: "He was led like a lamb to the slaughter, and like a sheep before its shearers is silent, so he opened not his mouth" (Isaiah); he describes the blows and wounds of his scourging: "By his stripes we are healed" (Isaiah); or his humility: "He had no form or majesty that we should look at him, and no beauty that we should desire him. He was a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief" (Isaiah); or that the people would not believe: "I have spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people" (Isaiah); or that he will rise from the dead: "In that day the root of Jesse shall stand as a signal for the peoples; he shall reign, and the nations shall hope in him, and his rest shall be glorious" (Isaiah); or concerning the time of resurrection: "We will find him ready like the dawn" (Hosea); or that he will sit at the right hand of the Father: "The Lord says to my Lord: 'Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool'" (Psalm); or when the possessor of all things is established: "Ask of me, and I will make the nations your heritage, and the ends of the earth your possession" (Psalm); or that he is shown to be the judge of all: "Give the king your justice, O God, and your righteousness to the royal son" (Psalm). I will not pursue more examples here, for the things announced about Christ are well known not only to all heretics but even to those who hold the truth.

excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 9
latin: Eadem regula ueritatis docet nos credere post patrem etiam in filium dei, Christum Iesum, dominum deum nostrum, sed dei filium; huius dei qui et unus et solus est, conditor scilicet rerum omnium, ut iam et superius expressum est. hunc enim Iesum Christum, iterum dicam huius dei filium, et in ueteri testamento legimus esse repromissum et in nouo testamento animaduertimus exhibitum, omnium sacramentorum umbras et figuras de praesentia corporatae ueritatis implentem. hunc enim Abrahae filium, hunc Dauid, non minus et uetera praedicta et euangelia testantur. ipsa Genesis, cum dicit: dabo et semini tuo; hunc quando luctatum ostendit hominem cum iacob; hunc, quando dicit: on deficiet princeps de Iuda, neque dux de Femoribus eius, donec ueniat is cui repromissum est, et ipse erit exspectatio gentium. hunc Moyses, cum dicit: prouide alium quem mittas; hunc idem, quando testatur, prophetam uobis, dicendo, suscitabit deus ex fratribus uestris: eum quasi me audite; hunc, quando dicit: videbitis uitam uestram pendentem nocte ac die, et non credetis ei. hunc Esaias: prodiet uirga de radice Iesse, et flos de radice etus ascendet; hunc eundem, quando dicit: ecce uirgo concipiet et pariet filium,; hunc, quando sanitates ab eo futuras collocat dicens: tunc aperientur oculi caecorum, et aures surdorum audient: tunc saliet claudus ut ceruus, et Diserta erit lingua mutorum; hunc, quando patientiae uirtutes expromit dicens: non audietur in plateis uox eius; harundinem quassatam non conteret, et linum fumigans non exstinguet; hunc, quando eius euangelia descripsit: e dzsponam uobis testamentum aeternum, sancta Daud fidelia; hunc, quando gentes in ipsum credituras prophetat: ecce posui eum in principium et praecipientem gentibus. gentes quae te non nouerunt inuocabunt te, et populi qui te nesciunt ad te confugient; hunc eundem, quando ad passionem eius exclamat dicens: sicut ouis ad occisionem ductus est, et sicut agnus coram tondente se sine uoce, sic non aperuit os suum in humilitate; hanc quando flagrorum eius ictus plagasque descripsit: liuore eius nos sanati sumus; aut humilitatem: et uidimus eum, et non erat ei species neque honor. homo in plaga et sciens ferre infirmitatem; aut quod populus non erat crediturus: tota die expandi manus meas ad populum non credentem; aut quod resurrecturus a mortuis: e erit in illa die radix Iesse, et qui surget imperare gentibus, in eum gentes sperabunt, et erit requies eius honor; aut cum tempus resurrectionis: quasi diluculo paratum inueniemus eum; aut quod sessurus ad dextram patris: dixit dominus domino meo: sede ad dexteram meam, donec ponam inimicos tuos scabellum pedum tuorum; aut cum possessor omnium collocatur: postula a me, et dabo tibi gentes hereditatem tuam, et possessionem tuam terminos terrae; aut quod iudex omnium ostenditur: deus iudicium tuum regi da, et iustitiam tuam filio regis. nec hoc in loco plura persequar, quae annuntiata de Christo omnibus haereticis sed et ipsis ueritatem tenentibus magis nota sunt.

excerpts.author: Novatian
english: I warn you: we are not to expect a different Christ in the gospel than this one whom the Creator promised beforehand in the letters of the Old Testament. The very things predicted about him have been fulfilled, and the things fulfilled were foretold in advance. Therefore I can truly and steadfastly say to these heretics who reject the authority of the Old Testament: "Who are you? Where are you from? By whom were you sent? Why did you want to come now? Why are you such a person? Or how could you come? Or why did you not go to your own people, unless you proved you have no people of your own by coming to strangers? What have you to do with the world of the Creator? What have you to do with the man of the Founder? What have you to do with the fabricated body, from which you strip away the hope of resurrection? Why do you come to a foreign servant and desire to seduce a foreign son? Why do you try to snatch me from the Lord? Why do you compel me to blaspheme and be impious toward the Father? What shall I gain from you in the resurrection, you who do not receive me yourself while I lose my body? If you wanted to save, you would have made a man to whom you could give salvation. If you desired to rescue from sin, you would have prevented me from sinning in the first place. What sanction of the law do you carry with you? What testimony of the prophetic voice do you have? Or what solid thing can I promise about you, since I see you coming as a phantom and not in solid reality? What then have you to do with the figure of a body, if you hate the body? You are defeated by bearing the very substance of the body you hated, whose mere likeness you also chose to take. You ought to have hated the imitation of the body if you hated the truth. For if you are someone else, you ought to have come in a different way, so that you would not be called the Son of the Creator, even if you had the image of flesh and body. Certainly, if you hated birth because you hated the union of the Creator's marriage, you ought to have refused even the imitation of man, who is born through the Creator's marriage." We therefore do not acknowledge the Christ of the heretics, who existed only in appearance and not in truth—since he did nothing true among the things he did, if he himself was a phantom and not the truth—nor the one who took nothing of our body into himself, because he received nothing from Mary, so that he did not come to us, since he did not appear in our substance; nor the one who, as other heretics claimed, put on heavenly or starry flesh. We see no salvation in him unless we also recognize the solid reality of our own body. Nor do we acknowledge any other whatsoever who bore some other body fabricated from the heretics' fictions. For both the birth of the Lord and his death itself refute all of them. For the Word, says John, became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14); therefore our body was truly in him, because the Word took our flesh. And blood flowed from his hands and feet and his side precisely so that he might be proven a sharer in our body, while he died under the laws of our death. Having been raised in the very same bodily substance in which he died, he is confirmed by the wounds of his body, and in his flesh he also demonstrated the laws of our resurrection, because he restored in his resurrection the body he had taken from us. The law of resurrection is established in the fact that Christ was raised in bodily substance as the pattern for the rest. Since it is written that flesh and blood do not inherit the kingdom of God, the substance of the flesh is not condemned—it was fashioned by divine hands so that it would not perish—but only the guilt of the flesh is justly condemned, which, through the voluntary rashness of man, rebelled against the laws of the divine law. That guilt is removed in baptism and in the dissolution of death, and the flesh returns to salvation as it is recalled to the state of innocence, having laid aside the mortality of sin.

latin: Sed illud admoneo, non alterum in euangelio Christum exspectandum fuisse, quam hunc a creatore ueteris testamenti litteris ante promissum; maxime cum et quae de ipso praedicta sunt impleta sint, et quae impleta sunt ante praedicta sint. ut merito haereticorum istorum testamenti ueteris auctoritatem respuentium nescio cui commenticio et ex fabulis anilibus ficto Christo atque fucato possim uere et constanter dicere: “quis es? unde es? a quo missus es? quare nunc uenire uoluisti? quare talis? uel qua uenire potuisti? uel quare non ad tuos abisti, nisi quod’ probasti tuos non habere, dum ad alienos uenis? quid tibi cum mundo creatoris? quid tibi cum homine conditoris? quid tibi cum figmento corporis, cui eripis spem resurrectionis? quid ad alienum uenis famulum, alienum sollicitare desideras filium? quid me a domino eripere conaris? quid me in patrem blasphemare atque impium esse compellis? aut quid sum a te in resurrectione consecuturus, qui me ipsum non recipio, dum corpus amitto? si saluare uis, fecisses hominem cui salutem dares. si a delicto eripere cupis, ante mihi ne delinquerem contulisses. quod autem tecum suffragium circumfers legis? quod habes testimonium propheticae uocis? aut quid mihi possum de te solidum repromittere, cum te uideam in phantasmate et non in soliditate uenisse? quid ergo tibi cum figura corporis, si corpus odisti? immo reuinceris corporis quod odisti circumferre substantiam, cuius suscipere uoluisti etiam figuram: odisse enim debueras corporis imitationem, si oderas ueritatem. quoniam si alter es, aliter uenire debueras, ne dicereris filius creatoris, si uel imaginem habuisses carnis et corporis. certe si oderas natiuitatem, quia creatoris oderas nuptiarum coniunctionem, recusare debueras etiam imitationem hominis, qui per nuptias nascitur creatoris.” neque igitur eum haereticorum agnoscimus Christum, qui in imagine (ut dicitur) fuit et non in ueritate:—nihil enim uerum eorum quae gessit fecerit, siipse phantasma et non ueritas fuit:— neque eum, qui nihil in se nostri corporis gessit, dum ex Maria nihil accepit, ne non nobis uenerit, dum non in nostra substantia uisus apparuit: neque illum, qui aetheream siue sideream, ut alii uoluerunt haeretici, induit carnem; nullam in illo nostro intellegamus salutem, si non etiam nostri corporis cognoscamus soliditatem: nec ullum omnino alterum, qui quoduis aliud ex figmento haereticorum gesserit corpus fabularum. omnes enim istos et natiuitas domini et mors ipsa confutat. nam et uerbum, inquit Ioannes, caro factum est, et habitauit in nobis; ut merito corpus nostrum in illo fuerit, quoniam quidem nostram carnem sermo suscepit. et sanguis idcirco de manibus ac pedibus atque ipso latere demanauit, ut nostri consors corporis probaretur, dum occasus nostri legibus moritur. qui dum in eadem substantia corporis, in qua moritur, resuscitatus ipsius corporis uulneribus comprobatur, etiam resurrectionis nostrae leges in sua carne monstrauit, qui corpus, quod ex nobis habuit, in sua resurrectione restituit. lex enim resurrectionis ponitur, dum Christus ad exemplum ceterorum in substantia corporis suscitatur. quoniam, cum caro ef sanguis non obtinere regnum dei scribitur, non carnis substantia damnata est, quae diuinis manibus, ne periret, exstructa est; sed sola carnis culpa merito reprehensa est, quae uoluntaria hominis temeritate contra legis diuinae iura grassata est. qua in baptismate et in mortis dissolutione sublata caro ad salutem reuertitur, dum ad statum innocentiae, deposita criminis mortalitate, reuocatur.

excerpts.author: Novatian
english: We do not define the substance of Christ's body in a way that makes Him only a man, because that would play into the hands of heretics who deny His divinity. We affirm that the Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God the Creator, was manifested in a true body, yet with the divinity of the Word mixed into that very flesh, so that He is also God according to the Scriptures (John 1:1-14; Colossians 1:15-20). It is a grave danger to call the Savior of the human race—the Lord and Prince of the world, to whom the Father has handed over all things, through whom all things were instituted, created, and ordered, the King of all ages and times, the Prince of all angels, before whom nothing exists except the Father—merely a man and to deny Him divine authority. That insult against the Son redounds to God the Father Himself, if the Father could not generate a Son who is God.

The blindness of heretics will not dictate the truth, nor will it strip from us what they refuse to see, simply because they see something else in Christ. They focus on His human weaknesses as if the divine virtues did not count; they recall the infirmities of the flesh but exclude the powers of divinity. But if the proof drawn from Christ's infirmities establishes that He is a man, then the proof gathered from His virtues must equally establish that He is God. If His sufferings demonstrate human fragility, why do His works not assert divine power? Unless the works succeed in proving He is God, the sufferings cannot succeed in proving He is a man. Whatever law governs one nature will be found to apply to the other; we cannot show Him to be a man from His passions unless we also approve Him as God from His virtues.

Therefore we must not lean toward one side and flee the other, for whoever excludes any portion of the truth will not hold the perfect truth. Scripture announces Christ as both God and man; it describes Jesus Christ as both man and God, the Lord Christ. It presents Him not only as the Son of God but also as the Son of Man, and not only as the Son of Man but also as the Son of God—so that, being from both, He may be both; lest, if He were only one, He could not be the other. Just as nature itself prescribes that we believe the man who comes from man, so the same nature prescribes that we believe the God who comes from God: lest, if He is not also God because He is from God, He is not even a man, though He is from man, and thus both are endangered when one is convicted of losing faith in the other.

Those who read that the Son of Man, Christ Jesus, is a man, let them also read that He is the same God and the Son of God. For just as, insofar as He is a man, He is from Abraham, so also, insofar as He is God, He is before Abraham (John 8:58). And just as, insofar as He is a man, He is the son of David, so also, insofar as He is God, He is the Lord of David (Psalm 110:1; Matthew 22:42-45). And just as, insofar as He is a man, He was made under the law and suffered sentence, so also, insofar as He is God, He possesses judgment over the living and the dead (Acts 10:42; 2 Timothy 4:1; 1 Peter 4:5). And just as, insofar as He is a man, He was born after the world, so also, insofar as He is God, He is said to have existed before the world (John 1:1-2; 17:5). And just as, insofar as He is a man, He was born from the seed of David, so also, insofar as He is God, the world is said to have been instituted through Him (John 1:3; Colossians 1:16; Hebrews 1:2). And just as, insofar as He is a man, He comes after many, so also, insofar as He is God, He is before all; and just as, insofar as He is a man, He is inferior to others, so also, insofar as He is God, He is greater than all (John 1:15, 30). And just as, insofar as He is a man, He ascends into heaven, so also, insofar as He is God, He descended from there; and just as, insofar as He is a man, He goes to the Father, so also, insofar as He is the Son, He obeys the Father (John 3:13; 6:38; 14:28; 16:28; Philippians 2:6-8). Just as the lowly traits in Him confirm human frailty, so the majestic traits in Him affirm divine power.

There is danger that, when we read of both natures, we believe only one and not the other. Since both are read in Christ, both must be believed, so that faith may be true only if it is perfect. If, from two realities, one ceases to be believed and we assume the lesser for belief, the rule of truth is disturbed; such rashness does not bring salvation but, in place of salvation, loss—a great danger of death will have flowed from the loss of faith.

excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 11
latin: Verum ne ex hoc quod dominum nostrum Iesum Christum dei creatoris filium in substantia ueri corporis exhibitum asserimus, aliis haereticis hoc in loco hominem tantum et solum defendentibus, atque ideo hominem illum nudum et solitarium probare cupientibus, aut manus dedisse aut loquendi materiam commodasse uideamur, non sic de substantia corporis ipsius exprimimus, ut solum et tantum hominem illum esse dicamus; sed ut diuinitate sermonis in ipsa con- ro cretione permixta etiam deum illum secundum scripturas esse teneamus. est enim periculum grande, saluatorem generis humani, totius dominum et principem mundi, cui a suo patre omnia tradita sunt et cuncta concessa, per quem instituta sunt uniuersa, creata sunt tota, digesta sunt cuncta, aeuorum omnium et temporum regem, angelorum omnium principem, ante quem nihil praeter patrem, hominem tantummodo dicere et auctoritatem illi diuinam in his abnegare. haec enim contumelia haereticorum ad ipsum quoque deum patrem redundabit, si deus pater filium deum generare non potuit. sed enim ueritati caecitas haereticorum nulla praescribet, nec quoniam in Christo aliquid tenent, aliquid non tenent, alterum uident, alterum non uident, eripietur nobis illud quod non uident, per illud quod uident. quasi hominis enim in illo fragilitates considerant, quasi dei uirtutes non computant; infirmitates carnis recolunt, potestates diuinitatis excludunt. quando si probatio haec ex infirmitatibus Christi illuc proficit, ut homo ex infirmitatibus comprobetur, probatio diuinitatis in illo collecta ex uirtutibus illuc proficiet, ut etiam deus ex operibus asseratur. si enim passiones ostendunt in illo humanam fragilitatem, cur opera non asserant in illo diuinam potestatem? ne, si hoc non profecerit ut deus ex uirtutibus asseratur, nec passiones proficiant ut etiam homo ex ipsis esse monstretur. quaecumque enim lex in alterutro fuerit posita, in altero inuenietur esse suscepta. periculum enim erit nec hominem illum ex passionibus ostendi, si non potuerit etiam deus ex uirtutibus approbari. non est ergo in unam partem inclinandum et ab alia parte fugiendum, quoniam nec tenebit perfectam ueritatem quisquis aliquam ueritatis excluserit portionem. tam enim scriptura etiam deum annuntiat Christum, quam etiam hominem ipsum annuntiat deum; tam hominem descripsit Iesum Christum, quam etiam deum quoque descripsit Christum dominum. quoniam nec dei tantum illum filium esse proponit, sed et hominis; nec hominis tantum dicit, sed et dei referre consueuit: ut dum ex utroque est, utrumque sit; ne si alterum tantum sit, alterum esse non possit. ut enim praescripsit ipsa natura hominem credendum esse, qui ex homine sit, ita eadem natura praescribit et deum credendum esse, qui ex deo sit: ne si non et deus fuerit, cum ex deo sit, iam nec homo sit, licet ex homine fuerit, et sic in alterutro utrumque periclitetur, dum alterum altero fidem perdidisse conuincitur. qui legunt ergo hominis filium hominem Christum Iesum, legant hunc eundem et deum et dei filium nuncupatum. nam quo modo est, qua homo, ex Abraham, sic est etiam, qua deus, ante ipsum Abraham. et quo modo, qua homo, filius Dauid, ita dominus Dauid, qua deus, nuncuet quo modo, qua homo, sub lege factus est, ita, et quo modo, qua homo, sententiam patitur, sic omne, qua deus, de uiuis et mortuis iudicium habere reperitur. et quo modo post mundum, qua homo, nascitur, sic ante mundum, qua deus, fuisse perhibetur. et quo modo ex semine Dauid, qua homo, genitus est, sic item per ipsum, qua deum, mundus dicitur institutus. et quo modo, qua homo, post multos, sic, qua deus, ante omnes; et quo modo ceteris, qua homo, inferior, sic omnibus, qua deus, maior. et quo modo in caelum, qua homo, ascendit, sic inde, qua deus, ante descendit; et quo modo ad patrem, qua homo, uadit, sic oboediens patri, qua filius, inde ita si mediocritates in illo approbant humanam fragilitatem, maiestates in illo affirmant diuinam potestatem. periculum est enim, cum utrumque legis, non utrumque sed alterum credidisse. ex quo quoniam utrumque in Christo legitur, utrumque creditur, ut fides ita demum uera sit, si et perfecta fuerit. nam si ex duobus, altero in fide cessante, unum, et quidem id quod est minus, ad credendum fuerit assumptum, perturbata regula ueritatis, temeritas ista non salutem contulerit, sed in uicem salutis de iactura: fidei periculum mortis grande conflauerit.

excerpts.author: Novatian
english: That Christ is God, is Proved by the Authority of the Old Testament Scriptures.

Why, then, should we hesitate to say what Scripture does not shrink from declaring? Why shall the truth of faith hesitate in that wherein the authority of Scripture has never hesitated? For, behold, Hosea the prophet says in the person of the Father: I will not now save them by bow, nor by horses, nor by horsemen; but I will save them by the Lord their God. Hosea 1:7 If God says that He saves by God, still God does not save except by Christ. Why, then, should man hesitate to call Christ God, when he observes that He is declared to be God by the Father according to the Scriptures? Yea, if God the Father does not save except by God, no one can be saved by God the Father unless he shall have confessed Christ to be God, in whom and by whom the Father promises that He will give him salvation: so that, reasonably, whoever acknowledges Him to be God, may find salvation in Christ God; whoever does not acknowledge Him to be God, would lose salvation which he could not find elsewhere than in Christ God. For in the same way as Isaiah says, Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and you shall call His name Emmanuel, which is, interpreted, God with us; Isaiah 7:14 so Christ Himself says, Lo, I am with you, even to the consummation of the world. Matthew 28:20 Therefore He is God with us; yea, and much rather, He is in us. Christ is with us, therefore it is He whose name is God with us, because He also is with us; or is He not with us? How then does He say that He is with us? He, then, is with us. But because He is with us He was called Emmanuel, that is, God with us. God, therefore, because He is with us, was called God with us, The same prophet says: Be strengthened, you relaxed hands, and you feeble knees; be consoled, you that are cowardly in heart; be strong; fear not. Lo, our God shall return judgment; He Himself shall come, and shall save you: then shall the eyes of the blind be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall hear; then shall the lame man leap as an hart, and the tongue of the dumb shall be eloquent. Since the prophet says that at God's advent these should be the signs which come to pass; let men acknowledge either that Christ is the Son of God, at whose advent and by whom these wonders of healings were performed; or, overcome by the truth of Christ's divinity, let them rush into the other heresy, and refusing to confess Christ to be the Son of God, and God, let them declare Him to be the Father. For, being bound by the words of the prophets, they can no longer deny Christ to be God. What, then, do they reply when those signs are said to be about to take place on the advent of God, which were manifested on the advent of Christ? In what way do they receive Christ as God? For now they cannot deny Him to be God. As God the Father, or as God the Son? If as the Son, why do they deny that the Son of God is God? If as the Father, why do they not follow those who appear to maintain blasphemies of that kind? Unless because in this contest against them concerning the truth, this is in the meantime sufficient for us, that, being convinced in any kind of way, they should confess Christ to be God, seeing they have even wished to deny that He is God. He says by Habakkuk the prophet: God shall come from the south, and the Holy One from the dark and dense mountain. Whom do they wish to represent as coming from the south? If they say that it is the Almighty God the Father, then God the Father comes from a place, from which place, moreover, He is thus excluded, and He is bounded within the straitnesses of some abode; and thus by such as these, as we have said, the sacrilegious heresy of Sabellius is embodied. Since Christ is believed to be not the Son, but the Father; since by them He is asserted to be in strictness a bare man, in a new manner, by those, again, Christ is proved to be God the Father Almighty. But if in Bethlehem, the region of which local division looks towards the southern portion of heaven, Christ is born, who by the Scriptures is also said to be God, this God is rightly described as coming from the south, because He was foreseen as about to come from Bethlehem. Let them, then, choose of the two alternatives, the one that they prefer, that He who came from the south is the Son, or the Father; for God is said to be about to come from the south. If the Son, why do they shrink from calling Him Christ and God? For the Scripture says that God shall come. If the Father, why do they shrink from being associated with the boldness of Sabellius, who says that Christ is the Father? Unless because, whether they call Him Father or Son, from his heresy, however unwillingly, they must needs withdraw if they are accustomed to say that Christ is merely man; when compelled by the facts themselves, they are on the eve of exalting Him as God, whether in wishing to call Him Father or in wishing to call Him Son.

excerpts.author: Novatian
english: John describes the birth of Christ: "The Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen His glory, the glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth" (John 1:14). He is also called the Word of God, just as the psalmist says, "My heart overflows with a good word," and the king's word is so named because he declares, "I speak my works to the king" (Psalm 45:1). Through Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made (John 1:3). As the Apostle says, whether thrones, dominions, rulers, or powers, whether visible or invisible, all things hold together through Him (Colossians 1:16). This is the Word who came to His own, yet His own did not receive Him; the world was made through Him, yet the world did not know Him (John 1:10–11). He was in the beginning with God, and the Word was God (John 1:1). Who then doubts? When the Gospel says, "The Word became flesh and dwelt among us," it means that Christ, whose birth this is, is man because He became flesh, and is unmistakably God because He is the Word of God. The Gospel especially joins both substances in the one birth of Christ. He comes forth like a bridegroom from his chamber and rejoices like a giant to run his course (Psalm 19:5); His going out is from the highest heaven and His return to the highest heaven. No one has ascended into heaven except the One who descended from heaven—the Son of Man who is in heaven—saying, "Father, glorify Me with the glory I had with You before the world existed" (John 17:5). The Word descended from heaven like a bridegroom to the flesh so that the Son of Man might ascend, through the assumption of flesh, to the place from which the Word of God had descended. By this mutual union the flesh bears the Word of God and the Son of God takes on the weakness of flesh; ascending with the flesh, His bride, to where He had descended without flesh, He receives again the glory He possessed before the world’s foundation, and God is most clearly proved. Moreover, the world itself, created after Him, is found to have been made through Him, confirming the divinity, glory, and authority of the One through whom the world was made. If Christ discerns the secrets of the heart, which belongs to God alone; if He forgives sins, which belongs to God alone; if He comes from heaven, which no mere man can do; if He says, "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30), which no mere man can say; if the Apostle Thomas, instructed by all proofs of Christ’s divinity, answers, "My Lord and my God"; if the Apostle Paul writes that Christ, who is over all, God blessed forever, came from the patriarchs according to the flesh (Romans 9:5); if Paul declares he was made an apostle not by men nor through a man, but through Jesus Christ; and if he insists he received the Gospel not from men nor through a man, but through Jesus Christ—then Christ is God. Therefore, in this matter one of two things must hold. Since it is manifest that all things were made through Christ, either He is before all things because all things were made through Him, and so He is rightly God; or, because He is a man, He is after all things, and so nothing was made through Him. But we cannot say nothing was made through Him, for Scripture attests that all things were made through Him. Therefore He is not after all things—that is, He is not merely a man, who comes after all things—but He is also God, because God is before all things. He is before all things because all things were made through Him; if He were only a man, nothing would have been made through Him. What answer can they give? That nothing was made through Him, so that He is only a man? How then can all things be made through Him? Therefore He is not only a man, but also God, since all things are made through Him. We must rightly understand that Christ is not only a man, who comes after all things, but also God, because all things were made through Him. How can you say He is only a man when you also see Him in the flesh, unless it is because, when both natures are observed, both should be believed?

excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 13
latin: Ac sic et Ioannes natiuitatem Christi describens, uerbum, inquit, caro factum est, et habitauit in nobis, et uidimus claritatem eius, claritatem tamquam unigeniti a patre, plenum gratia et ueritate. nam et uocatur nomen eius uerbum det: eructauit, inquit, cor meum uerbum bonum; ro quod uerbum regis nomine consequenter appellat inferendo, dico ego opera mea regi. per ipsum enim omnia facta sunt opera, ef sine ipso factum est nihil. siue enim, inquit apostolus, throni, siue dominationes, siue uirtutes, siue potestates, uisibilia et inuisibilia, omnia per ipsum constant. uerbum autem hoc illud est, quod zz sua uenit, et sui eum non receperunt. mundus enim per ipsum factus est, et mundus eum non cognouit. uerbum autem hoc erat in principio apud deum, et deus erat uerbum. quis igitur dubitet, cum in extrema parte dicitur, verbum caro Factum est, et habitauit in nobis, Christum, cuius est natiuitas, et quia caro factus est, esse hominem, et quia uerbum dei, deum incunctanter edicere esse; praesertim cum animaduertat scripturam euangelicam utramque istam substantiam in unam natiuitatis Christi foederasse concordiam? Hic est enim qui sicut sponsus egreditur de thalamo suo, exsultauit ut gigas ad currendum uam; a summo caelo egressio eius et usque ad summum regressio eius. quoniam usque ad summum, nec quisquam in caelum ascendit, nisi qui de caelo descendit, filius hominis, qui est in caelis, repetens hoc ipsum dicit: pater, clarifica me eo honore quo fui apud te antequam mundus esset. ac si de caelo descendit uerbum hoc tamquam sponsus ad carnem, ut per carnis assumptionem filius hominis illuc posset ascendere, unde dei filius uerbum descenderat, merito, dum per conexionem mutuam et caro uerbum dei gerit et filius dei fragilitatem carnis assumit, cum sponsa carne conscendens illuc, unde sine carne descenderat, recipit iam claritatem illam, quam dum ante mundi institutionem habuisse ostenditur, deus manifestissime comprobatur. et nihilominus, dum mundus ipse post illum institutus refertur, per ipsum creatus esse reperitur; quo ipso diuinitatis in ipso, per quem factus est mundus, et claritas et auctoritas comprobetur. + Quod si, cum nullius sit nisi dei cordis nosse secreta, Christus secreta conspicit cordis: quod si, cum nullius sit nisi dei peccata dimittere, idem Christus peccata dimittit: quod si, cum nullius sit hominis de caelo uenire, de caelo ueniendo descendit: quod si, cum nullius hominis haec uox esse possit, ego e pater unum sumus, hanc uocem de conscientia diuinitatis Christus solus edicit: quod si postremo omnibus diuinitatis Christi probationibus et rebus instructus apostolus Thomas, respondens Christo dominus meus et deus meus dicit: quod si et apostolus Paulus, quorum, inquit, patres et ex quibus Christus secundum carnem, qui est super omnia deus benedictus in saecula, in suis litteris scribit: quod si idem se apostolum non ab hominibus, aut per hominem, sed per Iesum Christum constitutum esse depromit: quod si idem euangelium non se ab hominibus didicisse aut per hominem, sed per Iesum Christum accepisse contendit: merito deus est Christus. Itaque hoc in loco ex duobus alterum constare debebit. cum enim manifestum sit omnia esse facta per Christum, aut ante omnia est, quoniam omnia per ipsum, et merito et deus est: aut quia homo est, post omnia est, et merito per ipsum nihil factum est. sed nihil per ipsum factum esse non possumus dicere, cum animaduertamus omnia per ipsum facta esse scriptum. non ergo post omnia est, id est non homo tantum est, qui post omnia est, sed et deus, quoniam deus ante omnia est. ante omnia est enim, quia per ipsum omnia; ne si homo tantum, nihil per ipsum; aut si omnia per ipsum, non homo tantum: quoniam si homo tantum, non omnia per ipsum, immo nihil per ipsum. quid ergo respondent? nihil per ipsum, ut homo sit tantum? quomodo ergo omnia per ipsum? ergo non homo tantummodo est, sed et deus, siquidem omnia sunt per ipsum. ut merito intellegere debeamus nec hominem esse Christum tantummodo, qui est post omnia, sed et deum, cum per ipsum facta sint omnia.......... quomodo enim aut ‘hominem tantummodo dicas...... cum illum etiam in carne conspicias; nisi quoniam si utrumque animaduertitur, utrumque merito credatur?

excerpts.author: Novatian
english: If Christ is merely human, how can he say, "Even if I testify on my own behalf, my testimony is valid, for I know where I came from and where I am going, but you do not know where I come from or where I am going. You judge by human standards"? (John 8:14-15). He also declares here that he will return to the place from which he came, having testified that he was sent from heaven. Thus he descends from the very place he came from, and he goes back to the place he descended from. If Christ were only a man, he could not have come from there, and consequently he could not return there either, since he never came from there in the first place. But by coming from a place no human can come from, he demonstrates that he came as God. Yet the Jews, ignorant of this very descent, have made these heretics their heirs — people to whom it is said: "You do not know where I come from or where I am going. You judge by human standards" (John 8:14-15). Both the heretics and the Jews insist that Christ's birth was purely fleshly, and so they conclude he is nothing but a man. They fail to consider that since a human being cannot originate in heaven so as to return there legitimately, the one who descended from heaven — from where no human can come — must be God.

If Christ is only a man, how can he say: "You are from below; I am from above. You are of this world; I am not of this world"? (John 8:23). If every human being belongs to this world, and Christ is in this world, does that make him merely human? By no means. Consider his claim: "I am not of this world." Would he be lying if he were of this world by virtue of being only a man? If he does not lie, then he is not of this world. Therefore he is not merely human, because he is not of this world. To leave no doubt about his identity, he explicitly states his origin: "I am from above" — that is, from heaven, where no human can originate, since human beings are not made in heaven. Consequently, the one who is from above is God, and for that reason he is not of this world. Nevertheless, in a certain sense he is of this world; thus Christ is not only God but also man. Rightly, just as he is not of this world according to the divinity of the Word, so he is of this world according to the frailty of the body he assumed. For humanity is joined with God, and God is united with humanity. Here Christ now emphasizes his divinity alone, because Jewish blindness saw only his flesh. In this present passage, passing over the frailty of his body that belongs to the world, he speaks solely of his divinity, which does not belong to the world. He does this so that, to the degree they were inclined to believe he was only a man, he might draw them to consider his divinity and come to believe he is God — overcoming their unbelief about his divinity by setting it in direct opposition, while temporarily setting aside mention of his human condition.

If Christ is only a man, how can he say: "I came forth from God and have come here," when it is established that human beings are made by God, not generated from God? Humanity did not proceed from God, but the Word of God did — concerning which it is said: "My heart overflows with a noble theme" (Psalm 45:1). Since this Word is from God, it rightly abides with God; and because it was not uttered idly, it rightly accomplishes all things. All things were made through it, and without it nothing was made (John 1:3). This Word, through whom all things were made, is God, because the one who proceeded is the Word, and the one who proceeded from God is God. If Christ is only a man, how can he say: "Whoever keeps my word will never see death"? (John 8:51). To never see death is nothing other than immortality. Immortality belongs to divinity, because divinity is itself immortal, and immortality is the fruit of divinity. But every human is mortal, and immortality cannot spring from what is mortal. Therefore immortality cannot arise from Christ as a mortal man. Yet he declares: "Whoever keeps my word will never see death." Consequently, Christ's Word bestows immortality, and through immortality it bestows divinity. If a mere mortal could not confer immortality on another, but Christ's Word does confer it, then he is not merely human — for a mere human could not grant what Christ's Word grants. By bestowing divinity through immortality, he proves himself God, offering a divinity that only God could confer.

If Christ is only a man, how can he say: "Before Abraham was, I am"? (John 8:58). No human being can exist before the one from whom he derives his existence, nor can anything precede the one from whom it takes its origin. Yet Christ, though descended from Abraham, claims to have existed before Abraham. Either he lies and deceives — if he was not before Abraham despite coming from Abraham — or he does not deceive, because he is also God, having existed before Abraham. If he were not God, then, being from Abraham, he could not have been before Abraham. If Christ is only a man, how can he say: "My sheep hear my voice; I know them, and they follow me. I give them eternal life, and they shall never perish"? (John 10:27-28). Every human is bound by the law of mortality and cannot preserve even himself forever, let alone another. Yet Christ promises to give salvation that lasts forever. If he does not give it, he is a liar; if he gives it, he is God. He does not deceive, for he fulfills his promise. Therefore he is God, the one who bestows eternal salvation — a salvation no mere human, unable to save even himself, could bestow on another.

If Christ is only a man, what are we to make of his claim: "I and the Father are one"? (John 10:30). How can the Father and the Son be one unless he is both God and the Son? One can be said to be one with the Father precisely because he is from the Father, because he is the Father's Son, because he is begotten of the Father, because he is found to have proceeded from the Father — and through that procession he is God. When the Jews considered this claim arrogant and blasphemous, because Christ revealed himself as God in these words, they picked up stones to stone him. But Christ vigorously refuted them with Scripture's own testimony and example. He said: "Is it not written in your Law, 'I have said you are gods'? If he called them 'gods' to whom the word of God came — and Scripture cannot be set aside — what about the one whom the Father set apart and sent into the world? Why then do you accuse me of blasphemy because I said, 'I am God's Son'?" (John 10:34-36, referencing Psalm 82:6). By these words he did not deny being God; on the contrary, he confirmed it. For if those who received God's word are called 'gods,' how much more is this one God, who surpasses them all? And he refuted the slanderous charge of blasphemy with a proper legal argument: he wants to be understood as God in the sense that he is the Son of God, not the Father himself. He said he was sent, and he showed that he performed many works from the Father — thereby making clear he is the Son, not the Father. In the final part of his defense he speaks as the Son, not the Father. So, regarding the charge of blasphemy, he identifies himself as the Son, not the Father; but regarding his divinity, by saying "I and the Father are one," he proves he is both the Son and God. Therefore he is God — yet God in such a way that he is the Son, not the Father.

excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 15
latin: Si homo tantummodo Christus, quomodo ait: etsi ego de me testificor, uerum est testimonium meum, quia scio unde uenerim et guo eam, uos ignoratis unde uenerim aut quo eam, uos secundum carnem iudicatis? ecce et hic illuc se dicit rediturum, unde se testificatur ante uenisse, missum scilicet de caelo. descendit ergo unde uenit, quo modo illuc uadit unde descendit. ex quo, si homo tantummodo Christus esset, non inde uenisset: atque ideo nec illuc abiret, quoniam non inde uenisset. ueniendo autem inde, unde homo uenire non potest, deum se ostendit uenisse. sed enim huius ipsius descensionis ignari et imperiti Iudaei heredes sibi haereticos istos reddiderunt, quibus dicitur: vos ignoratis unde ueniam, et quo eam: uos secundum carnem tudicatis. tam isti quam Iudaei, carnalem solam esse Christi natiuitatem tenentes, nihil aliud Christum esse quam hominem crediderunt, non considerantes illud, quoniam, cum de caelo homo non potuerit uenire, ut merito illuc posset redire, deum esse qui inde descenderit, unde homo uenire non potuerit. Si homo tantummodo Christus, quomodo dicit: vos ex inferioribus estis, ego desursum sum; uos de hoc mundo estis, ego non sum de hoc mundo? ideo autem si omnis homo ex hoc mundo est, et ideo in hoc mundo est Christus, an homo tantummodo est? absit. sed considera quod ait: ego non sum de hoc mundo. numquid ergo mentitur, cum ex hoc mundo sit, si homo tantummodo sit? aut si non mentitur, non est ex hoc mundo. non ergo homo tantummodo est, quia ex hoc mundo non est. sed ne lateret quis esset, expressit unde esset: ego, inquit, desursum sum; hoc est, de caelo, unde homo uenire non potest; non enim in caelo factus est. deus est ergo qui desursum est, et idcirco de hoc mundo non est. quamquam etiam quodam modo ex hoc mundo est; unde non deus tantum est Christus, sed et homo; ut merito, quo modo non est ex hoc mundo secundum uerbi diuinitatem, ita ex hoc mundo sit secundum suscepti corporis fragilitatem. homo est enim cum deo iunctus, et deus cum homine copulatus. sed idcirco nunc hic Christus in unam partem solius diuinitatis incubuit, quoniam caecitas Iudaica solam in Christo partem carnis aspexit, et inde in praesenti loco, silentio praeterita corporis fragilitate quae de mundo est, de sua sola diuinitate locutus est, quae de mundo non est: ut in quantum illi inclinauerant, ut hominem illum tantummodo crederent, in tantum illos Christus posset ad diuinitatem suam considerandam trahere, ut re deum crederent, uolens illorum incredulitatem circa diuinitatem suam, omissa interim commemoratione sortis humanae, solius diuinitatis oppositione superare. Si homo tantummodo Christus, quomodo dicit: ego ex deo prodii et ueni, cum constet hominem a deo factum esse, non ex deo processisse? ex deo autem homo quo modo non processit, sic dei uerbum processit; de quo dictum est: eructauit cor meum uerbum bonum. quod quoniam ex deo est, merito et apud deum est: quodque, quia non otiose prolatum est, merito omnia facit; omnia enim per ipsum facta sunt, et sine ipso factum est nihil. sed enim hoc uerbum, per quod facta sunt omnia, deo, dum qui processit sermo, deus est qui processit ex deo. si homo tantummodo Christus, quomodo ait: sz gués uerbum meum Seruauerit, mortem non uidebit in aeternum? mortem in aeternum non uidere, quid aliud quam immortalitas est? immortalitas autem diuinitati socia est, quia et diuinitas immortalis est, et immortalitas diuinitatis fructus est. sed enim omnis homo mortalis est; immortalitas autem ex mortali non potest esse. ergo ex Christo homine mortali immortalitas non potest nasci. sed qui uerbum custodierit, inquit, meum, mortem non uidebit in aeternum. ergo uerbum Christi praestat immortalitatem, et per immortalitatem praestat diuinitatem. quod si non potest exhibere ut immortalem alterum faciat ipse mortalis, hoc autem Christi uerbum exhibet pariter et praestat immortalitatem, non utique homo tantum est, qui praestat immortalitatem, quam, si tantummodo homo esset, praestare non posset. praestando autem diuinitatem per immortalitatem, deum se probat diuinitatem porrigendo, quam, nisi deus esset, praestare non posset. Si homo tantummodo Christus, quomodo inquit: ante Abraham ego sum? nemo enim hominum ante eum potest esse ex quo ipse est; nec potest fieri ut quicquam prius fuerit ante illum ex quo ipsum originem sumpsit. sed enim Christus, cum ex Abraham sit, ante Abraham esse se dicit. aut mentitur et fallit, si ante Abraham non fuit, qui ex Abraham fuit: aut non fallit, si etiam deus est, dum ante Abraham fuit. quod nisi fuisset, consequenter, cum ex Abraham fuisset, ante Abraham esse non posset. si homo tantummodo Christus, quomodo ait: ef ego agnoscam eas et sequuntur me meae; et ego uitam aeternam do illis, et numquam peribunt in perpetuum? sed enim cum omnis homo mortalitatis ro sit legibus alligatus, et idcirco in perpetuum se ipse seruare non possit, multo magis in perpetuum alterum seruare non poterit. at in perpetuum se Christus repromittit salutem daturum; quam si non dat, mendax est: si dat, deus est. sed non fallit; dat enim quod repromittit. deus est ergo, qui salutem perpetuam porrigit; quam homo, qui se ipsum seruare non potest, alteri praestare non poterit. Si homo tantummodo Christus, quid est, quod ait: ego e pater unum sumus? quomodo enim ego et pater unum sumus, Si non et deus est et filius? qui idcirco unum potest dici, dum ex ipso est, et dum filius eius est, et dum ex ipso nascitur, dum ex ipso processisse reperitur; per quod et deus est. quod cum inuidiosum Iudaei putassent, et blasphemum credidissent, eo quod se ostenderat his sermonibus Christus esse deum, ac propterea ad lapides concurrissent, et saxorum ictus inicere gestissent, exemplo et testimonio scripturarum aduersarios suos fortiter refutauit. sz zos, inquit, dixit deos ad quos det uerba facta sunt, et non potest solui scriptura; quem pater sanctificauit et misit in hunc mundum uos dicitis, quia blasphemas, quia dixi: filius dei sum ego? quibus uocibus neque se negauit deum, quin immo deum se esse firmauit. nam quia sine dubitatione dii esse dicuntur, ad quos uerba dei facta sunt, multo magis hic deus, qui melior illis omnibus inuenitur. et nihilominus calumniosam blasphemiam dispositione legitima congruenter refutauit: deum enim se sic intellegi uult, ut filium dei et non ipsum patrem uellet intellegi. missum enim se esse dixit, et multa opera se ex patre ostendisse monstrauit; ex quo non patrem se sed filium esse intellegi uoluit; ultima parte defensionis filii, non patris, fecit mentionem SUM. ita quod ad crimen blasphemiae pertinet, filium se non patrem dicit: quod autem ad diuinitatem spectet ipsius, ego e pater unum sumus dicendo, filium se esse et deum probauit. deus est ergo: deus autem sic, ut filius sit, non pater.

excerpts.author: Novatian
english: If Christ is only a man, how can he say: 'And everyone who sees and believes in me will not die eternally'? Yet the one who believes in a solitary and naked man is pronounced cursed; but the one who believes in Christ is not cursed, but is said to be one who will not die forever. From this it follows: if Christ is only a man, as the heretics want, how can whoever believes in him avoid eternal death, when the one who trusts in a man is held to be cursed? Or if the believer in Christ is not cursed but rather destined for the attainment of eternal life, as it is written, then Christ is not only a man but also God; for the one who believes in him both sets aside the danger of curse and advances to the fruit of righteousness. If Christ is only a man, how can he say that the Paraclete will take from his own what he will announce? For the Paraclete does not receive anything from a man, but imparts knowledge to men; the Paraclete does not learn future things from a man, but instructs men about future things. If the Paraclete were to receive from Christ-as-man what he is to announce, then Christ would be deceiving and misleading us in this very passage, since a man could give nothing to the Paraclete from whom the man himself must receive. But Christ does not deceive us, any more than he deceives, and the Paraclete has received from Christ what he will announce. Since the Paraclete has received from Christ what he announces, Christ is therefore greater than the Paraclete; for the Paraclete would not receive from Christ unless he were lesser than Christ. The fact that the Paraclete is lesser than Christ and receives from him what he proclaims proves that Christ is also God. This is a great testimony to Christ's divinity, since the Paraclete, found to be lesser than Christ, takes from him what he hands on to others. If Christ were only a man, then Christ would receive from the Paraclete what he would say, not the Paraclete from Christ.

If Christ is only a man, why did he lay down for us such a rule of belief, saying: 'This is eternal life, that they may know you, the one and true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent' (John 17:3)? If he had not wished to be understood as God also, why did he add 'whom you have sent, Jesus Christ'? For if he had not wished to be understood as God, he would have added 'whom you have sent, the man Jesus Christ.' But he did not add this, and Christ did not present himself to us as only a man, but joined himself to God, so that through this conjunction he might be understood as God, as he is. Therefore it must be believed, according to the prescribed rule, in the Lord, the one true God, and in the one whom he sent, Jesus Christ, consequently; for he would not have joined himself to the Father, as we said, unless he also wished to be understood as God. He would have separated himself from the Father if he had not wished himself to be understood as God. For he would have placed himself among men only, if he knew himself to be only a man, and he would not have joined himself to God if he did not also know himself to be God. Now he is silent about the man, because no one doubts that he is a man, and he joins himself to God deservedly, so that he might set a formula of his divinity for believers.

If Christ is only a man, how can he say: 'Now glorify me, Father, with the glory that I had with you before the world existed' (John 17:5)? If he had glory with God before the world existed and held splendor with the Father, then he existed before the world; for no one can have something unless he himself existed before, he who holds it. But Christ has glory before the institution of the world; therefore he existed before the institution of the world. For unless he existed before the institution of the world, he could not have had glory before the institution of the world, since he himself did not exist. Yet a man could not have had glory before the institution of the world, who came after the world; but Christ had it: therefore he was before the world. He is therefore not only a man, who was before the world; he is God, since he was before the world and held glory before the world. Let this not be called predestination, since it is not established. Let those who think this add it. But woe to those who add, just as to those who subtract, what is established. It cannot be said that what cannot be added is possible. Therefore, with predestination, which is not established, set aside, Christ existed in substance before the institution of the world. For he is the Word through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made. And even if it is said that he is glorious in predestination, and that predestination existed before the institution of the world, the order is preserved, and before this there will be a great number of men in glory; for Christ will be understood to be lesser through this destination than the rest, to whom he is posterior. Glory was in predestination, and Christ, who is the last, received this predestination in glory; for before this predestination of Christ in glory, Adam is seen to have been predestined, and Abel, and Enoch, and Noah, and Abraham, and the rest. For since with God the order of all persons and things is settled, before this predestination of Christ in glory many will be said to have been predestined, and in this way Christ will be found to be lesser than other men, who are better, greater, and more ancient than the angels themselves. Either all these things must be abolished, so that Christ's divinity may be taken away, or if these things cannot be abolished, Christ's own divinity must be restored to him by the heretics.

excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 16.
latin: Si homo tantummodo Christus, quomodo ipse dicit: et omnis qui uidet et credit in me non morietur in aeternum? sed enim qui in hominem solitarium credit et nudum, maledictus dicitur: hic autem, qui credit in Christum non maledictus, sed in aeternum non moriturus refertur. ex quo sl ro aut homo est tantum, ut haeretici uolunt, quomodo quisquis in eum credit non morietur in aeternum, cum maledictus esse teneatur qui confidit in homine? aut si non maledictus, sed potius ad aeternae uitae consecutionem, ut legitur, destinatus, non homo tantummodo Christus, sed et deus; in quem qui credit, et maledictionis periculum deponit, et ad fructum iustitiae accedit. Si homo tantummodo Christus, quomodo paracletum dicit de suo esse sumpturum quae nuntiaturus sit? neque enim paracletus ab homine quicquam accipit, sed homini scientiam paracletus porrigit; nec futura ab homine paracletus discit, sed de futuris hominem paracletus instruit. paraclitus a Christo homine quod nuntiet, quoniam paracleto homo nihil poterit dare a quo ipse homo debet accipere, et fallit in praesenti loco Christus et decipit, cum paracletum a se homine accepturum quae nuntiet dicit: aut non nos fallit, sicut nec fallit, et accepit paracletus a Christo quae nuntiet. sed si a Christo accepit quae nuntiet, maior ergo iam paracleto Christus est: quoniam nec paracletus a Christo acciperet, nisi minor Christo esset. minor autem Christo paracletus Christum etiam deum esse hoc ipso probat, a quo accepit quae nuntiat; ut testimonium Christo diuinitatis grande sit, dum minor Christo paraclitus repertus ab illo sumit quae ceteris tradit. quandoquidem si homo tantummodo Christus, a paracleto Christus acciperet quae diceret, non a Christo paracletus acciperet quae nuntiaret. Si homo tantummodo Christus, quare credendi nobis talem regulam posuit, quo diceret: haec est autem uita aeterna ut sciant te unum et uerum deum, et quem misisti Iesum Christum? si noluisset se etiam deum intellegi, cur addidit: e quem misisti Iesum Christum, nisi quoniam et deum accipi uoluit? quoniam si se deum nollet intellegi, addidisset: e quem misisti hominem Iesum Christum. nunc autem neque addidit, nec se hominem nobis tantummodo Christus tradidit, sed deo iunxit, ut et deum per hanc coniunctionem, sicut est, intellegi uellet. est ergo credendum, secundum praescriptam regulam, in dominum, unum uerum deum, et in eum quem misit Iesum Christum consequenter, qui se nequaquam patri, ut diximus, iunxisset, nisi deum quoque intellegi uellet. separasset enim ab eo, si deum intellegi se noluisset. inter homines enim tantummodo se collocasset, si hominem se esse tantummodo sciret, nec cum deo iunxisset, si se non et deum nosset. nunc et de homine tacet, quoniam hominem illum nemo dubitat, et deo se iungit merito, ut credituris diuinitatis suae formulam poneret. Si homo tantummodo Christus, quomodo dicit: e nunc honorifica me gloria quam habebam apud te priusquam mundus esset? si antequam mundus esset gloriam habuit apud deum et claritatem tenuit apud patrem, ante mundum fuit: nec enim habuisset gloriam, nisi ipse prius fuisset, qui gloriam posset tenere. nemo enim habere aliquid poterit, nisi ante ipse fuerit, qui aliquid tenet. sed enim Christus habet gloriam ante mundi institutionem; ergo ante institutionem mundi fuit. nisi enim ante institutionem mundi esset, ante mundi institutionem gloriam habere non posset, cum ipse non esset. sed enim homo gloriam ante mundi institutionem habere non potuit, qui post mundum fuit: Christus autem habuit: ante mundum igitur fuit. non igitur homo tantummodo fuit, qui ante mundum fuit: deus est igitur, quoniam ante mundum fuit et gloriam ante mundum tenuit. nec praedestinatio ista dicatur, quoniam nec posita est. aut addant hoc qui hoc putant. sed uae est adicientibus, quo modo et detrahentibus, positum. non potest ergo dici quod non potest adici. sublata ergo praedestinatione, quae non est posita, in substantia fuit Christus ante mundi institutionem. uerbum est enim per quod facta sunt omnia, et sine quo factum est nihil, quoniam et si in praedestinatione dicitur gloriosus, et ante mundi institutionem fuisse praedestinationem, ordo seruetur, et ante hunc erit multus numerus hominum in gloriam minor enim per istam destinationem Christus ceteris intellegetur, quibus posterior denotatur. gloria in praedestinatione fuit, praedestinationem istam in gloriam nouissimus Christus accepit: ante enim praedestinatus Adam esse cernetur, et Abel, et Enoch, et Noe, et Abraham, et reliqui ceteri. nam cum apud deum et personarum et rerum omnium ordo digestus sit, ante hanc praedestinationem Christi in gloriam multi praedestinati fuisse dicentur, et hoc pacto minor ceteris hominibus Christus esse deprehendetur, qui melior et maior et antiquior ipsis quoque angelis inuenitur. aut haec igitur omnia tollantur, ut Christo diuinitas auferatur: aut si haec tolli non possunt, Christo ab haereticis diuinitas propria reddatur.

excerpts.author: Novatian
english: Look at Moses: in another passage he reports that God was seen by Abraham. Yet no human being sees God and lives. So how could God have been seen? How can it be said he cannot be seen? The text says no man has ever seen him, and no one can see. If that is true, then the account is false—yet the vision was real. From this we can understand that the one seen was not the Father, who has never been seen, but the Son, who was accustomed to descend and to be seen because he had descended. For the Son is the image of the invisible God, so that the weakness and frailty of the human condition might become accustomed to seeing God the Father even then, in the image of God—that is, in the Son of God. Human frailty had to be nourished step by step through the image until it could reach that glory and someday see the Father, because great things are dangerous when they come suddenly. Even the light of the sun, breaking suddenly after darkness, does not reveal the day to unaccustomed eyes with its overwhelming brilliance; instead it blinds them. To prevent such harm to human eyes, the darkness is gradually broken and dispersed, and the rising of this light, increasing by moderate degrees, gently accustoms men's eyes to bear its full orb through the gradual increase of its rays. In the same way, Christ—the image of God and the Son of God—is seen by men insofar as he can be seen. And so the frailty and lowliness of the human lot are nourished, strengthened, and trained through him, so that they may eventually be able to see God the Father as well, once they have grown accustomed to beholding the Son; lest they be struck and cut off by the sudden, unbearable splendor of his majesty, and fail to see the Father whom they have always longed to see. It follows that the one who is seen is the Son; the Son of God is the Word of God; the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14); and this is Christ. What reason, then, could there be to doubt that he is called God, when he is confirmed as God in so many ways?

Consider also Hagar, Sarah's servant, cast out of the house and fleeing. An angel met her by a spring of water on the road to Shur, asked the cause of her flight, heard it, then offered her counsel of humility, gave her the hope of motherhood, promised that her offspring would be a great multitude, that Ishmael would be born to her, showed her a dwelling place, and described his future. The Scripture presents this figure as both angel and Lord and God (for he would not have promised the blessing of offspring unless he were both angel and God). Let the heretics explain what they make of this passage. Was it the Father whom Hagar saw, or not? God is named, but it is absurd to call God the Father an angel—unless they want to say an angel was substituted for him. How then could he be God if he was an angel, since that name is never given to angels? Unless the truth from both sides forces us to this conclusion: we must understand that it was the Son of God. Because he is from God, he is rightly called God, because he is the Son of God; because he is subject to the Father and announces the Father's will, he is proclaimed the Angel of Great Counsel (Isaiah 9:6). Therefore, if this passage fits neither the person of the Father—lest he be called an angel—nor the person of a mere angel—lest he be called God—but fits the person of Christ, who is both God because he is the Son of God, and Angel because he announces the Father's purpose, then the heretics must realize they are acting against the Scriptures. They say they believe Christ is an angel, yet refuse to call him God, even though they read in the Old Testament that he came often to visit the human race.

Moses adds further that God was seen by Abraham at the oak of Mamre, while he sat at the entrance of his tent at noon. Though he saw three men, he called one of them Lord. He washed their feet, offered them bread with butter and an abundance of milk, and urged them to eat as his guests. Afterward he heard that he would become a father, learned that Sarah his wife would bear a son by him, recognized the coming destruction of the Sodomites who deserved to suffer, and learned that God had descended because of the outcry against Sodom. In this episode, if the heretics want the Father to have been the one seen then, received in hospitality along with two angels, they have believed in a visible Father. But if it was an angel, since one of the three is called Lord, why is an angel called God—which is not customary? Unless it is so that the invisibility proper to God the Father may be preserved, and the lowliness proper to an angel may be set aside, and we believe that the Son of God, who is also God, was the one seen by Abraham and received as a guest. For what was to come, he was foreshadowing in the sacrament by becoming Abraham's guest, destined to come among Abraham's descendants; he washed their feet as proof that he was the one, returning in the sons the right of hospitality which the Father had once lent to him. So, to leave no doubt that this guest of Abraham was he, the account places him at the destruction of the Sodomites: "The Lord rained on Sodom and Gomorrah fire and sulfur from the Lord out of heaven" (Genesis 19:24). Thus the prophet also speaks in the person of God: "I will overthrow you, as the Lord overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah" (Amos 4:11). Therefore the Lord overthrew Sodom—that is, God overthrew Sodom. But in the overthrow of the Sodomites, the Lord rained fire from the Lord. This Lord who was seen by Abraham is God; this God is the guest seen by Abraham, certainly because he was touched. But since the Father, being invisible, was not seen then, the one who is accustomed to be touched and seen was seen and received in hospitality. And this Lord, who rained fire and sulfur on Sodom and Gomorrah, is the Son of God. He is the Word of God; the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14); and this is Christ. Therefore it was not the Father who was the guest with Abraham, but Christ; it was not the Father who was seen then, but the Son; and Christ was seen. Christ is rightly Lord and God, who was seen by Abraham in no other way than because, before him, the Word of God was begotten from God the Father.

Moreover, the same angel and God again consoled and visited Hagar, cast out of Abraham's house with the boy. When she had left the infant in the wilderness because the water in the skin was gone, and the child cried out, and she lifted up her voice and wept, Scripture says, "God heard the voice of the boy where he was" (Genesis 16:11). Having reported that it was God who heard the infant's voice, it adds: "The angel of the Lord called to Hagar from heaven" (Genesis 16:11)—identifying the angel as the one just called God, and naming him Lord whom it had placed as angel. And this angel and God promised Hagar greater comforts, saying, "Do not fear, for God has heard the voice of the boy where he is. Arise, lift up the boy, and hold him fast, for I will make him a great nation" (Genesis 16:17-18). If this angel is only an angel, why does he claim for himself the power to say, "I will make him a great nation," when that kind of power belongs to God and cannot belong to an angel? From this it is also confirmed that he is God who can do this. And to prove this very point, Scripture immediately adds: "God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of living water, and she went and filled the skin with water, and gave the boy a drink, and God was with the boy" (Genesis 16:19-20). If, then, this was God with the boy, who opened Hagar's eyes so she could see the well of living water and draw water because of the urgent necessity of thirst; and this God calls her from heaven; and he is called angel, when above, hearing the voice of the crying child, he was rather God—he is understood to be none other than both angel and God together. Since this cannot be fitting for the Father, who is only God, but can be fitting for Christ, who is not only God but also proclaimed an Angel, it clearly appears that it was not the Father who spoke to Hagar then, but rather Christ. Because he is God, the name of Angel also belongs to him, since he has been made the Angel of Great Counsel; and he is an Angel while he expounds the bosom of the Father, as John declares (John 1:18). For if John himself says that this same one, who expounds the Father's bosom, is the Word made flesh, in order that he might expound the Father's bosom, then Christ is rightly not only man but also Angel; and not only Angel, but also God, as is shown through the Scriptures, and is believed by us. Otherwise, if we refuse to accept that Christ spoke to Hagar then, we either make an angel into God, or count God the Father Almighty among the angels.
