excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 18.
latin: Ecce idem Moyses refert alio in loco, quod Abrahae uisus sit deus. quod nemo hominum deum uideat et utuat. potest deus, quomodo uisus est deus? quomodo uideri non potest? inquit, wdit umguam; hominum nemo, nec uidere potest. mentitur; ergo uere uisus est deus. ex quo intellegi potest, quod non pater uisus sit, qui numquam uisus est, sed filius, qui et descendere solitus est, et uideri quia descenderit. imago ro est enim éinuisibilis dei, ut mediocritas et fragilitas condicionis humanae deum patrem uidere aliquando iam tunc assuesceret in imagine dei, hoc est, in filio dei. gradatim enim et per incrementa fragilitas humana nutriri debuit per imaginem ad istam gloriam, ut deum patrem uidere possit aliquando, periculosa sunt enim quae magna sunt, si repentina sunt. nam etiam lux solis subita post tenebras splendore nimio insuetis oculis non ostendet diem, sed potius faciet caecitatem. quod ne in damnum humanorum contingat oculorum, paulatim disruptis et dissipatis tenebris, ortus luminaris istius mediocribus incrementis fallenter assurgens oculos hominum sensim assuefacit ad totum orbem suum ferendum per incrementa radiorum. sic ergo et Christus, id est imago dei et filius dei, ab hominibus inspicitur, qua poterat uideri. et ideo fragilitas et mediocritas sortis humanae per ipsum alitur, producitur, educatur, ut aliquando deum quoque ipsum patrem, assueta filium conspicere, possit, w est, uidere; ne maiestatis ipsius repentino et intolerabili fulgore percussa intercipi possit, ut deum patrem quem semper optauit uidere non possit. ex quo filius est hic qui uidetur; dei autem filius, dei uerbum est; dei autem uerbum caro factum est et habitauit in nobis: hic autem Christus est. quae, malum, ratio est ut dubitetur deus dici, qui tot modis deus intellegitur approbari? Ac si et Agar ancillam Sarae de domo eiectam pariter et fugatam angelus conuenit apud fontem aquae in uia Sur, fugae causas interrogat atque accipit, et post haec humilitatis consilia porrigit, spem praeterea illi materni nominis facit, quodque ex utero eius multum semen esset futurum spondet atque promittit, et quod Hismael ex illa nasci haberet, et cum ceteris aperit locum habitationis ipsius, actumque describit: hunc autem angelum et dominum scriptura proponit et deum (nam nec benedictionem seminis promisisset, nisi angelus et deus fuisset): quaerant quid in praesenti loco haeretici tractent. - pater fuit iste qui ab Agar uisus est, an non? quia deus positus sed absit deum patrem angelum dicere; ne alteri subsed angelum dicent fuisse. quomodo ergo deus erit, si angelus fuit, cum non sit hoc nomen angelis umquam concessum? nisi quoniam ex utroque latere nos ueritas in istam concludit sententiam, qua intellegere debeamus dei filium fuisse: qui, quoniam ex deo est, merito deus, quia dei filius, dictus sit, quoniam patri subditus et annuntiator paternae uoluntatis est, magni consilii angelus pronuntiatus est. ergo si hic locus neque personae patris congruit, ne angelus dictus sit, neque personae angeli, ne, deus pronuntiatus sit; personae autem Christi conuenit ut et deus sit, quia dei filius est, et angelus sit, quoniam paternae dispositionis annuntiator est: intellegere debent contra scripturas se agere haeretici, qui Christum cum dicant se et angelum credere, nolint illum etiam deum pronuntiare, quem in ueteri testamento ad uisitationem generis humani legunt\ saepe uenisse. Adhuc adiecit Moyses, Abrahae uisum deum apud quercum Mambre, sedente ipso ad ostium tabernaculi sui meridie, et nihilominus, cum tres conspexisset uiros, unum ex illis dominum nuncupasse; quorum cum pedes lauisset, cinericios panes cum butyro et ipsius copia lactis offert, et ut hospites retenti uescerentur, hortatur. post quae et quod pater futurus esset, audit; et quod Sara uxor eius paritura ex ipso filium esset, ediscit; et de exitu Sodomitarum, quae merebantur pati, recognoscit; et quod propter clamorem Sodomorum deus descendisset, addiscit. quo in loco si patrem uolunt uideri tunc fuisse cum angelis duobus hospitio receptum, patrem uisibilem haeretici crediderunt: si autem angelum, cum ex angelis tribus unus dominus nuncupatur, cur, quod non solet, angelus deus dicitur? nisi quoniam, ut deo patri inuisibilitas propria reddatur, et angelo propria mediocritas remittatur, non nisi dei filius, qui et deus est, Abrahae uisus et hospitio receptus esse credetur. quod enim erat futurus, meditabatur in sacramento Abrahae factus hospes, apud Abrahae filios futurus; cuius filiorum pedes, ad probationem quod ipse esset, abluit; reddens in filiis ius hospitalitatis, quod aliquando illi fenerauerat pater. unde et ne qua esset dubitatio quin iste Abrahae hospes fuisset, in Sodomitarum exitu ponitur: quoniam pluit dominus super Sodomam et Gomorram ignem et sulphur a domino de caelo. sic enim et prophetes ex persona dei: subuerti uos, inquit, sécut subuertit dominus Sodomam et Gomorram. dominus ergo Sodomam subuertit, id est, deus Sodomam subuertit: sed.in subuersione Sodomorum dominus pluit ignem a domino. hic autem dominus uisus est Abrahae deus: deus autem hic hospes est Abrahae uisus utique quia tactus. sed cum pater, quia inuisibilis, nec tunc utique uisus sit, uisus est et hospitio receptus et acceptus est, qui solitus est tangi et uideri: hic autem filius dei dominus a domino pluit super Sodomam et Gomorram sulphur atque ignem. hic autem dei uerbum est: uerbum autem dei caro factum est, et habitauit in nobis: hic autem Christus est. non pater igitur apud Abraham hospes, sed Christus fuit; nec tunc pater uisus est, sed filius; uisus autem est Christus. merito igitur Christus et dominus et deus est, qui non aliter Abrahae uisus est, nisi quia ante ipsum Abraham ex patre deo deus sermo generatus est. Adhuc, inquit, idem angelus et deus eandem Agar, fugatam de domo Abrahae cum puero, consolatur et uisitat. nam cum illa in solitudine exposuisset infantem, quia aqua defecisset ex utre, cumque puer ille clamasset, fletum et planctum leuasset, et audiuit, inquit scriptura, deus uocem pueri ae loco ubi erat. cum deum esse, qui uocem audisset infantis, rettulisset, adiecit: et uocauit angelus domini ipsam Agar de caelo; angelum referens esse quem deum dixerat, et~dominum pronuntians esse quem angelum collocarat.. quique angelus et deus adhuc ipsi Agar promittit maiora solacia, dicendo: ne timueris; exaudiui enim uocem pueri de loco ubi erat. surge, sume puerum, et tene: in gentem enim magnam faciam eum. hic angelus, si angelus tantum est, cur hoc sibi uindicat ut dicat: in gentem enim magnam faciam eum, cum hoc utique genus potentiae dei sit, angeli esse non possit? ex quo etiam deus confirmatur esse qui hoc potest facere. quoniam ut hoc ipsum comprobetur, adicitur per scripturam statim: e aperuit deus oculos eius, et uidit puteum aquae uiuae, et abiit, et impleuit utrem de puteo, et dedit puero, et erat deus cum puero. si ergo hic deus erat cum puero, qui aperuit oculos Agar, ut uideret puteum aquae uiuae et hauriret aquam propter urgentem sitis necessitatem; hic autem deus e caelo illam uocat; angelus dictus, cum superius uocem audiens clamantis pueri deus esset potius, non alius intellegitur quam angelus esse pariter et deus. quod cum patri competens et conueniens esse non possit, qui tantummodo deus est, competens autem esse possit Christo, qui non tantummodo deus sed et angelus pronuntiatus est, manifeste apparet non patrem ibi tunc locutum fuisse ad Agar, sed Christum potius, cum deus sit, cui etiam angeli competit nomen, quippe cum magni consili angelus factus sit; angelus autem sit, dum exponit sinum patris, sicut Ioannes edicit. si enim ipse Ioannes hunc eundem, qui sinum exponit patris, uerbum dicit carnem factum esse, ut sinum patris posset exponere, merito Christus non solum homo est, sed et angelus; nec angelus tantum, sed et deus per scripturas ostenditur, et a nobis hoc esse creditur, ne, si non Christum tunc locutum ad Agar uoluerimus accipere, aut angelum deum faciamus, aut deum patrem omnipotentem inter angelos computemus.

excerpts.author: Novatian
english: I could have expounded every heavenly Scripture and, so to speak, stirred up a vast forest of arguments about this kind of Christ's divinity; but my aim is not to debate this heresy at length. Instead, I intend to set out briefly the rule of truth concerning the person of Christ.

Even though I am eager to move on, I must not pass over the sign of his majesty that the Lord gave in the Gospel when he said, "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up" (John 2:19), or when he declared elsewhere, "I have authority to lay down my life and authority to take it up again; this command I received from my Father" (John 10:18). For who could claim the power to lay down his own life and take it up again simply because he received that command from the Father? Who could claim the power to rebuild the destroyed temple of his own body? Only the Word who is from the Father, who was with the Father, through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made. He is the imitator of the Father's works and virtues, the revealer of the invisible God, who descended from heaven and testified to what he had seen and heard. He did not come to do his own will, but the will of the Father who sent him for this very purpose: that, as the angel of the great counsel, he might unveil to us the laws of the heavenly mysteries. And because the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, Christ is proved to be not only human, since he is the Son of Man, but also God, since he is the Son of God.

If the apostle also calls Christ the firstborn of all creation (Colossians 1:15), how could he hold that title unless, according to his divinity, he proceeded from God the Father before all creation? If the heretics refuse this, they are forced to say that Christ is the firstborn of all creation as a mere human — something they cannot prove. Therefore, either he exists before all creation, so that he can be the firstborn of all creation, and is not merely human, since humanity comes after all creation; or he is only human and comes after all creation. And how can he be the firstborn of all creation unless it is according to that Word which precedes creation?

Thus the firstborn of all creation becomes flesh and dwells in us — that is, he assumes this human being who comes after all creation, and so dwells in us with him and in him. In this way neither the human is taken away from Christ, nor is the divinity denied. If he were only before all creation, the human would be subtracted from him; but if he were only human, the divinity that precedes all creation would be cut off. Consequently, both natures are united in Christ, both are joined together, both are bound fast; and rightly so, because in him there is something that surpasses creation, the concord of divinity and humanity appears as a pledge in him. For this reason the one who is called the mediator of God and humans is found to have joined God and human together in himself.

And when the same apostle says of Christ that, having stripped off the flesh, he disarmed the rulers and authorities and triumphed over them in himself, he did not present this stripping as pointless; he meant that Christ would be clothed again in the resurrection. Who, then, is the one who is stripped and then clothed again? Let the heretics ask. We know that the Word of God was clothed with the substance of flesh, and that the same Word was stripped of that same bodily material, which he took up again in the resurrection and, as it were, put on once more as a garment. If Christ had been only human, he would not have been stripped or clothed, for no one ever strips or clothes himself. It must be another who does the stripping or clothing from outside. From this it follows that the Word of God is the one who was stripped of the flesh and clothed again in the resurrection; he was stripped because he had already been clothed at his birth.

Therefore, in Christ it is God who clothes himself, and he must also be the one who is stripped; for the one who clothes himself is necessarily also the one who is stripped. He clothes and strips himself in the human being, as if with a tunic woven from a body. And so, consequently, the Word was, as we said, the one who is found to be clothed and stripped. He foretold this long ago in a blessing: "He will wash his robe in wine, and his garment in the blood of the grape" (Genesis 49:11). If the robe in Christ is the flesh, and the garment is the body, we must ask: whose body is the garment, and whose flesh is the robe? It is clear to us that the flesh is the robe and the body is the garment of the Word, who washed the substance of the body and the material of the flesh with the blood of the grape — that is, with wine — cleansing the passion of the assumed human. Since the garment is washed, the human is the one washed, because the garment that is washed is the flesh; but the one who washes is the Word of God, who became the wearer of the garment in order to wash it. Rightly, then, the human is declared from the substance that was received to be washed, so that from the authority of the Word who washed, it is shown that he is God.

excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 21.
latin: Et poteram quidem omnium scripturarum caelestium euentilare tractatus, et ingentem circa istam speciem Christi diuinitatis, ut ita dixerim, siluam commouere: nisi quoniam non tam mihi contra hanc haeresim propositum est dicere, quam breuiter circa personam Christi regulam ueritatis aperire. quamuis tamen ad alia festinem, illud non arbitror praetermittendum, quod in euangelio dominus ad significantiam suae maiestatis expressit dicendo: soluite templum hoc, et ego in triduo suscitabo illud; aut quando in alio loco et alia parte pronuntiat: potestatem habeo animam meam ponendi et rursus recipere eam. hoc enim mandatum accepi a patre. quis est enim, qui dicit animam suam se posse ponere aut animam suam posse se rursum recuperare, quia hoc mandatum acceperit a patre? aut quis dicit destructum corporis sui templum resuscitare rursum et reaedificare se posse? nisi quoniam sermo ille, qui ex patre, qui apud patrem, per quem facta sunt omnia, et sine quo factum est nihil, imitator paternorum operum atque uirtutum, mago inuisibilis dei, qui descendit de caelo, qui quae uidit et audiuit testificatus est, qui non uenit ut faceret suam uoluntatem, sed potius ut faciat patris uoluntatem, a quo missus ad hoc ipsum fuerat, ut magni consilii angelus factus arcanorum caelestium nobis iura reseraret, quique uerbum caro factus habttauit in nobis, ex nobis hic Christus non homo tantum, quia hominis filius, sed etiam deus, quia dei filius, comprobatur. Quod si et primogenitus omnis creaturae ab apostolo dictus sit Christus, quomodo omnis creaturae primogenitus esse potuit, nisi quoniam secundum diuinitatem ante omnem creaturam ex patre deo sermo processit? quod nisi ita haeretici acceperint, Christum hominem primogenitum omnis creaturae monstrare cogentur; quod facere non poterunt. aut igitur ante omnem est creaturam, ut primogenitus sit omnis creaturae, et non homo est tantum, quia homo post omnem creaturam est: aut homo tantum est, et est post omnem creaturam. et quomodo primogenitus est omnis creaturae, nisi secundum uerbum illud quod est ante creaturam? et ideo primogenitus omnis creaturae caro fit et habitat in nobis, hoc est, assumit hunc hominem qui est post omnem creaturam, et sic cum illo et in illo habitat in nobis, ut neque homo Christo subtrahatur, neque diuinitas negetur. nam si tantummodo ante omnem creaturam est, homo in illo subtractus est. si autem tantummodo homo est, diuinitas quae ante omnem creaturam est intercepta est. utrumque ergo in Christo confoederatum est, et utrumque coniunctum est, et utrumque conexum est, et merito, dum est in illo aliquid quod superat creaturam, pignerata in illo diuinitatis et humanitatis uidetur esse concordia. propter quam causam, qui mediator dei et hominum effectus exprimitur, in se deum et hominem sociasse reperitur. Ac si idem apostolus de Christo refert, ut exutus carnem potestates dehonestauit, palam triumphatis illis in semetipso, non utique otiose exutum carne proposuit, nisi quoniam et in resurrectione rursum indutum uoluit intellegi. quis est ergo iste exutus et rursus indutus? requirant haeretici. nos enim sermonem dei scimus indutum carnis substantiam, eundemque rursum exutum eadem corporis materia, quam rursus in resurrectione suscepit et quasi indumentum resumpsit. sed enim neque exutus neque indutus hominem Christus fuisset, si homo tantum fuisset. nemo enim umquam se ipso aut spoliatur aut induitur. sit enim necesse est aliud, quicquid aliunde aut spoliatur aut induitur. ex quo merito sermo dei fuit, qui exutus est carnem et in resurrectione rursus indutus; exutus autem, quoniam et in natiuitate fuerat indutus. itaque in Christo deus est qui induitur, atque etiam exutus sit oportet: propterea quod is qui induitur, pariter et exuatur necesse est. induitur autem et exuitur homine, quasi quadam contexti corporis tunica. ac propterea consequenter sermo fuit, ut diximus, dei, qui modo indutus, modo exutus esse reperitur. hoc enim etiam in benedictionibus ante praedixit: Lauabit stolam suam in uino, et in sanguine uuae amictum suum. si stola in Christo caro est, et amictum ipsum corpus est, requiratur, quis est ille cuius corpus amictum est, et stola caro? nobis enim manifestum est carnem stolam et corpus amictum uerbi fuisse, qui uuae sanguine, id est uino, lauit substantiam corporis et materiam carnis, abluens ex parte suscepti hominis passione. ex quo siquidem lauatur, homo est, quia amictum, quod lauatur, caro est: qui autem lauat, uerbum dei est, qui ut lauaret amictum, amicti susceptor effectus est. merito ex ea substantia, quae recepta est ut lauaretur, homo exprimitur, sic ut ex uerbi auctoritate, qui lauit, deus esse monstretur.

excerpts.author: Novatian
english: Why, though we appear to be rushing on to another part of the argument, do we skip over that passage in the apostle Paul? He writes of the one who, existing in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be seized, but emptied himself by taking the form of a servant, being made in human likeness; and found in appearance as a man, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to death — even death on a cross. Therefore God also highly exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father (Philippians 2:5-11).

"Who, existing in the form of God," he says. If Christ were merely a man, he would be in the image of God, not in the form — for we know that human beings are made according to the image, not the form, and even angels do not possess the form of God. Who, then, is this one who was found in the form of God, as we have said, unless he is that chief and noble Son of God above all, the Word of God, imitator of all the Father's works, who himself works just as his Father does, and so exists in the form of God the Father (as we have expressed it)? And rightly he is declared to be in the form of God, since he is above all and holds the divine power over all creation, and is God by the example of the Father. Yet this very status he received from the Father, so that he might be God over all, and Lord, and God in the form of God the Father, begotten and brought forth from him.

Therefore, although he existed in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God something to be seized. For even though he knew himself to be God from God the Father, he never compared or equated himself with God the Father, mindful that he is from his Father and that he possesses his very being because the Father gave it to him. Consequently, both before the assumption of flesh and after the assumption of the body — indeed, even after the resurrection itself — he rendered the same obedience to the Father in all things. By this it is proved that he never regarded his divinity as something to be grasped in order to make himself equal to God the Father; on the contrary, obedient and subject to every command and will of the Father, he was content even to take the form of a servant — that is, to become that man — and to assume the substance of flesh and body, which, born from the bondage of ancestral sins according to human nature, he undertook at his birth. At that time he also emptied himself, because he did not refuse to take on the frailty of the human condition.

If he had been born only as a man, he would not have been emptied; for a human being, when born, grows rather than is emptied. As he begins to be what he could not previously possess, he is not diminished but rather increased and enriched. But if Christ is emptied by being born, by taking the form of a servant, how can he be only a man? Of such a one it would more truly be said that he was enriched, not emptied, at birth — unless the authority of the divine Word, temporarily resting from exercising its powers in order to take on humanity, lowered itself for a time and laid aside its glory, while bearing the man it had assumed. He empties himself as he descends to injuries and insults, as he hears unspeakable things and suffers unworthy treatment. Yet the splendid fruit of that humility appears at once: he received the name that is above every name, which we certainly understand to be nothing other than the name of God (Philippians 2:9-10).

For since it belongs to God alone to be above all, it follows that the name which is above every name belongs to the one who is above all. That name, therefore, is the name of God — and consequently it belongs to the one who, existing in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be seized. For if Christ were not God, every knee would not bow to him — in heaven, on earth, and under the earth — nor would all creation, visible and invisible, be subjected to a mere man who remembered that he existed before humanity. From all this — while Christ is said to be in the form of God, while he is shown to have emptied himself in the birth according to the flesh, while it is declared that he received from the Father the name above every name, while it is shown that every knee of heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings bows and bends at his name, and that this very thing happens to the glory of God the Father — it follows necessarily that Christ is not a man merely because he became obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross; but also from these earlier realities that proclaim the divinity of Christ, the Lord Christ Jesus is shown to be God, which the heretics refuse to accept.

excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 22.
latin: Cur autem, licet ad aliam partem disputandi festinare uideamur, illum praetereamus apud apostolum locum? gui cum in forma dei esset, non rapinam arbitratus est aequalem se deo esse; sed semetipsum exinaniuit, formam serui accipiens, in similitudine hominum factus, et habitu tnwentus ut homo: humiliauit se, oboediens factus usque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis: propterea et deus illum superexaltauit, et dedit illi nomen quod est super omne nomen; ut in nomine Iesu omne genu flectatur caelestium terrestrium et infernorum, et omnis lingua confiteatur, quoniam dominus Iesus in gloria est dei patris. qui cum in forma dei esset, inquit. si homo tantummodo Christus, in imagine dei, non forma det rehominem enim scimus ad imaginem, non ad sed nec in angelis formam dei Quis ergo est iste, qui in forma dei, ut diximus, factus est legimus; nisi quoniam hic praecipuus atque generosus prae omnibus dei filius, uerbum dei, imitator omnium paternorum operum, dum et ipse operatur sicut et pater eius, in forma (ut expressimus) est dei patris. et merito in forma pronuntiatus est dei, dum et ipse super omnia, et omnis creaturae diuinam obtinens potestatem, et deus est exemplo patris; hoc ipsum tamen a patre proprio consecutus, ut omnium et deus esset, et dominus esset, et deus ad formam dei patris ex ipso genitus atque prolatus. hic ergo quamuis esset in forma dei, non est rapinam arbitratus aequalem se deo esse. qQuamuis enim se ex deo patre deum esse meminisset, numquam se deo patri aut comparauit aut contulit, memor se esse ex suo patre, et hoc ipsum, quod est, habere se, quia pater dedisset. inde denique et ante carnis assumptionem, sed et post assumptionem corporis, post ipsam praeterea resurrectionem, omnem patri in omnibus rebus oboedientiam praestitit pariter ac praestat. quo probatur numquam arbitratum illum esse rapinam quandam diuinitatem, ut aequaret se patri deo: quin immo contra, omni ipsius imperio et uoluntati oboediens atque subiectus, etiam ut formam serui susciperet contentus fuit—hoc est, hominem illum fieri—et substantiam carnis et corporis, quam ex paternorum secundum hominem delictorum seruitute uenientem nascendo suscepit. quo tempore se etiam exinaniuit, dum humanam condicionis fragilitatem suscipere non recusauit. quoniam si homo tantummodo natus fuisset, per hoc exinanitus non esset. homo enim nascens augetur, non exinanitur: nam dum incipit esse quod cum non esset habere non potuit, ut diximus, non exinanitur, sed potius augetur atque ditatur. at si Christus exinanitur in eo quod nascitur, formam serui accipiendo, quomodo homo tantummodo est? de quo uerius dictum fuisset, locupletatum illum esse tunc cum nasceretur, non exinanitum: nisi quoniam auctoritas diuini uerbi, ad suscipiendum hominem interim conquiescens, nec se suis uiribus exercens, deicit se ad tempus atque deponit, dum hominem fert quem suscepit. exinanit se, dum ad iniurias contumeliasque descendit, dum audit infanda, experitur indigna. cuius tamen humilitatis adest statim egregius fructus. accepit enim omen, quod est super omne nomen, quod utique non aliud intellegimus esse quam nomen dei. nam cum dei sit solius esse super omnia, consequens est, ut nomen illud quod est super omne nomen sit eius, qui super omnia est. dei est ergo nomen illud quod super,omne nomen est: quod nomen est eius utique consequenter, qui, cum in forma dei fuisset, non rapinam arbitratus est aequalem se deo esse. neque enim si non deus esset Christus, omne se in nomine eius genu flecteret, caelestium et terrestrium et infernorum: nec uisibilia aut inuisibilia, aut rerum omnium omnis creatura homini esset subiecta siue substrata, quae se ante hominem esse meminisset. ex quo dum iz forma dei esse Christus dicitur, et dum in natiuitatem secundum carnem se exinanisse monstratur, et dum id accepisse nomen a patre quod sit super omne nomen exprimitur, et dum in nomine eius omne genu caelestium, terrenorum et infernorum se flectere et curuare monstratur, et hoc ipsum in gloriam dei patris succurrere asseritur; consequenter non ex illo tantum homo est, quia oboediens patri factus est usque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis; sed ex his etiam rebus superioribus diuinitatem Christi sonantibus, dominus Christus Iesus et deus, quod haeretici nolunt, esse monstratur.

excerpts.author: Novatian
english: At this point I am free to collect arguments even from other heretical groups. Proof drawn from an opponent is especially firm, because it lets the truth be confirmed by the very enemies of truth themselves. Scripture makes it so clear that God exists that many heretics, overwhelmed by the magnitude and truth of the divine nature, have pushed their honors for him beyond all measure. They have gone so far as to proclaim not the Son but God the Father himself. Although this runs contrary to scriptural truth, it still stands as a great and principal argument for the divinity of Christ. He is so fully God, yet precisely as the Son of God born from God, that many heretics have accepted him as God in such a way that they thought he must be not the Son but the Father.

Let them consider, then, whether this one is God, whose authority has so moved certain people that they came to regard him as God the Father himself, as we noted earlier. They confessed the divinity in Christ without restraint and with abundant zeal, driven by the manifest divinity of Christ to think him the Father, because they perceived him to be God, the very one they read about as the Son. Other heretics have so embraced the manifest divinity of Christ that they declared he was without flesh, stripping away the whole man he assumed. They did this lest they diminish the power of the divine name in him, supposing that associating a human birth with him would weaken it. We do not approve of that view, but we do advance the argument that Christ is so fully God that some, once the man was removed, thought him to be only God, while others believed him to be God the Father himself.

The reason and balance of the heavenly scriptures show Christ to be God, but as the Son of God, and with the man assumed by God and also the Son, he is to be believed as a man as well. Because he came to humanity in order to be the mediator of God and men, he had to be one with humanity, and the Word had to become flesh. Only so could he establish harmony in himself between earthly and heavenly realities, binding the pledges of both sides in his own person and joining God to man and man to God. As a result, the Son of God, by assuming flesh, becomes the Son of man, and the Son of man, by receiving the Word of God, becomes the Son of God. The salvation of the human race, destined before the ages, finds its fulfillment in the Lord Jesus Christ, who is both God and man, and by this condition the human race is led to the fruit of eternal salvation.

excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 23.
latin: Hoc in loco licebit mihi argumenta etiam ex aliorum haereticorum parte conquirere. firmum est genus probationis, quod etiam ab aduersario sumitur, ut ueritas etiam ab ipsis inimicis ueritatis probetur. nam usque adeo hunc manifestum est in scripturis esse et deum tradi, ut plerique haereticorum, diuinitatis ipsius magnitudine et ueritate commoti, ultra modum extendentes honores eius, ausi sint non filium sed ipsum deum patrem promere uel putare. quod, etsi contra scripturarum ueritatem est, tamen diuinitatis Christi argumentum grande atque praecipuum est; qui usque adeo deus, sed qua filius dei natus ex deo, ut plerique illum (ut diximus) haeretici ita deum acceperint, ut non filium sed patrem pronuntiandum putarint. aestiment ergo an hic sit deus, cuius auctoritas tantum mouit quosdam, ut putarent illum, ut diximus superius, iam ipsum patrem deum, effrenatius et -effusius in Christo diuinitatem confitentes, ad hoc illos manifesta Christi diuinitate cogente, ut, quem filium legerent, quia deum animaduerterent, patrem putarent. alii quoque haeretici usque adeo Christi manifestam amplexati sunt diuinitatem, ut dixerint illum fuisse sine carne, et totum illi susceptum detraxerint hominem, ne decoquerent in illo diuini nominis potestatem, si humanam illi sociassent, ut arbitrabantur, natiuitatem. quod tamen nos non probamus; sed argumentum afferimus usque adeo Christum esse deum, ut quidam illum, subtracto homine, tantummodo putarint deum, quidam autem ipsum crediderint patrem deum: cum ratio et temperamentum scripturarum caelestium Christum ostendant deum, sed qua filium dei, et, assumpto a deo etiam filio hominis, credendum et hominem. quoniam si ad hominem ueniebat, ut mediator dei et hominum esse deberet, oportuit illum cum eo esse, et uerbum carnem fieri, ut in semetipso concordiam confibularet terrenorum pariter atque caelestium, dum utriusque partis in se conectens pignora et deum homini et hominem deo copularet; ut merito filius dei per assumptionem carnis filius hominis, et filius hominis per receptionem dei uerbi filius dei effici possit. salutem generis humani ante saecula destinatum, in domino Iesu Christo deo et homine inuenitur impleri, quo condicio generis humani ad fructum aeternae salutis posset adduci.

excerpts.author: Novatian
english: I believe the source of this heretical error is their refusal to acknowledge any difference between the Son of God and the son of man; otherwise, with a distinction drawn, both the man and God would be easily proven in Jesus Christ. They want the son of man to be identical with the Son of God, so that the man, the flesh, and that fragile substance may be declared to be the very Son of God. Because no distinction separates the son of man from the Son of God, but the son of man is claimed as God's Son, they assert that Christ is only a man and the same as the Son of God. By this they strive to exclude the truth that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14), and that his name shall be called Emmanuel, which means God with us (Matt. 1:23).

They put forward and allege the words recorded in Luke's Gospel, twisting them to assert not what is true but only what they wish: "The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the child to be born will be called holy, the Son of God" (Luke 1:35). They argue: if the angel tells Mary that what is born from her will be holy, then the substance of flesh and body comes from Mary; and this substance—that holy thing born of her—they claim is the Son of God. The man himself, they say, and that flesh of the body called holy, is the Son of God; so that whenever Scripture says "holy," we must understand Christ the son of man as a mere man, and whenever it presents the Son of God, we must perceive not God but a man.

But divine Scripture easily convicts and exposes the heretics' frauds and thefts. If the angel's words were only "the Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the child to be born will be called the Son of God," we might need a different line of argument and other weapons to defeat their snares and deceptions. But Scripture, abounding in heavenly fullness, strips itself of their calumnies; we simply stand on what is written and overcome these errors without doubt. For the angel did not say, as we have shown, merely "therefore the child to be born will be holy"; he added a conjunction: "therefore *and* the child to be born will be holy called the Son of God" (Luke 1:35). This shows that the holy thing born of her—this substance of flesh and body—is not primarily the Son of God, but secondarily; primarily the Son of God is the Word of God incarnate through that Spirit of whom the angel speaks: "The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you" (Luke 1:35).

This is the true Son of God, who is from God. When he assumes this holy thing and joins the son of man to himself, drawing him to himself and leading him across, he grants and makes the son of man the Son of God—which he was not by nature—by the union and mixture joined to himself. Thus the primacy of the divine name rests in the Spirit of the Lord who descends and comes; the sequence of the name belongs to the Son of God and man, and this one rightly becomes the Son of God because he is not primarily the Son of God. Therefore the angel, perceiving this arrangement and expediting the order of this mystery, did not confuse everything so as to leave no trace of distinction; he established a distinction, saying: "therefore and the child to be born will be holy, and will be called the Son of God" (Luke 1:35). Had he not dispensed this distribution with its proper measures but left it confused and mixed, he would have given heretics grounds to pronounce the son of man, as man, to be the same as the Son of God.

Now, expounding particularly, he clearly expressed the order and reason of so great a mystery, saying that the child to be born will be called holy, the Son of God, proving that the Son of God descends: who, when he received the son of man into himself, consequently made him the Son of God, because he associated and joined the son of man to himself, so that when the son of man adheres to the Son of God in birth, he might hold by this mixture what he could not possess by his own nature. Thus the angel's voice makes a distinction—which heretics reject—between the Son of God and the son of man, yet with their association, urging them to understand that Christ the son of man is a man, and also to recognize the Son of God, and that the man is the Son of God, that is, the Word of God, who (as Scripture says) is God. Therefore they should know Christ Jesus the Lord as woven and compacted from both, in the concord of both substances, mutually bound by the reciprocal covenant of their union, man and God—Scripture itself declaring this very truth.

excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 24.
latin: Sed erroris istius haereticorum inde, ut opinor, nata materia est, quia inter filium dei et filium hominis nihil arbitrantur interesse, ne facta distinctione et homo et deus Iesus Christus facile comprobetur. eundem enim atque ipsum, id est hominem filium hominis etiam filium dei, uolunt uideri, ut homo et caro et fragilis illa substantia eadem atque ipse filius dei esse dicatur; ex quo, dum distinctio filii hominis et filii dei nulla secernitur, sed ipse filius hominis dei filius uindicatur, homo tantummodo Christus idem atque filius dei asseratur. per quod nituntur excludere: uwerbum caro factum est et habitauit in nobis; et uocabitis nomen eius Emmanuel, quod est interpretatum nobiscum deus. Proponunt enim atque illa praetendunt, quae in euangelio Lucae relata sunt, ex quibus asserere conantur, non quod est, sed tantum illud quod uolunt esse: spiritus sanctus ueniet in te, et uirtus altissimi obumbrabit tibi; propterea et quod ex te nascetur sanctum, uocabitur filius dei. si ergo, inquiunt, angelus dei dicit ad Mariam, quod ex te nascetur sanctum, ex Maria est substantia carnis et corporis. hanc autem substantiam, id est sanctum hoc quod ex illa genitum est, filium dei esse proposuit. homo, inquiunt, ipse, et illa caro corporis, illud quod sanctum est dictum, ipsum est filius dei; ut et cum dicit scriptura sanctum, Christum filium hominis hominem intellegamus, et cum jiium dei proponit, non deum sed hominem percipere debeamus. Sed enim scriptura diuina haereticorum et fraudes et furta facile conuincit et detegit. si enim sic esset tantummodo: spiritus ueniet in te, et uirtus altissimi obumbrabit tibi; propterea quod nascetur ex te sanctum, uocabitur filius dei, fortasse alio esset nobis genere aduersus illos reluctandum, et alia nobis essent argumenta quaerenda et arma sumenda, quibus illorum et insidias et praestigias uinceremus. cum autem ipsa scriptura caelesti abundans plenitudine sese haereticorum istorum calumniis exuat, facile ipso quod scriptum est nitimur, et errores istos sine ulla dubitatione superamus. non enim dixit, ut iam expressimus, propterea quod ex te nascetur sanctum, sed adiecit coniunctionem: ait enim, propterea et quod ex te nascetur sanctum; ut illud ostenderet, non principaliter hoc sanctum, quod ex illa nascitur, id est istam carnis corporisque substantiam, filium dei esse, sed consequenter et in secundo loco: principaliter autem filium dei esse uerbum dei incarnatum per illum spiritum, de quo angelus refert: sf7zvitus ueniet in te, et uirtus altissimi obumbrabit tibi. Hic est enim legitimus dei filius, qui ex ipso deo est, qui dum Sanctum istud assumit et sibi filium hominis annectit et illum ad se rapit atque transducit, conexione sua et permixtione sociata praestat, et filium illum dei facit, quod ille naturaliter non fuit; ut principalitas nominis istius fs dei in spiritu sit domini, qui descendit et uenit; ut sequella nominis in filio dei et hominis sit, et merito consequenter hic filius dei factus sit, dum non principaliter filius dei est. atque ideo dispositionem istam angelus uidens et ordinem istum sacramenti expediens, non sic cuncta confundens ut nullum uestigium distinctionis collocarit, distinctionem posuit, dicendo: propterea et quod nascetur ex te sanctum, uocabitur filius dei: ne si distributionem istam cum libramentis suis non dispensasset, sed in confuso permixtam reliquisset, uere occasionem haereticis contulisset, ut hominis filium, qua homo est, eundem et dei et hominis filium pronuntiare deberent. nunc autem partiticulatim exponens, tam magni sacramenti ordinem atque rationem euidenter expressit, ut diceret, e quod ex te nascetur sanctum, uocabitur filius dei, probans quoniam filius dei descendit: qui dum filium hominis in se suscepit, consequenter illum filium dei fecit; quoniam illum filius sibi dei sociauit et iunxit, ut dum filius hominis adhaeret in natiuitate filio dei, ipsa permixtione feneratum et mutuatum teneret, quod ex natura propria possidere non posset. ac sic facta est angeli uoce, quod nolunt haeretici, inter filium dei hominisque, cum sua tamen sociatione, distinctio, urgendo illos uti Christum, hominis filium hominem, intellegant quoque dei filium, et hominem dei filium, id est dei uerbum (sicut scriptum est) deum, accipiant, atque ideo Christum Iesum dominum (ut ita dixerim) ex utroque contextum atque concretum, et in eadem utriusque substantiae concordia mutui ad inuicem foederis confibulatione sociatum, hominem et deum, scripturae hoc ipsum dicentis ueritate, cognoscant.

excerpts.author: Novatian
english: They argue that if Christ is not merely a man but also God, and yet Scripture reports that he died and rose again for us, then Scripture teaches us to believe that God died. Alternatively, if God cannot die, but Christ is reported to have died, then Christ cannot be God, since God cannot be conceived as having died. If they ever understood—or had ever understood—what they read, they would never speak so dangerously. But error is always marked by a sudden, reckless madness, and it is no surprise that those who have abandoned the legitimate faith descend into such dangerous statements.

After all, if Scripture presented Christ as God alone, with no admixture of human frailty, their twisted syllogism—"If Christ is God, and Christ died, therefore God died"—would carry some weight. But since Scripture constitutes Christ as both God and man, as we have shown repeatedly, it follows that what is immortal and incorruptible remains untouched. Who does not grasp that divinity is impassible, while human frailty is passible? Therefore, since Christ is understood to be a union of both the divine and the human—"the Word became flesh and dwelled among us" (John 1:14)—who cannot recognize without any teacher or interpreter that it was not the divine element in Christ that died, but the human?

Consider: if the divinity in Christ does not die, but only the substance of his flesh is extinguished, this parallels every other human being. We are not flesh alone, but flesh and soul; the flesh alone suffers the onset of death, while the incorrupt soul is seen to lie outside death's jurisdiction. The Lord himself confirmed this when he urged us to martyrdom and contempt for all human power: "Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul" (Matthew 10:28). If an immortal soul cannot be killed or destroyed in anyone else, even though the body and flesh alone can be killed, how much more certainly could the Word of God—who is God in Christ—never be killed at all, since only his flesh and body were slain?

If the soul possesses the nobility of immortality in every human being, rendering it unkillable, how much more does the nobility of the Word of God possess the power not to be killed? If human power is insufficient to kill the sacred power of God, and human cruelty fails to kill the soul, it must fail all the more to kill the Word of God. Since the soul itself—made through the Word of God—is not killed by men, the Word of God must all the more be believed indestructible. And if human cruelty can do no more against human beings than kill the body, how much more certainly will it prevail no further in Christ than to kill his body alone? The conclusion drawn from these facts is that only a man was killed in Christ, showing that the argument about mortality is misplaced.

Consider Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, acknowledged as mere men. Yet it is clear they live: "All of them live to God" (Luke 20:38), and death does not destroy the soul in them, which merely releases their bodies. Death could exercise its right over their bodies, but not over their souls; one element in them was mortal and therefore died, another was immortal and therefore is understood not to be extinguished. For this reason they are declared to live to God. How much more certainly, then, could death prevail against Christ only regarding the material of his body, and not against the divinity of his Word? For the power of death is broken wherever the authority of immortality intervenes.

excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 25.
latin: Ergo, inquiunt, si Christus non homo est tantum sed et deus, Christum autem refert scriptura mortuum pro nobis et resuscitatum, iam docet nos scriptura credere deum mortuum: aut si deus non moritur, Christus autem mortuus refertur, non erit Christus deus, quoniam deus non potest accipi mortuus. si umquam intellegerent aut intellexissent quod legunt, numquam tam periculose omnino loquerentur. sed erroris semper est abrupta dementia; et non est nouum si usque ad periculosa descendunt, qui fidem legitimam reliquerunt. si enim scriptura proponeret Christum tantummodo deum, et nulla in illo fragilitatis humanae sociatio esset permixta, merito illorum hic aliquid ualuisset sermo contortus, ‘si Christus deus, Christus autem mortuus, ergo mortuus est deus.’ sed cum non tantummodo illum, ut ostendimus iam frequenter, deum sed et hominem scriptura constituat, consequens est, quod immortale est, incorruptum mansisse teneatur. quis enim non intellegat, quod impassibilis sit diuinitas, passibilis uero sit humana fragilitas? cum ergo tam ex eo quod deus est, quam etiam ex illo quod homo est, Christus intellegatur esse permixtus et esse sociatus,—verbum enim caro factum est, et habitauit in nobis—quis non sine ullo magistro atque interprete ex sese facile cognoscat, non illud in Christo mortuum esse quod deus est, sed illud in illo mortuum esse quod homo est? quid enim si diuinitas in Christo non moritur, sed carnis solius substantia exstinguitur, quando et in ceteris hominibus, qui non sunt caro tantummodo, sed caro et anima, caro quidem sola incursum interitus mortisque patiatur, extra leges autem interitus et mortis anima incorrupta cernatur? hoc enim et ipse dominus, hortans nos ad martyrium et ad contemptum omnis humanae potestatis, aiebat: ne timueritis eos qui corpus occidunt, animam autem occidere non possunt. quod si anima immortalis occidi aut interfici non potest in quouis alio, licet corpus et caro sola possit interfici, quanto magis utique uerbum dei deus in Christo interfici omnino non potuit, cum caro sola et corpus occisum sit? si enim hanc habet generositatem immortalitatis anima in quouis homine, ut non possit interfici, multo magis hanc habet potestatem generositas uerbi dei, ut non possit occidi. nam si potestas hominum ad interficiendam sacram dei potestatem, et si crudelitas humana ad interficiendam animam deficit, multo magis ad dei uerbum interficiendum deficere debebit. nam cum ipsa anima, quae per dei uerbum facta est, ab hominibus non occiditur, multo magis utique uerbum dei perimi non posse credetur. et si plus non potest hominum cruenta saeuitia aduersus homines, quam ut tantummodo corpus occidat, quanto magis utique in Christo non ualebit, quam ut item tantummodo corpus occidat: ut, dum per haec colligitur non nisi hominem in Christo interfectum, appareat ad mortalitatem sermonem in loco non esse deductum. nam si Abraham, et Isaac, et Iacob, quos homines tantummodo constat fuisse, manifestum est uiuere—ommnes enim, inquit, illi uiuunt deo, nec mors in illis animam perimit, quae corpora ipsa soluit; ius enim suum exercere potuit in corpora, in animas exercere non ualuit: aliud enim in illis mortale, et ideo mortuum, aliud in illis immortale, et ideo intellegitur non exstinctum, ob quam causam uiuere deo pronuntiati et dicti sunt,—multo magis utique mors in Christum aduersum solam materiam corporis potuit ualere, aduersus diuinitatem sermonis non potuit se exercere. frangitur enim potestas mortis, ubi intercedit auctoritas immortalitatis.

excerpts.author: Novatian
english: I will also add that other part in which the heretic, as it were rejoicing with his own eye after losing the truth and the light, may recognize the total blindness of his error. For he repeatedly and frequently objects that it was said: 'I have been with you for so long a time, and you do not know me? Philip, whoever has seen me has seen the Father' (John 14:9). But what he does not understand, let him learn. Philip is blamed, and rightly and deservedly so, because he said: 'Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us.' For when had he ever heard or learned from Christ that Christ was the Father, since, on the contrary, he had heard and learned more frequently that Christ was the Son, not because he was the Father? For what the Lord said — 'If you have known me, you have also known my Father, and from now on you know him and have seen him' — he did not say so that he himself might be understood as the Father, but because whoever approaches the Son of God with total faith and total religion, in every way through that Son in whom he so believes, is going to come to the Father and will see him. For no one, he says, can come to the Father except through me (John 14:6), and therefore one is not only going to come to God the Father and know him, but also must hold and presume in mind and spirit as if he already knows the Father and has seen him. For divine Scripture often announces things not yet done as if they were already done, because they are going to be so, and it declares things that must happen in every way, not as if they were going to happen, but as if they had already happened. Finally, when Christ had not yet been born in the times of the prophet Isaiah, it was said: 'For a child has been born to us' (Isaiah 9:6); and when he had not yet come to Mary, it was said to the prophet: 'Behold, she has conceived and will bear a son' (Isaiah 7:14); and when Christ had not yet revealed the bosom of the Father, it was reported: 'His name will be called Angel of Great Counsel'; and when he had not yet suffered, it was proclaimed: 'He was led to slaughter' (Isaiah 53:7); and when the cross did not yet exist anywhere, it was said: 'All day long I have stretched out my hands to a disobedient people' (Isaiah 65:2; Romans 10:21); and when he had not yet been insultingly given drink, it was said: 'They gave me vinegar to drink' (Psalm 69:21); and when he had not yet been stripped, it was said: 'They cast lots for my garment' (Psalm 22:18), 'They numbered my bones' (Psalm 22:17), 'They pierced my hands and my feet' (Psalm 22:16). For divine Scripture, foreseeing, speaks of future things as done, because it knows they will come to pass, and of future perfections as perfect, which are certainly going to come. And therefore the Lord said in this present place: 'From now on you know him and have seen him.' For he said that the Father would be seen by whoever had followed the Son; not as if the Son himself were the Father seen, but because whoever would follow the Son and wished to be his disciple would receive the reward of being able to see the Father. For the Son is also the image of God the Father (Colossians 1:15; Hebrews 1:3), so that this may be added: just as the Father works, so the Son also works, and the Son is the imitator of all the Father's works; so that each one may have it as if he had already seen the Father, while he sees the one who always imitates the invisible Father in all works. But if Christ himself is the Father, how does he immediately add and say: 'Whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do, and will do greater works than these, because I am going to the Father' (John 14:12)? And he still adds: 'If you love me, keep my commandments: and I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Advocate' (John 14:15–16). And after these he also adds: 'If anyone loves me, he will keep my word: and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him' (John 14:23). Nor does he fail to add that also: 'But the Advocate, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you and remind you of all that I have said' (John 14:26). He premises that place to show that he is the Son, and rightly adds and says: 'If you loved me, you would rejoice, because I am going to the Father: for the Father is greater than I' (John 14:28). What, then, when he also adds: 'I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser: every branch in me that does not bear fruit he takes away, and every branch that bears fruit he prunes, that it may bear more fruit' (John 15:1–2)? He presses on and adds: 'As the Father has loved me, so I have loved you; abide in my love. If you keep my commandments, you will abide in my love, just as I have kept my Father's commandments and abide in his love' (John 15:9–10). He further introduces and says: 'I have called you friends, because all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you' (John 15:15). He gathers also this: 'But they will do all these things to you on account of my name, because they do not know the one who sent me' (John 15:21). These things, therefore, which clearly testify that he is not the Father but the Son, the Lord would never have added after those earlier words, if he had either remembered that he was the Father or wanted to be understood as the Father. Unless it was so that he might express that each one ought to have it as if he already held the Father, while seeing the image of God the Father through the Son, and as if he had seen the Father — since each one believing in the Son is exercised in the contemplation of the image, so that, having become accustomed to seeing the divinity through the image, he may progress and grow unto the perfect contemplation of God the Father Almighty — and because whoever drinks this in with mind and spirit and believes that all these things will be so, will have the Father whom he is going to see as if he had already seen him and already holds him here, as if he possesses what he knows he will certainly possess. But if he himself had been the Father, what reward would he promise as if it were future, which he had already granted and given? For since he says: 'Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God' (Matthew 5:8), he is caught promising the contemplation and vision of the Father. Therefore he had not yet given it: for why would he promise it if he had already given it? He would have given it if he were the Father; for he would have been seen and touched. But when Christ, while being touched and seen, still promises and says that whoever is pure in heart shall see God, this very fact proves that he is not the Father, who, being present while he was seen, was promising that whoever was pure in heart would see the Father. Therefore it was the Son, not the Father, who was promising these things; because the Son, who had something to be seen, was promising it: a promise that would have been superfluous unless he were the Son. For why would he promise the pure in heart that they would see the Father, if those who were present at that time were already seeing Christ the Father? But because he was the Son, not the Father, rightly the Son, because he is the image of God, was then visible, and the Father, because invisible, is promised and marked out to the pure in heart, that he may be seen. These things, then, are enough to have been said even against this heretic — a few things out of many. For a field, and indeed a broad and spread-out one, would be opened if we should wish to engage this heretic more fully; since, deprived of the light by two passages having been dug out, he is entirely overcome in the blindness of his doctrine.

latin: Adhuc adiciam illam quoque partem in qua dum haereticus quasi oculo quodam gaudet proprio, ueritatis et luminis amisso, totam caecitatem sui agnoscat erroris. identidem enim et frequenter opponit quia dictum sit: sano tempore uobiscum sum, et non agnoscitis me? Philippe, qui uidit me, uidit et patrem. sed quod non intellegit, discat. culpatur Philippus, et iure quidem meritoque, quia dixerit: domine, ostende nobis patrem, et sufficit nobis. quando enim ex Christo aut audierat istud aut didicerat, quasi esset pater Christus, cum contra magis, quod filius esset, non quia pater, frequenter audisset, et saepe didicisset? quod enim dixit dominus, s me cognouistis, et patrem meum cognouistis, et a modo nostis illum, et uidistis illum, non sic dixerat ut se patrem uellet intellegi, sed quoniam qui penitus et plene et cum tota fide et tota religione accessit ad dei filium, omnibus modis per ipsum filium, in quem sic credit, ad patrem peruenturus sit, eundemque uisurus. nemo enim, inquit, potest uenire ad patrem nisi per me, et ideo ad patrem deum non tantum uenturus est, et cogniturus ipsum patrem, sed etiam sic tenere debet, atque ita animo ac mente praesumere, quasi iam nouerit patrem pariter et uiderit. Saepe enim scriptura diuina, quae nondum facta pro factis annuntiat, quia sic futura sunt, et quae omnibus modis fieri habent, non quasi futura sint, praedicat, sed quasi facta sint, narrat. denique cum nondum temporibus Isaiae prophetae Christus natus fuisset, quia puer, aiebat, natus est nobis; et cum nondum accessum esset ad Mariam, e accessit ad propheten, dicebat, e concepit, et peperit filium. et cum nondum sinum patris Christus exposuisset, referebat: e uocabitur nomen eius magni consili angelus. et cum nondum fuisset passus, guas? outs, pronuntiabat, ad iugulationem adductus est. et cum adhuc crux nusquam esset, aiebat: Tota die expandi manus meas ad populum non credentem., et cum nondum iniuriose potatus fuisset, s7fz, ait, mea potauerunt me aceto. et cum spoliatus adhuc non fuisset, dicebat, super uestem meam miserunt sortem: et dinumerauerunt ossa mea: effoderunt manus meas et pedes. prouidens enim scriptura diuina pro factis dicit, quae futura scit, et pro perfectis dicit, quae futura habet, quae sine dubitatione uentura sunt. et ideo dominus in praesenti loco dicebat: a modo nostis illum, et uidistis. dicebat enim uisum iri ab eo patrem, quisquis filium secutus fuisset; non quasi filius ipse esset pater uisus, sed quod praemium consecuturus esset, quisquis illum sequi et discipulus eius esse uoluisset, ut uidere patrem posset. nam et imago est dei patris, ut his etiam illud accedat, quoniam sicut pater operatur, ita operatur et filius, et imitator est filius omnium operum paternorum; ut perinde habeat unusquisque, quasi iam uiderit patrem, dum eum uidet qui inuisibilem patrem in omnibus operibus semper imitatur. Ceterum si ipse pater est Christus, quomodo confestim adicit et dicit: gud credit in me, opera quae ego facio et ipse Faciet, et maiora his faciet, quia ego ad patrem uado? et adhuc subnectit: si diligitis me, praecepta mea seruate: et ego rogabo patrem, et alium aduocatum dabit uobis. post quae etiam illud subnectit: s quis me diligit, sermonem meum custodiet: et pater meus diliget illum, et ad eum ueniemus, et mansionem apud illum Jaciemus. nec non etiam subdidit illud quoque: aduocatus autem ille spiritus sanctus, quem missurus est pater, ille uos docebit et commemorabit- omnia quaecumque dixero. praemittit adhuc istum locum, quo ostendat se esse filium, et merito subdidit, et dicit: s me diligeretis, gauderetis, quia eo ad patrem: quia pater maior me est. quid autem cum etiam ila subnectit: ego sum uitis uera, et pater meus agricola: omne sarmentum in me non afferens fructum tollit illud, et omne fructtSerum purgat, ut fructum ampliorem ferat? instat adhuc et adicit: sicut dilexit me pater, et ego dilexi uos; manete in mea caritate; si mandata mea seruaueritis, manebitis in mea caritale, sicut ego patris mandata seruaui, et maneo in eius caritate. adhuc ingerit, et dicit: dixi autem uos amicos, quia omnia quae audiui a patre meo, nota uobis feci. aggregat etiam hoc: sed haec omnia facient uobis propter nomen meum, quia ignorant eum qui me misit. Haec ergo numquam post illa euidenter illum non patrem sed filium esse testantia dominus subdidisset, si aut patrem se esse meminisset, aut patrem se uellet intellegi. nisi quoniam ut illud exprimeret, perinde unumquemque iam habere debere, dum imaginem dei patris per filium uidet, atque si uiderit patrem—quandoquidem unusquisque credens in filium exerceatur in imaginis contemplatione, ut assuefactus ad diuinitatem uidendam imagine proficere possit et crescere usque ad dei patris omnipotentis perfectam contemplationem,—et quoniam, qui hoc animo ac mentecombiberit et de omnibus sic futurum esse crediderit, patrem, quem uisurus sit, quasi iam quodammodo uiderit et hic iam sic habeat, quasi teneat, quod habiturum se pro certo sciat. Ceterum, si ipse pater fuisset, quid quasi futurum praemium repromittebat, quod iam praestiterat et dederat? nam quoniam dicit: beati mundo corde, quia ipsi deum uidebunt, polliceri deprehenditur contemplationem et aspectum patris. ergo nondum dederat: cur enim repromitteret, si iam dedisset? dederat enim, si pater esset; uidebatur enim, et contingebatur. quando autem, dum contingitur ipse Christus et uidetur, repromittit tamen et dicit, quoniam qui mundo fuerit corde, deum uidebit, hoc ipso probat patrem se non esse, qui tunc praesens cum uideretur repromittebat, quod patrem uisurus esset quisquis mundo corde fuisset. erat ergo repromittens haec non pater sed filius; quia qui filius erat, quod uideri habebat repromittebat: cuius repromissio superuacua fuisset, nisi filius fuisset. cur enim repromittebat mundis ut uiderent patrem, Si iam tunc qui praesentes erant, patrem Christum uidebant? sed quia filius erat, non pater, merito et filius, quia imago dei, tunc uidebatur, et pater, quia inuisibilis, mundis corde, ut uideretur, repromittitur et notatur. Haec igitur satis sit etiam aduersus istum haereticum dictasse, pauca de multis. campus enim, et quidem latus ac fusus, aperietur, plenius haereticum istum si agitare uoluerimus; quandoquidem duobus istis locis quibusdam effossis luminibus orbatus, totus sit in doctrinae suae caecitate superatus.

excerpts.author: Novatian
english: The logic of reason and the authority of faith, built on the Lord's own words and writings, urge us to believe in the Holy Spirit as well. The church was promised this Spirit long ago, but he was given at the appointed times. He was promised through the prophet Joel (Joel 2:28-29), but given through Christ. "In the last days," God says, "I will pour out my Spirit upon my servants and handmaids." The Lord himself commanded: "Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive anyone's sins, they are forgiven; if you retain anyone's sins, they are retained" (John 20:22-23). The Lord Christ calls this Spirit the Paraclete, and declares him to be the Spirit of truth. He is not new in the Gospel, nor was he given for the first time then. This same Spirit accused the people through the prophets, and acted as advocate for the nations through the apostles. The people deserved accusation because they had despised the law; those who believe from the nations deserve the Spirit's advocacy because they strive to attain the law of the Gospel. There is a real difference in his operations, because changing times bring different reasons for his action; yet he himself is not different, nor is he another while doing these things. He is one and the same, distributing his offices across times, occasions, and moments.

Finally, the apostle Paul says: "Having the same spirit of faith, as it is written, 'I believed, therefore I spoke,' we also believe, therefore we also speak." The Spirit is one and the same, present in the prophets and the apostles, except that there he was present only for a moment, but here he remains always. There he did not dwell permanently in them; here he stays in them forever. There he was distributed in measure; here he is poured out entirely. There he was given sparingly; here he is lavished generously. He was not given before the Lord's resurrection, but was bestowed through Christ's resurrection (John 14:16-17). Jesus said, "I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Advocate to be with you forever, the Spirit of truth." And: "When the Advocate comes, whom I will send you from the Father, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father." And: "If I do not go away, the Advocate will not come to you; but if I go, I will send him to you" (John 16:7-8). And: "When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all truth." Because the Lord was about to ascend into heaven, he necessarily gave the Paraclete to the disciples, so that he would not leave them as orphans—something unfitting—and abandon them without an Advocate and guardian.

He is the one who strengthened their souls and minds, who distinguished the sacraments of the Gospel, who was the illuminator of divine things within them. By him they were confirmed so that for the Lord's name they feared neither prisons nor chains; indeed, they trampled the powers of the world and its torments, armed and strengthened by him. They carried within themselves the gifts which this same Spirit distributes and directs to Christ's bride, the church, like ornaments. He is the one who establishes prophets in the church, instructs teachers, directs tongues, produces virtues and healings, works miraculous deeds, grants discernment of spirits, provides governance, suggests counsels, and composes and arranges all the other gifts of the charisms. Thus he makes the Lord's church perfect and complete in every way and in all things.

This is the one who, in the form of a dove, came upon the Lord after his baptism and remained, dwelling in Christ alone, full and entire, not diminished by any measure or portion. He was distributed and sent with all his abundance, so that others might receive a share of graces from him. The fountain of the Holy Spirit remains in Christ, so that from him the veins of gifts and works might flow, the Holy Spirit dwelling abundantly in Christ. The prophet Isaiah foretold this: "The Spirit of wisdom and understanding shall rest upon him, the Spirit of counsel and might, the Spirit of knowledge and piety, and he shall fill him with the Spirit of the fear of God" (Isaiah 11:2). The same truth appears in another place, spoken in the Lord's own person: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; because he has anointed me, he has sent me to preach good news to the poor." Similarly David says: "Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions" (Psalm 45:7). About this the apostle Paul writes: "Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him," and: "Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom."

He is the one who works the second birth from water, a seed of divine generation, the consecrator of heavenly birth, the pledge of the promised inheritance, and a kind of guarantee of eternal salvation. He makes us God's temple and his house. He intercedes for us before God with inexpressible groans, fulfilling the office of advocate and presenting the gifts of defense. Given to dwell in our bodies, he is the effecter of sanctity. By doing this in us, he brings our bodies to eternity and to the resurrection of immortality, while accustoming them to mix with heavenly virtue and associate with the divine eternity of the Holy Spirit. For our bodies are trained in him and through him to advance toward immortality, as they learn to discipline themselves moderately according to his decrees.

He is the one who opposes the flesh, because the flesh resists him. He restrains insatiable desires, breaks immoderate lusts, extinguishes illicit ardors, conquers flaming impulses, rejects drunkenness, repels avarice, drives away luxurious revelries, binds charities, constrains affections, repels sects, establishes the rule of truth, conquers heretics, casts out the wicked, and guards the Gospels. About this same Spirit the apostle says: "We have not received the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God." He exults: "I think that I also have the Spirit of God." He says: "The spirits of prophets are subject to prophets." He reports: "The Spirit explicitly says that in later times some will depart from the faith, paying attention to deceitful spirits and teachings of demons." No one who is cautious in this Spirit has ever said, "Anathema to Jesus"; no one has denied Christ the Son of God or repudiated the Creator God; no one has uttered words against the Scriptures; no one has established other sacrilegious decrees; no one has written different laws. Whoever blasphemes against this Spirit will not have forgiveness, not only in this age but also in the age to come.

This Spirit bears witness to Christ in the apostles, shows the constant faith of religion in the martyrs, includes the admirable continence of sealed chastity in the virgins, and guards the incorrupt and uncontaminated laws of the Lord's doctrine in the rest. He destroys heretics, corrects the perverse, accuses the faithless, exposes hypocrites, corrects the wicked, and guards the church incorrupt and inviolable in the sanctity of perpetual virginity and truth (1 Corinthians 12:3).
