excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 29
latin: Sed enim ordo rationis et fidei auctoritas digestis uocibus et litteris domini admonet nos post haec credere etiam in spiritum sanctum, olim ecclesiae repromissum, sed statutis temporum opportunitatibus redditum. est enim per Ioelem prophetam repromissus, sed per Christum redditus. in nouissimis, inquit, diebus effundam de spiritu meo super seruos et ancillas meas. dominus autem: accipite spiritum sanctum; quorum remiseritis peccata, erunt remissa; et quorum retinueritis, erunt retenta. hunc autem spiritum sanctum dominus Christus modo paracletum appellat, modo spiritum ueritatis esse pronuntiat. qui non est in euangelio nouus, sed nec noue datus. nam hic ipse et in prophetis populum accusauit, et in apostolis aduocationem gentibus praestitit. nam illi ut accusarentur merebantur, quia contempserant legem: et qui ex gentibus credunt, ut patrocinio spiritus adiuuentur merentur, quia ad euangelicam peruenire gestiunt legem. differentia sane in illo genera officiorum, quoniam in temporibus differens ratio causarum: nec ex hoc tamen ipse diuersus, qui haec sic gerit, nec alter est, dum sic agit, sed unus atque ipse est, diuidens officia sua per tempora et rerum occasiones atque momenta. denique apostolus Paulus: habentes, inquit, eundem spiritum, sicut scriptum est: credidi, propter quod locutus sum, et nos credimus, ideo loquimur. vnus ergo et idem spiritus, qui in prophetis et apostolis; nisi quoniam ibi ad momentum, hic semper. ceterum ibi, non ut semper in illis inesset, hic, ut in illis semper maneret: et ibi mediocriter distributus, hic totus effusus; ibi parce datus, hic large commodatus; nec tamen ante resurrectionem’ domini exhibitus, sed per resurrectionem Christi contributus. rogabo enim aiebat, patrem, et alium aduocatum dabit uobis, ut uobiscum sit in aeternum, spiritum ueritatis. et: cum uenerit aduocatus ile, quem ego missurus sum uobis a patre meo, spiritum ueritatis, qui de patre meo procedit. et: si non abiero ego, aduocatus ille non ueniet ad uos: si autem ego abiero, remittam illum ad uos. et: cum uenerit spiritus ueritatis, ille uos diriget in omnem ueritatem. et quoniam dominus in caelos esset abiturus, paracletum discipulis necessario dabat, ne illos quodammodo pupillos, quod minime decebat, relinqueret, et sine aduocato et quodam tutore desereret. Hic est enim qui ipsorum animos mentesque firmauit, qui -euangelica sacramenta distinxit, qui in ipsis illuminator rerum diuinarum fuit, quo confirmati pro nomine domini nec carceres nec uincula timuerunt; quin immo ipsas saeculi potestates et tormenta calcauerunt, armati iam scilicet per ipsum atque firmati, habentes in se dona, quae hic idem spiritus ecclesiae Christi sponsae quasi quaedam ornamenta distribuit et dirigit. hic est enim qui prophetas in ecclesia constituit, magistros erudit, linguas dirigit, uirtutes et sanitates facit, opera mirabilia gerit, discretiones spirituum porrigit, gubernationes contribuit, consilia suggerit, quaeque alia sunt charismatum dona componit et digerit; et ideo ecclesiam domini undique et in omnibus perfectam et consummatam facit. Hic est qui in modum columbae, posteaquam dominus baptizatus est, super eum uenit et mansit, habitans in solo Christo plenus et totus, nec in aliqua mensura aut portione mutilatus, sed cum tota sua redundantia cumulate distributus et missus, ut ex illo delibationem quandam gratiarum ceteri consequi possint, totius sancti spiritus in Christo fonte remanente, ut ex illo donorum atque operum uenae ducerentur, spiritu sancto in Christo affluenter habitante. hoc etenim iam prophetans Esaias aiebat: et requiescit, inquit, super eum spiritus sapientiae et intellectus, spiritus consili et uirtutis, spiritus scientiae et pietatis, et implebit eum spiritus timoris dei, hoc idem atque ipsum et alio in loco ex persona ipsius domini: spiritus domini super me; propter quod unxit me, euangelizare pauperibus misit me. similiter Dauid: propterea unxit te, deus, deus tuus oleo laetitiae a consortibus tuis. de hoc apostolus Paulus: guz enim spiritum Christi non habet, hic non est eius; et: vbi spiritus domini, tht libertas. Hic est qui operatur ex aquis secundam natiuitatem, semen quoddam diuini generis, et consecrator caelestis natiuitatis, pignus promissae hereditatis, et quasi chirographum quoddam aeternae salutis; qui nos dei faciat templum, et nos eius efficiat domum. qui interpellat diuinas aures pro nobis gemitibus ineloquacibus, aduocationis implens officia, et defensionis exhibens munera, inhabitator corporibus nostris datus, et sanctitatis effector; qui id agens in nobis ad aeternitatem et ad resurrectionem immortalitatis corpora nostra producat, dum illa in se assuefacit cum caelesti uirtute misceri, et cum spiritus sancti diuina aeternitate sociari. erudiuntur enim in illo et per ipsum corpora nostra ad immortalitatem proficere, dum ad decreta ipsius discunt se moderanter temperare. hic est enim "qui contra carnem desiderat, quia caro contra ipsum repugnat. hic est qui inexplebiles cupiditates coercet, immoderatas libidines frangit, illicitos ardores exstinguit, flagrantes impetus uincit, ebrietates reicit, auaritias repellit, luxuriosas comissationes fugat, caritates nectit, affectiones constringit, sectas repellit, regulam ueritatis expedit, haereticos reuincit, improbos foras exspuit, euangelia custodit. De hoc idem apostolus: on enim spiritum mundi accepimus, sed spiritum qui ex deo est. de hoc exsultat, et dicit: puto autem quia et ego spiritum dei habeo. de hoc dicit: et spiritus prophetarum prophetis subiectus est. de hoc refert: spiritus autem manifeste dicit, quia in nouissimis temporibus recedent quidam a fide, attendentes spiritibus seductoribus, doctrinis daemoniorum, in hypocrisi mendacia loguentium, cautertatam in hoc spiritu positus nemo umquam dicit anathema Iesum: nemo negauit Christum dei filium, aut repudiauit creatorem deum: nemo contra scripturas ulla sua uerba depromit: nemo alia et sacrilega decreta constituit: nemo diuersa iura conscribit. in hunc quisquis blasphemauerit, remissionem non habet, non tantum in isto saeculo, uerum etiam nec in futuro. hic in apostolis Christo testimonium reddit, in martyribus constantem fidem religionis ostendit, in uirginibus admirabilem continentiam signatae castitatis includit, in ceteris incorrupta et incontaminata doctrinae dominicae iura custodit, haereticos destruit, peruersos corrigit, infideles arguit, simulatores ostendit, improbos quoque corrigit, ecclesiam incorruptam et inuiolatam perpetuae uirginitatis et ueritatis sanctitate custodit.

excerpts.author: Novatian
english: We have spoken briefly about the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, keeping our statement concise and avoiding lengthy debate, though we could have expanded far more and argued at greater length because the entire Old and New Testament bears witness that the true faith stands exactly as we hold it. Yet since heretics who fight against the truth habitually drag the sincere tradition and the catholic faith into controversy, scandalized that Christ is also God and is both proclaimed in Scripture and believed by us to be so, we must dispute that Christ is God in a way that neither impedes the truth of Scripture nor our own faith, by which the one God is promised in Scripture and is held and believed by us. Both those who claim that Jesus Christ is the Father himself and those who insist that he is only a man have drawn the roots and causes of their error from this same point: when they observed that Scripture says there is one God, they concluded they could preserve that conviction only by deciding that Christ must be either a mere man or actually God the Father. That is how they habitually gather their slanders, striving to validate their own error. Those who call Jesus Christ the Father argue like this: if there is one God and Christ is God, then Christ is the Father, because there is one God; but if Christ is not the Father, then since Christ is the Son of God, two Gods appear to be introduced contrary to Scripture. Those who contend that Christ is only a man argue from the opposite direction: if the Father is one and the Son another, and the Father is God and Christ is God, then two Gods are introduced, the Father and the Son; and if there is one God, then Christ must be a man, so that the Father may rightly be the one God. In truth, the Lord is crucified between these two thieves just as he was once fixed on the cross, and so he receives the sacrilegious insults of these heretics from both sides. Yet neither the holy Scriptures nor we ourselves supply the causes of their perdition and blindness if they either refuse to see or cannot see the truths plainly set in the midst of the divine letters. We know, read, believe, and hold that there is one God who made heaven and earth alike, because we know no other and never will. 'I am,' he says, 'God, and there is no just and saving one besides me' (Isaiah 44:6). Again: 'I am the first and the last, and there is no God besides me' (Isaiah 44:6). 'Who is like me?' (Isaiah 44:7). 'Who has measured heaven with a span and the earth with a fist? Who has weighed the mountains in a balance and the hills in scales?' (Isaiah 40:12). And Hezekiah prayed: 'that all may know that you alone are God' (Isaiah 37:16, 20). The Lord himself says: 'Why do you ask me about what is good? There is only one who is good' (Matthew 19:17). The apostle Paul also says: 'He alone has immortality and dwells in unapproachable light, whom no one has seen or can see' (1 Timothy 6:16). And elsewhere: 'A mediator implies more than one party, but God is one' (Galatians 3:20). But just as we hold, read, and believe this, so we must not pass over any part of the heavenly Scriptures, for we must not refuse the marks of Christ's divinity placed there, lest by corrupting the authority of Scripture we be found to have corrupted the integrity of the holy faith. Therefore we believe, because it is most faithful, that Jesus Christ the Son of God is our Lord and God: in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God (John 1:1). He was in the beginning with God. And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14). And Thomas cried, 'My Lord and my God!' (John 20:28). And again: 'From whom are the patriarchs, and from whom, according to the flesh, comes the Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever' (Romans 9:5). What then shall we say? Does Scripture propose two Gods? How then does it say there is one God? Or does it not also say that Christ is God? How then was it said to Christ, 'My Lord and my God'? Unless we hold all this with proper reverence and sound reasoning, we will rightly be thought to have given a scandal to heretics, not from any fault in the heavenly Scriptures, which never fail, but from the presumption of human error by which heretics choose to be heretics. First, this must be thrown back at those who presume to manufacture a controversy about two Gods for us. It is written, and they cannot deny it, that there is one Lord (Deuteronomy 6:4; 1 Corinthians 8:6). What then do they think of Christ? That he is the Lord, or that he is not the Lord at all? But they do not doubt that he is the Lord; therefore, if their reasoning is true, there are already two Lords. How then is there one Lord according to Scripture? Christ is called the one Teacher; yet we read that the apostle Paul is also a teacher (1 Timothy 2:7; 2 Timothy 1:11). So there is not one Teacher; by their logic we count two. How then is Christ the one Teacher according to Scripture? One God is called good in Scripture; but in the same Scriptures Christ is also called good (Mark 10:18). So if they reason correctly, there is not one good but two. How then is one good God affirmed according to the faith of Scripture? If they do not think that the fact there is one Lord can be reconciled with Christ being Lord; nor that the fact there is one Teacher can be reconciled with Paul being a teacher; nor that the fact there is one Good can be reconciled with Christ being called good; then by the same reasoning let them understand that the fact there is one God cannot be invalidated by the fact that Christ is declared to be God.

excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 30
latin: Et haec quidem de patre et de filio et de spiritu sancto breuiter sint nobis dicta, et strictim posita, et non longa disputatione porrecta. latius enim potuerunt porrigi, et propensiore disputatione produci, quandoquidem ad testimonium, quod ita se habeat fides uera, totum et uetus et nouum testamentum possit adduci. sed quia obluctantes aduersus ueritatem semper haeretici sincerae traditionis et catholicae fidei controuersiam solent trahere, scandalizati in Christum, quod etiam deus et per scripturas asseratur et a nobis hoc esse credatur, merito a nobis (ut omnis a fide nostra auferri possit haeretica calumnia) de eo quod et deus sit Christus sic est disputandum, ut non impediat scripturae ueritatem, sed nec nostram fidem, qua unus deus et per scripturas promitur, et a nobis tenetur et creditur. tam enim illi qui Iesum Christum ipsum deum patrem dicunt, quam etiam illi qui hominem illum tantummodo esse uoluerunt, erroris sui et peruersitatis origines et causas inde rapuerunt, quia cum animaduerterent scriptum esse quod unus sit deus, non aliter putauerunt istam tenere se posse sententiam, nisi aut hominem tantum Christum, aut certe deum patrem putarent esse credendum. sic enim calumnias suas colligere consueuerunt, ut errorem proprium approbare nitantur. et quidem illi qui Iesum Christum patrem dicunt, ista praetendunt: si unus deus, Christus autem deus, pater est Christus, quia unus deus: si non pater sit Christus, dum et deus filius Christus, duo dii contra scripturas introducti esse uideantur. qui autem hominem tantummodo Christum esse contendunt, ex diuerso sic colligunt: si alter pater, alter est filius, pater autem deus, et Christus deus, non ergo unus deus, sed duo dii introducuntur pariter, pater et filius; ac si unus deus, consequenter homo Christus, ut merito pater sit deus unus. re uera quasi inter duos latrones cruci figitur dominus, quo modo fixus aliquando est: et ita excipit haereticorum istorum ex utroque latere sacrilega conuicia. Sed neque scripturae sanctae, neque nos causas illis perditionis et caecitatis afferimus, si qua in medio diuinarum ro litterarum euidenter posita aut uidere nolunt, aut uidere non possunt. nos enim et scimus et legimus et credimus et tenemus unum esse deum, qui fecit caelum pariter ac terram, quoniam nec alterum nouimus aut nosse (cum nullus sit) aliquando poterimus. ego sum, inquit, deus: e non est praeter me iustus et saluans. et alio in loco: ego primus et nouissimus, et praeter me non est deus. quis sicut ego? et: quis mensus est palmo caelum, et terram pugillo? quis suspendit montes in pondere, et nemora in statera? et Ezechias: ut sciant omnes quia tu es deus solus. ipse praeterea dominus: quid me interrogas de bono? unus deus bonus. apostolus quoque Paulus: guz solus, inquit, habet immortalitatem, et lucem habitat inaccessibilem; quem uidit hominum nemo, nec uidere potest. et alio in loco: mediator autem unius non est; deus autem unus est. sed quo modo hoc tenemus et legimus et credimus, sic scripturarum caelestium nullam partem praeterire debemus: quippe cum etiam illa quae in scripturis sunt posita Christi diuinitatis insignia nullo modo debemus recusare, ne scripturarum auctoritatem corrumpendo integritatem fidei sanctae corrupisse teneamur. et hoc ergo credamus, siquidem fidelissimum, dei filium Iesum Christum dominum et deum nostrum: quoniam zz principio erat uerbum, et uerbum erat apud deum, et deus erat uerbum. hoc erat in principio apud deum. et uerbum caro factum est, et habitauit in nobis. et: dominus meus et deus meus. et: quorum patres, et ex quibus Christus secundum carnem, qui est super omnia deus benedictus in saecula. Quid ergo dicemus? numquid duos deos scriptura proponit? quomodo ergo dicit, quia deus unus est? aut numquid non et Christus deus est? quomodo ergo, dominus meus et deus meus, Christo dictum est? totum igitur hoc nisi cum propria ueneratione et legitima disputatione teneamus, merito scandalum haereticis praebuisse credemur, non utique ex scripturarum caelestium uitio, quae numquam fallunt, sed humani erroris praesumptione, qua haeretici esse uoluerunt. et in primis illud retorquendum in istos qui duorum nobis deorum controuersiam facere praesumunt. scriptum est, quod negare non possunt, quoniam unus est dominus. de Christo ergo quid sentiunt? dominum esse, aut illum omnino non esse? sed dominum illum omnino non dubitant: ergo si uera est illorum ratiocinatio, iam duo sunt domini.. quomodo igitur iam secundum scripturas unus est dominus? et magister unus Christus est dictus; attamen legimus, quod magister sit etiam apostolus Paulus. non ergo iam unus magister: duos enim magistros secundum ista colligimus. quomodo igitur secundum scripturas unus magister Christus? unus in scripturis bonus dictus est deus; sed iisdem in scripturis bonus etiam Christus positus est. non igitur, si recte colligunt, unus bonus, sed etiam duo boni. quomodo igitur secundum scripturarum fidem unus bonus esse refertur? ac si non putant aliqua ratione offici posse ei quod unus dominus est, per illud quod est dominus et Christus; neque ei quod unus est magister, per illud quod est magister et Paulus; aut illi quod unus est bonus, per illud quod bonus sit nuncupatus et Christus; eadem ratione intellegant offici non posse ab illo quod unus est deus, ei quod deus pronuntiatus est et Christus.

excerpts.author: Novatian
english: God the Father is the founder and creator of all things. He alone has no origin, and he is invisible, boundless, immortal, eternal, and the one true God. Nothing can surpass his greatness, his majesty, or his power, nor can anything even be compared to them. When the Father chose, his Son the Word was born. The Son is not a sound made by striking the air or a voice forced from human vocal cords; he is recognized as the very substance of the power that God brought forth. The mysteries of this holy and divine birth were not learned by any apostle, discovered by any prophet, known by any angel, or recognized by any creature. They are known to the Son alone, because he alone knows the Father's secrets.

Since the Son was born from the Father, he is always in the Father. I say "always" to prove that he was born, not that he is innate. The one who exists before all time must be said to have always been in the Father, because time cannot be assigned to one who precedes time. The Father is always the Father; otherwise he would not always be the Father. He also precedes the Son, since the one who has no origin must precede the one who has an origin. At the same time, the Son is lesser, because he knows he exists in the Father and owes his existence to being born. Through the Father, though he has an origin, he stands near in birth, since he is born from the Father who alone has no origin.

When the Father willed it, the Son proceeded from the Father. He who was in the Father, because he was from the Father, was afterwards with the Father, because he proceeded from him. This is the divine substance named the Word, through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made. All things come after him because they exist through him, so he is rightly before all things, yet after the Father, since all things were made through him. The one who proceeded from the Father, from whose will all things were made, is God proceeding from God. He constitutes the second person after the Father as the Son, but he does not take away from the Father the fact that he is the one God.

If the Son had not been born, and were compared to the Father who is innate, equality in both would produce two innates and therefore two Gods. If he had not been generated, and were compared to the one who is not generated, they would be found equal and would constitute two ungenerated Gods, so Christ would have made two Gods. If he were without origin like the Father, he would be a principle of all things like the Father, making two principles and therefore two Gods. If he were not the Son but the Father generating another Son from himself, comparison with the Father would produce two Fathers and therefore two Gods. If he were invisible like the Father, comparison would show two invisibles and therefore two Gods. If he were incomprehensible or shared any other attribute of the Father, he would rightly stir up the controversy about two Gods that they invent.

But as it is, whatever the Son is, he is not from himself, because he is not innate; he is from the Father, because he is generated. Whether as the Word, or as power, or as wisdom, or as light, or as Son, whatever he is, he is not from anywhere else but from the Father, as we said above. He owes his origin to his Father, so he could not create a division in the divine nature into two Gods. By being born, he received his origin from the one who is the one God. Because he is both the only-begotten and the firstborn from the one who has no origin and is therefore the one, the principle, and the head of all things, he proclaimed one God. That one God is not under any principle or beginning; rather, he is the beginning and principle of all things, and the Son confirmed this.

In the end, the Son is the one who does nothing by his own choice, does nothing by his own counsel, and does not come from himself. He obeys all the Father's commands and precepts. So although his birth proves he is the Son, his obedient submission proves he is the minister of the Father's will, from whom he came. By rendering himself obedient to the Father in all things, he shows the one God, the Father, through his obedience, even though he himself is God. He derives his origin from the Father, so he could not make two Gods, because he did not create two origins. He received the principle of his birth before all time from the one who has no origin.

The innate one is the principle for all others, and God the Father alone is that innate one, existing outside all origin. The Son who is born comes from him. By coming from the one who has no origin, the Son proves that the Father is the principle from whom he himself exists. Even though the Son is God, he shows one God, the Father, whom he confirmed to be without origin. Therefore the Son is God, but precisely in being born so that he may be God. He is Lord, but precisely in being born from the Father so that he may be Lord. He is also an angel, but destined from his Father to announce the great counsel of God. His divinity is handed down in such a way that it does not appear to have produced two Gods through any discord or inequality.

The Father subjected all things to him as a Son. While the Son himself is subjected to his Father along with the things subjected to him, he is proven to be the Father's Son. Over everything else he is found to be both Lord and God. Since all things were entrusted to this one who is God, and the Son receives all things subjected to him and refers them back to the Father, he returns the whole authority of divinity to the Father. The one true and eternal God, the Father, is thus shown. From him alone this power of divinity was sent out, handed down and directed to the Son, and through communion it returns again to the Father's substance. The Son is shown to be God, the one to whom divinity was handed down and extended. Yet nonetheless the one God, the Father, is proven, because that majesty and divinity gradually, by a reciprocal movement, return to the Father who gave them, sent back and turned by the Son himself. So rightly God the Father is the God of all, and the principle of his own Son, whom he begot as Lord. The Son is the God of all the rest, because God the Father placed him over all things. Thus Christ Jesus, the mediator of God and humanity, holds all creation subjected to himself by the Father's own power, by which he is God. With all creation subjected to him, he is found in harmony with his Father, God, briefly affirming the one, only, and true God, his Father, remaining in what was also heard.

excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 31
latin: Est ergo deus pater omnium institutor et creator, solus originem nesciens, inuisibilis, immensus, immortalis, aeternus, unus deus; cuius neque magnitudini neque maiestati neque uirtuti quicquam, non dixerim praeferri, sed nec comparari potest. ex quo, quando ipse uoluit, sermo filius natus est: qui non in sono percussi aeris, aut tono coactae de uisceribus uocis accipitur, sed in substantia prolatae a deo uirtutis agnoscitur. cuius sacrae et diuinae natiuitatis arcana nec apostolus didicit, nec prophetes comperit, nec angelus sciuit, nec creatura cognouit; filio soli nota sunt, qui patris secreta cognoulit. Hic ergo, cum sit genitus a patre, semper est in patre. semper autem sic dico, ut non innatum, sed natum probem. sed qui ante omne tempus est, semper in patre fuisse dicendus est: nec enim tempus illi assignari potest, qui ante Semper enim in patre, ne pater non semper sit quia ‘et pater illum etiam praecedit, quod necesse est quoniam antecedat necesse est eum, qui habet originem, ille qui originem nescit; simul ut hic minor sit, dum in illo esse se scit, habens originem, quia nascitur, et per patrem quodam modo, quamuis originem habet, qua nascitur, uicinus in natiuitate, dum ex eo patre, qui originem solus non habet, nascitur. hic ergo quando pater uoluit, processit ex patre: et qui in patre fuit, quia ex patre fuit, cum patre postmodum fuit, quia ex patre processit, substantia scilicet illa diuina, cuius nomen est uerbum, per quod facta sunt omnia, et sine quo factum est nihil. omnia enim post ipsum sunt, quia per ipsum sunt, et merito ipse est ante omnia, sed post patrem, quando per illum facta sunt omnia. qui processit ex eo, ex cuius uoluntate facta sunt omnia, deus utique procedens ex deo, secundam personam efficiens post patrem, qua filius, sed non eripiens illud patri, quod unus est deus. Si enim natus non fuisset, innatus comparatus cum eo qui esset innatus, aequatione in utroque ostensa, duos faceret innatos, et ideo duos faceret deos. si non genitus esset, collatus cum eo qui genitus non esset, et aequales inuenti, duos deos merito reddidissent non geniti; atque ideo duos Christus reddidisset deos. si sine origine esset ut pater, inuentus et ipse principium omnium ut pater, duo faciens principia, duos ostendisset nobis consequenter et deos. aut si et ipse filius non esset, sed pater generans de se alterum filium, merito collatus cum patre et tantus denotatus, duos patres effecisset, et ideo duos approbasset etiam deos. si inuisibilis fuisset, cum inuisibili collatus, par expressus, duos inuisibiles ostendisset, et ideo duos comprobasset et deos. si incomprehensibilis, si et cetera quaecumque sunt patris, merito, dicimus, duorum deorum quam isti confingunt controuersiam suscitasset. nunc autem quicquid est, non ex se est, quia nec innatus est, sed ex patre est, quia genitus est. siue dum uerbum est, siue dum uirtus est, siue dum sapientia est, siue dum lux est, siue dum filius est, et quicquid horum est, dum non aliunde est, quam, sicut diximus iam superius, ex patre, patri suo originem suam debens, discordiam diuinitatis de numero duorum deorum facere non potuit, qui ex illo, qui est unus deus, originem nascendo contraxit. quo genere, dum et unigenitus est et primogenitus ex illo est qui, quia originem non habet, unus est omnium rerum et principium et caput, idcirco unum deum asseruit, quem non sub ullo principio aut initio, sed initium potius et principium rerum omnium comprobauit. Idem est denique quod nihil ex arbitrio suo gerit, nec ex consilio suo facit, nec a se uenit, sed imperiis paternis omnibus et praeceptis oboedit: ut quamuis probet illum natiuitas filium, tamen morigera oboedientia asserat illum paternae uoluntatis, ex quo est, ministrum. ita dum se patri in omnibus obtemperantem reddit, quamuis sit et deus, unum tamen deum patrem de oboedientia sua ostendit, ex quo et originem traxit. Et ideo duos deos facere non potuit, quia nec duas origines fecit, qui ex eo, qui originem non habet, principium natiuitatis ante omne tempus accepit. nam cum id sit principium ceteris quod innatum est (quod deus solus pater est, qui extra originem est, ex quo hic est qui natus est), dum qui ex illo nascitur merito ex eo uenit, qui originem non habet, principium probans illud esse, ex quo ipse est, etiamsi deus est qui natus est, unum tamen deum ostendit, quem hic qui natus est esse sine origine comprobauit. Est ergo deus, sed in hoc ipsum genitus, ut esset deus. est et dominus, sed in hoc ipsum natus ex patre, ut esset dominus. est et angelus, sed ad annuntiandum magnum dei consilium €x patre suo angelus destinatus. cuius sic diuinitas traditur, ut non aut dissonantia aut inaequalitate diuinitatis duos deos reddidisse uideatur. subiectis enim ei quasi filio omnibus rebus a patre, dum ipse cum his, quae illi subiecta sunt, patri suo subicitur, patris quidem sui filius probatur; ceterorum autem et dominus et deus esse reperitur. ex quo dum huic qui est deus omnia substrata traduntur, et cuncta sibi subiecta filius accepta refert patri, totam diuinitatis auctoritatem rursus patri remittit. unus deus ostenditur uerus et aeternus pater, a quo solo haec uis diuinitatis emissa, etiam in filium tradita et directa, rursum substantiae per communionem ad patrem reuoluitur. deus quidem ostenditur filius, cui diuinitas tradita et porrecta conspicitur; et tamen nihilominus unus deus pater probatur, dum gradatim reciproco meatu illa maiestas atque diuinitas ad patrem, qui dederat eam, rursum ab illo ipso filio missa reuertitur et retorquetur; ut merito deus pater omnium deus sit, et principium ipsius quoque filii sui, quem dominum genuit: filius autem ceterorum omnium deus sit, quoniam omnibus illum deus pater praeposuit, quem genuit. ita mediator dei et hominum Christus Iesus, omnis creaturae subiectam sibi habens a patre proprio potestatem, qua deus est, cum tota creatura subdita sibi, concors patri suo deo inuentus, unum et solum et uerum deum patrem suum, manente in illo quod etiam auditus est, breuiter approbauit.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Once God's goodness looked out for humanity by knowing it, the goodness added a further claim to its own proclamation: it had first prepared a dwelling for human beings, then a very great one, and finally an even greater one. The purpose was that a person might first exercise and grow in a great dwelling as if it were a smaller one, and so advance from God's goodness — that is, the great — to the highest expression of that goodness — that is, the greater dwelling. The goodness also appointed the best possible minister for its good work: its own Word. 'My heart has uttered the best word,' it says. Let Marcion recognize from this the first, best fruit — certainly of the best tree. The most ignorant peasant grafts a bad shoot onto a good one, but the shoot of blasphemy will not prevail; it will wither along with its craftsman, and in that way the nature of the good tree will prove itself. Look at the sum of things and see what kind of fruit the Word has produced: God said, 'Let it be,' and it came to be, and God saw that it was good — not as though he did not know it was good unless he saw it, but because it was good he saw it, honoring and sealing and bestowing the goodness of the works with the dignity of his gaze (Genesis 1:3; Genesis 1:31). Thus he also blessed what he had benefited, so that all of God might be commended to you as good in both speaking and doing. The Word did not yet know how to speak evil, because it did not know how to do evil. We will see the causes that demanded this from God as well. Meanwhile the world consists entirely of good things, sufficiently demonstrating how much good was being prepared for the one for whom all this was being prepared. Who, finally, is worthy to inhabit God's works except God's own image and likeness? That image, too, goodness — and indeed the more operative goodness — brought about, not with an imperial decree but with a familiar hand, preceded by a coaxing word: 'Let us make humanity in our image and likeness.' Goodness spoke; goodness formed clay into so great a substance of flesh, constructed from a single material with so many qualities; goodness breathed into the soul — not a dead one, but a living one; goodness placed humanity in charge of all things to be enjoyed and ruled, and also to be named; goodness added further delights so that, although possessing the whole world, humanity might linger in more pleasant places, transferred into paradise — already then from the world into the church; the same goodness also looked out for help, lest anything not good remain. 'It is not good for the human to be alone,' it says (Genesis 2:18). God knew that sex would be profitable for the man, and thereafter for the church. But the law that you accuse, that you twist into controversies — goodness imposed that, too, consulting for the human's sake, so that he might cling to God, lest he seem not so much free as cast off, equal to his servants, the other animals, released by God and freed from disgust. Rather, goodness intended that the human alone might glory, because he alone was worthy to receive the law from God, and that as a rational creature capable of intellect and knowledge, he might also be contained by rational freedom, subject to the one who had subjected all things to him. Goodness equally prescribed the plan for observing this law: 'On the day you eat of it, you will die by death' (Genesis 2:17). For it most kindly demonstrated the outcome of transgression, lest ignorance of the danger assist negligence in obedience. Furthermore, if the reason for imposing the law came first, the observance of it followed as well, so that punishment might be ascribed to transgression — which, however, the one who had foretold it beforehand did not want to happen. Therefore recognize the goodness of our God, at least up to this point, from the good works, from the good blessings, from the indulgences, from the providences, from the good and kind laws and warnings.

excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 4. The Next Stage Occurs in the Creation of Man by the Eternal Word. Spiritual as Well as Physical Gifts to Man. The Blessings of Man's Free-Will.
latin: Igitur cum cognoscendo deo hominem prospexisset bonitas dei ipsius, etiam hoc praeconio suo addidit, quod prius domicilium homini commentata est aliquam [postmodum] molem maximam, postmodum et maiorem, ut in magna tamquam in minore proluderet atque proficeret et ita de bono dei, id est de magno, ad optimum quoque eius, id est ad maius habitaculum, promoueretur. adhibet operi bono optimum etiam ministrum, sermonem suum: eructauit, inquit, cor meum sermonem optimum. agnoscat hinc primum fructum optimum, utique optimae arboris, Marcion. imperitissimus rusticus quidem malam in bonam inseruit. sed non ualebit blasphemiae surculus; arescet cum suo artifice et ita se bonae arboris natura testabitur. aspice ad summam, qualia sermo fructificauerit: et dixit deus: fiat, et factum est, et uidit deus quia bonum, non quasi nesciens bonum nisi uideret, sed quia bonum, ideo uidens, honorans et consignans et dispungens bonitatem operum dignatione conspectus. sic et benedicebat quae benefaciebat, ut tibi totus deus commendaretur, bonus et dicere et facere. male dicere adhuc sermo non norat, quia nec malefacere. uidebimus causas, quae hoc quoque a deo exegerunt. interim mundus ex bonis omnibus constitit, satis praemonstrans, quantum boni pararetur illi, cui praeparabatur hoc totum. quis denique dignus incolere dei opera quam ipsius imago et similitudo? eam quoque bonitas et quidem operantior operata est, non imperiali uerbo, sed familiari manu, etiam uerbo blandiente praemisso: faciamus hominem ad imaginem et similitudinem nostram. bonitas dixit; bonitas finxit de limo in tantam substantiam carnis, ex una materia tot qualitatibus exstructam; bonitas inflauit in animam, non mortuam, sed uiuam; bonitas praefecit uniuersis fruendis atque regnandis, etiam cognomiuandis; bonitas amplius delicias adiecit homini, ut, quamquam totius orbis . possidens, in amoenioribus moraretur, translatus in paradisum — iam tunc de mundo in ecclesiam —; eadem bonitas et adiutorium prospexit, ne quid non boni. non est enim, inquit, bonum solum esse hominem. sciebat illi sexum Mariae et deinceps ecclesiae profuturum. sed et quam arguis legem, quam in controuersias torques, bonitas irrogauit, consulens homini, quo deo adhaereret, ne non tam liber quam abiectus uideretur, aequandus famulis suis, ceteris animalibus, solutis a deo et ex fastidio liberis, sed ut solus homo gloriaretur, quod solus dignus fuisset, qui legem a deo sumeret, utque animal rationale, intellectus et scientiae capax, ipsa quoque libertate rationali contineretur, ei subiectus, qui subiecerat illi omnia. cuius legis obseruandae consilium bonitas pariter adscripsit: qua die autem ederitis, morte moriemini. benignissime enim demonstrauit exitum transgressionis, ne ignorantia periculi neglegentiam iuuaret obsequii. porro si legis imponendae ratio praecessit, sequebatur etiam obseruandae, ut poena transgressioni adscriberetur, quam tamen euenire noluit qui ante praedixit. I agnosce igitur bonitatem dei nostri interim uel bucusque ex operibus bonis, ex benedictionibus bonis, ex indulgentiis, ex prouidentiis, ex legibus et praemonitionibus bonis et benignis.\'

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: So let's turn to the questions, all of you—you dogs the apostle kicks out for barking against the God of truth. These are the bones of the arguments you gnaw on: If God is good, knows the future, and has the power to stop evil, why did He let man—His image and likeness, indeed His very substance through the soul’s judgment—slip from obedience to the law into death, tricked by the devil? If He is good, He would not want such a thing to happen; if He foresees, He would not be ignorant of it coming; if He is able, He could drive it away. Under those three conditions of divine majesty, the disaster could not have happened. But it did happen. Therefore, the opposite conclusion stands: God cannot be believed to be good, or prescient, or powerful. To the exact degree that such a thing would not have happened if God were truly good, prescient, and able, to that degree it happened because He is not such a God. So first we must defend these attributes in the Creator—goodness, prescience, and power—since they are the ones called into doubt. I will not linger here; Christ’s own definition leads the way, and the proof starts from His works. The Creator’s works testify to both His goodness—by which He is good, as we have shown—and His power, by which He is so great, and indeed created from nothing. Even if He used some pre-existing matter, as some claim, it still counts as creation from nothing, because those things were not what they are now. Ultimately, He is so great because He is good, and so powerful because He is God—all things are His, which is why He is called omnipotent. What about prescience? It has as many witnesses as there are prophets. What title to prescience could be greater than the Author of all things, who foreknows everything by disposing it and disposes everything by foreknowing it? He certainly foreknew that very transgression; otherwise He would not have entrusted its warning under the threat of death. So if these faculties existed in God—faculties before which no evil could or should have happened to man—and yet it happened anyway, let us examine man’s condition. Perhaps the disaster came through man rather than through God, since it could not come through God. I find that God instituted man as free, possessing his own judgment and his own power. I see no image and likeness of God in him more clearly than the form of that status. He was not expressed toward the uniform God by face and bodily lines, which vary so widely across the human race, but in that substance he drew from God Himself—the soul—he was sealed to the form of God, guaranteeing freedom of judgment and power. The law God then gave confirmed this status. Law would not be given to someone who did not have obedience to the law in his power, nor would the threat of death be attached to transgression if contempt for the law were not also entrusted to man’s freedom of judgment. You find the same pattern in the Creator’s later laws. He sets good and evil, life and death, before man. Nor is the whole order of discipline arranged through precepts by the calling, threatening, and exhorting God in any other way than to address a free and voluntary human being capable of both obedience and contempt.

excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 5. Marcion's Cavils Considered. His Objection Refuted, I.e., Man's Fall Showed Failure in God. The Perfection of Man's Being Lay in His Liberty, Which God Purposely Bestowed on Him. The Fall Imputable to Man's Own Choice.
latin: Iam hinc ad quaestiones t omnes, o canes, quos foras apostolus expellit, latrantes in deum ueritatis. haec sunt argumentationum ossa, quae obroditis: (si deus bonus et praescius futuri et auertendi mali potens, cur hominem, et quidem imaginem et similitudinem suam, immo et substantiam suam, per animae scilicet censum, passus est labi de, obsequio legis in mortem, circumuentum a diabolo? si enim et bonus, qui euenire tale quid nollet, et praescius, qui euenturum non ignoraret, et potens, qui depellere ualeret, nullo modo euenisset quod sub his tribus condicionibus diuinae maiestatis euenire non posset. quod si euenit, absolutum est e contrario deum neque bonum credendum neque praescium neque potentem; siquidem in quantum nihil tale euenisset, si talis deus, id est bonus et praescius et potens, in tantum ideo euenit, quia non talis deus), ad haec prius est istas species in creatore defendere, quae in dubium uocantur, bonitatem dico et praescientiam et potentiam. nec immorabor huic articulo, praeeunte definitione etiam ipsius Christi ex operibus ineundae probationis. opera creatoris utrumque testantur, et bonitatem eius, qua bona, sicut ostendimus, et potentiam, qua tanta, et quidem ex nihilo. nam et si ex aliqua materia, ut quidam uolunt, hoc ipso tamen ex nihilo; dum non id fuerunt, quod sunt. postremo uel sic magna, dum bona, uel sic deus potens, dum omnia ipsius, unde et omnipotens. de praescientia uero quid dicam, quae tantos habet testes, quantos fecit prophetas? quamquam quis praescientiae titulus in omnium auctore. qui uniuersa utique (et) disponendo praesciit et praesciendo disposuit? certe ipsam transgressionem, quam nisi praescisset. nec cautionem eius delegasset sub metu mortis. igitur si et fuerunt in deo istae facultates, prae quibus nihil mali euenire homini aut potuisset aut debuisset, et nihilominus euenit. uideamus et hominis condicionem, ne per illam potius euenerit quod per deum euenire non potuit. liberum et sui arbitrii et suae potestatis inuenio hominem a deo institutum, nullam magis imaginem et similitudinem dei in illo animaduertens quam eiusmodi status formam. neque enim facie et corporalibus lineis, tam uariis in genere humano, ad uniformem deum expressus est, sed in ea substantia, quam ab ipso deo traxit, id est anima, ad formam dei, spondentis et arbitrii sui libertatem et potestatem, signatus est. hunc statum eius confirmauit etiam ipsa lex tunc a deo posita. non enim poneretur lex ei, qui non haberet obsequium debitum legi in sua potestate, nec rursus comminatio mortis transgressioni adscriberetur, si non et contemptus legis in arbitrii libertatem homini deputaretur. sic et in posteris legibus creatoris inuenias. proponentis ante hominem bonum et malum, uitam et mortem. sed nec alias totum ordinem disciplinae per praecepta dispositum a uocante deo, et minante et hortante, nisi et ad obsequium et ad contemptum libero et uoluntario homini.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: The logic runs like this: evil erupted later, and only then did God's goodness begin to engage the adversary. That same justice of God also found another task — now directing goodness in opposition to the adversary — so that, once its freedom is set aside (the freedom by which God is good of his own accord, dispensing favor according to each person's merits: offering it to the worthy, denying it to the unworthy, withdrawing it from the ungrateful, and thereby exacting vengeance on all rivals), the whole work of justice becomes the management of goodness. What it condemns by judging, what it punishes by condemning, what you call raging — all of it profits the good, not the evil. Finally, the fear of judgment drives toward the good, not the evil. For goodness did not suffice to commend itself; now it labors under the adversary. Even if it is commendable in itself, it is not also preservable, because it is now conquerable by the adversary — unless some power of fear were present to compel even the unwilling to seek and guard the good. With so many allurements of evil conquering the good, who would pursue what he could despise with impunity? Who would guard what he could lose without danger? The road of evil is broad and far more traveled: would not everyone stumble onto it if nothing were feared on it? We tremble at the Creator's terrible threats, and we are hardly torn away from evil. What if he threatened nothing? Would you call this justice evil because it does not favor evil? Would you deny this is good because it looks out for the good? What kind of god do you want? What kind would suit evildoers? Under whom would sins rejoice? At whom would the devil mock? Would you judge that god good who could make man more evil by the security of sin? Who is the author of good, if not also the exactor? Therefore who is a stranger to evil, if not also an enemy? Who is an enemy, if not also a conqueror? Who is a conqueror, if not also a punisher? Thus the whole God is good, so long as he is entirely for the good. Thus finally he is all-powerful, because he is powerful both to help and to harm. It is less to be only beneficial, because he can do nothing else but benefit. With what confidence could I hope for good from such a one, if he can only do that? How could I pursue the reward of innocence, if I do not also fear the punishment of guilt? I must distrust, lest the one who lacked the power for either part fail to reward either. So far justice is also the fullness of divinity itself, exhibiting God as perfect — both Father and Lord: Father by clemency, Lord by discipline; Father with gentle power, Lord with severity; Father to be loved piously, Lord to be feared necessarily — to be loved because he prefers mercy to sacrifice, and to be feared because he does not want sin; to be loved because he prefers the sinner's repentance to death, and to be feared because he does not want his sinners who are no longer repenting. Therefore the law defines both: you shall love God, and you shall fear God. He set one thing before the supplicant, another before the transgressor.

excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 13. Further Description of the Divine Justice; Since the Fall of Man It Has Regulated the Divine Goodness. God's Claims on Our Love and Our Fear Reconciled.
latin: At enim ut malum postea erupit atque inde iam coepit bonitas dei cum aduersario agere, aliud quoque negotium eadem illa iustitia dei nacta est, iam secundum aduersationem dirigendae bonitatis, ut, seposita libertate eius, qua et ultro deus bonus, pro meritis cuiusque pensetur, dignis offeratur, indignis denegetur, ingratis auferatur, proinde omnibus aemulis uindicetur. ita omne hoc iustitiae opus procuratio bonitatis est: quod iudicando damnat, quod damnando punit, quod, ut dicitis. saeuit, utique bono, non malo proficit. denique timor iudicii ad bonum, non ad malum confert. non enim sufficiebat bonum per semetipsum commendari. iam sub aduersario laborans. nam et si commendabile per semetipsum, non tamen et conseruabile, quia expugnabile iam per aduersarium, nisi uis aliqua praeesset timendi, quae bonum etiam nolentes adpetere et custodire compelleret. ceterum tot inlecebris mali expugnantibus bonum quis illud appeteret, quod impune contemneret? quis custodiret quod sine periculo amitteret? legis mali uiam latam et multo frequentiorem: nonne omnes illa laberentur. si nihil in illa timeretur? horremus terribiles minas creatoris, et uix a malo auellimur. quid, si nihil minaretur? hanc iustitiam malum dices, quae malo non fauet? hanc bonum negabis, quae bono prospicit? qualem oportet deum uelles? qualem malis expediret? sub quo delicta gauderent? cui dia- , bolus inluderet? illum bonum iudicares deum, qui hominem posset magis malum facere securitate delicti? quis boni auctor, nisi qui et exactor? proinde quis mali extraneus, nisi qui et inimicus? quis inimicus, nisi qui et expugnator? quis expugnator, nisi qui et punitor? sic totus deus bonus est, dum pro bono omnia est. sic denique omnipotens, quia et iuuandi et laedendi potens. minus est tantummodo prodesse, quia non aliud quid possit quam prodesse. de eiusmodi qua fiducia bonum sperem, si hoc solum potest? quomodo innocentiae mercedem secter, si non et nocentiae spectem? diffidam necesse est, ne nec alteram partem remuneret qui utramque non ualuit. usque adeo iustitia etiam plenitudo est diuinitatis ipsius, exhibens deum perfectum, et patrem et dominum, patrem clementia dominum disciplina, patrem potestate blanda dominum seuera, patrem diligendum pie dominum timendum necessarie, diligendum, quia malit misericordiam quam sacrificium, et timendum. quia nolit peccatum, diligendum, quia malit paenitentiam peccatoris quam mortem, et timendum, quia nolit peccatores sui iam non paenitentes. ideo lex utrumque definit : diliges deum et: timebis deum. aliud obsecutori proposuit, aliud exorbitatori.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Dismiss these facts and you still see the whole economy of God the Judge—or, to put it more worthily, the defender of that catholic and supreme goodness which the Marcionites refuse to recognize in the same God who rains on the good and the bad and makes his sun rise on the just and the unjust (Matthew 5:45), a feat no other god can match. Even if Marcion dared to cut this saying of Christ out of the Creator's Gospel, the world itself is written large and read by every conscience. And the Creator's patience will stand as evidence against Marcion at the judgment—the patience that waits for a sinner's repentance rather than death and prefers mercy to sacrifice, turning aside the doom ordained for Nineveh, granting Hezekiah a reprieve through his tears, and restoring the Babylonian tyrant's kingdom after he repented. I mean the mercy that spared Saul's doomed son out of devotion to the people, that pardoned David when he confessed his guilt over Uriah's house, that restored Israel again and again whenever it judged and whenever it rebuked. So do not merely stare at the Judge to convert and to the highest examples: mark when he avenges, weigh when he indulges; set leniency against severity. Bring both together in the Creator and you will find in him the very thing that makes you believe in another god. Come, then, to an inspection of his teachings, disciplines, precepts, and counsels. You may object that these are also fixed by human laws. But Moses and God stand before every Lycurgus and Solon; no later generation fails to receive from the origins. Yet my Creator did not learn from your god to command: You shall not kill, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal, you shall not bear false witness, you shall not covet what belongs to another, honor your father and mother, and love your neighbor as yourself. To these chief counsels of innocence and chastity, justice and piety, are added the prescriptions of humanity: every seventh year servitudes are released into freedom; at the same time the land is spared, yielding its place to the needy; even the ox treading grain is unmuzzled for the fruit of its present labor—so that humanity, premeditated in the treatment of beasts, might more easily instruct the refreshment of human beings.

excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 17. Trace God's Government in History and in His Precepts, and You Will Find It Full of His Goodness.
latin: Haec ita dispecta totum ordinem dei iudicis operarium et, ut dignius dixerim, protectorem catholicae et summae illius bonitatis ostendunt, quam (ut) semotam a iudiciariis sensibus et in suo statu puram nolunt Marcionitae in eodem deo agnoscere, pluente super bonos et malos et solem suum oriri faciente super iustos et iniustos, quod alius deus omnino non praestat. nam etsi hoc quoque testimonium Christi in creatorem Marcion. de euangelio eradere ausus est, sed ipse mundus inscriptus est et omni a conscientia legitur. et erit haec ipsa patientia creatoris in iudicium Marcionis, illa patientia, quae expectat paenitentiam potius peccatoris quam mortem et mauult misericordiam quam sacrificium, auertens destinatum iam exitium Niniuitis et largiens spatium uitae Ezechiae lacrimis et restituens statum regni Babylonis tyranno paenitentia functo: illam dico misericordiam, quae et filium Saulis moriturum ex deuotione populo concessit et Dauid delicta in domum Uriae confessum uenia liberauit et ipsum Israhel totiens restituit quotiens iudicauit, totiens refouit quotiens et increpuit. non solum igitur iudicem aspiciens conuertere et ad optimi exempla: notans cum ulciscitur considera cum indulget; repende austeritati lenitatem. cum utrumque conueneris in creatore, inuenies in eo et illud, propter quod alterum deum credis. ueni denique ad inspectationem doctrinarum disciplinarum praeceptorum consiliorumque eius. dices forsitan haec etiam humanis legibus determinari. sed ante Lycurgos et Solonas omnes Moyses et deus. nulla posteritas non a primordiis accipit. tamen non a tuo deo didicit creator meus praescribere : non occides, non adulterabis, non furaberis, non falsum testimonium dices, alienum non concupisces, honora patrem et matrem, et diliges proximum tuum ut temetipsum. ad haec innocentiae et pudicitiae, iustitiae et pietatis principalia consulta accedunt etiam humanitatis praescripta, cum septimo quoque anno seruitia libertate soluuntur, cum eodem tempore agro parcitur egenis cedendo locum, (cum) boui etiam terenti uincula oris remittuntur ad fructum praesentis laboris, quo facilius in pecudibus praemeditata humanitas in hominum refrigeria erudiretur.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Therefore, in prohibiting the making of any likeness of things in heaven, on earth, or in the waters, He also reveals the reasons — those very substances that restrain idolatry — for He immediately adds: 'You shall not worship them nor serve them.' (Numbers 21:8-9) The bronze serpent, which the Lord later commanded Moses to make, did not fall under the heading of idolatry; it was a remedy for those being plagued by serpents. I pass over the figure of that remedy. Likewise, the golden Cherubim and Seraphim fashioned on the Ark were simply ornamentation, adapted to the Mercy Seat; they had causes far removed from the condition of idolatry on account of which a likeness is forbidden. They do not appear to violate the law against prohibited likenesses, because they were not caught in that state of likeness for which the likeness is prohibited.

We have spoken of the rational institution of sacrifices, which called people away from idols to perform duties for God. Had He rejected those duties again, saying, 'What is the multitude of your sacrifices to Me?' (Isaiah 1:11), He would have shown He never properly exacted them for Himself. For He says, 'I do not drink the blood of bulls,' since elsewhere He says, 'The eternal God neither hungers nor thirsts.' True, He accepted Abel's offerings and smelled Noah's burnt offerings with pleasure, but what was that pleasure — the flesh of sheep, the odor of burning victims? No: the simple, God-fearing heart of the offerers, which came from God, and the sweet fragrance of their intent, were reckoned as grace to God — not what was done as if He needed it, but the purpose for which it was done, namely, the honor of God. If a client offers a trifling gift to a rich man or king who desires nothing, does the gift's quantity and quality insult the recipient, or does the title of duty delight him? But if a client offers gifts, whether voluntarily or by the king's own decree, and observes the king's solemnities — yet without faith, without a pure heart, without full obedience in other respects — is it not inevitable that the king or rich man will cry out: 'What is the multitude of your gifts to me? I am full of your solemnities, your feast days, and your Sabbaths'? (Isaiah 1:13-14) They celebrated these according to their own desire, not the religion of God, making them their own, not God's. Therefore He demonstrated a conditional and rational rejection of the very rites He had prescribed to be administered.

excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 22. The Brazen Serpent and the Golden Cherubim Were Not Violations of the Second Commandment. Their Meaning.
latin: Proinde et similitudinem uetans fieri omnium. quae in caelo et in terra et in aquis. ostendit et causas. [idolatriae scilicet substantiam cohibentes.] subicit enim: non adorabitis ea neque seruietis illis. serpentis autem aenei effigies postea praecepta Moysi a domino non ad idolatriae titulum pertinebat, sed ad remediandos eos, qui a serpentibus infestabantur. et taceo de figura remedii. sic et Cherubin et Seraphin aurea in arcae figuratum exemplum; certe simplex ornamentum. adcommodata suggestui, longe diuersas habendo causas ab idolatriae condicione, ob quam\' similitudo prohibetur, non uidentur similitudinum prohibitarum legi refragari, non in eo similitudinis statu deprehensa, ob quem similitudo prohibetur. diximus de sacrificiorum rationali institutione, auocante scilicet ab idolis ad deum officia ea, quae si rursus eiecerat dicens: quo mihi multitudinem sacrificiorum uestrorum? hoc ipsum uoluit intellegi, quod non sibi ea proprie exegisset. non enim bibam, inquit, sanguinem taurorum, quia et alibi ait: deus aeternus non esuriet nec sitiet. nam etsi ad oblationes Abelis aduertit et holocausta Noe odoratus est libenter, quae iocunditas siue uiscerum berbicinorum siue nidoris ardentium uictimarum? sed animus simplex et deum metuens offerentium ea, quae a deo habebant et pabuli et suauis olentiae, gratiae apud deum deputabatur, non. quae fiebant exigentem, sed illud, propter quod fiebant, ob honorem dei scilicet. si cliens diuiti aut regi nihil desideranti tamen aliquid uilissimi munusculi obtulerit, quantitas et qualitas muneris infuscabit diuitem et regem, an delectabit titulus officii? at si cliens ei munera (uel) ultro uel etiam indicta ordine suo offerat et sollemnia regis obseruet, non ex fide tamen nec corde puro nec pleno circa cetera quoque obsequio, nonne consequens, ut rex ille uel diues exclamet: quo mihi multitudinem munerum tuorum? *** plenus sum et sollemnitates et dies festos et uestra sabbata dicendo, quae secundum libidinem suam, non secundum religionem dei celebrando sua iam, non dei fecerant. condicionalem idcirco et rationalem demonstrauit recusationem eorum. % quae administranda praescripserat.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: I will now settle the rest briefly. You gather up whatever petty, weak, and unworthy details you can find to tear down the Creator, but a simple, certain reason answers them all: God could not enter human life unless He took on human senses and affections, through which He could temper the force of His majesty — force utterly intolerable to human mediocrity — with humility. Such things are unworthy of God in themselves, yet necessary for man; that makes them worthy of God after all, because nothing is more worthy of God than human salvation. I would argue this at length if I were debating pagans — though the dispute with heretics is not much different — but since you already believe that God has walked among men in the form and full order of the human condition, your own faith should convince you that God conformed Himself to humanity. For if God, the more exalted One, has cast down the height of His majesty with such humility that He submitted even to death, and to death on a cross, why do you not think that some smallnesses were fitting for our God as well — smallnesses far more tolerable than the Jewish insults, crosses, and graves? Are these the smallnesses that should now prejudice Christ, subjected to human passions, into being the very God whose human weaknesses you reproach? We also confess that Christ always acted in the name of God the Father; He was conversing with the patriarchs and prophets from the beginning. He is the Son of the Creator, the Word of God, whom the Father brought forth from Himself and made His Son, placing Him over all His disposition and will, diminishing Him slightly below the angels, as it is written (Psalm 8:5; Hebrews 2:7). By this diminution the Father also appointed Him to the very things you condemn as merely human, learning already from the beginning what He would be in the end. He is the One who descended, the One who asked, the One who demanded, the One who swore. Moreover, because the Father has never been seen by anyone, the common Gospel itself testifies, with Christ saying: "No one has known the Father except the Son" (John 1:18; Matthew 11:27). For He had also declared in the Old Testament: "No one will see God and live" (Exodus 33:20), defining the invisible Father, in whose authority and name He Himself was the God who was seen as the Son of God. Among us, too, Christ is accepted in the person of Christ, because He is ours in that very way. Therefore, whatever you demand as worthy of God will be found in the invisible, unapproachable, peaceful Father — the philosophers' God, so to speak — but whatever you condemn as unworthy will be attributed to the Son, the One seen and heard and interacted with, the Father's arbiter and minister, blending in Himself man and God: God in virtues, man in smallnesses, so that He confers on man exactly as much as He detracts from God. Finally, the whole shame of my God, in your eyes, is the sacrament of human salvation. God conversed with men so that man might learn to act divinely. God acted on equal terms with man so that man might be able to act on equal terms with God. God was found small so that man might become great. You who disdain such a God do not know whether you believe in a crucified God by faith. How great, then, is your perversity toward both orders of the Creator? You despise Him as a judge, and you reproach the severity of the judge — severity congruent with the merits of the cases — as savagery; you demand a most excellent God. And you turn the leniency of His benignity — leniency congruent with the capacity of human mediocrity — into something worthless, so that you may depreciate the smallness. Neither the great nor the moderate pleases you, neither the judge nor the friend. What if the same things are now detected in your own God? We have already shown that He is a judge in His own book, and that a judge is necessarily severe, and that the severe one is certainly savage, if indeed He is savage.

latin: Iam nunc, ut et cetera compendio absoluam, quaecumque adhuc ut pusilla et infirma et indigna colligitis ad destructionem creatoris, simplici et certa ratione proponam: deum non potuisse humanos congressus inire, nisi humanos et sensus et adfectus suscepisset, per quos uim maiestatis suae, intolerabilem utique humanae mediocritati, humilitate temperaret. I sibi quidem indigna, homini autem necessaria, et ita iam deo digna, quia nihil tam dignum deo quam salus hominis. de isto pluribus retractarem, si cum ethnicis agerem, — quamquam et cum haereticis non multo diuersa congressio — sed quatenus et ipsi deum in figura et in reliquo ordine humanae condicionis deuersatum iam credidistis, non exigetis utique diutius persuaderi deum conformasse semetipsum humanitati, sed de uestra fide reuincimini. si enim deus, et quidem sublimior, tanta humilitate fastigium maiestatis suae strauit, ut etiam morti subiceretur, et morti crucis, cur non putetis nostro quoque deo aliquas pusillitates congruisse, tolerabiliores tamen ludaicis contumeliis et patibulis et sepulcris? an hae sunt pusillitates, quae iam hinc praeiudicare debebunt Christum humanis passionibus obiectum eius dei esse, cui humanitates exprobrantur a uobis? nam et profitemur Christum semper egisse in dei patris nomine, ipsum ab initio conuersatum, ipsum congressum cum patriarchis et prophetis, filium creatoris, sermonem eius, quem ex semetipso proferendo filium fecit et exinde omni dispositioni suae uoluntatique praefecit, diminuens illum modico citra angelos, sicut apud eum scriptum est. qua diminutione in haec quoque dispositus est a patre, quae ut humana reprehenditis, ediscens iam inde a primordio [iam inde hominem] quod erat futurus in fine. ille est, qui descendit, ille, qui interrogat, ille, qui postulat, ille, qui iurat. ceterum quia patrem nemini uisum etiam commune testabitur euangelium, dicente Christo: nemo cognouit patrem nisi filius. ipse enim et ueteri testamento pronuntiarat: deum nemo uidebit et uiuet, patrem inuisibilem determinans, in cuius auctoritate et nomine ipse erat deus, qui uidebatur dei filius. sed et penes nos Christus in persona Christi accipitur, quia et hoc modo noster est. igitur quaecumque exigitis deo digna, habe- Ii buntur in patre inuisibili incongressibilique et placido et, ut ita dixerim, philosophorum deo, quaecumque autem ut indigna reprehenditis, deputabuntur in filio et uiso et audito et congresso, arbitro patris et ministro, miscente in semetipso hominem et deum, in uirtutibus deum, in pusillitatibus hominem, ut tantum homini conferat quantum deo detrahit. totum denique\' dei mei penes uos dedecus sacramentum est humanae salutis. conuersabatur deus (humane,) ut homo diuine agere doceretur. ex aequo agebat deus cum homine, ut homo ex aequo agere cum deo posset. deus pusillus inuentus est, ut homo maximus fieret. qui talem deum dedignaris, nescie, an ex fide credas deum crucifixum. quanta itaque peruersitas uestra erga utrumque ordinem creatoris? iudicem eum desi-, gnatis, et seueritatem iudicis secundum merita causarum congruentem pro saeuitia exprobratis; deum optimum exigitis. et lenitatem eius benignitati congruentem, pro captu mediocritatis humanae deiectius conuersatam, ut pusillitatem depretiatis. nec magnus uobis placet nec modicus, nec iudex nec amicus. quid, si nunc eadem et in uestro deprehendantur? iudicem quidem et illum esse iam ostendimus in libello suo et de iudice necessarie seuerum et de seuero scilicet saeuum, si tamen saeuum.

excerpts.author: Lactantius
english: Let the starting point of our work, then, be the next question in order: whether the world is ruled by the power of one God or of many. No one who is truly wise and exercises reason fails to understand that there is a single Being who both founded all things and governs them with the very same power by which he created them. What need could there be for many to sustain the government of the world? One might suppose that if there were several, each would possess less strength and force; but that is exactly what proponents of many gods must claim, because if each cannot bear the helm of so vast a burden without the help of the others, they are necessarily weak. God, however, is eternal Mind, perfect and complete in virtue from every angle. If that is true, he must be one. Absolute power or virtue retains its own firmness; what is solid lacks nothing, and what is perfect admits no addition. Who would doubt that the mightiest king is the one who holds dominion over the whole world? And not without reason: all things everywhere belong to him, and all resources from every quarter flow to him alone. If many were to divide the world, each would certainly command less wealth and less strength, confined within a prescribed portion. The same holds for gods: if there are many, they are less powerful, since each has only as much as the others. The perfect nature of virtue can reside only in that which contains the whole, not in that which holds a mere fragment. Since God is perfect, as he must be, he cannot be anything but one, so that all things may be in him. Consequently, the virtues and powers of many gods would have to be weaker, because each lacks exactly as much as the others possess; the more there are, the smaller each becomes. Moreover, the supreme power of reality and divine strength cannot be divided even once. Whatever undergoes division must also undergo destruction. But destruction is remote from God, because he is incorruptible and eternal; therefore divine power cannot be divided. God is therefore one, since nothing else can possess equal power. Yet those who posit many gods claim that they have divided offices among themselves. We will debate all those claims in their proper place. For now I hold to the point at hand: if they have divided offices, the result is the same—no single one can suffice for all. Hence the one who cannot govern all things when the rest cease to act is not perfect. It follows that the world requires the perfect virtue of one, not the weakness of many. Anyone who thinks this vast magnitude cannot be ruled by a single being is mistaken and fails to grasp the greatness of divine strength and majesty. If the one God could make the world, he can certainly rule what he made. Consider the immensity of this divine work: though nothing existed before, it was brought into being from nothing by God's virtue and counsel—a work that could not have been begun or completed by anyone but one. Once this is grasped, it becomes clear that ruling what one has established is far easier than establishing it in the first place. Someone might object that not even a work as immense as the world could have been fashioned except by many. Let him imagine any multitude, any greatness, any magnitude of power, virtue, and majesty distributed among many; I gather all of it into one and declare that it exists in him, so that he possesses those qualities to a degree that cannot be thought or spoken. In this matter we fail both in perception and in language, because the human heart cannot grasp so great a light of understanding, nor can mortal tongue explain such things; yet we must understand and say this much. I see what might be said in opposition: that those many are exactly as we wish the one to be. But that cannot happen in any way, because the power of each cannot advance further when it encounters the powers of the others. Each must have his own limits, which he cannot cross, or if he crosses them he drives another back by his own boundaries. Those who believe in many gods do not see that it is possible for them to will different things, from which dispute and conflict would arise—just as Homer invented gods warring among themselves, some wanting Troy taken, others resisting. Therefore the world must be ruled by the decision of one. Unless the power of individual parts is referred to a single providence, the totality itself cannot hold together, each caring for nothing beyond what pertains to him—just as no military force can have more than one leader and ruler. If a single army had as many commanders as legions, cohorts, wedges, and wings, the battle line could not even be formed, each refusing danger, nor could it be easily directed or controlled, because all would follow their own counsels, whose diversity would harm more than help. So in this command of nature, unless there is one to whom the care of the whole sum is referred, all things will dissolve and collapse. To say the world is ruled by the will of many is like saying that a single body has many minds, because its members have many and varied functions, so that individual minds are thought to govern individual senses, and many affections—anger, desire, joy, fear, pity—are thought to be operated by as many minds. If someone actually says this, he does not even seem to possess the one mind he has. But if one mind in a single body governs so many things and attends to all simultaneously, why would anyone think the world cannot be ruled by one but can be by many? Because the defenders of many gods understand this, they say those gods preside over individual things and parts, yet insist there is still one supreme ruler. Then the rest are not gods at all, but satellites and ministers whom that one greatest and most powerful Being has appointed to those offices, to serve his command and nods. If all are not equal, then they are not all gods; the same thing cannot both serve and rule. If God is the name of the highest power, he must be incorruptible, perfect, impassible, subject to nothing. Therefore those whom necessity compels to obey the greatest God are not gods. But since those who think this way are not mistaken in vain, we will reveal the cause of their error shortly. Now we will confirm the unity of divine power with testimonies.

excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 3. Whether the universe is governed by the power of one God or of many.

excerpts.author: Lactantius
english: So let our work begin with the second question that follows: whether the world is ruled by the power of one God or of many. No one who is wise and consults reason fails to see that there is one who both founded all things and governs them with the same virtue by which he founded them. What need is there for many to sustain the rule of the world? One might suppose that if there are several, each has less nerve and strength; but those who want many gods do so because it is necessary for them to be weak, since no single one can bear the helm of so great a burden without the help of the rest. God, however, who is eternal mind, is perfect and complete virtue in every respect. If that is true, there must be one. Absolute power or virtue retains its own firmness. What is solid lacks nothing; what is perfect admits nothing further. Who would doubt that the king who holds command of the whole world is most powerful? And not without reason: all things everywhere are his, and all resources from every quarter are gathered to him alone. But if many divide the world, each will certainly have less wealth and less strength, since each is confined to his allotted portion. The same holds for gods: if there are many, they will be weaker, because each has no more in himself than the others have. Perfect virtue can reside only in that which contains the whole, not in that which contains a mere part. If God is perfect, as he must be, he cannot be anything but one, so that all things may be in him. Therefore the virtues and powers of the gods must be inferior, for each lacks exactly as much as resides in the others: the more there are, the smaller they become. The supreme power of things and divine strength cannot be divided even once. Whatever undergoes division must also undergo destruction. But destruction is far from God, because he is incorruptible and eternal; therefore divine power cannot be divided. God is one, if nothing else can possess as much power. Yet those who think there are many say they have divided offices among themselves. We will dispute all these points in their proper place. For now I hold to what belongs to the present argument: if they have divided offices, the matter returns to the same point, so that no one of them can suffice for all things. He will not be perfect who cannot govern all things when the others are absent. Thus ruling the world requires the perfect virtue of one, not the weakness of many. Whoever thinks this great magnitude cannot be ruled by one is mistaken and does not understand how great the strength and power of divine majesty is, if he supposes that the singular God who could make the world cannot rule what he made. But if he conceives in his mind how great the immensity of this divine work is—how, when nothing previously existed, it was brought into being from nothing by the virtue and counsel of God, a work that could not have been begun and completed except by one—he will then understand that it is far easier for it to be ruled by one than it was to be established by one. Someone may say that not even so immense a work as the world could have been made without many. Let him imagine whatever multitude, whatever greatness, whatever magnitude of power, virtue, and majesty he pleases in many; I gather it all into one and say it exists in one, so that there is as much of those things in him as cannot be thought or spoken. In this matter we fail both in sense and in words, because the human heart cannot grasp such great light of understanding, nor can mortal tongue grasp the explanation of such great things; yet we ought to understand and say this very thing. I see again what might be said on the contrary: that those many are such as we want the one to be. But this cannot happen in any way, because the power of each will not be able to advance further when met by the powers of the others. Each must have his own limits, which he cannot cross, or if he crosses them he drives another back with his own boundaries. Those who believe in many gods do not see that it is possible for them to will something different, from which a dispute and contest would arise among them, just as Homer fashioned gods fighting among themselves when some wanted Troy taken and others resisted. Therefore the world must be ruled by the decision of one. Unless the power of individual parts is referred to one providence, the whole itself cannot hold together, each caring for nothing more than what belongs to him—just as even a military force cannot have more than one leader and ruler. If in one army there were as many commanders as legions, cohorts, wedges, and wings, first the battle line could not be formed, each refusing his own danger, nor would it be easy to rule or temper, because all would follow their own counsels, whose diversity harms more than it helps. So in this command of nature, unless there is one to whom the care of the whole sum is referred, all things will dissolve and collapse. To say that the world is ruled by the decision of many is like affirming that in one body there are many minds, because there are many and varied ministries of the members, so that individual minds are believed to rule individual senses of the body, and also many affections by which we are moved—to anger, desire, joy, fear, pity—so that as many minds are thought to operate. If someone said that, he would not even be seen to have the one mind that is alone. But if in one body one mind possesses the governance of so many things and is attentive to all at once, why would anyone think the world cannot be ruled by one but can be ruled by many? Because those who assert the gods understand this, they say the gods preside over individual things and parts, yet there is one excellent ruler. Now therefore the others would not be gods but satellites and ministers, whom that one greatest and most powerful of all has placed over those offices to serve his command and nods. If all are not equal, then not all are gods: it cannot be the same thing that serves and that dominates. If God is the name of the highest power, he must be incorruptible, perfect, impassible, subject to nothing. Therefore those whom necessity compels to obey the greatest God are not gods. But because those who think this are not mistaken in vain, we will reveal the cause of this error a little later. Now we will confirm the unity of divine power with testimonies.
