rectorem. quodsi in uno exercitu tot fuerint imperatores quot legiones, quot cohortes, quot cunei, quot alae, primum nec instrui poterit acies uno quoque periculum recusante nec regi facile aut temperari, quod suis propriis consiliis utantur omnes, quorum diuersitate plus noceant quam prosint: sic in hoc rerum naturae imperio nisi unus fuerit ad quem totius summae cura referatur, uniuersa soluentur et conruent. dicere autem multorum arbitrio regi mundum tale est, quale si quis adfirmet in uno corpore multas esse mentes, quoniam multa et uaria sint ministeria membrorum, ut singulos corporis sensus singulae mentes regere credantur, item multi adfectus, quibus commoueri solemus uel ad iram uel ad cupiditatem uel ad laetitiam uel ad metum uel ad miserationem, ut in his omnibus totidem mentes putentur operari. quod si quis profecto dicat, ne ipsam quidem quae una est habere uideatur. quodsi in uno corpore tantarum rerum gubernationem mens una possidet et uniuersis simul intenta est, cur aliquis existimet mundum non posse ab uno regi, a pluribus posse? quod quia intellegunt isti adsertores deorum, ita eos praeesse singulis rebus ac partibus dicunt, ut tamen unus sit rector eximius. iam ergo ceteri non dii erunt, sed satellites ac ministri, quos ille unus maximus ac potens omnium iis officiis praefecerit, ut ipsi eius imperio ac nutibus seruiant. si uniuersi pares non sunt, non igitur dii omnes sunt: nec enim potest hoc idem esse quod seruit et quod dominatur. nam si deus nomen est summae potestatis, incorruptibilis esse debet, perfectus inpassibilis nulli rei subiectus. ergo dii non sunt quos parere um maximo deo necessitas cogit. sed quia non frustra falluntur qui hoc ita putant, causam huius erroris paulo post aperiemus. nunc unitatem diuinae potestatis testimoniis conprobemus.
excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 3. Whether the universe is governed by the power of one God or of many.

excerpts.author: Lactantius
english: We should set aside the prophets’ testimony, lest the proof appear inadequate to those who reject it entirely. Let us turn instead to the authors our opponents themselves invoke—the poets and philosophers—and call them as witnesses to the truth. From them we must establish one God, not because they possessed the truth, but because truth’s power is so great that no one can be so blind as to miss the divine clarity forced upon their eyes. The poets, though they decked the gods in verse and magnified their deeds with highest praise, still confess again and again that all things are held together and governed by a single spirit or mind. Orpheus, most ancient of the poets and a peer of the gods themselves—tradition says he sailed with the Argonauts alongside Castor and Hercules—calls the true and great God ‘Protogonos’, because nothing was generated before him, but all things were generated from him. He also names him ‘Phaneta’, because when nothing yet existed, he first appeared and stood forth from the infinite. Unable to conceive his origin and nature, Orpheus said he was born of vast air: ‘Protogonos Phaethon, son of immeasurable air’; he had nothing further to say. This God, he says, is the parent of all the gods, for whose sake he founded heaven and provided for his children a common dwelling and seat: ‘He built an imperishable house for the immortals’. Guided by nature and reason, Orpheus recognized a supreme power, the creator of heaven and earth. He could not name Jupiter as the first principle, since Jupiter was born of Saturn; nor Saturn, who was said to be born of heaven; nor dare he make heaven itself the first god, because he saw heaven as a world-element that itself required an author. This reasoning led him to that firstborn God, to whom he assigns and attributes sovereignty. Homer offers nothing for the truth, for he wrote of human, not divine, matters. Hesiod might have, since he compressed the gods’ genealogy into a single book; yet he gave no account that did not begin with Chaos—a confused mass of raw, disordered matter—when he ought first to have explained what Chaos is, and whence, when, and how it began to exist. For just as all things are ordered and fashioned by some craftsman, so this matter itself must have been fashioned by someone. Who made it, if not God, to whose power all things are subject? But Hesiod shrinks back, dreading the unknown truth. He did not pour out that song on Helicon by the Muses’ impulse, as he wished to seem, but came prepared and deliberate. Our first poet, Virgil, was not far from the truth. Of the highest God, whom he named Mind and Spirit, he wrote: ‘In the beginning the Spirit nourishes heaven and earth and the fields and the shining globe of the moon and the Titan stars; the Mind, infused throughout, stirs the whole mass and mingles with the great body’. And lest anyone mistake which Spirit wields such power, he declared elsewhere: ‘For God passes through all lands and sea-tracts and deep heaven; from him flocks and herds and men and every kind of wild beast, each living thing new-born, are summoned to life’. Ovid, too, at the start of his great work, without disguising the name, acknowledges that the world was ordered by God, whom he calls the world’s maker and craftsman of things. If Orpheus or our own poets, led by nature, had defended perpetually what they perceived, they would have held the same doctrine we follow, having grasped the truth. So much for the poets. Now to the philosophers, whose authority is weightier and judgment surer, because they are thought to have studied not fictions but the investigation of truth. Thales of Miletus, one of the Seven Sages and said to be the first to seek natural causes, said water is the source from which all things are born, but God is the Mind that formed all things from water. Thus he placed the matter of things in moisture and fixed the principle and cause of generation in God. Pythagoras defined God as: ‘The Mind that pervades all parts of the world and all nature, diffused throughout, from which all living creatures receive life’. Anaxagoras says God is an infinite Mind that moves itself. Antisthenes grants many popular gods, but one natural God—that is, the craftsman of the whole. Cleanthes and Anaximenes name the highest God as Ether; our poet assented to this view: ‘Then the Almighty Father, with fertilizing rains, descended into the joyful lap of his Ether-bride, and the great offspring is nourished, mingled with the great body’. Chrysippus calls God the natural power endowed with divine reason, sometimes divine necessity; Zeno calls God the natural and divine law. Though all their opinions are uncertain, they converge on the same point: they agree that there is one Providence. Whether you call it Nature, or Ether, or Reason, or Mind, or Fatal Necessity, or Divine Law, or anything else, it is the same thing we call God. Nor does the diversity of names obstruct, since all are referred by their meaning to one reality. Aristotle, though he contradicts himself and says and thinks opposing things, still testifies that one Mind presides over the world. Plato, judged the wisest of all, defends the monarchy openly and plainly, and does not name Ether, or Reason, or Nature, but calls him God, from whom this world was made perfect and wonderful. Cicero, following and imitating him in many places, frequently confesses God and calls him Supreme in the books he wrote on the laws, arguing that the world is ruled by him when he discusses the nature of the gods: ‘Nothing is more excellent than God. Therefore the world must be ruled by him. For God is subject to no nature, nor obedient to it. Therefore he himself rules all nature.’ That God exists we do not doubt; nor can God himself, as we understand him, be understood in any other way than as a certain Mind, free and separated from all mortal concretion, perceiving and moving all things. Seneca, the keenest Stoic among the Romans, how often does he extol the highest God with deserved praise! When discussing premature death he says: ‘Do you not understand the authority and majesty of your judge, the ruler of earth and heaven and all the gods, from whom those divine powers which we singly adore and worship are suspended?’ Also in his Exhortations: ‘When he laid the first foundations of this most beautiful world and began to order it, so that all things might go under their leaders, although he himself had extended through his whole body, nevertheless God generated the ministers of his kingdom.’ And how many other things he said about God, similar to ours! I omit them now, because they fit better elsewhere. For the present it is enough to show that men of the highest genius have touched the truth and almost grasped it, unless they were dragged back by custom’s corrupt and perverse opinions, by which they believed there were other gods and that the things God made for human use were to be held and worshipped as gods.

excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 5. Of the testimonies of poets and philosophers.

excerpts.author: Lactantius
english: We now turn to the divine testimonies. First, however, I will cite one piece of evidence that resembles the divine both because of its great antiquity and because the man I shall name was enrolled among the gods. In Cicero, the pontiff U. Cotta argues against the Stoics concerning religions and the variety of opinions usually held about the gods. He follows the Academic practice of rendering everything uncertain. He states that there were five Mercurys; after enumerating four in order, he identifies the fifth as the one who killed Argus. On that account, this figure fled to Egypt and handed down laws and letters to the Egyptians. The Egyptians call him Thoyth; from him their first month of the year—September—received its name. He also founded a city that is still called, in Greek, the City of Mercury, and the Pheneatae worship him religiously. Although he was a man, he was the most ancient and the most thoroughly instructed in every kind of learning, so that his knowledge of many arts and sciences earned him the surname Trismegistus. He wrote many books pertaining to the knowledge of divine things. In them he asserts the majesty of the highest and singular God, addressing him by the very names we use for the Lord and Father. Lest anyone seek his name, he declared that God is anonymous, because the divine nature has no need of a proper name on account of its unity. His own words are: "O se Oso; one, indeed, one, not needing a name, is anonymous." Therefore, God does not have a name, because he is alone; there is no need for a proper title unless a multitude requires distinction, so that each person may be designated by a unique mark and appellation. But because God is always one, "God" is his proper name.

It remains to produce testimonies from the sacred and prophetic writings that are far more certain. Perhaps those against whom we argue do not consider poets credible, since they invent fictions, nor philosophers, because they could have erred, being men themselves. M. Varro, than whom no one more learned ever lived, not even among the Greeks, wrote books on divine matters addressed to C. Caesar the pontifex maximus. When discussing the quindecimvirs, he states that the Sibylline books were not the work of a single Sibyl. They bear one name, "Sibylline," because the ancients called all female prophets Sibyls, either from the name of one Delphid or from the announcing of the counsels of the gods. For they called the gods not "Osouc" but "theos," and counsel not "boulēn" but "boullan," in the Aeolic dialect. Hence the Sibyl was, as it were, a "theoboulēn"—a divine counsel. Moreover, there were ten Sibyls, and Varro enumerated them all under the authorities who wrote about each. The first was Persian, mentioned by Nicanor, who wrote the deeds of Alexander of Macedon. The second was Libyssa, recalled by Euripides in the prologue to the Lamia. The third was the Delphid, discussed by Chrysippus in his book on divination. The fourth was Cimmerian, in Italy, named by Naevius in his books on the Punic War and by Piso in his annals. The fifth was the Erythraean, whom Apollodorus of Erythrae affirmed to be his fellow citizen; she prophesied to the Greeks bound for Ilium that Troy would fall and that Homer would write falsehoods. The sixth was Samian, recorded by Eratosthenes in the ancient annals of the Samians. The seventh was the Cumaean, named Amalthea, also called Herophile or Demophile by others. She brought nine books to King Tarquinius Priscus and demanded three hundred philippeos for them. The king scorned the high price and mocked the woman's madness. In his presence she burned three of the books and asked the same price for the remaining six. Tarquin, thinking her even more insane, was moved to buy the rest for three hundred gold pieces. The number of books later increased when the Capitol was rebuilt; volumes were collected from all cities, Italian and Greek, especially from Erythrae, and brought to Rome under whatever Sibyl's name they bore. The eighth was the Hellespontian, born in the Troad, in the village of Marmessa near the city of Gergithium; Heraclides of Pontus places her in the times of Solon and Cyrus. The ninth was the Phrygian, who prophesied at Ancyra. The tenth was the Tiburtine, named Albunea, worshiped as a goddess at Tibur near the banks of the river Anio; her image is said to have been found in the whirlpool holding a book in her hand. The songs of all these Sibyls are both corrupted and preserved, except those of the Cumaean. Her books the Romans keep hidden; no one but the quindecimvirs may inspect them. There are individual books for each Sibyl, but because they are all inscribed with the name "Sibyl," they are believed to be the work of one, and are confused so that they cannot be distinguished or assigned to their proper authors—except for the Erythraean, who inserted her true name into her verse and proclaimed herself Erythraean, though she was born in Babylon. We too shall cite the Sibyls without distinction wherever their testimonies are needed.

All these Sibyls proclaim one God, above all the Erythraean, who is held more famous and noble than the rest. Fenestella, a most diligent writer on the quindecimvirs, says that when the Capitol was restored, the consul C. Curio reported to the senate that legates should be sent to Erythrae to recover the Sibyl's songs. Accordingly P. Gabinius, M. Otacilius, and L. Valerius were dispatched; they brought back to Rome about a thousand verses copied from private collections. We have shown above that Varro attests the same. In these verses, which the legates brought to Rome, the following testimonies concerning one God appear: "One God, who alone rules, immense, ungenerated." This is the only highest God, who made heaven and distinguished it with lights: "But God alone, one, most high, who made heaven, the sun, and the stars, and the moon, and the fruitful earth, and the waters of the sea." Because he alone is the builder of the world and the artificer of all things, whether they consist in it or are in it, he testifies that he alone ought to be worshiped: "Honor him, the only one, the leader of the world." "Who alone is from eternity and to eternity." Likewise, another Sibyl, whoever she may be, when she claims to bring the voice of God to men, declares: "For I am the only God, and there is no other God." I would now produce the testimonies of the other Sibyls, if these did not suffice and if I were not reserving them for more opportune places. But since we defend the cause of truth against those who, straying from the truth, serve false religions, what proof should we employ more effectively against them than to convict them by the testimonies of their own gods?

nonam Phrygiam, quae uaticinata sit Ancyrae; decimam Tiburtem nomine Albuneam, quae Tiburi colatur ut dea iuxta ripas amnis Anienis, cuius in gurgite simulacrum eius inuentum esse dicitur tenens in manu librum. arum onmium Sibyllarum carmina et teruntur et habentur, praeterquam Cymaeae, cuius libri a Romanis occultantur nec eos ab ullo nisi a quindecimuiris inspici fas habent. et sunt singularum singuli libri: quos, quia Sibyllae nomine inscribuntur, unius esse credunt, suntque confusi nec discerni ac suum cuique adsignari potest nisi Erythraeae, quae et nomen suum uerum carmini inseruit et Erythraeam se nominatuiri praelocuta est, cum esset orta Babylone. sed et IlOS confuse Sibyllam dicemus, sicubi testimoniis earum ruent abutendum. omnes igitur hae Sibyllae unum deum praedicant, maxime tamen Erythraea, quae celebrior inter ceteras ac nobilior habetur, siquidem Fenestella diligentissimus scriptor de quindecim uiris dicens ait restituto Capitolio rettulisse ad senatum C. Curionem consulem, ut legati Erythras mitterentur, qui carmina Sibyllae conquisita Romam deportarent: itaque missos esse P. Gabinium M. Otacilium L. Valerium, qui descriptos a priuatis uersus circa mille Romam deportarunt. idem dixisse Varronem supra ostendimus. in his ergo uersibus quos Romam legati adtulerunt de uno deo haec sunt testimonia: εἷς θεός, ὂς μόνος ἄρχει, ὐπερμεγέθης ἀγένητος. hunc esse solum summum deum, qui caelum fecerit luminibusque distinxerit: ἀλλὰ θεὸς μόνος εἶς πανυπέρτατος, ὃς πεποίηκεν οὐρανὸν ἡέλιὸν τε καὶ ἀστέρας, ἠδέ σελήνην, καρποφόρον γαῖαν τε καὶ ὕδατος οἴδματα πόντου. qui quoniam solus sit aedificator mundi et artifex rerum uel quibus constat uel quae in eo sunt, solum coli oportere testatur: αὐτὸν τὸν μόνον ὄντα σέβεσθ᾽ ἡγήτορα κόσμου. ὃς μόνος εἰς αἰῶνα καὶ ἐξ αἰῶνος ἐτύχθη. item alia Sibylla quaecumque est cum perferre se ad homines uocem dei diceret, sic ait: μοῦνος γὰρ θεὸς εἰμὶ καὶ οὐκ ἔστι θεὸς ἄλλος. Exequerer nunc testimonia ceterarum, nisi et haec sufticerent et illa opportunioribus locis reseruarem. sed cum defendamus causam ueritatis aput eos qui aberrantes a ueritate falsis religionibus seruiunt, quod genus probationis aduersus eos magis adhibere debemus quam ut eos deorum suorum testimoniis reuincamus?
excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 6. Of divine testimonies, and of the Sibyls and their predictions.

excerpts.author: Lactantius
english: So many and such weighty witnesses confirm that the world is governed by the power and providence of one God. Plato declares in the Timaeus that this God's power and majesty are so great that no one can conceive them in mind or express them in words, because the power is excessive and inestimable. If anyone still doubts whether anything is difficult or impossible for God, consider: he devised such great and wondrous works by providence, established them by virtue, perfected them by reason, now sustains them by spirit, and moderates them by power — a being incomprehensible, ineffable, and known adequately to no one but himself.

When I reflect often on such majesty, those who worship gods sometimes strike me as so blind, so unthinking, so foolish, and not much different from mute beasts. They believe that beings born from the union of male and female can possess some divine majesty and virtue, even though the Erythraean Sibyl says, 'No man formed from the thighs and womb of a woman can be God.' Since this is true, it follows that Hercules, Apollo, Bacchus, Mercury, and Jupiter himself — along with the rest — were men, because they were born of two sexes.

What could be more remote from God than the very work he gave mortals for propagating offspring, a work that cannot exist without bodily substance? If the gods are immortal and eternal, what need is there for another sex — namely, to generate? What need is there for progeny, since they lack no succession, being forever? In humans and other animals, the diversity of sex, union, and generation serves no other purpose than to preserve all kinds of living things by mutual succession, because they are subject to mortality. But for God, who is eternal, neither another sex nor succession is necessary.

Someone will object: 'So that he may have ministers or those over whom he can rule.' Then what need is there for the female sex, since God, who is omnipotent as he is called, can procreate sons without the use or work of a woman? If he has granted certain small animals the ability to be born from leaves and sweet herbs and to gather them with their mouths, why would anyone think that God himself cannot generate except by the mixture of another sex?

Therefore, no one is so thoughtless as not to understand that those whom the ignorant and foolish call and worship as gods were mortals. 'How, then,' someone asks, 'were they believed to be gods?' Precisely because they were the greatest and most powerful kings, and on account of the merits of their virtues, or gifts, or discovered arts. Since they were dear to those they ruled, they were consecrated to memory. If anyone doubts this, let him consider their deeds and actions, which both ancient poets and historians have handed down.

unde mihi de tanta maiestate saepius cogitanti qui deos colunt interdum uideri solent tam caeci, tam incogitabiles, tam excordes, tam non multum a mutis animalibus differentes, qui credant eos qui geniti sint maris ac feminae coitu aliquid maiestatis diuinaeque uirtutis habere potuisse, cum Sibylla Erythraea dicat: ou οὐ δύνατ\' ἀνδρὸς ἑϰ μηρῶν μήτρας τε θεὸς τετυπωμένος εἶναι. quod si est uerum, sicuti est, apparet Herculem Apollinem Liberum Mercurium Iouemque ipsum cum ceteris homines fuisse, quoniam sunt ex duobus sexibus nati. quid est autem a deo tam remotum quam id opus, quod ipse ad propagandam subolem mortalibus tribuit et quod sine substantia corporali nullum potest esse? excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 8. That God is without a body, nor does he need difference of sex for procreation.

excerpts.author: Lactantius
english: Who, then, is so senseless as to imagine that he reigns in heaven who ought not even to have reigned on earth? It was not without humour that a certain poet wrote of the triumph of Cupid: in which book he not only represented Cupid as the most powerful of the gods, but also as their conqueror. For having enumerated the loves of each, by which they had come into the power and dominion of Cupid, he sets in array a procession, in which Jupiter, with the other gods, is led in chains before the chariot of him, celebrating a triumph. This is elegantly pictured by the poet, but it is not far removed from the truth. For he who is without virtue, who is overpowered by desire and wicked lusts, is not, as the poet feigned, in subjection to Cupid, but to everlasting death. But let us cease to speak concerning morals; let us examine the matter, in order that men may understand in what errors they are miserably engaged. The common people imagine that Jupiter reigns in heaven; both learned and unlearned are alike persuaded of this. For both religion itself, and prayers, and hymns, and shrines, and images demonstrate this. And yet they admit that he was also descended from Saturn and Rhea. How can he appear a god, or be believed, as the poet says, to be the author of men and all things, when innumerable thousands of men existed before his birth — those, for instance, who lived during the reign of Saturn, and enjoyed the light sooner than Jupiter? I see that one god was king in the earliest times, and another in the times that followed. It is therefore possible that there may be another hereafter. For if the former kingdom was changed, why should we not expect that the latter may possibly be changed, unless by chance it was possible for Saturn to produce one more powerful than himself, but impossible for Jupiter so to do? And yet the divine government is always unchangeable; or if it is changeable, which is an impossibility, it is undoubtedly changeable at all times.

Is it possible, then, for Jupiter to lose his kingdom as his father lost it? It is so undoubtedly. For when that deity had spared neither virgins nor married women, he abstained from Thetis only in consequence of an oracle which foretold that whatever son should be born from her would be greater than his father. And first of all there was in him a want of foreknowledge not befitting a god; for had not Themis related to him future events, he would not have known them of his own accord. But if he is not divine, he is not indeed a god; for the name of divinity is derived from god, as humanity is from man. Then there was a consciousness of weakness; but he who has feared, must plainly have feared one greater than himself. But he who does this assuredly knows that he is not the greatest, since something greater can exist. He also swears most solemnly by the Stygian marsh: Which is set forth the sole object of religious dread to the gods above. What is this object of religious dread? Or by whom is it set forth? Is there, then, some mighty power which may punish the gods who commit perjury? What is this great dread of the infernal marsh, if they are immortal? Why should they fear that which none are about to see, except those who are bound by the necessity of death? Why, then, do men raise their eyes to the heaven? Why do they swear by the gods above, when the gods above themselves have recourse to the infernal gods, and find among them an object of veneration and worship? But what is the meaning of that saying, that there are fates whom all the gods and Jupiter himself obey? If the power of the Parcæ is so great, that they are of more avail than all the heavenly gods, and their ruler and lord himself, why should not they be rather said to reign, since necessity compels all the gods to obey their laws and ordinances? Now, who can entertain a doubt that he who is subservient to anything cannot be greatest? For if he were so, he would not receive fates, but would appoint them. Now I return to another subject which I had omitted. In the case of one goddess only he exercised self-restraint, though he was deeply enamoured of her; but this was not from any virtue, but through fear of a successor. But this fear plainly denotes one who is both mortal and feeble, and of no weight: for at the very hour of his birth he might have been put to death, as his elder brother had been put to death; and if it had been possible for him to have lived, he would never have given up the supreme power to a younger brother. But Jupiter himself having been preserved by stealth, and stealthily nourished, was called Zeus, or Zen, not, as they imagine, from the fervor of heavenly fire, or because he is the giver of life, or because he breathes life into living creatures, which power belongs to God alone; for how can he impart the breath of life who has himself received it from another source? But he was so called because he was the first who lived of the male children of Saturn. Men, therefore, might have had another god as their ruler, if Saturn had not been deceived by his wife. But it will be said the poets feigned these things. Whoever entertains this opinion is in error. For they spoke respecting men; but in order that they might embellish those whose memory they used to celebrate with praises, they said that they were gods. Those things, therefore, which they spoke concerning them as gods were feigned, and not those which they spoke concerning them as men; and this will be manifest from an instance which we will bring forward. When about to offer violence to Danae, he poured into her lap a great quantity of golden coins. This was the price which he paid for her dishonour. But the poets who spoke about him as a god, that they might not weaken the authority of his supposed majesty, feigned that he himself descended in a shower of gold, making use of the same figure with which they speak of showers of iron when they describe a multitude of darts and arrows. He is said to have carried away Ganymede by an eagle; it is a picture of the poets. But he either carried him off by a legion, which has an eagle for its standard; or the ship on board of which he was placed had its tutelary deity in the shape of an eagle, just as it had the effigy of a bull when he seized Europa and conveyed her across the sea. In the same manner, it is related that he changed Io, the daughter of Inachus, into a heifer. And in order that she might escape the anger of Juno, just as she was, now covered with bristly hair, and in the shape of a heifer, she is said to have swam over the sea, and to have come into Egypt; and there, having recovered her former appearance, she became the goddess who is now called Isis. By what argument, then, can it be proved that Europa did not sit on the bull, and that Io was not changed into a heifer? Because there is a fixed day in the annals on which the voyage of Isis is celebrated; from which fact we learn that she did not swim across the sea, but sailed over. Therefore they who appear to themselves to be wise because they understand that there cannot be a living and earthly body in heaven, reject the whole story of Ganymede as false, and perceive that the occurrence took place on earth, inasmuch as the matter and the lust itself is earthly. The poets did not therefore invent these transactions, for if they were to do so they would be most worthless; but they added a certain color to the transactions. For it was not for the purpose of detraction that they said these things, but from a desire to embellish them. Hence men are deceived; especially because, while they think that all these things are feigned by the poets, they worship that of which they are ignorant. For they do not know what is the limit of poetic licence, how far it is allowable to proceed in fiction, since it is the business of the poet with some gracefulness to change and transfer actual occurrences into other representations by oblique transformations. But to feign the whole of that which you relate, that is to be foolish and deceitful rather than to be a poet.

But grant that they feigned those things which are believed to be fabulous, did they also feign those things which are related about the female deities and the marriages of the gods? Why, then, are they so represented, and so worshipped? Unless by chance not the poets only, but painters also, and statuaries, speak falsehoods. For if this is the Jupiter who is called by you a god, if it is not he who was born from Saturn and Ops, no other image but his alone ought to have been placed in all the temples. What meaning have the effigies of women? What the doubtful sex? In which, if this Jupiter is represented, the very stones will confess that he is a man. They say that the poets have spoken falsely, and yet they believe them: yes, truly they prove by the fact itself that the poets did not speak falsely; for they so frame the images of the gods, that, from the very diversity of sex, it appears that these things which the poets say are true. For what other conclusion does the image of Ganymede and the effigy of the eagle admit of, when they are placed before the feet of Jupiter in the temples, and are worshipped equally with himself, except that the memory of impious guilt and debauchery remains for ever? Nothing, therefore, is wholly invented by the poets: something perhaps is transferred and obscured by oblique fashioning, under which the truth was enwrapped and concealed; as that which was related about the dividing of the kingdoms by lot. For they say that the heaven fell to the share of Jupiter, the sea to Neptune, and the infernal regions to Pluto. Why was not the earth rather taken as the third portion, except that the transaction took place on the earth? Therefore it is true that they so divided and portioned out the government of the world, that the empire of the east fell to Jupiter, a part of the west was allotted to Pluto, who had the surname of Agesilaus; because the region of the east, from which light is given to mortals, seems to be higher, but the region of the west lower. Thus they so veiled the truth under a fiction, that the truth itself detracted nothing from the public persuasion. It is manifest concerning the share of Neptune; for we say that his kingdom resembled that unlimited authority possessed by Mark Antony, to whom the senate had decreed the power of the maritime coast, that he might punish the pirates, and tranquillize the whole sea. Thus all the maritime coasts, together with the islands, fell to the lot of Neptune. How can this be proved? Undoubtedly ancient stories attest it. Euhemerus, an ancient author, who was of the city of Messene, collected the actions of Jupiter and of the others, who are esteemed gods, and composed a history from the titles and sacred inscriptions which were in the most ancient temples, and especially in the sanctuary of the Triphylian Jupiter, where an inscription indicated that a golden column had been placed by Jupiter himself, on which column he wrote an account of his exploits, that posterity might have a memorial of his actions. This history was translated and followed by Ennius, whose words are these: Where Jupiter gives to Neptune the government of the sea, that he might reign in all the islands and places bordering on the sea.

The accounts of the poets, therefore, are true, but veiled with an outward covering and show. It is possible that Mount Olympus may have supplied the poets with the hint for saying that Jupiter obtained the kingdom of heaven, because Olympus is the common name both of the mountain and of heaven. But the same history informs us that Jupiter dwelt on Mount Olympus, when it says: At that time Jupiter spent the greatest part of his life on Mount Olympus; and they used to resort to him there for the administration of justice, if any matters were disputed. Moreover, if any one had found out any new invention which might be useful for human life, he used to come there and display it to Jupiter. The poets transfer many things after this manner, not for the sake of speaking falsely against the objects of their worship, but that they may by variously colored figures add beauty and grace to their poems. But they who do not understand the manner, or the cause, or the nature of that which is represented by figure, attack the poets as false and sacrilegious. Even the philosophers were deceived by this error; for because these things which are related about Jupiter appeared unsuited to the character of a god, they introduced two Jupiters, one natural, the other fabulous. They saw, on the one hand, that which was true, that he, forsooth, concerning whom the poets speak, was man; but in the case of that natural Jupiter, led by the common practise of superstition, they committed an error, inasmuch as they transferred the name of a man to God, who, as we have already said, because He is one only, has no need of a name. But it is undeniable that he is Jupiter who was born from Ops and Saturn. It is therefore an empty persuasion on the part of those who give the name of Jupiter to the Supreme God. For some are in the habit of defending their errors by this excuse; for, when convinced of the unity of God, since they cannot deny this, they affirm that they worship Him, but that it is their pleasure that He should be called Jupiter. But what can be more absurd than this? For Jupiter is not accustomed to be worshipped without the accompanying worship of his wife and daughter. From which his real nature is evident; nor is it lawful for that name to be transferred there, where there is neither any Minerva nor Juno. Why should I say that the peculiar meaning of this name does not express a divine, but human power? For Cicero explains the names Jupiter and Juno as being derived from giving help; and Jupiter is so called as if he were a helping father — a name which is ill adapted to God: for to help is the part of a man conferring some aid upon one who is a stranger, and in a case where the benefit is small. No one implores God to help him, but to preserve him, to give him life and safety, which is a much greater and more important matter than to help.

And since we are speaking of a father, no father is said to help his sons when he begets or brings them up. For that expression is too insignificant to denote the magnitude of the benefit derived from a father. How much more unsuitable is it to God, who is our true Father, by whom we exist, and whose we are altogether, by whom we are formed, endued with life, and enlightened, who bestows upon us life, gives us safety, and supplies us with various kinds of food! He has no apprehension of the divine benefits who thinks that he is only aided by God. Therefore he is not only ignorant, but impious, who disparages the excellency of the supreme power under the name of Jupiter. Wherefore, if both from his actions and character we have proved that Jupiter was a man, and reigned on earth, it only remains that we should also investigate his death. Ennius, in his sacred history, having described all the actions which he performed in his life, at the close thus speaks: Then Jupiter, when he had five times made a circuit of the earth, and bestowed governments upon all his friends and relatives, and left laws to men, provided them with a settled mode of life and grain, and given them many other benefits, and having been honoured with immortal glory and remembrance, left lasting memorials to his friends, and when his age was almost spent, he changed his life in Crete, and departed to the gods. And the Curetes, his sons, took charge of him, and honoured him; and his tomb is in Crete, in the town of Cnossus, and Vesta is said to have founded this city; and on his tomb is an inscription in ancient Greek characters, Zan Kronou, which is in Latin, Jupiter the son of Saturn. This undoubtedly is not handed down by poets, but by writers of ancient events; and these things are so true, that they are confirmed by some verses of the Sibyls, to this effect:—
Inanimate demons, images of the dead, Whose tombs the ill-fated Crete possesses as a boast.

Cicero, in his treatise concerning the Nature of the Gods, having said that three Jupiters were enumerated by theologians, adds that the third was of Crete, the son of Saturn, and that his tomb is shown in that island. How, therefore, can a god be alive in one place, and dead in another; in one place have a temple, and in another a tomb? Let the Romans then know that their Capitol, that is the chief head of their objects of public veneration, is nothing but an empty monument.

Let us now come to his father who reigned before him, and who perhaps had more power in himself, because he is said to be born from the meeting of such great elements. Let us see what there was in him worthy of a god, especially that he is related to have had the golden age, because in his reign there was justice in the earth. I find something in him which was not in his son. For what is so befitting the character of a god, as a just government and an age of piety? But when, on the same principle, I reflect that he is a son, I cannot consider him as the Supreme God; for I see that there is something more ancient than himself — namely, the heaven and the earth. But I am in search of a God beyond whom nothing has any existence, who is the source and origin of all things. He must of necessity exist who framed the heaven itself, and laid the foundations of the earth. But if Saturn was born from these, as it is supposed, how can he be the chief God, since he owes his origin to another? Or who presided over the universe before the birth of Saturn? But this, as I recently said, is a fiction of the poets. For it was impossible that the senseless elements, which are separated by so long an interval, should meet together and give birth to a son, or that he who was born should not at all resemble his parents, but should have a form which his parents did not possess.

excerpts.author: Lactantius
english: Given the established facts about these men, it is clear how they first came to be called gods. Since no kings existed before Saturn or Uranus because the human population was sparse and people lived a rustic life without any ruler, there is no doubt that in those early times men began to offer the king himself — and indeed the whole nation — the highest praises and honors, even calling them gods. They did this either because of the miracle of virtue — a belief the rude and simple people genuinely held — or, as often happens, out of flattery toward present power or gratitude for benefits that had civilized humanity. Afterward, because those kings had been dear to the people whose lives they had shaped, their deaths left a great longing. Consequently, men fashioned images of them to find some solace in contemplating these likenesses, and, carried further by love, they began to honor the memory of the dead — both to appear grateful to their benefactors and to entice their successors toward the desire to rule well. Cicero teaches this in *On the Nature of the Gods*, saying that human life and common custom adopted the practice of elevating excellent men to heaven by fame and will on account of their benefits; from this came Hercules, Castor, Pollux, Aesculapius, and Liber. In another passage he adds that in most cities one can see that the memory of brave men was consecrated with the honors of immortal gods, either to sharpen virtue or so that the best men might more readily face danger for the republic's sake. By this reasoning the Romans consecrated their Caesars and the Moors their kings. Thus religions gradually arose: those who had first known these men initiated their own children and grandchildren into the rite, then all posterity, until finally these supreme kings were worshipped in every province because of the fame of their names. Privately, individual peoples or cities worshipped their own founders — whether men distinguished by strength or women remarkable for chastity — with the utmost veneration: the Egyptians honored Isis, the Moors Iuba, the Macedonians Cabirus, the Carthaginians Urania, the Latins Faunus, the Sabines Sancus, the Romans Quirinus; likewise the Athenians honored Minerva, the Samians Juno, the Paphian people Venus, the Lemnians Vulcan, the Naxians Liber, and the Delians Apollo. In this way diverse sacred rites were adopted across peoples and regions, because men wished to be grateful to their leaders but could find no other honors to confer upon those who no longer lived. Moreover, the piety of successors contributed greatly to the error: wishing to appear born of divine stock, they bestowed divine honors on their parents and ordered them to be worshipped. Can anyone doubt how the religions of the gods were instituted, when one reads in Virgil Aeneas commanding his companions: "Now pour libations to Jupiter with prayers and invoke Anchises as father"? To Anchises was attributed not only immortality but also power over the winds: "Let us ask for winds, and declare that these sacred rites I have established in the city be brought to him every year in his temples." Liber, Pan, Mercury, and Apollo did the same, and afterward their successors followed suit. Poets added to this, lifting these figures to heaven in songs composed for pleasure, just as flatterers praise even bad kings with mendacious panegyrics. This evil originated among the Greeks, whose levity, armed with rhetorical skill and abundance of speech, stirred up incredible clouds of falsehoods. Admiring them, men adopted their sacred rites and handed them down to all nations. On account of this vanity the Sibyl rebukes them: "O Greece, why do you trust in leaders of men? Why offer vain gifts to the dead? Do you sacrifice to idols? Who put this plan in your mind, to perform these rites while abandoning the face of the great God?" Marcus Tullius, who was not only a consummate orator but also a philosopher — indeed the sole imitator of Plato — did not hesitate in the book where he consoled himself for his daughter's death to say that the gods publicly worshipped were men. His testimony must be judged most serious, since he held the augural priesthood and himself worshipped and venerated those same gods. In a few verses he gave us two things: by professing that he would consecrate his daughter's image in the same manner as the ancients had consecrated theirs, he taught that those gods were dead and revealed the origin of vain superstition. When he says that we see many men and women from the human race numbered among the gods, and that we venerate their most august shrines in cities and fields, let us agree with the wisdom of those whose genius and inventions have given us a whole life cultivated and established by laws and institutions. If any creature was ever worthy of consecration, she certainly was. If the progeny of Cadmus, Amphitryon, or Tyndareus was to be raised to heaven by fame, then this same honor must surely be given to her — and I will do it, placing you, the best and most learned of all, in the assembly of the immortal gods themselves, with their approval, in the opinion of all mortals, I will consecrate her. Perhaps someone will claim that Cicero was delirious from excessive grief. But that entire speech — perfect in doctrine, examples, and the very manner of speaking — came from a steady mind and sound judgment, and this very statement shows no sign of grief. I do not think he could have written so variously, so copiously, so ornately unless his grief had been softened by reason itself, the consolation of friends, and the passage of time. What, moreover, when he says the same thing in *On the Republic* and *On Glory*? In *On the Laws*, following Plato to establish laws that would make a city just and wise, he sanctioned religion thus: "Let them worship the gods who have always been considered heavenly, and also those whom merit has placed in heaven: Hercules, Liber, Aesculapius, Castor, Pollux, Quirinus." Similarly in the *Tusculan Disputations*, when he said that almost the whole heaven is filled with the human race, he added: "If indeed we scrutinize ancient things and draw out from them what the writers of Greece have produced, those very gods of the nations, who are considered to have originated from us, will be found to have gone to heaven." Since their tombs are shown in Greece, he says, remember — because you have been initiated — what is handed down in the mysteries: then you will finally understand how far this extends. He testified, evidently appealing to Atticus's conscience, that from the mysteries themselves one can understand that all those who are worshipped were men. When he confessed without hesitation about Hercules, Liber, Aesculapius, Castor, and Pollux, and about Apollo and Jupiter as their fathers, and similarly about Neptune, Vulcan, Mars, and Mercury, whom he called the gods of the nations, he feared to speak openly. Therefore he says this extends far, so that we may understand the same concerning Jupiter and the other more ancient gods. If the ancients consecrated their memory in the same manner as he says he will consecrate his daughter's image and name, such error can be forgiven in the grieving, but not in the believing. For who is so foolish as to think that the consensus and applause of innumerable fools can open heaven to the dead, or that anyone can give what he himself does not possess to another? Among the Romans, Julius was made a god because it pleased that wicked man Antony; Quirinus was made a god because it seemed right to the shepherds — though one was a twin brother and the other a parricide of his father. But if Antony had not been consul, Gaius Caesar would have been denied even the honor due a dead man for his merits to the republic, by the counsel of his father-in-law Piso and his relative Lucius Caesar, who forbade his funeral, and of the consul Dolabella, who overthrew the column — that is, Caesar's tomb — in the forum and purified the forum. Ennius declares that Romulus was longed for by his people; the people, grieving their lost king, cry out: "O Romulus, Romulus, tell us what kind of guardian of the fatherland the gods produced in you! You brought us within the boundaries of light, O father, O begetter, O blood relative of the gods." Because of this longing it was more easily believed that Julius Proculus was lying — he had been suborned by the fathers to announce to the people that he had seen the king in a form more august than human, and that the king had commanded them to build him a temple, declaring himself a god and called Quirinus. By this deed he persuaded the people that Romulus had gone to the gods, and freed the senate from the suspicion of regicide.

latin: Quibus ex rebus cum constet illos homines fuisse, non est obscurum qua ratione dii coeperint nominari. si enim nulli reges ante Saturnum uel Uranum fuerunt propter hominum raritatem, qui agrestem uitam sine ullo rectore uiuebant, non est dubium quin illis temporibus homines regem ipsum totamque gentem mactare summis laudibus ac nonis honoribus coeperint, ut etiam deos appellarent siue ob miraculum uirtutis — hoc uere putabant rudes adhuc et simplices — siue, ut fieri solet, in adulationem praesentis potentiae siue ob beneficia quibus erant ad humanitatem conpositi. deinde ipsi reges cum cari fuissent iis quorum uitam composuerant, magnum sui desiderium mortui reliquerunt. itaque homines eorum simulacra finxerunt, ut haberent aliquod ex imaginum contemplatione solacium, progressique longius per amorem memoriam defunctorum colere coeperunt, ut et gratiam referre bene meritis uiderentur et successores eorum adlicerent ad bene imperandi cupiditatem. quod Cicero de natura deorum docet dicens: suscepit autem uita hominum consuetudoque communis, ut beneficiis excellentis uiros in caelum fama ac uoluntate tollerent. hinc Hercules, hinc Castor, hinc Pollux, hinc Aesculapius, hinc Liber. et alio loco: atque in plerisque ciuitatibus intellegi potest acuendae uirtutis gratia aut quo libentius rei publicae causa periculum adiret optimus quisque, uirorum fortium memoriam honore deorum inmortalium consecratam. hac scilicet ratione Romani Caesares suos consecrauerunt et Mauri suos reges. sic paulatim religiones esse coeperunt, dum illi primi qui eos nouerant eo ritu suos liberos ac nepotes, deinde omnes posteros imbuerunt, et hi tandem summi reges ob celebritatem nominis in prouinciis omnibus colebantur. priuatim uero singuli populi gentis aut urbis suae conditores, seu uiri fortitudine insignes erant seu feminae castitate mirabiles, summa ueneratione coluerunt, ut Aegyptus Isidem, Mauri Iubam, Macedones Cabirum, Poeni Uraniam, Latini Faunum, Sabini Sancum, Romani Quirinum, eodem utique modo Athenae Mineruam, Samos Iunonem, Paphos Venerem, Vulcanum Lemnos, Liberum Naxos, Apollinem Delos. sic per populos atque regiones uaria sacra suscepta sunt, dum homines grati esse in suos principes cupiunt et quos alios honores uita carentibus deferant, inuenire non possunt. praeterea pietas eorum qui successerant plurimum contulit ad errorem: qui ut • diuina stirpe nati uiderentur, diuinos honores parentibus detulerunt deferrique iusserunt. an potest aliquis dubitare, quomodo religiones deorum sint institutae, cum apud Maronem legat Aeneae uerba sociis imperantis: nunc pateras libate Ioui precibusque uocate Anchisen genitorem —? cui non tantum immortalitatem, uerum etiam uentorum tribuit potestatem: poscamus uentos, atque haec me sacra quotannis urbe uelit posita templis sibi ferre dicatis. idem scilicet de Ioue Liber et Pan et Mercurius et Apollo fecerunt ac postea de his ipsis successores eorum. accesserunt etiam poetae et compositis ad uoluptatem carminibus in caelum eos sustulerunt, sicut faciunt qui apud reges etiam malos panegyricis mendacibus adulantur. quod malum a Graecis ortum est, quorum leuitas instructa dicendi facultate et copia incredibile est quantas mendaciorum nebulas excitauerit. itaque admirati eos et susceperunt primi sacra illorum et uniuersis gentibus tradiderunt. ob hanc uanitatem Sibylla sic eos increpat: Ἑλλὰς δὴ, τί πέποιθας ἐπ᾽ ἀνδράσιν ἡγεμόνεσσι; πρὸς τί δὲ δῶρα μάταια καταφθιμένοις πορίζεις; θύεις εἰδώλοις; τίς σοι πλάνον ἐν φρεσὶ θῆκεν ταῦτα τελεῖν προλιπόντα θεοῦ μεγάλοιο πρόσωπον. M. Tullius, qui non tantum perfectus orator, sed etiam philosophus fuit, siquidem solus extitit Platonis imitator, in eo libro quo se ipse de morte filiae consolatus est, non dubitauit dicere deos qui publice colerentur homines fuisse. quod ipsius testimonium eo debet grauissimum iudicari, quod et augurale habuit sacerdotium et eosdem se colere uenerarique testatur. itaque intra paucos uersiculos duas res nobis dedit. nam dum imaginem filiae eodem se modo consecraturum esse profitetur quo illi a ueteribus sint consecrati, et illos mortuos esse docuit et originem uanae superstitionis ostendit. cum uero inquit et mares et feminas complures ex hominibus in deorum numero esse uideamus et eorum in urbibus atque agris augustissima delubra ueneremur, adsentiamur eorum sapientiae quorum ingeniis et inuentis omnem uitam legibus et institutis excultam constitutamque habemus. quod si ullum umquam animal consecrandum fuit, illud profecto fuit. si Cadmi progenies aut Amphitryonis aut Tyndari in caelum tollenda fama fuit, huic idem honos certe dicandus est. quod quidem faciam teque omnium optimam doctissimam adprobantibus diis inmortalibus ipsis in eorum coetu locatam ad opinionem omnium mortalium consecrabo. fortasse dicat aliquis prae nimio luctu delirasse Ciceronem. atquin illa omnis oratio et doctrina et exemplis et ipso loquendi genere perfecta non aegri, sed constantis animi ac iudicii fuit et haec ipsa sententia nullum praefert indicium doloris. neque enim puto illum tali uarie, tam copiose, tam ornate scribere potuisse, nisi luctum eius et ratio ipsa et consolatio amicorum et longitudo temporis mitigasset. quid quod idem dicit in libris de re publica, idem de gloria? nam de legibus, quo in opere Platonem secutus leges uoluit ponere, quibus putaret usuram esse iustam et sapientem ciuitatem, de religione ita sanxit: diuos et eos qui caelestes semper habiti sunt colunto et ollos quos endo caelo merita locauerunt, Herculem Liberum Aesculapium Castorem Pollucem Quirinum. item in Tusculanis, cum diceret totum paene caelum humano genere conpletum, si uero inquit scrutari uetera et ex illis ea quae scriptores Graeciae prodiderunt eruere coner, ipsi illi maiorum gentium di qui habentur hinc a nobis profecti in caelum reperientur. quare quoniam demonstrantur sepulchra in Graecia, reminiscere, quoniam es initiatus, quae tradantur mysteriis: tum denique quam hoc late pateat intelleges. testatus est uidelicet Attici conscientiam, ex ipsis mysteriis intellegi posse quod omnes illi homines fuerint qui coluntur, et cum de Hercule Libero Aesculapio Castore Polluce incunctanter fateretur, de Apolline ac Ioue patribus eorum, item de Neptuno Uulcano Marte Mercurio, quos maiorum gentium deos appellauit, timuit aperte coner. et idcirco ait late hocpatere, ut idem de Ioue ceterisque antiquioribus diis intellegamus, quorum memoriam si eadem ratione ueteres consecrauerunt, qua se imaginem nomenque filiae consecraturum esse dicit, ignosci maerentibus potest, credentibus non potest. quis enim tam demens, qui consensu et plaCitO innumerabilium stultorum aperiri caelum mortuis arbitretur aut aliquem quod ipse non habeat dare alteri posse? apud Romanos deus Iulius, quia hoc scele- rato homini placuit Antonio, deus Quirinus, quia hoc pastoribus uisum est, cum alter gemini fratris extiterit, alter patriae parricida. quodsi non consul fuisset Antonius, Gaius Caesar pro suis in rem publicam meritis etiam defuncti hominis honore caruisset, et quidem consilio Pisonis soceri et Lucii Caesaris propinqui, qui uetabant funus ei fieri, et Dolabellae consulis, qui columnam in foro id est tumulum eius euertit ac forum expiauit. nam Romulum desiderio suis fuisse declarat Ennius, apud quem populus amissum regem dolens haec loquitur: o Romule, Romule die, qualem te patriae custodem di genuerunt! tu produxisti nos intra luminis oras, o pater, o genitor, o sanguen dis oriundum. ob hoc desiderium facilius creditum est Iulio Proculo mentienti, qui subornatus a patribus est, ut nuntiaret plebi uidisse se regem humano habitu augustiorem eumque mandasse ad populum, ut sibi delubrum fieret, se deum esse et Quirinum uocari. quo facto et ipsi populo persuasit Romulum ad deos abisse et senatum suspicione caedis regiae liberauit.
excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 15. How they who were men obtained the name of gods.

excerpts.author: Lactantius
english: I turn now to Rome's own cults, having already addressed the common ones. Divine honors were bestowed on the wolf that nursed Romulus — and one might accept that, if the actual animal were the object of worship. But Livy records that the image honored was not the wolf's body but the mind and character of Larentia. She was Faustulus' wife, and because of the shame attached to her body, the shepherds called her 'Lupa' — that is, a prostitute; hence the word 'lupanar' for a brothel. The Romans followed the Athenian precedent in shaping this figure: when the prostitute Leaena killed a tyrant at Athens, they could not lawfully erect her statue in a temple, so they set up an effigy of the animal whose name she bore. Thus the Athenians made a monument from a name; the Romans made one from a profession. A feast day was dedicated to her name, and the Larentalia were instituted. Nor do the Romans worship only this prostitute; they also worship Faula, whom Verrius records as the mistress of Hercules. What kind of immortality is this that even harlots attain? Flora, after amassing great wealth through prostitution, made the Roman people her heir and left a sum whose annual interest would fund games on her birthday — the games called Floralia. The Senate found this shameful, so it was decided to derive a pretext from the name itself, to lend some dignity to a disgraceful thing. They invented a goddess presiding over flowers who must be placated so that crops, trees, and vines might flourish. The poet in the Fasti followed this coloring, telling how a noble nymph named Chloris, wed to Zephyr, received from her husband the dominion over all flowers as a bridal gift. The story is told honorably, but it is believed shamefully and basely; such veils must not deceive us when we seek the truth. Accordingly those games are celebrated with all lasciviousness, fittingly commemorating a harlot. For beyond the license of speech that pours out every obscenity, prostitutes strip naked at the crowd's demand, act as mimes, and are held in public view with shameful movements until the spectators are sated. Tatius consecrated the image of Cloacina, found in the Cloaca Maxima; ignorant of whose likeness it was, he named her from the place. Tullus Hostilius fashioned and worshiped Pavor and Pallor. What can one say of this, except that it befitted a man who always kept his gods at hand, as people commonly wish? This differs from Marcus Marcellus' consecration of Honor and Virtue in the honesty of the names, yet agrees in the substance. The Senate, in the same vanity, placed Mind among the gods — a Mind which, if they truly possessed it, would never have led them to undertake such rites. Cicero calls it a bold and great design of the Greeks to have consecrated images of Cupids and Loves in the gymnasia; he was plainly flattering Atticus and mocking a friend. For it was neither great nor a design at all, but the lost and desperate wickedness of shameless men who prostituted their own children — whom they ought to have trained in honor — to the lust of youth. From such men came the demand that gods of shame be worshiped precisely in those places where naked bodies lie exposed to corrupt eyes, and at that age which is simple and unwary, more easily caught in snares than able to guard against them. What wonder if every vice flowed from a people among whom vices themselves are religious — not only not avoided, but actually worshiped? Therefore Cicero added, as if the Greeks excelled in prudence: 'Virtues ought to be consecrated, not vices.' But if you accept that, Marcus Tullius, do you not see that vices will burst in alongside virtues, because evils cling to goods and are more powerful in human minds? And if you forbid the consecration of vices, Greece will answer that she worships some gods to gain their help, others to avert their harm — the perpetual excuse of those who make their evils into gods, as the Romans do with Rust and Fever. So if vices are not to be consecrated — a point I grant — then neither should virtues. For virtues do not possess wisdom or feeling in themselves, nor do they dwell within walls or mud-built shrines; they must be lodged in the heart and grasped inwardly, lest they become false when placed outside a man. Therefore I mock that famous law of yours which you phrase thus: 'But for the man to whom ascent to heaven is given, let there be temples of Mind, Virtue, Piety, Faith.' Yet these cannot be separated from man. If they are to be worshiped, they must exist in man himself. If they exist outside him, what use is it to worship what you lack? Virtue is to be worshiped, not the image of virtue; and it is to be worshiped not by sacrifice, incense, or formal prayer, but by will and purpose alone. For what is worshiping virtue except comprehending it with the mind and holding it fast? Each person achieves this the moment he begins to will it. This alone is the worship of virtue: for no religion or reverence is due except to the one God. Why then, wisest of men, occupy space with superfluous buildings that could serve human needs? Why appoint priests to tend vain and senseless things? Why immolate victims? Why spend such sums fabricating and worshiping images? The human heart is a stronger and more incorruptible temple: let it be adorned, let it be filled with true divinities. These false consecrations follow of necessity. For those who worship virtues this way — that is, who chase shadows and images of virtues — cannot hold the true virtues themselves. Hence there is no virtue in anyone, vices reigning everywhere; no faith, each seizing everything for himself; no piety, greed and lust driving men to poison and the sword, sparing neither kin nor parents; no peace, no concord, public wars raging and private hatreds flaming to bloodshed; no chastity, unbridled lusts defiling every sex and every part of the body. And yet they do not cease to worship the very things they flee and hate. They offer incense and the pinch of fingertips to things they ought to abhor with their inmost senses — an error springing from ignorance of the highest and chief Good. When the Gauls occupied the city and the Romans were besieged on the Capitol, they made catapults from women's hair and consecrated a temple to Venus Calva. Thus they do not perceive how empty their religions are, even from the fact that they mock them with such follies. Perhaps they learned from the Lacedaemonians to invent gods from events. When the Lacedaemonians besieged the Messenians, and the Messenians slipped out by deceit to plunder Lacedaemon, they were routed by Spartan women. The Lacedaemonians, discovering the trick, pursued. Armed women went out to meet them at a distance. Seeing their husbands preparing for battle, thinking them Messenians, the women bared their bodies. The men, recognizing their wives and inflamed to lust, mingled with them promiscuously, still armed — there was no time to distinguish — just as the young men sent earlier with the virgins, from whom the Partheniae were born. In memory of this deed they erected a temple and image to Venus Armata: which, though born of a shameful cause, seems more honorable than consecrating Venus Calva. At the same time an altar was set up to Jupiter the Baker, because he had warned them in a quiet moment to bake all their grain into bread and throw it into the enemy camp; this done, the siege was lifted, the Gauls despairing of starving the Romans. What mockery of religion is this? If I were its defender, what could I complain of more gravely than that the divine numen has sunk to such contempt as to be ridiculed by the most shameful names? Who would not laugh at Fornax the oven-goddess, or rather at learned men busying themselves with the Fornacalia? Who can keep from laughter on hearing of the goddess Muta? They say she is the mother of the Lares, and call her Lara or Larunda. What can she grant a worshipper who cannot speak? They also worship Iaca, who betrayed her brother to Hercules about the cattle theft and won divinity for her treachery; and Cunina, who guards infants in cradles and averts the evil eye; and Stercutus, who first taught the art of manuring fields; and Tutinus, in whose shameful lap brides sit, as if the god must first taste their chastity; and a thousand other monsters — so that we might say those who undertook to worship these are more foolish than the Egyptians, who venerate monstrous and ridiculous images. Even those have some semblance. What of those who worship an unshaped, rude stone named Terminus? This is the stone Saturn is said to have swallowed, and not without reason is he honored. When Tarquinius wished to build the Capitol, many gods' shrines stood on the site; he consulted them by augury whether they would yield to Jupiter. The others yielded; Terminus alone stood fast. Hence the poet calls him the immovable rock of the Capitol. From this very fact we see how great Jupiter is — to whom not even a stone yielded, perhaps trusting that he had freed it from his father's jaws. So when the Capitol was built, a hole was left in the roof above Terminus, that he might enjoy the open sky since he had not yielded — a sky which not even those who thought the stone enjoyed it could enjoy themselves. Public supplication is therefore made to him as guardian of boundaries, though he is not only a stone but sometimes a mere stake. What can we say of those who worship such things, except that they themselves are rather stones and stakes?
