english: Moses reports elsewhere that God appeared to Abraham, even though no human being can see God and live. How can God be seen if no one has ever seen Him or is able to see Him? The claim that God was seen would be a lie—unless it was truly God who appeared. From this we understand that the one seen was not the Father, who has never been seen, but the Son, who is accustomed to descend and to be seen precisely because He has descended. He is the image of the invisible God, given so that the frailty and limitation of our human condition might gradually become accustomed to seeing God the Father in the image of God, that is, in the Son of God (John 1:14). Human weakness had to be nurtured step by step toward that glory, so that it might someday be able to see the Father; for great things are dangerous when they come suddenly. Even the sun's light, bursting forth after darkness, does not reveal the day to unaccustomed eyes but blinds them instead. To prevent such damage to human eyes, the rising of this heavenly light ascends gently, its rays increasing little by little, accustoming our vision to bear its full brilliance. In the same way Christ, the image and Son of God, is seen by human beings insofar as He can be seen. Through Him our frailty is nourished, developed, and trained, so that—once accustomed to seeing the Son—we may someday see God the Father Himself, and not be struck down by the sudden, intolerable splendor of His majesty, which would rob us of the vision we have always longed for. Therefore the one seen is the Son; the Son of God is the Word of God; the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and this is Christ (John 1:14). What perverse reasoning doubts that He should be called God, when He is attested as God in so many ways?

Consider Hagar, Sarah's servant, cast out and fleeing. An angel met her at a spring on the road to Shur, questioned her about her flight, gave her counsel of humility, promised her the name "mother" and a multitude of descendants through Ishmael, and showed her where he would dwell (Genesis 16:7-14). Scripture calls this figure both angel and Lord and God—for He would not have promised the blessing of seed unless He were both angel and God. Let heretics examine who is at work here. Was it the Father whom Hagar saw? God is named, but it is absurd to call the Father an angel, lest they invent a second angel. How can He be God if He is an angel, since the name "God" is never given to angels? Unless the truth from both sides compels the conclusion that this is the Son of God: because He is from God He is rightly called God; because He is the Son He is called the Angel of Great Counsel, since He is subject to the Father and announces the Father's will (Isaiah 9:6). This passage fits neither the Father (lest He be called an angel) nor a mere angel (lest he be called God); it fits Christ, who is both God as the Son of God and angel as the announcer of the Father's purpose. Heretics who confess Christ as an angel yet refuse to call Him God act against the Scriptures, which record His frequent visits to humanity in the Old Testament.

Moses adds that God appeared to Abraham at the oaks of Mamre while he sat at his tent door at noon. Abraham saw three men, called one of them Lord, washed their feet, and set before them bread, butter, and abundant milk, urging them to eat as guests (Genesis 18:1). Afterwards he heard that he would become a father, that Sarah would bear a son, and learned of the coming destruction of the Sodomites and that God had descended because of their outcry. If heretics insist the Father was seen there alongside two angels, they make the Father visible. But if it was an angel, why is one of the three called Lord and addressed as God—something never done for a mere angel? The only coherent explanation is that the Son of God, who is also God, appeared to Abraham and was received as a guest, preserving the Father's invisibility and the angel's proper mediocrity. He was anticipating, in a sacramental sign, His future dwelling among Abraham's descendants; He washed their feet as proof of who He was, returning in the sons the right of hospitality the Father had once extended to Him. Lest any doubt remain that this guest was He, the account continues with the destruction of Sodom: the Lord rained fire and sulfur on Sodom and Gomorrah from the Lord in heaven (Genesis 19:24). The prophets speak in God's person: "I will overthrow you as the Lord overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah" (Amos 4:11). Thus the Lord overthrew Sodom—that is, God overthrew Sodom—yet in that overthrow the Lord rained fire from the Lord. This Lord whom Abraham saw and touched was God; the Father, being invisible, was not seen. The one seen and received, the one accustomed to be touched and seen, is the Son of God, who rained fire from the Lord. He is the Word of God; the Word became flesh and dwelt among us; this is Christ (John 1:14). So it was not the Father who was Abraham's guest, but Christ; not the Father who was seen, but the Son; and Christ was seen. Rightly, then, Christ is Lord and God, seen by Abraham in no other way than as the Word, God from God, begotten of the Father before all time.

Again, the same angel and God consoled and visited Hagar after she was cast out with her boy. When the water ran out and the child cried, God heard the boy's voice from where he lay (Genesis 16:7-14). Scripture first says God heard; then it says the angel of the Lord called to Hagar from heaven—identifying the angel as the one just called God, and calling Him Lord whom it had just called angel. This angel and God promises greater comfort: "Do not fear; I have heard the boy's voice. Rise, take him, hold him; I will make him a great nation." If this figure is only an angel, how can he claim the divine prerogative of making a great nation? That power belongs to God alone, confirming that He is God. To prove the point, Scripture immediately adds: God opened Hagar's eyes, she saw a well of living water, filled the skin, gave the boy drink, and God was with the boy (Genesis 16:7-14). The same God who opened her eyes called her from heaven; the one called angel is the same one who, moments before, heard the boy's cry as God. This identity cannot belong to the Father, who is only God and never appears; but it fits Christ, who is not only God but also designated Angel, since He is the Angel of Great Counsel and reveals the Father's bosom, as John testifies (John 1:18). John says the Word made flesh is the one who reveals the Father's bosom. Therefore Christ is not only man, but also angel; not only angel, but also God, as Scripture demonstrates and we believe—lest, refusing to accept that Christ spoke to Hagar, we either make a mere angel into God or count the Almighty Father among the angels.

nisi quoniam, ut deo patri inuisibilitas propria reddatur, et angelo propria mediocritas remittatur, non nisi dei filius, qui et deus est, Abrahae uisus et hospitio receptus esse credetur. quod enim erat futurus, meditabatur in sacramento Abrahae factus hospes, apud Abrahae filios futurus; cuius filiorum pedes, ad probationem quod ipse esset, abluit; reddens in filiis ius hospitalitatis, quod aliquando illi fenerauerat pater. unde et ne qua esset dubitatio quin iste Abrahae hospes fuisset, in Sodomitarum exitu ponitur: quoniam pluit dominus super Sodomam et Gomorram ignem et sulphur a domino de caelo. sic enim et prophetes ex persona dei: subuerti uos, inquit, sécut subuertit dominus Sodomam et Gomorram. dominus ergo Sodomam subuertit, id est, deus Sodomam subuertit: sed.in subuersione Sodomorum dominus pluit ignem a domino. hic autem dominus uisus est Abrahae deus: deus autem hic hospes est Abrahae uisus utique quia tactus. sed cum pater, quia inuisibilis, nec tunc utique uisus sit, uisus est et hospitio receptus et acceptus est, qui solitus est tangi et uideri: hic autem filius dei dominus a domino pluit super Sodomam et Gomorram sulphur atque ignem. hic autem dei uerbum est: uerbum autem dei caro factum est, et habitauit in nobis: hic autem Christus est. non pater igitur apud Abraham hospes, sed Christus fuit; nec tunc pater uisus est, sed filius; uisus autem est Christus. merito igitur Christus et dominus et deus est, qui non aliter Abrahae uisus est, nisi quia ante ipsum Abraham ex patre deo deus sermo generatus est. Adhuc, inquit, idem angelus et deus eandem Agar, fugatam de domo Abrahae cum puero, consolatur et uisitat. nam cum illa in solitudine exposuisset infantem, quia aqua defecisset ex utre, cumque puer ille clamasset, fletum et planctum leuasset, et audiuit, inquit scriptura, deus uocem pueri ae loco ubi erat. cum deum esse, qui uocem audisset infantis, rettulisset, adiecit: et uocauit angelus domini ipsam Agar de caelo; angelum referens esse quem deum dixerat, et~dominum pronuntians esse quem angelum collocarat.. quique angelus et deus adhuc ipsi Agar promittit maiora solacia, dicendo: ne timueris; exaudiui enim uocem pueri de loco ubi erat. surge, sume puerum, et tene: in gentem enim magnam faciam eum. hic angelus, si angelus tantum est, cur hoc sibi uindicat ut dicat: in gentem enim magnam faciam eum, cum hoc utique genus potentiae dei sit, angeli esse non possit? ex quo etiam deus confirmatur esse qui hoc potest facere. quoniam ut hoc ipsum comprobetur, adicitur per scripturam statim: e aperuit deus oculos eius, et uidit puteum aquae uiuae, et abiit, et impleuit utrem de puteo, et dedit puero, et erat deus cum puero. si ergo hic deus erat cum puero, qui aperuit oculos Agar, ut uideret puteum aquae uiuae et hauriret aquam propter urgentem sitis necessitatem; hic autem deus e caelo illam uocat; angelus dictus, cum superius uocem audiens clamantis pueri deus esset potius, non alius intellegitur quam angelus esse pariter et deus. quod cum patri competens et conueniens esse non possit, qui tantummodo deus est, competens autem esse possit Christo, qui non tantummodo deus sed et angelus pronuntiatus est, manifeste apparet non patrem ibi tunc locutum fuisse ad Agar, sed Christum potius, cum deus sit, cui etiam angeli competit nomen, quippe cum magni consili angelus factus sit; angelus autem sit, dum exponit sinum patris, sicut Ioannes edicit. si enim ipse Ioannes hunc eundem, qui sinum exponit patris, uerbum dicit carnem factum esse, ut sinum patris posset exponere, merito Christus non solum homo est, sed et angelus; nec angelus tantum, sed et deus per scripturas ostenditur, et a nobis hoc esse creditur, ne, si non Christum tunc locutum ad Agar uoluerimus accipere, aut angelum deum faciamus, aut deum patrem omnipotentem inter angelos computemus.

excerpts.author: Novatian
excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 21.
english: I could certainly range through all the heavenly Scriptures and stir up a vast forest, so to speak, on this aspect of Christ's divinity, but my aim is not to write against this heresy; it is to lay out briefly the rule of truth concerning the person of Christ. Even though I am hurrying on to other matters, I cannot pass over what the Lord said in the gospel to reveal his majesty: "Destroy this temple, and I will raise it up in three days" (John 2:19), or when he declared elsewhere: "I have authority to lay down my life and to take it up again, for this command I received from my Father" (John 10:18). Who can say he has the power to lay down his own life and take it up again because he received that command from the Father? Who can claim he can raise and rebuild the destroyed temple of his own body? Only the Word who is from the Father, who was with the Father, through whom all things were made and without whom nothing was made (John 1:1-3), the imitator of the Father's works and virtues, the messenger of the invisible God, who came down from heaven and testified to what he saw and heard (John 3:13, 31-32), who came not to do his own will but the will of the Father who sent him (John 6:38), so that as the angel of the great counsel he might reveal to us the laws of the heavenly secrets, and who, becoming flesh, dwelt among us (John 1:14). In this way Christ is proved not only human, because he is the Son of Man, but also God, because he is the Son of God.

But if the apostle also calls Christ the firstborn of all creation (Colossians 1:15), how could he be the firstborn of all creation unless, according to his divinity, he proceeded from God the Father before all creation? If the heretics refuse to accept this, they will be forced to show that Christ is the firstborn of all creation as a mere human, which they cannot do. Therefore, either he is before all creation, so that he is the firstborn of all creation, and not only human, because humanity comes after all creation; or he is only human and comes after all creation. And how can he be the firstborn of all creation except according to that Word which is before creation? And so the firstborn of all creation becomes flesh and dwells among us, that is, he takes on this human who comes after all creation, and thus he dwells among us with him and in him, so that neither the human is subtracted from Christ, nor is the divinity denied. For if he is only before all creation, the human is subtracted from him. But if he is only human, the divinity which is before all creation is cut off. Both, therefore, are united in Christ, both are connected, both are joined, and rightly so: since there is something in him that surpasses creation, the concord of divinity and humanity appears to be pledged in him. For this reason, the one who is expressed as the mediator of God and humans is found to have associated God and human in himself (1 Timothy 2:5).

And if the same apostle reports of Christ that, having stripped off the flesh, he disarmed the powers and authorities, making a public spectacle of them, triumphing over them in himself (Colossians 2:15), he did not present that stripping as pointless unless he also meant to be understood as being clothed again in the resurrection. Who, then, is the one who is stripped and clothed again? Let the heretics ask. For we know that the Word of God was clothed with the substance of flesh, and the same Word was stripped of that same bodily material, which he took up again in the resurrection and, as it were, put on again like a garment. But certainly Christ would not have been stripped or clothed if he were only human. No one ever strips or clothes himself; there must be something else, whatever is put on or taken off from outside. It follows, then, that the Word of God was the one who was stripped of flesh and clothed again in the resurrection; stripped, because he had also been clothed in the nativity. And so in Christ, God is the one who clothes himself, and also the one who strips himself; for the one who clothes himself must also be able to strip himself. He clothes and strips himself with human flesh, as with a tunic of a woven body. And therefore, consequently, the Word was, as we said, of God, who is found now clothed, now stripped.

For he also predicted this beforehand in the blessings: "He will wash his robe in wine, and his garment in the blood of the grape" (Genesis 49:11). If the robe in Christ is flesh, and the garment is the body, let it be asked: whose body is the garment, and whose flesh is the robe? For it is clear to us that the flesh was the robe and the body was the garment of the Word, who washed the substance of the body and the material of the flesh with the blood of the grape, that is, with wine, cleansing the passion of the assumed human. From this, since he is washed, he is human, because the garment that is washed is flesh; but the one who washes is the Word of God, who, in order to wash the garment, became the wearer of the garment. Rightly, therefore, from the substance that was received to be washed, the human is expressed, so that from the authority of the Word who washed, God is shown to be.

latin: Et poteram quidem omnium scripturarum caelestium euentilare tractatus, et ingentem circa istam speciem Christi diuinitatis, ut ita dixerim, siluam commouere: nisi quoniam non tam mihi contra hanc haeresim propositum est dicere, quam breuiter circa personam Christi regulam ueritatis aperire. quamuis tamen ad alia festinem, illud non arbitror praetermittendum, quod in euangelio dominus ad significantiam suae maiestatis expressit dicendo: soluite templum hoc, et ego in triduo suscitabo illud; aut quando in alio loco et alia parte pronuntiat: potestatem habeo animam meam ponendi et rursus recipere eam. hoc enim mandatum accepi a patre. quis est enim, qui dicit animam suam se posse ponere aut animam suam posse se rursum recuperare, quia hoc mandatum acceperit a patre? aut quis dicit destructum corporis sui templum resuscitare rursum et reaedificare se posse? nisi quoniam sermo ille, qui ex patre, qui apud patrem, per quem facta sunt omnia, et sine quo factum est nihil, imitator paternorum operum atque uirtutum, mago inuisibilis dei, qui descendit de caelo, qui quae uidit et audiuit testificatus est, qui non uenit ut faceret suam uoluntatem, sed potius ut faciat patris uoluntatem, a quo missus ad hoc ipsum fuerat, ut magni consilii angelus factus arcanorum caelestium nobis iura reseraret, quique uerbum caro factus habttauit in nobis, ex nobis hic Christus non homo tantum, quia hominis filius, sed etiam deus, quia dei filius, comprobatur. Quod si et primogenitus omnis creaturae ab apostolo dictus sit Christus, quomodo omnis creaturae primogenitus esse potuit, nisi quoniam secundum diuinitatem ante omnem creaturam ex patre deo sermo processit? quod nisi ita haeretici acceperint, Christum hominem primogenitum omnis creaturae monstrare cogentur; quod facere non poterunt. aut igitur ante omnem est creaturam, ut primogenitus sit omnis creaturae, et non homo est tantum, quia homo post omnem creaturam est: aut homo tantum est, et est post omnem creaturam. et quomodo primogenitus est omnis creaturae, nisi secundum uerbum illud quod est ante creaturam? et ideo primogenitus omnis creaturae caro fit et habitat in nobis, hoc est, assumit hunc hominem qui est post omnem creaturam, et sic cum illo et in illo habitat in nobis, ut neque homo Christo subtrahatur, neque diuinitas negetur. nam si tantummodo ante omnem creaturam est, homo in illo subtractus est. si autem tantummodo homo est, diuinitas quae ante omnem creaturam est intercepta est. utrumque ergo in Christo confoederatum est, et utrumque coniunctum est, et utrumque conexum est, et merito, dum est in illo aliquid quod superat creaturam, pignerata in illo diuinitatis et humanitatis uidetur esse concordia. propter quam causam, qui mediator dei et hominum effectus exprimitur, in se deum et hominem sociasse reperitur. Ac si idem apostolus de Christo refert, ut exutus carnem potestates dehonestauit, palam triumphatis illis in semetipso, non utique otiose exutum carne proposuit, nisi quoniam et in resurrectione rursum indutum uoluit intellegi. quis est ergo iste exutus et rursus indutus? requirant haeretici. nos enim sermonem dei scimus indutum carnis substantiam, eundemque rursum exutum eadem corporis materia, quam rursus in resurrectione suscepit et quasi indumentum resumpsit. sed enim neque exutus neque indutus hominem Christus fuisset, si homo tantum fuisset. nemo enim umquam se ipso aut spoliatur aut induitur. sit enim necesse est aliud, quicquid aliunde aut spoliatur aut induitur. ex quo merito sermo dei fuit, qui exutus est carnem et in resurrectione rursus indutus; exutus autem, quoniam et in natiuitate fuerat indutus. itaque in Christo deus est qui induitur, atque etiam exutus sit oportet: propterea quod is qui induitur, pariter et exuatur necesse est. induitur autem et exuitur homine, quasi quadam contexti corporis tunica. ac propterea consequenter sermo fuit, ut diximus, dei, qui modo indutus, modo exutus esse reperitur. hoc enim etiam in benedictionibus ante praedixit: Lauabit stolam suam in uino, et in sanguine uuae amictum suum. si stola in Christo caro est, et amictum ipsum corpus est, requiratur, quis est ille cuius corpus amictum est, et stola caro? nobis enim manifestum est carnem stolam et corpus amictum uerbi fuisse, qui uuae sanguine, id est uino, lauit substantiam corporis et materiam carnis, abluens ex parte suscepti hominis passione. ex quo siquidem lauatur, homo est, quia amictum, quod lauatur, caro est: qui autem lauat, uerbum dei est, qui ut lauaret amictum, amicti susceptor effectus est. merito ex ea substantia, quae recepta est ut lauaretur, homo exprimitur, sic ut ex uerbi auctoritate, qui lauit, deus esse monstretur.

excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 22.
english: But why, even though we seem to be rushing on to another part of the discussion, do we skip over that passage in the apostle? He writes of the one who, existing in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be seized; but he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in human likeness, and, found in appearance as a man, he humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross (Philippians 2:5-8). Therefore God also highly exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father (Philippians 2:9-11).

The text says, ‘Who, when he was in the form of God.’ If Christ were only a man, he would be in the image of God, not in the form—for we know that man was made according to the image, not according to the form, nor do angels possess the form of God. Who, then, is this one who was found in the form of God, as we have said and as we read? It can only be the preeminent and noble Son of God, the Word of God, the imitator of all the Father’s works, who himself works just as his Father does, and is therefore in the form (as we have expressed it) of God the Father. And rightly was he declared to be in the form of God, since he himself is above all things and holds the divine power over all creation, and is God, an example of the Father. Yet this very status he received from his own Father, that he might be both God and Lord of all, and God in the form of God the Father, begotten and brought forth from him.

Therefore, although he existed in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as a thing to be grasped. For even though he knew himself to be God from God the Father, he never compared or equated himself with God the Father, mindful that he is from his Father and that he possesses his very being because the Father gave it to him. Consequently, both before the assumption of flesh and after the assumption of the body, and after the resurrection itself, he rendered obedience to the Father in all things, and continues to render it. This proves that he never considered it a seizure to claim a certain divinity in order to make himself equal to God the Father. On the contrary, being obedient and subject to every command and will of the Father, he was content even to take the form of a servant—that is, to become a man—and to assume the substance of flesh and body, which, by being born, he took on from the bondage of the Father’s sins according to man. At that time he also emptied himself, by not refusing to take on the frailty of the human condition.

For if he had been born only as a man, he would not have been emptied; a man, when born, grows, he is not emptied. For while he begins to be what he was not, he cannot possess what he did not have; as we have said, he is not emptied but rather grows and is enriched. But if Christ is emptied in his birth by taking the form of a servant, how can he be only a man? Of such a one it would have been more truly said that he was enriched, not emptied, when he was born—unless it is because the authority of the divine Word, resting for a time in order to assume humanity and not exercising his own powers, lowered himself for a time and laid them aside, while bearing the man he had assumed. He empties himself as he descends to injuries and insults, as he hears blasphemies and endures indignities. Yet the fruit of that humility appears at once. For he received the name that is above every name, which we understand to be none other than the name of God. Since it belongs to God alone to be above all things, it follows that the name which is above every name belongs to him who is above all things. That name, therefore, is God’s; and it belongs, consequently, to him who, existing in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as a thing to be grasped.

For if Christ were not God, every knee would not bow to him—in heaven and on earth and under the earth—nor would all creation, visible and invisible, every creature, be subjected or made subject to a mere man who remembered that he existed before man. From the fact that Christ is said to be in the form of God, and that he is shown to have emptied himself in his birth according to the flesh, and that it is declared he received from the Father the name that is above every name, and that every knee of heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings is shown to bow and bend at that name, and that this very thing is asserted to happen to the glory of God the Father—it follows, consequently, that he is not a man only because he became obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross. From these preceding realities, which proclaim the divinity of Christ, the Lord Christ Jesus is shown to be God, which the heretics refuse to accept.

latin: Cur autem, licet ad aliam partem disputandi festinare uideamur, illum praetereamus apud apostolum locum? gui cum in forma dei esset, non rapinam arbitratus est aequalem se deo esse; sed semetipsum exinaniuit, formam serui accipiens, in similitudine hominum factus, et habitu tnwentus ut homo: humiliauit se, oboediens factus usque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis: propterea et deus illum superexaltauit, et dedit illi nomen quod est super omne nomen; ut in nomine Iesu omne genu flectatur caelestium terrestrium et infernorum, et omnis lingua confiteatur, quoniam dominus Iesus in gloria est dei patris. qui cum in forma dei esset, inquit. si homo tantummodo Christus, in imagine dei, non forma det rehominem enim scimus ad imaginem, non ad sed nec in angelis formam dei Quis ergo est iste, qui in forma dei, ut diximus, factus est legimus; nisi quoniam hic praecipuus atque generosus prae omnibus dei filius, uerbum dei, imitator omnium paternorum operum, dum et ipse operatur sicut et pater eius, in forma (ut expressimus) est dei patris. et merito in forma pronuntiatus est dei, dum et ipse super omnia, et omnis creaturae diuinam obtinens potestatem, et deus est exemplo patris; hoc ipsum tamen a patre proprio consecutus, ut omnium et deus esset, et dominus esset, et deus ad formam dei patris ex ipso genitus atque prolatus. hic ergo quamuis esset in forma dei, non est rapinam arbitratus aequalem se deo esse. qQuamuis enim se ex deo patre deum esse meminisset, numquam se deo patri aut comparauit aut contulit, memor se esse ex suo patre, et hoc ipsum, quod est, habere se, quia pater dedisset. inde denique et ante carnis assumptionem, sed et post assumptionem corporis, post ipsam praeterea resurrectionem, omnem patri in omnibus rebus oboedientiam praestitit pariter ac praestat. quo probatur numquam arbitratum illum esse rapinam quandam diuinitatem, ut aequaret se patri deo: quin immo contra, omni ipsius imperio et uoluntati oboediens atque subiectus, etiam ut formam serui susciperet contentus fuit—hoc est, hominem illum fieri—et substantiam carnis et corporis, quam ex paternorum secundum hominem delictorum seruitute uenientem nascendo suscepit. quo tempore se etiam exinaniuit, dum humanam condicionis fragilitatem suscipere non recusauit. quoniam si homo tantummodo natus fuisset, per hoc exinanitus non esset. homo enim nascens augetur, non exinanitur: nam dum incipit esse quod cum non esset habere non potuit, ut diximus, non exinanitur, sed potius augetur atque ditatur. at si Christus exinanitur in eo quod nascitur, formam serui accipiendo, quomodo homo tantummodo est? de quo uerius dictum fuisset, locupletatum illum esse tunc cum nasceretur, non exinanitum: nisi quoniam auctoritas diuini uerbi, ad suscipiendum hominem interim conquiescens, nec se suis uiribus exercens, deicit se ad tempus atque deponit, dum hominem fert quem suscepit. exinanit se, dum ad iniurias contumeliasque descendit, dum audit infanda, experitur indigna. cuius tamen humilitatis adest statim egregius fructus. accepit enim omen, quod est super omne nomen, quod utique non aliud intellegimus esse quam nomen dei. nam cum dei sit solius esse super omnia, consequens est, ut nomen illud quod est super omne nomen sit eius, qui super omnia est. dei est ergo nomen illud quod super,omne nomen est: quod nomen est eius utique consequenter, qui, cum in forma dei fuisset, non rapinam arbitratus est aequalem se deo esse. neque enim si non deus esset Christus, omne se in nomine eius genu flecteret, caelestium et terrestrium et infernorum: nec uisibilia aut inuisibilia, aut rerum omnium omnis creatura homini esset subiecta siue substrata, quae se ante hominem esse meminisset. ex quo dum iz forma dei esse Christus dicitur, et dum in natiuitatem secundum carnem se exinanisse monstratur, et dum id accepisse nomen a patre quod sit super omne nomen exprimitur, et dum in nomine eius omne genu caelestium, terrenorum et infernorum se flectere et curuare monstratur, et hoc ipsum in gloriam dei patris succurrere asseritur; consequenter non ex illo tantum homo est, quia oboediens patri factus est usque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis; sed ex his etiam rebus superioribus diuinitatem Christi sonantibus, dominus Christus Iesus et deus, quod haeretici nolunt, esse monstratur.

excerpts.author: Novatian
excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 23.
english: At this point I am allowed to collect arguments even from the side of other heretics. A proof drawn from an opponent is especially solid, because then the truth is established even by the enemies of truth themselves. Scripture makes it so clear that God exists that many heretics, overwhelmed by the magnitude and truth of his divinity, have carried their honors for him beyond all measure and have dared to proclaim or imagine not the Son but God the Father himself. That view contradicts the truth of Scripture, yet it stands as a great and principal argument for the divinity of Christ. He is so truly God, yet precisely as the Son of God born from God, that many heretics (as I said) have accepted him as God in such a way that they thought he ought to be called not the Son but the Father. Let them consider, then, whether this is the God whose authority has so moved certain people that they thought him, as I said above, to be God the Father himself, confessing the divinity in Christ without restraint and with such fullness that the manifest divinity of Christ compelled them to regard the One they read of as the Son — because they perceived him as God — as the Father. Other heretics have likewise embraced the manifest divinity of Christ so completely that they said he was without flesh, and they stripped away the whole man assumed by him, lest they diminish the power of the divine name in him by associating a human birth with him, as they supposed. We do not approve of that; but we offer the argument that Christ is so much God that some have thought him to be only God, with the man removed, while others have believed him to be God the Father himself. For the reason and balance of the heavenly scriptures show Christ to be God, but as the Son of God, and with the man also assumed by God the Son, he is to be believed to be a man as well. Since he came to human beings in order to be the mediator of God and men, it was necessary for him to be with them, and for the Word to become flesh, so that in himself he might establish harmony between earthly and heavenly things, while joining the pledges of both sides in himself and linking God to men and men to God; so that the Son of God, by the assumption of flesh, may become the Son of men, and the Son of men, by the reception of the Word of God, may become the Son of God. The salvation of the human race, destined before the ages, is found fulfilled in the Lord Jesus Christ, who is both God and man, and by that condition the human race may be brought to the fruit of eternal salvation.

latin: Hoc in loco licebit mihi argumenta etiam ex aliorum haereticorum parte conquirere. firmum est genus probationis, quod etiam ab aduersario sumitur, ut ueritas etiam ab ipsis inimicis ueritatis probetur. nam usque adeo hunc manifestum est in scripturis esse et deum tradi, ut plerique haereticorum, diuinitatis ipsius magnitudine et ueritate commoti, ultra modum extendentes honores eius, ausi sint non filium sed ipsum deum patrem promere uel putare. quod, etsi contra scripturarum ueritatem est, tamen diuinitatis Christi argumentum grande atque praecipuum est; qui usque adeo deus, sed qua filius dei natus ex deo, ut plerique illum (ut diximus) haeretici ita deum acceperint, ut non filium sed patrem pronuntiandum putarint. aestiment ergo an hic sit deus, cuius auctoritas tantum mouit quosdam, ut putarent illum, ut diximus superius, iam ipsum patrem deum, effrenatius et -effusius in Christo diuinitatem confitentes, ad hoc illos manifesta Christi diuinitate cogente, ut, quem filium legerent, quia deum animaduerterent, patrem putarent. alii quoque haeretici usque adeo Christi manifestam amplexati sunt diuinitatem, ut dixerint illum fuisse sine carne, et totum illi susceptum detraxerint hominem, ne decoquerent in illo diuini nominis potestatem, si humanam illi sociassent, ut arbitrabantur, natiuitatem. quod tamen nos non probamus; ut merito filius dei per assumptionem carnis filius hominis, et filius hominis per receptionem dei uerbi filius dei effici possit. salutem generis humani ante saecula destinatum, in domino Iesu Christo deo et homine inuenitur impleri, quo condicio generis humani ad fructum aeternae salutis posset adduci.

excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 24.
english: I think the source of this heretical error is that they see no difference between the Son of God and the son of man, so that, once a distinction is made, both the man and God, Jesus Christ, can be easily proven. They want the same person—the human son of man—to be also the Son of God, so that the man, the flesh, and that fragile substance may be declared identical with the Son of God. Since no distinction between the son of man and the Son of God is recognized, but the son of man is vindicated as the Son of God, Christ is asserted to be only a man, the same as the Son of God. By this they try to exclude the truth that “the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), and that “you will call his name Emmanuel, which is interpreted God with us” (Matthew 1:23).

They bring forward and allege the passages recorded in Luke’s Gospel, trying to prove not what is true but only what they want to be true: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one to be born will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35). They argue: if the angel of God tells Mary that what is born of her will be holy, then the substance of flesh and body comes from Mary. This substance—that is, this holy thing born of her—they claim is the Son of God. The man himself, they say, and that flesh of the body, the thing called holy, is the Son of God; so that when Scripture says ‘holy,’ we should understand Christ the son of man to be a man, and when it presents the Son of God, we should perceive not God but a man.

But divine Scripture easily convicts and exposes the heretics’ frauds and thefts. If the text were only: “The Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one born of you will be called the Son of God,” then we might need a different kind of argument against them, and we would have to seek other arguments and take up other weapons to overcome their snares and deceptions. But since Scripture itself, abounding with heavenly fullness, strips off the calumnies of these heretics, we readily rely on what is written and overcome these errors without any doubt.

For, as we have already shown, the angel did not say merely “therefore the holy one born of you will be called the Son of God,” but added a conjunction: “therefore and the holy one born of you will be called the Son of God.” This shows that the holy thing born of her—that is, this substance of flesh and body—is not primarily the Son of God, but secondarily. Primarily, the Son of God is the Word of God incarnate through that Spirit of whom the angel speaks: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1:35). This is the true Son of God, who is from God. He assumes this holy thing, attaches the son of man to himself, draws him to himself, and translates him; by his own connection and commingling he grants and makes the son of man the Son of God, which he was not by nature. Thus the primacy of this divine name resides in the Spirit of the Lord who descends and comes; the sequence of the name belongs to the Son of God and man, and this Son of God is deservedly made, since he is not primarily the Son of God.

Therefore the angel, seeing this arrangement and unfolding the order of this sacrament, did not confuse everything so as to leave no trace of distinction, but established a distinction, saying: “therefore and the holy one born of you will be called the Son of God.” If he had not dispensed this distribution with its proper weights but had left it confused and mixed, he would have truly given the heretics an occasion to declare that the son of man, as man, is the same as the Son of God. But now, expounding particularly, he clearly expressed the order and reason of so great a sacrament, so that he said, “the holy one born of you will be called the Son of God,” proving that the Son of God descends. When he received the son of man into himself, he consequently made him the Son of God, because he associated and joined the son of man to himself, so that when the son of man adheres to the Son of God in birth, he might hold by this mixture what he could not possess by his own nature.

And so, by the angel’s voice—which the heretics do not want—a distinction is made between the Son of God and the son of man, even with their association. This urges them to understand that Christ the son of man is a man, and also to perceive that he is the Son of God, and that the man is the Word of God, who, as Scripture says, is God. Therefore they should recognize Christ Jesus the Lord, as it were, woven and compacted from both, and in the concord of both substances mutually bound by the interlocking of a reciprocal covenant—man and God—Scripture itself declaring this very thing with truth.

english: The source of this heretical error, I believe, is their refusal to recognize any distinction between the Son of God and the son of man. They think that by erasing the difference, they can easily prove Jesus Christ to be both man and God. They want the son of man to be identical with the Son of God, so that the man, the flesh, and that fragile human substance may be declared the very Son of God. Since they will not separate the son of man from the Son of God, but instead vindicate the son of man as the Son of God, they end up asserting that Christ is only a man, yet the same as the Son of God. By this maneuver they try to set aside the testimony that "the Word became flesh and dwelt among us" (John 1:14), and that "you will call his name Emmanuel, which means God with us" (Matt 1:23).

They put forward and allege the words recorded in Luke's Gospel, trying to prove not what is true, but only what they wish to be true: "The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one to be born will be called the Son of God" (Luke 1:35). "If," they argue, "the angel of God tells Mary that what is born of her is holy, then the substance of flesh and body comes from Mary. And this substance—that holy thing born of her—is proposed to be the Son of God. The man himself, they say, and that flesh of the body, that which is called holy, is the Son of God. Thus when Scripture says 'holy,' we are to understand Christ the son of man to be a man; and when it presents the Son of God, we are to perceive not God, but a man."

But divine Scripture easily convicts and exposes the heretics' frauds and thefts. If the text were merely: "The Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore what is born of you will be called the Son of God," we might have needed another kind of argument against them, and would have had to seek other proofs and take up other weapons to overcome their snares and deceptions. But since Scripture itself, abundant with heavenly fullness, strips off the calumnies of these heretics, we rely confidently on what is written and overcome these errors without any doubt.

For the angel did not say, as we have already shown, merely "therefore what is born of you will be holy"; he added a conjunction: "therefore *and* what is born of you will be holy" (Luke 1:35). He did this to show that the holy thing born of her—that is, this substance of flesh and body—is *not primarily* the Son of God, but secondarily. Primarily, the Son of God is the Word of God incarnate through that Spirit of whom the angel speaks: "The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you" (Luke 1:35). This is the true Son of God, who is from God. When he assumes this holy thing and joins the son of man to himself, drawing him up to himself, he grants and makes him the Son of God—which he was not by nature—so that the primacy of this divine name may reside in the Spirit of the Lord who descends and comes, while the sequence of the name belongs to the Son of God and man. Thus he deservedly *becomes* the Son of God, since he is not primarily the Son of God.

Therefore the angel, perceiving this arrangement and unfolding the order of this great mystery, did not confuse everything so as to leave no trace of distinction. Instead he marked a distinction, saying: "therefore *and* what will be born of you will be holy, [and] will be called the Son of God" (Luke 1:35). Had he not dispensed this distribution with its proper weights, but left it confused and mixed, he would have truly given the heretics grounds to declare that the son of man, insofar as he is man, is the same as the Son of God. But now, by expounding particularly, he has clearly expressed the order and reason of so great a sacrament, so as to say: "what is born of you will be holy, [and] will be called the Son of God"—proving that the Son of God descends. When he receives the son of man into himself, he consequently makes him the Son of God, because he associates and joins this son to himself, so that when the son of man adheres to the Son of God in birth, he may hold by this mixture what he could not possess by his own nature.

And so, by the angel's voice—what the heretics do not want—a distinction is made between the Son of God and the son of man, yet with their association, urging them to understand that Christ the son of man is a man, and also the Son of God; and that the man is the Word of God, who, as Scripture says, is God. Therefore they may know Christ Jesus the Lord to be composed and concreted from both, and in the concord of both substances, mutually bound by the interweaving of a reciprocal covenant, man and God—Scripture itself speaking this very thing with truth.

excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 28
english: I will now include another section. In it the heretic glories as though with his own eye, yet having lost truth and light he may come to recognize the full blindness of his error. He repeatedly objects that the Lord said, "I have been with you all this time, and still you do not know me? Philip, whoever has seen me has seen the Father" (John 14:9). Let him learn what he fails to understand. Philip is blamed, and justly so, because he said, "Lord, show us the Father, and that will be enough for us." When had he ever heard or learned from Christ that Christ was the Father? On the contrary, he had often heard and learned that he was the Son, not the Father. The Lord said, "If you have known me, you will know my Father also; from now on you do know him and have seen him" (John 14:7). He did not speak this way to be understood as the Father, but because whoever approaches the Son of God with complete faith and complete devotion will reach the Father through the Son, in whom he believes, and will see him. Jesus said, "No one comes to the Father except through me" (John 14:6). Therefore anyone who comes to God the Father will not only come and know the Father, but must also hold and presume in mind and heart as if he already knows and sees the Father. Divine Scripture often announces what has not yet happened as if it were already done, because it will certainly happen; it narrates what must happen in every way not as future but as already accomplished. Long before Christ was born in Isaiah's time, it said, "A child is born to us" (Isa 9:6). Before he had come to Mary, it told the prophet, "He came, and she conceived and bore a son" (Isa 7:14). Before Christ had revealed the Father's bosom, it declared, "His name will be called Angel of Great Counsel" (Isa 9:6 LXX). Before he had suffered, it proclaimed, "He was led like a lamb to the slaughter" (Isa 53:7). Before the cross existed, it said, "All day long I have stretched out my hands to a disobedient people" (Isa 65:2; Rom 10:21). Before he had been given vinegar to drink, it said, "They gave me vinegar for my thirst" (Ps 69:21). Before he had been stripped, it said, "They cast lots for my garment" (Ps 22:18), "they numbered my bones" (Ps 22:17), "they pierced my hands and feet" (Ps 22:16). Divine Scripture foreknows the future and speaks of future deeds as already done, of future perfections as already perfect, without any doubt. Therefore the Lord said in this passage, "From now on you know him and have seen him" (John 14:7). He meant that the Father would be seen by anyone who followed the Son—not that the Son himself was the Father seen, but that whoever followed him and chose to be his disciple would receive the reward of seeing the Father. The Son is the image of God the Father (Col 1:15; Heb 1:3), so that we may add: just as the Father works, so the Son works, and the Son imitates all the Father's works (John 5:19). Thus each person may have it as if he already saw the Father when he sees the one who always imitates the invisible Father in every work.

But if Christ himself were the Father, how could he immediately add, "Whoever believes in me will do the works I do, and greater works than these, because I am going to the Father" (John 14:12)? He also adds, "If you love me, keep my commandments, and I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Advocate" (John 14:15–16). After that he adds, "If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him" (John 14:23). He also adds, "The Advocate, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send, will teach you and remind you of everything I have said" (John 14:26). He anticipates this passage to show that he is the Son, and rightly adds, "If you loved me, you would rejoice that I am going to the Father, for the Father is greater than I" (John 14:28). What then when he also adds, "I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser. Every branch in me that bears no fruit he takes away, and every branch that does bear fruit he prunes, so that it may bear more fruit" (John 15:1–2)? He further adds, "As the Father loved me, so I have loved you; abide in my love. If you keep my commandments, you will abide in my love, just as I kept my Father's commandments and abide in his love" (John 15:9–10). He also says, "I have called you friends, because I have made known to you everything I heard from my Father" (John 15:15). He adds, "They will do all these things to you on account of my name, because they do not know the one who sent me" (John 15:21). The Lord would never have added these things, which plainly testify that he is not the Father but the Son, if he had remembered being the Father or wanted to be understood as the Father—unless he wanted to express that each person ought to hold it as if he already saw the Father when he sees the image of God the Father through the Son, and as if he saw the Father. For every believer in the Son is exercised in contemplating the image, so that, becoming accustomed to seeing the divinity in the image, he may advance and grow until he reaches the perfect contemplation of God the Father Almighty. And whoever drinks this in with mind and heart and believes that all these things will be so, will possess the Father he is to see as if he had already seen him and already holds him, because he knows for certain that he will possess him.

But if he himself were the Father, what future reward would he promise when he had already given and bestowed it? Since he says, "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God" (Matt 5:8), he is caught promising the contemplation and vision of the Father. Therefore he had not yet given it; why would he promise it if he had already given it? He would have given it if he were the Father; he would have been seen and touched. Yet while Christ himself was being touched and seen, he still promised that the pure in heart will see God. This very fact proves he is not the Father, who, though present and seen, promised that the pure in heart would see the Father. So it was not the Father but the Son who promised these things; because he was the Son, he promised what he was destined to be seen—a promise that would have been superfluous if he were not the Son. Why would he promise the pure in heart that they would see the Father, if those present were already seeing the Father in Christ? But because he was the Son, not the Father, and rightly the Son because he is the image of God, he was seen at that time, while the Father, being invisible, is promised to the pure in heart so that he may be seen and recognized. This is enough, even against this heretic—a few points out of many. For a field, broad and spacious, will open if we wish to engage this heretic more fully; since, blinded by the removal of two passages, he is utterly overcome by the blindness of his doctrine.

Haec ergo numquam post illa euidenter illum non patrem sed filium esse testantia dominus subdidisset, si aut patrem se esse meminisset, aut patrem se uellet intellegi. nisi quoniam ut illud exprimeret, perinde unumquemque iam habere debere, dum imaginem dei patris per filium uidet, atque si uiderit patrem—quandoquidem unusquisque credens in filium exerceatur in imaginis contemplatione, ut assuefactus ad diuinitatem uidendam imagine proficere possit et crescere usque ad dei patris omnipotentis perfectam contemplationem,—et quoniam, qui hoc animo ac mentecombiberit et de omnibus sic futurum esse crediderit, patrem, quem uisurus sit, quasi iam quodammodo uiderit et hic iam sic habeat, quasi teneat, quod habiturum se pro certo sciat. Ceterum, si ipse pater fuisset, quid quasi futurum praemium repromittebat, quod iam praestiterat et dederat? nam quoniam dicit: beati mundo corde, quia ipsi deum uidebunt, polliceri deprehenditur contemplationem et aspectum patris. ergo nondum dederat: cur enim repromitteret, si iam dedisset? dederat enim, si pater esset; uidebatur enim, et contingebatur. quando autem, dum contingitur ipse Christus et uidetur, repromittit tamen et dicit, quoniam qui mundo fuerit corde, deum uidebit, hoc ipso probat patrem se non esse, qui tunc praesens cum uideretur repromittebat, quod patrem uisurus esset quisquis mundo corde fuisset. erat ergo repromittens haec non pater sed filius; quia qui filius erat, quod uideri habebat repromittebat: cuius repromissio superuacua fuisset, nisi filius fuisset. cur enim repromittebat mundis ut uiderent patrem, Si iam tunc qui praesentes erant, patrem Christum uidebant? sed quia filius erat, non pater, merito et filius, quia imago dei, tunc uidebatur, et pater, quia inuisibilis, mundis corde, ut uideretur, repromittitur et notatur. Haec igitur satis sit etiam aduersus istum haereticum dictasse, pauca de multis. campus enim, et quidem latus ac fusus, aperietur, plenius haereticum istum si agitare uoluerimus; quandoquidem duobus istis locis quibusdam effossis luminibus orbatus, totus sit in doctrinae suae caecitate superatus.

english: The order of reason and the authority of faith, once we have taken in the Lord's own words and letters, urge us to believe also in the Holy Spirit. He was promised to the church long ago, but given at the times God appointed. He is promised through the prophet Joel, but given through Christ. "In the last days," God says, "I will pour out my Spirit on my servants and handmaids" (Joel 2:28-29). And the Lord himself said, "Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive anyone's sins, they are forgiven; if you retain them, they are retained" (John 20:22-23). The Lord Christ calls this same Spirit now the Paraclete, now the Spirit of truth. He is not new in the gospel, nor was he given anew. For this very Spirit accused the people through the prophets, and through the apostles he gave advocacy to the nations. The people deserved accusation because they had despised the law; the Gentiles who believe deserve the Spirit's patronage because they strive to attain the law of the gospel. There is a real difference in the kinds of duties he performs, because the reason for his action changes with the times. Yet he himself is not different, nor does he become another; he remains one and the same, dividing his offices across times, occasions, and moments. As the apostle Paul says, "Having the same Spirit... as it is written: 'I believed, therefore I spoke,' we also believe, therefore we also speak" (2 Cor 4:13). So it is one and the same Spirit who is in the prophets and the apostles — only there he was present for a moment, here he abides always. There he was not given to stay in them permanently; here he is given to remain in them always. There he was distributed in measure; here he is poured out fully. There he was given sparingly; here he is bestowed lavishly. He was not bestowed before the Lord's resurrection, but was given through Christ's resurrection. For Jesus said, "I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Advocate to be with you forever, the Spirit of truth" (John 14:16-17). And: "When the Advocate comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father" (John 15:26). And: "If I do not go away, the Advocate will not come to you; but if I go, I will send him to you" (John 16:7). And: "When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all truth" (John 16:13). Because the Lord was about to ascend to heaven, he necessarily gave the Paraclete to the disciples, so he would not leave them like orphans — which would be unfitting — abandoning them without an Advocate and guardian. This is the One who strengthened their souls and minds, who distinguished the gospel sacraments, who was the illuminator of divine things in them. Confirmed by him in the Lord's name, they feared neither prisons nor chains; indeed they trampled the powers of the world and its torments, armed and strengthened through him, bearing the gifts which this same Spirit distributes and directs to Christ's church, the bride, as her ornaments. He is the One who establishes prophets in the church, teaches teachers, directs tongues, produces virtues and healings, works miracles, extends discernment of spirits, supplies governance, suggests counsels, and composes and arranges all the other charismatic gifts — thus making the Lord's church perfect and complete in every way and everywhere.

This is the One who, in the form of a dove, came upon Jesus and remained after his baptism, dwelling in Christ alone, full and entire, not mutilated in any measure or portion, but distributed and sent with all his abundance. He did this so that others might receive a share of grace from him, while the fountain of the whole Holy Spirit remains in Christ, so that from him the veins of gifts and works may flow, the Holy Spirit dwelling abundantly in Christ. For Isaiah already prophesied this: "The Spirit of wisdom and understanding shall rest on him, the Spirit of counsel and might, the Spirit of knowledge and piety, and he will fill him with the Spirit of the fear of God" (Isa 11:2-3). This same identical Spirit speaks in another place in the person of the Lord himself: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to bring good news to the poor" (Luke 4:18). Similarly David: "Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of joy beyond your companions" (Ps 45:7). About this the apostle Paul says: "Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him" (Rom 8:9); and: "Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom" (2 Cor 3:17). This is the One who works a second birth from water, a seed of divine generation, and the consecrator of heavenly birth, a pledge of the promised inheritance, and as it were a deed of eternal salvation. He makes us God's temple and his house. He intercedes for us before God with inarticulate groans, fulfilling the office of advocacy and exhibiting the gifts of defense. He is given to inhabit our bodies and to effect our sanctification. Doing this in us, he brings our bodies to eternity and to the resurrection of immortality, accustoming them to be mixed with heavenly virtue and associated with the divine eternity of the Holy Spirit. For our bodies are instructed in him and through him to advance toward immortality, as they learn to govern themselves moderately according to his decrees. This is the One who opposes the flesh, because the flesh resists him. He restrains insatiable desires, breaks immoderate lusts, extinguishes illicit passions, conquers flaming impulses, rejects drunkenness, repels avarice, drives out luxurious revelries, binds charities, constrains affections, repels sects, establishes the rule of truth, conquers heretics, casts out the wicked, guards the gospels. About this same Spirit the apostle says: "We have not received the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God" (1 Cor 2:12). He exults: "I think that I also have the Spirit of God" (1 Cor 7:40). He says: "The spirits of prophets are subject to prophets" (1 Cor 14:32). He reports: "The Spirit explicitly says that in later times some will depart from the faith, paying attention to deceitful spirits and teachings of demons, through the hypocrisy of liars" (1 Tim 4:1-2). Caution is placed in this Spirit so that no one ever says 'Anathema' to Jesus: no one denies Christ the Son of God, or repudiates the Creator God; no one speaks words against the Scriptures; no one establishes other sacrilegious decrees; no one writes divergent laws. Whoever blasphemes against this Spirit has no forgiveness, not only in this age but also in the age to come. This Spirit bears witness to Christ in the apostles, shows the constant faith of religion in the martyrs, seals admirable continence of chastity in virgins, guards the incorrupt and uncontaminated rights of the Lord's doctrine in all others, destroys heretics, corrects the perverse, accuses the faithless, exposes hypocrites, corrects the wicked, and guards the church incorrupt and inviolate in the holiness of perpetual virginity and truth.

latin: Sed enim ordo rationis et fidei auctoritas digestis uocibus et litteris domini admonet nos post haec credere etiam in spiritum sanctum, olim ecclesiae repromissum, sed statutis temporum opportunitatibus redditum. est enim per Ioelem prophetam repromissus, sed per Christum redditus. in nouissimis, inquit, diebus effundam de spiritu meo super seruos et ancillas meas. dominus autem: accipite spiritum sanctum; quorum remiseritis peccata, erunt remissa; et quorum retinueritis, erunt retenta. hunc autem spiritum sanctum dominus Christus modo paracletum appellat, modo spiritum ueritatis esse pronuntiat. qui non est in euangelio nouus, sed nec noue datus. nam hic ipse et in prophetis populum accusauit, et in apostolis aduocationem gentibus praestitit. nam illi ut accusarentur merebantur, quia contempserant legem: et qui ex gentibus credunt, ut patrocinio spiritus adiuuentur merentur, quia ad euangelicam peruenire gestiunt legem. differentia sane in illo genera officiorum, quoniam in temporibus differens ratio causarum: nec ex hoc tamen ipse diuersus, qui haec sic gerit, nec alter est, dum sic agit, sed unus atque ipse est, diuidens officia sua per tempora et rerum occasiones atque momenta. denique apostolus Paulus: habentes, inquit, eundem spiritum, sicut scriptum est: credidi, propter quod locutus sum, et nos credimus, ideo loquimur. vnus ergo et idem spiritus, qui in prophetis et apostolis; nisi quoniam ibi ad momentum, hic semper. ceterum ibi, non ut semper in illis inesset, hic, ut in illis semper maneret: et ibi mediocriter distributus, hic totus effusus; ibi parce datus, hic large commodatus; nec tamen ante resurrectionem’ domini exhibitus, sed per resurrectionem Christi contributus. rogabo enim aiebat, patrem, et alium aduocatum dabit uobis, ut uobiscum sit in aeternum, spiritum ueritatis. et: cum uenerit aduocatus ile, quem ego missurus sum uobis a patre meo, spiritum ueritatis, qui de patre meo procedit. et: si non abiero ego, aduocatus ille non ueniet ad uos: si autem ego abiero, remittam illum ad uos. et: cum uenerit spiritus ueritatis, ille uos diriget in omnem ueritatem. et quoniam dominus in caelos esset abiturus, paracletum discipulis necessario dabat, ne illos quodammodo pupillos, quod minime decebat, relinqueret, et sine aduocato et quodam tutore desereret. Hic est enim qui ipsorum animos mentesque firmauit, qui -euangelica sacramenta distinxit, qui in ipsis illuminator rerum diuinarum fuit, quo confirmati pro nomine domini nec carceres nec uincula timuerunt; quin immo ipsas saeculi potestates et tormenta calcauerunt, armati iam scilicet per ipsum atque firmati, habentes in se dona, quae hic idem spiritus ecclesiae Christi sponsae quasi quaedam ornamenta distribuit et dirigit. hic est enim qui prophetas in ecclesia constituit, magistros erudit, linguas dirigit, uirtutes et sanitates facit, opera mirabilia gerit, discretiones spirituum porrigit, gubernationes contribuit, consilia suggerit, quaeque alia sunt charismatum dona componit et digerit; et ideo ecclesiam domini undique et in omnibus perfectam et consummatam facit. Hic est qui in modum columbae, posteaquam dominus baptizatus est, super eum uenit et mansit, habitans in solo Christo plenus et totus, nec in aliqua mensura aut portione mutilatus, sed cum tota sua redundantia cumulate distributus et missus, ut ex illo delibationem quandam gratiarum ceteri consequi possint, totius sancti spiritus in Christo fonte remanente, ut ex illo donorum atque operum uenae ducerentur, spiritu sancto in Christo affluenter habitante. hoc etenim iam prophetans Esaias aiebat: et requiescit, inquit, super eum spiritus sapientiae et intellectus, spiritus consili et uirtutis, spiritus scientiae et pietatis, et implebit eum spiritus timoris dei, hoc idem atque ipsum et alio in loco ex persona ipsius domini: spiritus domini super me; propter quod unxit me, euangelizare pauperibus misit me. similiter Dauid: propterea unxit te, deus, deus tuus oleo laetitiae a consortibus tuis. de hoc apostolus Paulus: guz enim spiritum Christi non habet, hic non est eius; et: vbi spiritus domini, tht libertas. Hic est qui operatur ex aquis secundam natiuitatem, semen quoddam diuini generis, et consecrator caelestis natiuitatis, pignus promissae hereditatis, et quasi chirographum quoddam aeternae salutis; qui nos dei faciat templum, et nos eius efficiat domum. qui interpellat diuinas aures pro nobis gemitibus ineloquacibus, aduocationis implens officia, et defensionis exhibens munera, inhabitator corporibus nostris datus, et sanctitatis effector; qui id agens in nobis ad aeternitatem et ad resurrectionem immortalitatis corpora nostra producat, dum illa in se assuefacit cum caelesti uirtute misceri, et cum spiritus sancti diuina aeternitate sociari. erudiuntur enim in illo et per ipsum corpora nostra ad immortalitatem proficere, dum ad decreta ipsius discunt se moderanter temperare. hic est enim "qui contra carnem desiderat, quia caro contra ipsum repugnat. hic est qui inexplebiles cupiditates coercet, immoderatas libidines frangit, illicitos ardores exstinguit, flagrantes impetus uincit, ebrietates reicit, auaritias repellit, luxuriosas comissationes fugat, caritates nectit, affectiones constringit, sectas repellit, regulam ueritatis expedit, haereticos reuincit, improbos foras exspuit, euangelia custodit. De hoc idem apostolus: on enim spiritum mundi accepimus, sed spiritum qui ex deo est. de hoc exsultat, et dicit: puto autem quia et ego spiritum dei habeo. de hoc dicit: et spiritus prophetarum prophetis subiectus est. de hoc refert: spiritus autem manifeste dicit, quia in nouissimis temporibus recedent quidam a fide, attendentes spiritibus seductoribus, doctrinis daemoniorum, in hypocrisi mendacia loguentium, cautertatam in hoc spiritu positus nemo umquam dicit anathema Iesum: nemo negauit Christum dei filium, aut repudiauit creatorem deum: nemo contra scripturas ulla sua uerba depromit: nemo alia et sacrilega decreta constituit: nemo diuersa iura conscribit. in hunc quisquis blasphemauerit, remissionem non habet, non tantum in isto saeculo, uerum etiam nec in futuro. hic in apostolis Christo testimonium reddit, in martyribus constantem fidem religionis ostendit, in uirginibus admirabilem continentiam signatae castitatis includit, in ceteris incorrupta et incontaminata doctrinae dominicae iura custodit, haereticos destruit, peruersos corrigit, infideles arguit, simulatores ostendit, improbos quoque corrigit, ecclesiam incorruptam et inuiolatam perpetuae uirginitatis et ueritatis sanctitate custodit.

english: I have spoken briefly about the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, setting things forth succinctly without lengthy debate, though I could have treated the matter more extensively and argued it more fully, since the entire Old and New Testament can be summoned as witness that the true faith stands exactly as I have stated. However, because heretics who battle against the truth habitually drag the sincere tradition and the Catholic faith into controversy, scandalized by Christ because He is also God and is so proclaimed in Scripture and believed by us, we must rightly dispute that Christ is God in a way that impedes neither the truth of Scripture nor our own faith — the faith that holds and believes one God promised through the Scriptures. Both those who claim Jesus Christ is the Father Himself and those who insist He was merely a man have seized the roots and causes of their error and perversity from this very point: when they observed that Scripture writes there is one God, they thought they could maintain that confession only by deciding Christ must be either a mere man or the Father Himself. Thus they habitually gather their calumnies so as to try to validate their own error.

Those who call Jesus Christ the Father argue like this: if there is one God, and Christ is God, then Christ is the Father, because there is one God; but if Christ is not the Father, then — since Christ is the Son of God — two Gods appear to be introduced contrary to the Scriptures. Those who contend Christ is only a man reason the opposite way: if the Father is one and the Son another, and the Father is God and Christ is God, then two Gods are introduced together, the Father and the Son; and if there is one God, then Christ must consequently be a man so that the Father alone may be the one God. In truth the Lord is crucified between these two thieves just as He once was crucified, and so He receives the sacrilegious insults of these heretics from both sides. Yet neither the Holy Scriptures nor we supply the causes of their perdition and blindness if they either refuse to see or are unable to see the truths plainly set in the midst of the divine letters.

For we know, read, believe, and hold that there is one God who made heaven and earth alike, since we know no other and never will be able to know one, for none exists. 'I am,' He says, 'God, and there is no just and saving one besides Me' (Isaiah 44:6). And in another place: 'I am the first and the last, and there is no God besides Me. Who is like Me?' (Isaiah 44:6). And: 'Who has measured the heavens with a span, and the earth with a fist? Who has suspended the mountains in a balance, and the forests in a scale?' (Isaiah 40:12). And Hezekiah: 'that all may know that You are the only God' (Isaiah 37:16, 20). Moreover the Lord Himself: 'Why do you ask Me about what is good? There is one good God' (Matthew 19:17). The Apostle Paul also: 'He alone has immortality and dwells in unapproachable light, whom no human has seen or can see' (1 Timothy 6:16). And in another place: 'A mediator is not of one, but God is one' (Galatians 3:20).

But just as we hold, read, and believe this, so we must not pass over any part of the heavenly Scriptures: we must not refuse the signs of Christ's divinity placed in the Scriptures, lest by corrupting the authority of the Scriptures we be found to have corrupted the integrity of the holy faith. Therefore we should believe, since it is most faithful, that Jesus Christ, the Son of God, is our Lord and God: because in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God (John 1:1). This was in the beginning with God. And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14). And: 'My Lord and my God' (John 20:28). And: 'of whom are the fathers, and from whom Christ came according to the flesh, who is over all, God blessed forever' (Romans 9:5).

What then shall we say? Do the Scriptures propose two Gods? How then does it say there is one God? Or is Christ not God? How then was it said to Christ, 'My Lord and my God'? Therefore, unless we hold all this with proper reverence and legitimate reasoning, we will be thought to have given a scandal to the heretics — not because of any fault in the heavenly Scriptures, which never deceive, but because of the presumption of human error by which the heretics chose to be. First of all, this must be thrown back at those who presume to manufacture a controversy about two Gods for us. It is written, which they cannot deny, that there is one Lord (Deuteronomy 6:4; 1 Corinthians 8:6). What then do they think of Christ? That He is the Lord, or that He is not at all? But they do not doubt that He is the Lord; therefore, if their reasoning is true, there are already two Lords. How then is there one Lord according to the Scriptures? And Christ is said to be one Master; yet we read that the Apostle Paul is also a Master (1 Corinthians 4:15; 2 Timothy 1:11). So there is not one Master; for we infer two Masters from these things. How then is Christ one Master according to the Scriptures? One God is said to be good in the Scriptures; but in the same Scriptures Christ is also said to be good. Therefore, if they reason correctly, there is not one good but two goods. How then is there one good according to the faith of the Scriptures? And if they do not think any office can be attributed to the fact that there is one Lord through the fact that Christ is Lord; nor to the fact that there is one Master through the fact that Paul is Master; nor to the fact that there is one good through the fact that Christ is called good — by the same reasoning they should understand that an office cannot be taken away from the fact that there is one God by the fact that Christ is pronounced God.

latin: Et haec quidem de patre et de filio et de spiritu sancto breuiter sint nobis dicta, et strictim posita, et non longa disputatione porrecta. latius enim potuerunt porrigi, et propensiore disputatione produci, quandoquidem ad testimonium, quod ita se habeat fides uera, totum et uetus et nouum testamentum possit adduci. sed quia obluctantes aduersus ueritatem semper haeretici sincerae traditionis et catholicae fidei controuersiam solent trahere, scandalizati in Christum, quod etiam deus et per scripturas asseratur et a nobis hoc esse credatur, merito a nobis (ut omnis a fide nostra auferri possit haeretica calumnia) de eo quod et deus sit Christus sic est disputandum, ut non impediat scripturae ueritatem, sed nec nostram fidem, qua unus deus et per scripturas promitur, et a nobis tenetur et creditur. tam enim illi qui Iesum Christum ipsum deum patrem dicunt, quam etiam illi qui hominem illum tantummodo esse uoluerunt, erroris sui et peruersitatis origines et causas inde rapuerunt, quia cum animaduerterent scriptum esse quod unus sit deus, non aliter putauerunt istam tenere se posse sententiam, nisi aut hominem tantum Christum, aut certe deum patrem putarent esse credendum. sic enim calumnias suas colligere consueuerunt, ut errorem proprium approbare nitantur. et quidem illi qui Iesum Christum patrem dicunt, ista praetendunt: si unus deus, Christus autem deus, pater est Christus, quia unus deus: si non pater sit Christus, dum et deus filius Christus, duo dii contra scripturas introducti esse uideantur. qui autem hominem tantummodo Christum esse contendunt, ex diuerso sic colligunt: si alter pater, alter est filius, pater autem deus, et Christus deus, non ergo unus deus, sed duo dii introducuntur pariter, pater et filius; ac si unus deus, consequenter homo Christus, ut merito pater sit deus unus. re uera quasi inter duos latrones cruci figitur dominus, quo modo fixus aliquando est: et ita excipit haereticorum istorum ex utroque latere sacrilega conuicia. Sed neque scripturae sanctae, neque nos causas illis perditionis et caecitatis afferimus, si qua in medio diuinarum ro litterarum euidenter posita aut uidere nolunt, aut uidere non possunt. nos enim et scimus et legimus et credimus et tenemus unum esse deum, qui fecit caelum pariter ac terram, quoniam nec alterum nouimus aut nosse (cum nullus sit) aliquando poterimus. ego sum, inquit, deus: e non est praeter me iustus et saluans. et alio in loco: ego primus et nouissimus, et praeter me non est deus. quis sicut ego? et: quis mensus est palmo caelum, et terram pugillo? quis suspendit montes in pondere, et nemora in statera? et Ezechias: ut sciant omnes quia tu es deus solus. ipse praeterea dominus: quid me interrogas de bono? unus deus bonus. apostolus quoque Paulus: guz solus, inquit, habet immortalitatem, et lucem habitat inaccessibilem; quem uidit hominum nemo, nec uidere potest. et alio in loco: mediator autem unius non est; deus autem unus est. sed quo modo hoc tenemus et legimus et credimus, sic scripturarum caelestium nullam partem praeterire debemus: quippe cum etiam illa quae in scripturis sunt posita Christi diuinitatis insignia nullo modo debemus recusare, ne scripturarum auctoritatem corrumpendo integritatem fidei sanctae corrupisse teneamur. et hoc ergo credamus, siquidem fidelissimum, dei filium Iesum Christum dominum et deum nostrum: quoniam zz principio erat uerbum, et uerbum erat apud deum, et deus erat uerbum. hoc erat in principio apud deum. et uerbum caro factum est, et habitauit in nobis. et: dominus meus et deus meus. et: quorum patres, et ex quibus Christus secundum carnem, qui est super omnia deus benedictus in saecula. Quid ergo dicemus? numquid duos deos scriptura proponit? quomodo ergo dicit, quia deus unus est? aut numquid non et Christus deus est? quomodo ergo, dominus meus et deus meus, Christo dictum est? totum igitur hoc nisi cum propria ueneratione et legitima disputatione teneamus, merito scandalum haereticis praebuisse credemur, non utique ex scripturarum caelestium uitio, quae numquam fallunt, sed humani erroris praesumptione, qua haeretici esse uoluerunt. et in primis illud retorquendum in istos qui duorum nobis deorum controuersiam facere praesumunt. scriptum est, quod negare non possunt, quoniam unus est dominus. de Christo ergo quid sentiunt? dominum esse, aut illum omnino non esse? sed dominum illum omnino non dubitant: ergo si uera est illorum ratiocinatio, iam duo sunt domini.. quomodo igitur iam secundum scripturas unus est dominus? et magister unus Christus est dictus; attamen legimus, quod magister sit etiam apostolus Paulus. non ergo iam unus magister: duos enim magistros secundum ista colligimus. quomodo igitur secundum scripturas unus magister Christus? unus in scripturis bonus dictus est deus; sed iisdem in scripturis bonus etiam Christus positus est. non igitur, si recte colligunt, unus bonus, sed etiam duo boni. quomodo igitur secundum scripturarum fidem unus bonus esse refertur? ac si non putant aliqua ratione offici posse ei quod unus dominus est, per illud quod est dominus et Christus; neque ei quod unus est magister, per illud quod est magister et Paulus; aut illi quod unus est bonus, per illud quod bonus sit nuncupatus et Christus; eadem ratione intellegant offici non posse ab illo quod unus est deus, ei quod deus pronuntiatus est et Christus.
