excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 31
english: God the Father is the founder and creator of all things. He alone has no origin; he is invisible, immense, immortal, eternal, the one God. Nothing can be preferred to his magnitude, majesty, or power, nor can anything even be compared with them. From him, when he so willed, his Son the Word was born. The Word is not a sound made by struck air or a tone forced from the throat; he is recognized as the very substance of the power that God produced. The secrets of this sacred, divine birth are known to the Son alone, who knows the Father's secrets; no apostle learned them, no prophet discovered them, no angel knew them, no creature perceived them. Since he is generated by the Father, the Son always exists in the Father. I say "always" not to suggest he is innate, but to prove he is generated. Because he exists before all time, he must be said to have always been in the Father; no time can be assigned to one who is before time itself. The Father always precedes him, because the one who has no origin precedes the one who has an origin. At the same time, the Son is lesser, since he knows he exists in the Father, having an origin because he is born. Through the Father, though he has an origin by which he is born, he stands near in birth, since he is born from the Father who alone has no origin. When the Father willed, the Son proceeded from the Father. He who was in the Father because he was from the Father came to be with the Father because he proceeded from him — that divine substance named the Word, through whom all things were made and without whom nothing was made. All things come after him because they exist through him; rightly he is before all things, but after the Father, since all things were made through him. The one who proceeded from the Father, from whose will all things were made, is God proceeding from God, constituting a second person after the Father, namely the Son, yet not depriving the Father of being the one God. If the Son had not been born, he would have been innate; compared with the innate Father, equality would appear in both, making two innates and therefore two Gods. If he had not been generated, he would be comparable to the ungenerated Father; found equal, they would constitute two ungenerated Gods, and Christ would have made two Gods. If he were without origin like the Father, he would be another principle of all things, yielding two principles and consequently two Gods. If he were not the Son but the Father generating another Son from himself, then compared with the Father and marked as equally great, he would produce two Fathers and thus two Gods. If he were invisible like the Father, the two would be expressed as equal, showing two invisibles and therefore two Gods. If he were incomprehensible, or possessed any other attribute of the Father, we say he would rightly have stirred up a controversy over two Gods. But as it stands, whatever the Son is, he is not from himself, because he is not innate; he is from the Father, because he is generated. Whether as Word, power, wisdom, light, or Son — whatever he is — he comes from nowhere else but the Father, owing his origin to his Father, as said above. Therefore he could not introduce a discord in divinity amounting to two Gods, since by being born he received his origin from the one God. Because he is both only-begotten and first-begotten from the one who, having no origin, is the one principle and head of all things, he affirmed one God. That God is not under any principle or beginning; rather, he is the beginning and principle of all things. Finally, this same Son does nothing on his own initiative, acts on no counsel of his own, comes from himself in no way; he obeys all the Father's commands and precepts. Thus, although his birth proves him to be the Son, his obedient subjection asserts him to be the minister of the Father's will, from whom he exists. By rendering himself obedient to the Father in all things, he shows one God, the Father, through his obedience — even though he himself is also God — because he derives his origin from the Father. Consequently he could not make two Gods, because he did not create two origins; he received the principle of his birth before all time from the one who has no origin. The innate one is the principle for all others; God the Father alone is that innate one, existing outside all origin, and from him comes the one who is born. The one born from him rightly comes from the one without origin, proving that one to be the principle from which he himself exists. Even though the one born is God, he demonstrates one God — the one whom the Son himself acknowledges as without origin. He is God, but precisely in being generated so that he might be God. He is Lord, but precisely in being born from the Father so that he might be Lord. He is also an angel, but one destined from his Father to announce the great counsel of God. His divinity is handed down in such a way that it does not appear to have produced two Gods through any discord or inequality. The Father subjected all things to him as Son; while he himself, together with the things subjected to him, submits to his Father, he is proven to be the Father's Son, yet he is found to be both Lord and God over the rest. All things are entrusted to him as God; the Son receives all things subjected to him and refers them back to the Father, thereby remitting the whole authority of divinity to the Father. Thus one God is shown, true and eternal, the Father. From him alone this power of divinity went forth; it was also handed down and directed to the Son, and through communion it returns again to the Father's substance. The Son is shown to be God, the one to whom divinity was handed down and extended; yet nonetheless one God, the Father, is proven, because that majesty and divinity, by a gradual reciprocal movement, return to the Father who gave it, sent back and turned by the Son himself. Rightly, then, God the Father is the God of all, and the principle of his own Son, whom he begot as Lord; the Son is the God of all the rest, because God the Father placed him, whom he begot, over all things. So Christ Jesus, the mediator of God and men, holds all creation subjected to himself by the Father's own power, by which he is God. With all creation subjected to him, he is found in harmony with his Father, God, acknowledging his one, only, and true God, the Father, remaining in that which has also been heard, briefly.

latin: Est ergo deus pater omnium institutor et creator, solus originem nesciens, inuisibilis, immensus, immortalis, aeternus, unus deus; cuius neque magnitudini neque maiestati neque uirtuti quicquam, non dixerim praeferri, sed nec comparari potest. ex quo, quando ipse uoluit, sermo filius natus est: qui non in sono percussi aeris, aut tono coactae de uisceribus uocis accipitur, sed in substantia prolatae a deo uirtutis agnoscitur. cuius sacrae et diuinae natiuitatis arcana nec apostolus didicit, nec prophetes comperit, nec angelus sciuit, nec creatura cognouit; filio soli nota sunt, qui patris secreta cognoulit. Hic ergo, cum sit genitus a patre, semper est in patre. semper autem sic dico, ut non innatum, sed natum probem. sed qui ante omne tempus est, semper in patre fuisse dicendus est: nec enim tempus illi assignari potest, qui ante Semper enim in patre, ne pater non semper sit quia ‘et pater illum etiam praecedit, quod necesse est quoniam antecedat necesse est eum, qui habet originem, ille qui originem nescit; simul ut hic minor sit, dum in illo esse se scit, habens originem, quia nascitur, et per patrem quodam modo, quamuis originem habet, qua nascitur, uicinus in natiuitate, dum ex eo patre, qui originem solus non habet, nascitur. hic ergo quando pater uoluit, processit ex patre: et qui in patre fuit, quia ex patre fuit, cum patre postmodum fuit, quia ex patre processit, substantia scilicet illa diuina, cuius nomen est uerbum, per quod facta sunt omnia, et sine quo factum est nihil. omnia enim post ipsum sunt, quia per ipsum sunt, et merito ipse est ante omnia, sed post patrem, quando per illum facta sunt omnia. qui processit ex eo, ex cuius uoluntate facta sunt omnia, deus utique procedens ex deo, secundam personam efficiens post patrem, qua filius, sed non eripiens illud patri, quod unus est deus. Si enim natus non fuisset, innatus comparatus cum eo qui esset innatus, aequatione in utroque ostensa, duos faceret innatos, et ideo duos faceret deos. si non genitus esset, collatus cum eo qui genitus non esset, et aequales inuenti, duos deos merito reddidissent non geniti; atque ideo duos Christus reddidisset deos. si sine origine esset ut pater, inuentus et ipse principium omnium ut pater, duo faciens principia, duos ostendisset nobis consequenter et deos. aut si et ipse filius non esset, sed pater generans de se alterum filium, merito collatus cum patre et tantus denotatus, duos patres effecisset, et ideo duos approbasset etiam deos. si inuisibilis fuisset, cum inuisibili collatus, par expressus, duos inuisibiles ostendisset, et ideo duos comprobasset et deos. si incomprehensibilis, si et cetera quaecumque sunt patris, merito, dicimus, duorum deorum quam isti confingunt controuersiam suscitasset. nunc autem quicquid est, non ex se est, quia nec innatus est, sed ex patre est, quia genitus est. siue dum uerbum est, siue dum uirtus est, siue dum sapientia est, siue dum lux est, siue dum filius est, et quicquid horum est, dum non aliunde est, quam, sicut diximus iam superius, ex patre, patri suo originem suam debens, discordiam diuinitatis de numero duorum deorum facere non potuit, qui ex illo, qui est unus deus, originem nascendo contraxit. quo genere, dum et unigenitus est et primogenitus ex illo est qui, quia originem non habet, unus est omnium rerum et principium et caput, idcirco unum deum asseruit, quem non sub ullo principio aut initio, sed initium potius et principium rerum omnium comprobauit. Idem est denique quod nihil ex arbitrio suo gerit, nec ex consilio suo facit, nec a se uenit, sed imperiis paternis omnibus et praeceptis oboedit: ut quamuis probet illum natiuitas filium, tamen morigera oboedientia asserat illum paternae uoluntatis, ex quo est, ministrum. ita dum se patri in omnibus obtemperantem reddit, quamuis sit et deus, unum tamen deum patrem de oboedientia sua ostendit, ex quo et originem traxit. Et ideo duos deos facere non potuit, quia nec duas origines fecit, qui ex eo, qui originem non habet, principium natiuitatis ante omne tempus accepit. nam cum id sit principium ceteris quod innatum est (quod deus solus pater est, qui extra originem est, ex quo hic est qui natus est), dum qui ex illo nascitur merito ex eo uenit, qui originem non habet, principium probans illud esse, ex quo ipse est, etiamsi deus est qui natus est, unum tamen deum ostendit, quem hic qui natus est esse sine origine comprobauit. Est ergo deus, sed in hoc ipsum genitus, ut esset deus. est et dominus, sed in hoc ipsum natus ex patre, ut esset dominus. est et angelus, sed ad annuntiandum magnum dei consilium €x patre suo angelus destinatus. cuius sic diuinitas traditur, ut non aut dissonantia aut inaequalitate diuinitatis duos deos reddidisse uideatur. subiectis enim ei quasi filio omnibus rebus a patre, dum ipse cum his, quae illi subiecta sunt, patri suo subicitur, patris quidem sui filius probatur; ceterorum autem et dominus et deus esse reperitur. ex quo dum huic qui est deus omnia substrata traduntur, et cuncta sibi subiecta filius accepta refert patri, totam diuinitatis auctoritatem rursus patri remittit. unus deus ostenditur uerus et aeternus pater, a quo solo haec uis diuinitatis emissa, etiam in filium tradita et directa, rursum substantiae per communionem ad patrem reuoluitur. deus quidem ostenditur filius, cui diuinitas tradita et porrecta conspicitur; et tamen nihilominus unus deus pater probatur, dum gradatim reciproco meatu illa maiestas atque diuinitas ad patrem, qui dederat eam, rursum ab illo ipso filio missa reuertitur et retorquetur; ut merito deus pater omnium deus sit, et principium ipsius quoque filii sui, quem dominum genuit: filius autem ceterorum omnium deus sit, quoniam omnibus illum deus pater praeposuit, quem genuit. ita mediator dei et hominum Christus Iesus, omnis creaturae subiectam sibi habens a patre proprio potestatem, qua deus est, cum tota creatura subdita sibi, concors patri suo deo inuentus, unum et solum et uerum deum patrem suum, manente in illo quod etiam auditus est, breuiter approbauit.

english: Therefore God the Father is the founder and creator of all, the only one who knows no origin, invisible, immense, immortal, eternal, one God; nothing can be compared to His magnitude, His majesty, or His power, let alone preferred above them. When He Himself willed, the Word His Son was born from Him: He is not apprehended in the sound of struck air or in the tone of a voice forced from the viscera, but is recognized in the substance of the power brought forth from God. The secrets of His sacred and divine birth were not learned by the apostle, not discovered by the prophet, not known by the angel, not recognized by any creature; they are known to the Son alone, who has known the Father's secrets. This Son, then, since He is begotten of the Father, is always in the Father. I say 'always' so that I may prove He is begotten, not innate. But He who exists before all time must be said to have been in the Father always; for time cannot be assigned to one who is before all time. The Father precedes Him, for it is necessary that the one who has an origin be preceded by the One who knows no origin; at the same time the Son is lesser, since He knows He exists in the Father, having an origin because He is begotten, and through the Father He is in some sense near in His birth, because He is begotten of the Father who alone lacks an origin. So then, when the Father willed, He proceeded from the Father; and He who was in the Father, because He was from the Father, was afterwards with the Father because He proceeded from the Father — that divine substance whose name is the Word, through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made. For all things come after Him, because they are through Him, and He is rightly before all things, yet after the Father, since all things were made through Him. He who proceeded from Him, from whose will all things were made, is God proceeding from God, constituting a second person after the Father as Son, yet not robbing the Father of what belongs to Him, that He is one God. For if the Son had not been begotten, an innate being compared with another innate would display equality on both sides, making two innate beings and therefore two Gods. If He had not been generated, He would be compared with the One who is not generated; equals would be found, and two ungenerated Gods would rightly result. If He were without origin like the Father, He would be found to be the principle of all things like the Father, producing two principles and consequently showing us two Gods. Or if the Son were not the Son but the Father generating another Son from Himself, rightly compared with the Father and marked as equally great, He would make two Fathers and therefore would approve two Gods. If He were invisible, compared with the Invisible He would appear equal, revealing two invisible beings and therefore proving two Gods. If He were incomprehensible, or possessed any of the Father's other attributes whatsoever, He would rightly raise the controversy of two Gods which these men invent. But now whatever He is, He is not from Himself, because He is not innate, but from the Father, because He is begotten. Whether He is the Word, or Power, or Wisdom, or Light, or the Son, and whatever else He may be, since He is from nowhere else but from the Father, as we have already said above, owing His origin to His Father, He could not create a division of the Godhead into two Gods, since He received His origin by being begotten from the One who is one God. By this very fact, because He is both Only-begotten and Firstborn from the One who, having no origin, is the one source and principle and head of all things, He affirmed one God, whom He proved to be not under any principle or beginning but rather the beginning and principle of all things. In the end He does nothing of His own will, He does nothing from His own counsel, He does not come from Himself, but obeys all the Father's commands and precepts: so that, although His birth proves Him to be the Son, yet His submissive obedience asserts Him to be the minister of the Father's will, from whom He comes. Thus while He renders Himself obedient to the Father in all things, although He is God He shows one God the Father by His obedience, from whom He also drew His origin. And therefore He could not make two Gods, because He did not make two origins, but received the principle of His birth before all time from the One who has no origin. For since the Father is the principle of all things in that He is innate — God the Father alone existing outside all origin, from whom comes the One who is begotten — the One who is begotten from Him rightly comes from the One who lacks an origin, proving Him to be the principle from which He Himself comes; and even though the begotten One is God, He still shows one God, whom He has proved to be without origin. So the Son is God, but He is begotten in order to be God; He is Lord, but He is born of the Father in order to be Lord; He is the Angel, but He is destined by the Father as the Angel to announce the great counsel of God. His divinity is handed down in such a way that it does not appear to have produced two Gods by any discrepancy or inequality of divinity. For since all things are subjected to Him as Son by the Father, while He Himself is subjected to the Father together with the things subjected to Him, He is proved to be His Father's Son; yet He is found to be the Lord and God of all other things. From the moment all things are placed beneath Him, who is God, and He receives all things subjected to Himself and refers them back to the Father, He returns the whole authority of divinity to the Father once more. The one true and eternal God the Father is shown, from whom alone this power of divinity was sent forth, even into the Son, and through communion it circles back to the Father's substance. The Son is shown to be God, to whom divinity was handed down and extended; and yet nonetheless the one God the Father is proved, because gradually, in a reciprocal movement, that majesty and divinity return to the Father who gave them, sent back and turned back by the Son Himself; so that the Father is rightly the God of all things, and the principle of His own Son whom He begot as Lord; and the Son is the God of all other things, because the Father has set Him over all things, the One whom He begot. Thus Christ Jesus, the mediator of God and men, having all creation subjected to Him by the power from His own Father through which He is God, and being found in harmony with His Father God together with all creation subjected to Him, briefly approved the one and only true God, His Father, abiding in what He had also been heard to say.

Si enim natus non fuisset, innatus comparatus cum eo qui esset innatus, aequatione in utroque ostensa, duos faceret innatos, et ideo duos faceret deos. si non genitus esset, collatus cum eo qui genitus non esset, et aequales inuenti, duos deos merito reddidissent non geniti; atque ideo duos Christus reddidisset deos. si sine origine esset ut pater, inuentus et ipse principium omnium ut pater, duo faciens principia, duos ostendisset nobis consequenter et deos. aut si et ipse filius non esset, sed pater generans de se alterum filium, merito collatus cum patre et tantus denotatus, duos patres effecisset, et ideo duos approbasset etiam deos. si inuisibilis fuisset, cum inuisibili collatus, par expressus, duos inuisibiles ostendisset, et ideo duos comprobasset et deos. si incomprehensibilis, si et cetera quaecumque sunt patris, merito, dicimus, duorum deorum quam isti confingunt controuersiam suscitasset. nunc autem quicquid est, non ex se est, quia nec innatus est, sed ex patre est, quia genitus est. siue dum uerbum est, siue dum uirtus est, siue dum sapientia est, siue dum lux est, siue dum filius est, et quicquid horum est, dum non aliunde est, quam, sicut diximus iam superius, ex patre, patri suo originem suam debens, discordiam diuinitatis de numero duorum deorum facere non potuit, qui ex illo, qui est unus deus, originem nascendo contraxit. quo genere, dum et unigenitus est et primogenitus ex illo est qui, quia originem non habet, unus est omnium rerum et principium et caput, idcirco unum deum asseruit, quem non sub ullo principio aut initio, sed initium potius et principium rerum omnium comprobauit. Idem est denique quod nihil ex arbitrio suo gerit, nec ex consilio suo facit, nec a se uenit, sed imperiis paternis omnibus et praeceptis oboedit: ut quamuis probet illum natiuitas filium, tamen morigera oboedientia asserat illum paternae uoluntatis, ex quo est, ministrum. ita dum se patri in omnibus obtemperantem reddit, quamuis sit et deus, unum tamen deum patrem de oboedientia sua ostendit, ex quo et originem traxit. Et ideo duos deos facere non potuit, quia nec duas origines fecit, qui ex eo, qui originem non habet, principium natiuitatis ante omne tempus accepit. nam cum id sit principium ceteris quod innatum est (quod deus solus pater est, qui extra originem est, ex quo hic est qui natus est), dum qui ex illo nascitur merito ex eo uenit, qui originem non habet, principium probans illud esse, ex quo ipse est, etiamsi deus est qui natus est, unum tamen deum ostendit, quem hic qui natus est esse sine origine comprobauit. Est ergo deus, sed in hoc ipsum genitus, ut esset deus. est et dominus, sed in hoc ipsum natus ex patre, ut esset dominus. est et angelus, sed ad annuntiandum magnum dei consilium €x patre suo angelus destinatus. cuius sic diuinitas traditur, ut non aut dissonantia aut inaequalitate diuinitatis duos deos reddidisse uideatur. subiectis enim ei quasi filio omnibus rebus a patre, dum ipse cum his, quae illi subiecta sunt, patri suo subicitur, patris quidem sui filius probatur; ceterorum autem et dominus et deus esse reperitur. ex quo dum huic qui est deus omnia substrata traduntur, et cuncta sibi subiecta filius accepta refert patri, totam diuinitatis auctoritatem rursus patri remittit. unus deus ostenditur uerus et aeternus pater, a quo solo haec uis diuinitatis emissa, etiam in filium tradita et directa, rursum substantiae per communionem ad patrem reuoluitur. deus quidem ostenditur filius, cui diuinitas tradita et porrecta conspicitur; et tamen nihilominus unus deus pater probatur, dum gradatim reciproco meatu illa maiestas atque diuinitas ad patrem, qui dederat eam, rursum ab illo ipso filio missa reuertitur et retorquetur; ut merito deus pater omnium deus sit, et principium ipsius quoque filii sui, quem dominum genuit: filius autem ceterorum omnium deus sit, quoniam omnibus illum deus pater praeposuit, quem genuit. ita mediator dei et hominum Christus Iesus, omnis creaturae subiectam sibi habens a patre proprio potestatem, qua deus est, cum tota creatura subdita sibi, concors patri suo deo inuentus, unum et solum et uerum deum patrem suum, manente in illo quod etiam auditus est, breuiter approbauit.

excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 19. Argument: Moreover, the Poets Have Called Him the Parent of Gods and Men, the Creator of All Things, and Their Mind and Spirit. And, Besides, Even the More Excellent Philosophers Have Come Almost to the Same Conclusion as the Christians About the Unity of God.
english: I hear the poets also proclaim one Father of gods and men, and that the mind of mortals takes its character from whatever day the Parent of all has ordained (Virgil, Aeneid 6.724–725). What of the Mantuan Maro? Does he not speak more openly, more directly, more truly? "In the beginning," he says, "heaven and earth" and the rest of the world's members "are nourished by a spirit within, and an infused mind stirs them. From this comes the race of men and beasts, and every other kind of animal" (Aeneid 6.724–727). Elsewhere he names that mind and spirit God; for it is true: "God goes through all lands and tracts of sea and deep heaven. From him come men and beasts, from him come rain and fire" (Aeneid 6.727–729). What else do we proclaim about God but that he is mind, reason, and spirit? Let us review, if you please, the teachings of the philosophers, and you will find that, for all their different vocabularies, they converge on this single conclusion. I pass over those crude ancients who earned a reputation for wisdom merely through their sayings. Take Thales of Miletus as the first, the first to debate heavenly matters. Thales said the origin of things is water, but God is the mind that fashioned everything from water. Here is a reason concerning water and spirit higher and more sublime than any human could have discovered; it was handed down by God. You see the leading philosopher's view in full accord with ours. Anaximenes next, and after him Diogenes of Apollonia, posit air as God, infinite and immense. Their consensus on divinity is likewise similar. Anaxagoras calls the description and motion of the infinite mind God. Pythagoras says God is the soul that pervades the whole nature of things and attends to it, from which the life of all animals is also derived. Xenophanes is known for handing down that all infinite things are God with mind; Antisthenes, that there are many popular gods but one natural and principal God; Zeuxippus [corrected to Speusippus], that the natural, animate power by which all things are governed is known as God. What of Democritus? Although he was the first inventor of atoms, does he not often speak of nature, which crafts images, and intelligence, as God? Strato likewise posits nature; even Epicurus, who either imagines gods as idle or nonexistent, nevertheless sets nature above them. Aristotle varies, yet still assigns a single power: sometimes he calls mind God, sometimes the world, sometimes he places God over the world. Aristotle of Pontus also varies, sometimes attributing the first principle to the world, sometimes to the divine mind. Heraclides of Pontus likewise ascribes the divine mind to God, though in various ways. Theophrastus, Zeno, Chrysippus, and Cleanthes are multiform as well; but they all circle back to the unity of providence. For Cleanthes discusses God as mind, sometimes as soul, sometimes as ether, most often as reason. Zeno, his master, holds that natural and divine law, and sometimes ether, sometimes reason, is the principle of all things. Again, by interpreting Juno as air, Jupiter as heaven, Neptune as sea, fire as Vulcan, and showing the other popular gods to be elements, he seriously indicts and refutes the public error. Chrysippus does much the same: he believes the divine power, rational nature, the world, and fatal necessity are God, and he imitates Zeno's physiological interpretation of the songs of Hesiod, Homer, and Orpheus. The Babylonian Diogenes also teaches the exposition and discussion of Jupiter's birth and Minerva's origin, and that such names are not divine at all. The Socratic Xenophon denies that the form of the true God can be seen, and therefore ought not to be sought. The Stoic Aristo says God cannot be comprehended at all. Both, in their desperation to understand, have sensed the majesty of God. Plato's discourse on God, on things themselves, and on their names is more open; it would be wholly heavenly, were it not sometimes sullied by an admixture of civic persuasion. Accordingly, in the Timaeus, God is the parent of the world, the artificer of the soul, the fabricator of heavenly and earthly things—difficult to find because of his too great and incredible power, and impossible to speak of publicly once found, he says. We have much the same, for we know God and call him the Parent of all, and we never preach publicly unless asked.

latin: Audio poetas quoque « unum patrem divum atque hominum » praedicantes, et « talem esse mortalium mentem qualem parens omnium diem duxerit. » Quid Mantuanus Maro? nonne apertius, proximius, verius? « Principio, ait, coelum et terras, » et caetera mundi membra « spiritus intus alit, et infusa mens agitat. Inde hominum pecudumque genus » et quidquid aliud animalium. Idem alio loco, mentem istam et spiritum, Deum nominat; haec enim vera sunt: Deum namque ire per omnes Terrasque tractusque maris coelumque profundum. Unde homines, et pecudes, unde imber et ignis. Quid aliud et a nobis Deus, quam mens et ratio et spiritus praedicatur? Recenseamus, si placet, disciplinas philosophorum, deprehendes eos, etsi sermonibus variis, ipsis tamen rebus in hanc unam coire et conspirare sententiam. (XII) Omitto illos rudes et veteres qui de suis dictis sapientes esse meruerunt. Sit Thales Milesius omnium primus, qui primus omnium de coelestibus disputavit. Is Milesius Thales rerum initium aquam dixit; Deum autem eam mentem quae ex aqua cuncta formaverit. Eho! altior et sublimior aquae et spiritus ratio, quam ab homine potuerit inveniri; a Deo traditum. Vides Philosophi principalis nobiscum penitus opinionem consonare. Anaximenes deinceps, et post Apolloniates Diogenes, aera Deum statuunt, infinitum et immensum. Horum quoque similis de divinitate consensio est. Anaxagorae vero descriptio et motus infinitae mentis Deus dicitur. Et Pythagorae Deus est animus, per universam rerum naturam commeans et intentus: ex quo etiam animalium omnium vita capiatur. Xenophanem notum est omne infinitum cum mente Deum tradere; et Antisthenem, populares deos multos, sed naturalem unum praecipuum; Zeuxippum [ imp. Spensippum], vim naturalem, animalem, qua omnia regantur, Deum nosse. Quid Democritus? quamvis atomorum primus inventor,26 nonne plerumque naturam, quae imagines fundat, et intelligentiam, Deum loquitur? Straton quoque et ipse naturam: etiam Epicurus ille qui deos aut otiosos fingit aut nullos, naturam tamen superponit. Aristoteles variat, et adsignat tamen unam potestatem. Nam interim mentem, mundum interim Deum dicit, interim mundo Deum praeficit. Aristoteles Ponticus variat, alias mundo, alias menti divinae tribuens principatum. Heraclides Ponticus quoque Deo divinam mentem, quamvis varie, adscribit. Theophrastus, et Zenon, et Chrysippus, et Cleanthes, sunt et ipsi multiformes; sed ad unitatem providentiae omnes revolvuntur. Cleanthes enim mentem, modo animum, modo aethera, plerumque rationem Deum disseruit. Zenon, ejusdem magister, naturalem legem atque divinam, et aethera interim, interdumque rationem, vult omnium esse principium. Item interpretando Junonem aera, Jovem coelum, Neptunum mare, ignem esse Vulcanum, et caeteros similiter vulgi deos elementa esse monstrando, publicum arguit graviter et revincit errorem. Eadem fere Chrysippus, vim divinam, rationalem naturam, et mundum interim, et fatalem necessitatem Deum credit, Zenonemque interpretatione physiologiae in Hesiodi, Homeri Orpheique carminibus imitatur. (XIII) Babylonio etiam Diogeni disciplina est exponendi et disserendi Jovis partum et ortum Minervae, et hoc genus caeterarum rerum vocabula esse, non deorum. (XIV) Nam Socraticus Xenophon formam Dei veri negat videri posse, et ideo quaeri non oportere. Aristo Stoicus , comprehendi omnino non posse. Uterque majestatem Dei, intelligendi desperatione; senserunt. Platoni apertior de Deo et rebus ipsis et nominibus oratio est; et quae tota esset coelestis, nisi persuasionis civilis nonnumquam admixtione sordesceret. Platoni itaque in Timaeo Deus est ipso suo nomine mundi parens, artifex animae, coelestium terrenorumque fabricator; quem et invenire difficile, prae nimia et incredibili potestate; et, cum inveneris, in publicum dicere impossibile praefatur. (XV) Eadem fere et ista quae nostra sunt nam et Deum novimus et parentem omnium dicimus, et numquam publice, nisi interrogati, praedicamus.

english: These impure spirits, demons, hide under statues and consecrated images, as magicians, philosophers, and Plato have shown. By their breath they seize authority, as if a divinity were present, while they inspire prophets, haunt temples, sometimes animate the fibers of entrails, govern the flights of birds, control lots, and produce oracles wrapped in many falsehoods. For they both deceive and are deceived, so that they do not confess the true truth they know, to their own perdition. Thus they weigh down from heaven and call people away from the true God to material things; they disturb life, disturb everyone, secretly penetrate even bodies, and as thin spirits they fabricate diseases, terrify minds, and distort limbs, so that they may compel worship of themselves: so that by the smell of altars, or by the sacrifices of fattened animals once sated, they may seem to have cured what they themselves had bound. These are also the raving ones you see rushing out in public; prophets, too, even without a temple, rave just so, frenzy just so, spin just so. The demonic instigation in them is equal, but the form of their madness differs. You also know those things I told you a little while ago about them: that Jupiter would renew games because of a dream, that the Castors would appear with horses, that a matron's girdle would follow a ship. Most of you know all this because the demons themselves confess it about themselves whenever we drive them out of bodies by the torments of words and the fires of prayer. Saturn himself, Serapis, Jupiter, and whatever demons you worship, conquered by pain, declare what they are; nor do they lie, especially with some of you present, to their own shame. Believe them as witnesses when they confess the truth about themselves: they are demons. For when adjured by the true and only God, they shudder unwillingly in wretched bodies, and either leap out immediately or fade away gradually, as the faith of the sufferer assists or the grace of the healer inspires. Thus they flee in haste from the neighborhood of Christians, whom they had long harassed in gatherings through you. Therefore, implanted in the minds of the unskilled, they secretly sow hatred of us through fear: for it is natural to hate those you fear, and to attack those you dread, if you can. Thus they occupy minds and block hearts, so that people begin to hate us before they know us, so that they cannot know us, nor imitate us, nor condemn us.

latin: Isti igitur impuri spiritus, daemones, ut ostensum a magis, a philosophis, et a Platone, sub statuis et imaginibus consecrati delitescunt, et afflatu suo auctoritatem, quasi praesentis numinis, consequuntur, dum inspirantur interim vatibus, dum fanis immorantur, dum nonnumquam extorum fibras animant, avium volatus gubernant, sortes regunt, oracula efficiunt falsis pluribus involuta. Nam et falluntur et fallunt, ut et nescientes sinceram veritatem, et quam sciunt, in perditionem sui non confitentes. Sic a coelo deorsum gravant, et a Deo vero ad materias avocant, vitam turbant, omnes inquietant, irrepentes etiam corporibus occulte, ut spiritus tenues, morbos fingunt, terrent mentes, membra distorquent, ut ad cultum sui cogant: ut nidore altarium, vel hostiis pecudum saginati remissis, quae constrinxerant curasse videantur. Hi sunt et furentes, quos in publicum videtis excurrere; vates et ipsi absque templo sic insaniunt, sic bacchantur, sic rotantur. Par et in illis instigatio daemonis, sed :ARGUMENTUM dispar furoris. De ipsis etiam illa quae paulo ante tibi dicta sunt, ut Jupiter ludos repeteret ex somnio, ut cum equis Castores viderentur, ut cingulum matronae navicula sequeretur. Haec omnia sciunt plerique pars vestrum, ipsos daemonas de semetipsis confiteri, quoties a nobis et tormentis verborum et orationis incendiis de corporibus exiguntur. Ipse Saturnus, et Serapis, et Jupiter, et quidquid daemonum colitis, victi dolore, quod sunt eloquuntur: nec utique in turpitudinem sui, nonnullis praesertim vestrum assistentibus, mentiuntur. Ipsis testibus, esse eos daemonas, de se verum confitentibus credite. Adjurati enim per Deum verum et solum, inviti miseris corporibus inhorrescunt: et vel exsiliunt statim, vel evanescunt gradatim, prout fides patientis adjuvat, aut gratia curantis aspirat. Sic Christianos de proximo fugitant, quos longe in coetibus per vos lacessebant. Ideo inserti mentibus imperitorum, odium nostri serunt occulte per timorem: naturale est enim et odisse, quem timeas; et quem metueris, infestare, si possis. Sic occupant animos, et obstruunt pectora, ut ante nos incipiant homines odisse, quam nosse: ne cognitos aut imitari possint, aut damnare non possint.

excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 3. Whether the universe is governed by the power of one God or of many.
english: Let the second and following question be the starting point of our work: whether the world is governed by the power of one God or of many. No one who is truly wise and exercises reason can fail to recognize that there is a single Being who both founded all things and governs them with the very power by which he created them. What need would there be for many to sustain the governance of the world? Unless one supposes that if there were several, each would possess less strength and vigor—a concession that proponents of many gods are forced to make, since individually they could not bear the helm of so vast a mass without the help of the others. God, however, is eternal mind, and from every angle he is perfect, consummate virtue. If that is true, he must be one. Absolute power or virtue retains its own firmness; what is solid lacks nothing, and what is perfect admits no addition. Who doubts that the mightiest king is he who holds command over the whole world? And not without reason: all things everywhere belong to him, and all resources from every quarter are gathered to him alone. If more than one were to divide the world, each would certainly possess less wealth and less strength, confined as each is to an allotted portion. The same holds for gods: if they were many, each would be weaker, having no more in himself than the others possess. The perfect nature of virtue can reside only in that which contains the whole, not in that which holds but a small part of the whole. Since God is perfect, as he must be, he cannot be anything but one, so that all things may be in him. Consequently, the virtues and powers of many gods would necessarily be inferior, for each would lack exactly as much as the others contain; the more there are, the smaller each becomes. Moreover, the supreme power of the universe and divine strength cannot be divided even once. Whatever undergoes division necessarily undergoes destruction. But destruction is utterly foreign to God, because he is incorruptible and eternal; therefore divine power cannot be divided. God is one, then, if nothing else can possess equal power. Those who argue for many gods claim that offices are divided among them, a matter we will dispute in its proper place. For now I hold this point, which bears on the present argument: if offices are divided, the case reduces to the same problem—no single one can suffice for all. A being who cannot govern all things when the others fail is not perfect. Thus the world requires the perfect virtue of one, not the weakness of many. Anyone who thinks this immense magnitude cannot be ruled by one is deceived and fails to grasp the strength and power of divine majesty. If a single God could make the world, he can certainly govern what he made. Once one conceives in his mind the immensity of this divine work—how, though nothing existed before, it was formed from nothing by God's virtue and counsel, a work that could be begun and completed by one alone—he will understand all the more easily that what was established by one is far more easily governed by one. Someone may object that even the making of so immense a world could not have been accomplished by fewer than many. However many or great he imagines them, whatever magnitude, power, virtue, and majesty he distributes among them, I gather all of it into one and declare that it exists in one, so that there is in him as much of those qualities as can be neither thought nor expressed. In this matter we fail both in perception and in language, for the human breast cannot grasp so great a light of understanding, nor can mortal tongue compass the explanation of such things; yet we must understand and speak this truth. I see again what might be urged on the contrary: that those many are each such as we would have the one be. But this is impossible, because the power of each cannot advance further when confronted by the powers of the others. Each must have his own limits, which he cannot transgress; if he does transgress, he simply drives another back within his own bounds. Those who believe in many gods do not see that it becomes possible for them to will different things, giving rise to dispute and conflict among them—just as Homer invented gods warring with one another, some wanting Troy taken, others resisting. The world must therefore be governed by the judgment of one. Unless the power of the individual parts is referred to a single providence, the whole cannot hold together, each part caring for nothing beyond what properly belongs to it, just as no army can function with more than one leader and ruler. If in one army there were as many commanders as there are legions, cohorts, wedges, or wings, the battle line could not even be drawn up, each commander shirking danger, and it would be impossible to direct or control them, since all would follow their own counsels, whose diversity would harm more than help. So in this command of nature, unless there is one to whom the care of the whole is referred, all things will dissolve and collapse. To say that the world is governed by the judgment of many is like asserting that one body contains many minds because its members perform many and varied functions—as if separate minds were thought to rule the separate senses of the body, and as many minds as there are emotions—anger, desire, joy, fear, pity—were thought to operate within us. If someone actually said that, he would not even seem to possess one mind himself. But if one mind in a single body governs so many things and attends to all simultaneously, why should anyone think the world cannot be governed by one but can be by many? Because the advocates of many gods recognize this, they say the gods preside over individual things and parts, yet insist there is still one supreme ruler. Then the others are not gods at all, but satellites and ministers whom that one greatest and most powerful has placed over those offices to serve his command and bidding. If all are not equal, they are not all gods; the same thing cannot be both servant and master. For if God is the name of highest power, he must be incorruptible, perfect, impassible, subject to nothing. Therefore those whom necessity compels to obey the greatest God are not gods. Yet because those who think this way are not deceived in vain, we will reveal the cause of their error shortly. Now we will confirm the unity of divine power with testimonies.

excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 5. Of the testimonies of poets and philosophers.
english: We should set aside the prophets' testimonies, because for those who refuse to believe at all such proof would appear less adequate. Instead, let us turn to the very authors whom our opponents habitually cite against us and call them as witnesses to the truth—I mean the poets and philosophers. From them we must establish that there is one God, not because they possessed the truth, but because the power of truth itself is so great that no one can be so blind as to miss the divine clarity forced upon his eyes.

Although the poets adorned their gods with songs and magnified their deeds with the highest praises, they nevertheless very often confess that all things are contained and governed by a single spirit or mind. Orpheus, the most ancient of the poets and a contemporary of the gods themselves—tradition says he sailed with the Argonauts alongside Castor and Hercules—calls the true and great God ‘Firstborn’, because nothing was generated before Him, but all things were generated from Him. He also names Him ‘Phaneta’, because when nothing else yet existed, He first appeared and stood forth from the infinite. Since Orpheus could not conceive that origin and nature in his mind, he declared that this God was born from the vast air: ‘Firstborn Phaethon, son of boundless air’; he simply had nothing further to say. He asserts that this God is the parent of all the gods, for whose sake He founded heaven and provided for His children so that they might share a common dwelling and seat: ‘He built an imperishable home for the immortals’. Guided by nature and reason, he therefore understood that there exists a supreme power, the creator of heaven and earth. He could not proclaim Jupiter as the first principle, since Jupiter was born of Saturn, nor Saturn, since Saturn was born of heaven; yet he dared not make heaven itself the first god, because he saw that heaven is an element of the world and therefore itself requires an author. This reasoning led him to that Firstborn God, to whom he assigns and attributes sovereignty.

Homer can give us nothing that pertains to the truth, for he wrote of human rather than divine matters. Hesiod might have done so, since he encompassed the genealogy of the gods in a single work, yet he nevertheless offered nothing that did not take its starting point from Chaos—a confused mass of raw, disordered matter—when he ought first to have explained Chaos itself: whence, when, and how it began to exist or subsist. For just as all things are disposed, ordered, and fashioned by some craftsman, so the matter itself must have been fashioned by someone. Who else could have made it but God, to whose power all things are subject? But Hesiod shrank back from this, because he dreaded the unknown truth. That song he poured out on Helicon was not delivered by the instinct of the Muses, as he wished to appear; he came to it after meditation and preparation.

Our first poet, Vergil, was not far from the truth. Of the highest God, whom he names Mind and Spirit, he writes: ‘In the beginning the Spirit nourishes heaven and earth and the plains and the shining globe of the moon and the Titan stars; the Mind, infused throughout, stirs the whole mass and mingles with the great body’. And lest anyone be ignorant of who this Spirit is, who wields such power, Vergil declares in another place: ‘For God goes through all lands and the tracts of the sea and the deep heaven; from Him flocks, herds, men, every kind of wild beast, and each living thing that is born are summoned’. Ovid likewise, at the start of his renowned work, openly confesses that the world was fashioned by God, whom he calls the Maker of the world and the Craftsman of things. If Orpheus or our own poets, who perceived these things by nature, had defended them forever, they would have held the same doctrine we follow, having grasped the truth.

But enough of the poets. Let us turn to the philosophers, whose authority is weightier and judgment more certain, because they are believed to have studied not fictitious things but to have investigated the truth. Thales of Miletus, one of the Seven Sages and said to be the first to inquire into natural causes, declared that water is the source from which all things were born, and that God is the Mind that formed all things from water. Thus he placed the matter of things in moisture and established the principle and cause of generation in God. Pythagoras defined God as the Mind that pervades all parts of the world and all nature, from which all living creatures receive life. Anaxagoras says God is an infinite Mind that moves itself. Antisthenes acknowledges many popular gods, yet one natural God—that is, the Craftsman of the whole. Cleanthes and Anaximenes identify the highest God with ether, an opinion our poet Vergil embraced: ‘Then the Almighty Father, with fertile rains, descended into the joyous bosom of His ether bride, and the great fetus is nourished, mingled with the great body’. Chrysippus calls God the natural force endowed with divine reason, sometimes divine necessity; Zeno calls God the natural and divine law. Although the opinions of all these men are uncertain, they nevertheless converge on the same point: they agree that there is a single Providence. For whether you call it Nature, or Ether, or Reason, or Mind, or Fatal Necessity, or Divine Law, or anything else, it is the same reality we call God. Nor does the diversity of names hinder, since by their very signification all are reduced to one.

Aristotle, though he disagrees with himself and utters and thinks contradictory things, nevertheless testifies that one Mind presides over the world. Plato, judged the wisest of all, openly and plainly defends the monarchy of God; he does not name Ether, or Reason, or Nature, but God as He is: ‘From Him this world was made perfect and wonderful’. Cicero, following and imitating Plato in many respects, frequently confesses God and calls Him supreme in the books he wrote On the Laws; and he argues that the world is ruled by Him when he discusses the nature of the gods, in this way: ‘Nothing is more excellent than God. Therefore the world must be ruled by Him. For God is not subject to any nature, nor is He obedient to it. Therefore He Himself rules all nature.’ Because He is God, we must understand Him thus: ‘A mind freed and liberated, separated from all mortal concretion, perceiving and moving all things.’

Annaeus Seneca, the keenest Stoic among the Romans, how often he pursues the highest God with deserved praise! When discussing premature death he says: ‘Do you not understand the authority and majesty of your Judge, the Ruler of earth and heaven and all the gods, from whom those divine powers that we adore and worship are suspended?’ Again, in his Exhortations: ‘When God laid the first foundations of this beautiful world and began to order it, so that all things might go under their leaders, although He had extended Himself throughout the whole body, nevertheless He generated the ministers of His kingdom.’ And how many other things he said about God, similar to ours! I pass them by now because they are more opportune in other places. For the present it is enough to demonstrate that men of the highest genius have touched the truth and almost grasped it, unless they were dragged back by the corrupt and perverse opinions of custom—opinions by which they believed there were other gods, and that the things God made for human use, as if they possessed sensation, ought to be regarded and worshiped as gods.

excerpts.author: Lactantius

excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 6. Of divine testimonies, and of the Sibyls and their predictions.
english: Now we turn to the divine testimonies, but first I must produce one witness who resembles them both in his great antiquity and in the fact that he was elevated from humanity to divinity. In Cicero's work, the pontiff U. Cotta argues against the Stoics on the subject of religion and the variety of opinions about the gods; adopting the Academic method of making everything uncertain, he declares that there were five Mercurys. After listing four in order, he identifies the fifth as the one who killed Argus, fled to Egypt, and gave the Egyptians their laws and letters. The Egyptians call him Thoyth, and from him their first month—September—took its name. He also founded a city still called in Greek the City of Mercury, and the Pheneatae worship him devoutly. Though he was a man, he was the most ancient and thoroughly versed in every kind of learning, so that his knowledge of many arts and sciences earned him the surname Trismegistus. He wrote many books on the knowledge of divine things, in which he asserts the majesty of the highest and singular God, calling him by the very names we use for the Lord and Father. Lest anyone ask for his name, he said it is anonymous, because it does not require the property of a name, owing to its very unity. His words are: "O the one God; one, indeed, is the one who does not need a name." Therefore God has no name, because he is alone, nor is a proper title needed, except when a multitude demands a distinction so that each person may be designated by a unique mark and appellation. But for God, because he is always one, the proper name is God.

It remains to bring forward testimonies from the sacred and prophetic poems, which are far more certain. Perhaps those against whom we argue do not think poets should be trusted, as if they invent vain things, nor philosophers, since they could have erred, being men themselves. Marcus Varro, than whom no one more learned ever lived—not even among the Greeks—in his books on divine matters addressed to Gaius Caesar the pontifex maximus, when speaking of the quindecimvirs, says the Sibylline books were not the work of one Sibyl, but are called by the single name "Sibylline" because all female prophets were called Sibyls by the ancients, either from the name of one Delphid or from the announcing of the counsels of the gods. For they called the gods not Osouc but theos, and counsel not boulēn but boulēn, in the Aeolic dialect. Thus the Sibyl is said to be, as it were, theoboulē. Moreover, there were ten Sibyls in number, and he enumerated them all under the authors who wrote about each. The first was from Persia, mentioned by Nicanor, who wrote the deeds of Alexander of Macedon; the second was Libyssa, whom Euripides recalls in the prologue of the Lamia; the third was Delphid, of whom Chrysippus speaks in his book on divination; the fourth was the Cimmerian in Italy, named by Naevius in his books on the Punic War and by Piso in his annals; the fifth was the Erythraean, whom Apollodorus of Erythrae affirms was his fellow citizen, and who prophesied to the Greeks sailing for Ilium that Troy would fall and that Homer would write falsehoods; the sixth was the Samian, of whom Eratosthenes writes in the ancient annals of the Samians; the seventh was the Cumaean, named Amalthea, also called Herophile or Demophile by others, who brought nine books to King Tarquinius Priscus and demanded three hundred philippeos for them. The king despised the magnitude of the price and ridiculed the woman's insanity; she burned three of them in his sight and asked the same price for the remaining six. Tarquinius thought her even more insane; but when she persevered at the same price after burning three more, he was moved and bought the surviving books for three hundred gold pieces. Their number was later increased when the Capitol was rebuilt, for they were collected and brought to Rome from all cities, Italian and Greek, and especially from Erythrae, under the name of whatever Sibyl they were. The eighth was the Hellespontian, born in the Troad, in the village of Marmesso near the city of Gergithium, whom Heraclides of Pontus places in the time of Solon and Cyrus; the ninth was the Phrygian, who prophesied at Ancyra; the tenth was the Tiburtine, named Albunea, worshiped as a goddess at Tibur near the banks of the Anio, whose image is said to have been found in the whirlpool holding a book in her hand. The poems of all the Sibyls are both worn and preserved, except those of the Cumaean, whose books the Romans keep hidden, and it is not lawful for anyone but the quindecimvirs to inspect them. There are individual books for each Sibyl, but because they are all inscribed with the name of the Sibyls, they are believed to be the work of one, and are confused, nor can they be distinguished and assigned to each—except for the Erythraean, who inserted her true name into the poem and proclaimed herself the Erythraean, though she was born in Babylon. Even so, we will speak of the Sibyl indistinctly whenever we must use their testimonies.

All these Sibyls proclaim one God, especially the Erythraean, who is the most famous and noble among them. The diligent writer Fenestella, in his account of the quindecimvirs, says that when the Capitol was restored, the consul Gaius Curio reported to the senate that legates should be sent to Erythrae to recover the Sibyl's poems and bring them to Rome. Accordingly Publius Gabinius, Marcus Otacilius, and Lucius Valerius were dispatched; they brought back about a thousand verses copied from private collections. Varro confirms this above. In these verses which the legates brought to Rome, the testimonies concerning one God are these: "One God, who alone rules, immense, unbegotten." This is the only highest God, who made heaven and distinguished it with lights: "But God alone is one, most high, who made heaven, the sun, and the stars, the moon, the fruitful earth, and the waters of the sea." Since he alone is the builder of the world and the artisan of all things, whether those that constitute it or those within it, he testifies that he alone must be worshiped: "Honor the one who is the only ruler of the world." He alone is from eternity and to eternity. Likewise another Sibyl, whoever she may be, when she declared that she was bringing the voice of God to men, said: "For I am the only God, and there is no other God." I would now produce the testimonies of the other Sibyls, were these not sufficient and were I not reserving those for more opportune places. But since we defend the cause of truth against those who, straying from the truth, serve false religions, what kind of proof ought we to employ against them more than to convict them by the testimonies of their own gods?

excerpts.author: Lactantius

excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 8. That God is without a body, nor does he need difference of sex for procreation.
english: The sheer number and authority of the witnesses confirm that the world is governed by the power and providence of one God. Plato declares in the *Timaeus* that this God's power and majesty are so vast that no one can grasp them with the mind or express them in words, because his power is excessive and beyond estimate. Should anyone still doubt whether anything is difficult or impossible for God, consider who he is: by providence he devised the world, by virtue he established it, by reason he perfected it, and now he sustains it by his Spirit, governs it by his power, and remains incomprehensible, ineffable, and known fully to no one but himself. Reflecting often on such majesty, I find that those who worship gods sometimes appear blind, thoughtless, foolish — hardly different from mute animals. They believe that beings born from the union of male and female can possess divine majesty and virtue, even though the Erythraean Sibyl says: "God cannot be formed from the thighs of a man and the womb of a woman." Since that is true, it follows that Hercules, Apollo, Liber, Mercury, and Jupiter himself — along with the rest — were merely human, because they were born of two sexes. What could be more alien to God than the very act he gave mortals for propagating offspring, an act that cannot exist without bodily substance? If the gods are immortal and eternal, what need have they for the other sex — namely, to generate? What need for progeny, since they lack nothing and will always exist? In humans and all other living creatures, the difference of sexes, intercourse, and birth serve no other purpose than to preserve each kind through mutual succession, because mortality condemns them to perish. But for God, who is eternal, neither a second sex nor succession is necessary. Someone may object that God needs a female sex in order to have ministers or subjects to rule. But if God is omnipotent, as he is called, he can beget sons without any use or work of a woman. He granted certain tiny creatures the power to be born from leaves and sweet herbs and to gather them with their mouths; why should anyone think God himself cannot generate except by the mixture of the other sex? Therefore, no one is so thoughtless as to miss the point: those whom the ignorant and foolish call and worship as gods were mortals. "How then," one asks, "did they come to be believed as gods?" Because they were the greatest and most powerful kings. On account of the merits of their virtues, their benefactions, or the arts they discovered, they were dear to those they ruled, and so they were consecrated to memory. If anyone doubts this, let him examine their deeds and actions, which both ancient poets and historians have handed down.

unde mihi de tanta maiestate saepius cogitanti qui deos colunt interdum uideri solent tam caeci, tam incogitabiles, tam excordes, tam non multum a mutis animalibus differentes, qui credant eos qui geniti sint maris ac feminae coitu aliquid maiestatis diuinaeque uirtutis habere potuisse, cum Sibylla Erythraea dicat: ou οὐ δύνατ\' ἀνδρὸς ἑϰ μηρῶν μήτρας τε θεὸς τετυπωμένος εἶναι. quod si est uerum, sicuti est, apparet Herculem Apollinem Liberum Mercurium Iouemque ipsum cum ceteris homines fuisse, quoniam sunt ex duobus sexibus nati. quid est autem a deo tam remotum quam id opus, quod ipse ad propagandam subolem mortalibus tribuit et quod sine substantia corporali nullum potest esse? dii ergo si sunt inmortales et aeterni, quid opus est altero sexu — nimirum ut generent? ipsa progenie quid opus est, cum successione non egeant qui semper sunt futuri? nam profecto in hominibus ceterisque animantibus diuersitas sexus et coitio et generatio nullam habet aliam rationem nisi ut omnia genera uiuentium, quoniam sunt condicione mortalitatis obitura, mutua possint successione seruari, deo autem, qui est sempiternus, neque alter sexus neque successio necessaria est. dicet aliquis ut habeat uel ministros uel in quos possit ipse dominari.\' quid igitur sexu opus est feminino, cum deus, qui est omnipotens ut uocatur, sine usu et opera feminae possit. filios procreare? nam si quibusdam minutis animalibus id praestitit, ut sibi e foliis natos et suauibus herbis ore legant, cur existimet aliquis ipsum deum nisi ex permixtione sexus alterius non posse generare? illos igitur quos inperiti et insipientes tamquam deos et nuncupant et adorant, nemo est tam inconsideratus quin intellegat fuisse mortales. \'quomodo ergo\' inquiet aliquis \'dii crediti sunt?\' nimirum quia reges maximi ac potentissimi fuerunt, ob merita uirtutum suarum aut munerum aut artium repertarum, cum cari fuissent iis quibus inperitauerant, in memoriam sunt consecrati. quod si quis dubitat, res eorum gestas et facta consideret, quae uniuersa tam poetae quam historici ueteres prodiderunt.

excerpts.author: Lactantius

english: Once it is established that these figures were human, the reason they came to be called gods is clear. Before Saturn or Uranus, there were no kings because the human population was so sparse that people lived a rustic life without any ruler. In those early times, therefore, men began to honor their king and their whole community with the highest praises and honors, so that they even called them gods — whether out of wonder at their virtue (the rude and simple people truly believed this), or out of flattery toward present power, as often happens, or because of the benefits by which these rulers had civilized humanity. When those kings died, they left behind a great longing in the people whose lives they had ordered. Consequently, men fashioned images of them to find some solace in contemplating their likenesses; then, driven further by love, they began to venerate the memory of the dead, both to appear grateful to their benefactors and to entice successors with the desire to rule well. Cicero teaches this in On the Nature of the Gods, saying that human life and common custom adopted the practice of raising excellent men to heaven by fame and will because of their benefits — hence Hercules, Castor, Pollux, Aesculapius, Liber. Elsewhere he adds that in most cities one can see that the memory of brave men was consecrated with the honors of immortal gods to encourage virtue and so that the best men would more readily face danger for the republic. By this same logic the Romans consecrated their Caesars and the Moors their kings. Thus religions gradually arose: the first generation who knew these rulers taught the rite to their children and grandchildren, then to all posterity, until those most famous kings were worshiped in every province because of the renown of their names. Privately, individual peoples or cities honored their own founders — whether men distinguished by bravery or women remarkable for chastity — with the highest veneration: the Egyptians Isis, the Moors Juba, the Macedonians Cabirus, the Carthaginians Urania, the Latins Faunus, the Sabines Sancus, the Romans Quirinus; likewise the Athenians Minerva, the Samians Juno, the Paphian Venus, the Lemnians Vulcan, the Naxians Liber, the Delians Apollo. So various sacred rites spread among peoples and regions, because men wished to be grateful to their princes but could find no other honors to bestow on the lifeless. Moreover, the piety of successors greatly fueled the error: wanting to appear of divine stock, they paid divine honors to their parents and ordered them to be worshiped. Can anyone doubt how the religions of the gods were instituted, when we read Aeneas commanding his companions in Virgil: "Now pour libations to Jupiter and invoke the father Anchises"? To Anchias he attributed not only immortality but also power over the winds: "Let us ask for winds, and let these rites, which I wish established in the city's temples, be offered to him every year." Liber, Pan, Mercury, and Apollo did the same, and afterward their successors. Poets also contributed; composing songs for pleasure, they elevated these figures to heaven, just as flatterers praise even bad kings with mendacious panegyrics. This evil originated with the Greeks, whose levity, armed with rhetorical skill and abundance of language, stirred up incredible clouds of falsehood. Admiring them, men adopted their sacred rites and passed them on to all nations. Because of this vanity the Sibyl rebukes them: "O Greece, what do you trust in, relying on leaders? Why do you offer vain gifts to the dead? Do you sacrifice to idols? Who put this plan in your mind, abandoning the face of the great God?" Marcus Tullius — not only a consummate orator but also a philosopher, the sole imitator of Plato — in the book where he consoled himself for his daughter's death, did not hesitate to say that the gods worshiped publicly were men. His testimony carries the greatest weight because he held the augural priesthood and attests that he himself worshiped and venerated them. In a few verses he gives us two things: while professing that he will consecrate his daughter's image in the same manner as the ancients consecrated theirs, he teaches that those figures were dead and reveals the origin of vain superstition. When he says we see many men and women from the human race in the number of the gods, and we venerate their most august temples in cities and fields, let us agree with the wisdom of those whose genius and inventions have cultivated and established our whole life with laws and institutions. If any mortal was ever to be consecrated, this one surely was. If the offspring of Cadmus, Amphitryon, or Tyndareus was raised to heaven by fame, then the same honor ought to be given to her — which I will do, and with the approval of the immortal gods themselves I will place you, most excellent and learned, in their assembly, in the opinion of all mortals, I will consecrate. Someone might claim that Cicero spoke deliriously from excessive grief. But that entire speech — perfect in doctrine, examples, and the very manner of speaking — came from a steady mind and sound judgment, and this very statement shows no sign of grief. I do not think he could have written so varied, so copious, so ornate a work unless his grief had been softened by reason itself, the consolation of friends, and the passage of time. What of the fact that he says the same in On the Republic and On Glory? In On the Laws, where he followed Plato to establish laws for a just and wise city, he sanctioned this concerning religion: "Let them worship the gods and those who have always been considered heavenly, and those whom merit has placed in heaven — Hercules, Liber, Aesculapius, Castor, Pollux, Quirinus." Similarly in the Tusculan Disputations, when he said almost the whole heaven is filled with the human race, he added that if we investigate ancient things and extract what Greek writers have recorded, we will find that those very gods of the nations, considered to have originated from us, have gone to heaven. Since their tombs are shown in Greece, remember — since you have been initiated — what is handed down in the mysteries: then you will finally understand how far this extends. He testified, evidently appealing to Atticus's conscience, that from the mysteries themselves it can be understood that all those who are worshiped were men; and when he freely confessed this concerning Hercules, Liber, Aesculapius, Castor, and Pollux, concerning Apollo and Jupiter their fathers, and concerning Neptune, Vulcan, Mars, and Mercury, whom he called the gods of the nations, he feared to speak openly. Therefore he says this extends far, so that we may understand the same concerning Jupiter and the other more ancient gods, whose memory — if the ancients consecrated it in the same manner as he says he will consecrate his daughter's image and name — can be forgiven to the grieving but not to the believing. For who is so foolish as to think that the consensus and applause of innumerable fools can open heaven to the dead, or that anyone can give what he himself does not have to another? Among the Romans, Julius was made a god because it pleased the wicked Antony; Quirinus was made a god because it seemed good to the shepherds — one the twin brother, the other the parricide of his fatherland. If Antony had not been consul, Gaius Caesar would have been denied even the honors of a dead man for his services to the republic, blocked by the counsel of his father-in-law Piso, his relative Lucius Caesar (who forbade his funeral), and the consul Dolabella (who overthrew the column, that is the tomb, in the forum and purified the forum). Ennius declares that Romulus was deeply desired by his people; the people, grieving their lost king, cry out: "O Romulus, Romulus, tell us what kind of guardian of the fatherland the gods produced in you! You brought us within the boundaries of light, O father, O begetter, O blood kin of the gods." Because of this longing, it was more easily believed that Julius Proculus was lying — suborned by the fathers to announce to the plebs that he had seen the king in a form more august than human, and that the king had commanded them to build him a shrine, saying he was a god and should be called Quirinus. By this act he persuaded the people that Romulus had gone to the gods and freed the senate from the suspicion of the king's murder.

memoriam honore deorum inmortalium consecratam. hac scilicet ratione Romani Caesares suos consecrauerunt et Mauri suos reges. sic paulatim religiones esse coeperunt, dum illi primi qui eos nouerant eo Sancum, Romani Quirinum, eodem utique modo Athenae Mineruam, Samos Iunonem, Paphos Venerem, Vulcanum Lemnos, Liberum Naxos, Apollinem Delos. sic per populos atque regiones uaria sacra suscepta sunt, dum homines grati esse in suos principes cupiunt et quos alios honores uita carentibus deferant, inuenire non possunt. praeterea pietas eorum qui successerant plurimum contulit ad errorem: qui ut • diuina stirpe nati uiderentur, diuinos honores parentibus detulerunt deferrique iusserunt. an potest aliquis dubitare, quomodo religiones deorum sint institutae, cum apud Maronem legat Aeneae uerba sociis imperantis: nunc pateras libate Ioui precibusque uocate Anchisen genitorem —? cui non tantum immortalitatem, uerum etiam uentorum tribuit potestatem: poscamus uentos, atque haec me sacra πρόσωπον. M. Tullius, qui non tantum perfectus orator, sed etiam philosophus fuit, siquidem solus extitit Platonis imitator, in eo libro quo se ipse de morte filiae consolatus est, non dubitauit dicere deos qui publice colerentur homines fuisse. quod ipsius testimonium eo debet grauissimum iudicari, quod et augurale habuit sacerdotium et eosdem se colere uenerarique testatur. itaque intra paucos uersiculos duas res nobis dedit. nam dum imaginem filiae eodem se modo consecraturum esse profitetur quo illi a ueteribus sint consecrati, et illos mortuos esse docuit et originem uanae superstitionis ostendit. cum uero inquit et mares et feminas complures ex hominibus in deorum numero esse uideamus et eorum in urbibus atque agris augustissima delubra ueneremur, adsentiamur eorum sapientiae quorum ingeniis et inuentis omnem uitam legibus et institutis excultam constitutamque habemus. quod si ullum umquam animal consecrandum fuit, illud profecto fuit. si Cadmi progenies aut Amphitryonis aut Tyndari in caelum tollenda fama fuit, huic idem honos certe dicandus est. quod quidem faciam teque omnium optimam doctissimam adprobantibus diis inmortalibus ipsis in eorum coetu locatam ad opinionem omnium mortalium consecrabo. fortasse dicat aliquis prae nimio luctu delirasse Ciceronem. atquin illa omnis oratio et doctrina et exemplis et ipso loquendi genere perfecta non aegri, sed constantis animi ac iudicii fuit et haec ipsa sententia nullum praefert indicium doloris. neque enim puto illum tali uarie, tam copiose, tam ornate scribere potuisse, nisi luctum eius et ratio ipsa et consolatio amicorum et longitudo temporis mitigasset. quid quod idem dicit in libris de re publica, idem de gloria? nam de legibus, quo in opere Platonem secutus leges uoluit ponere, quibus putaret usuram esse iustam et sapientem ciuitatem, de religione ita sanxit: diuos et eos qui caelestes semper habiti sunt colunto et ollos quos endo caelo merita locauerunt, Herculem Liberum Aesculapium Castorem Pollucem Quirinum. item in Tusculanis, cum diceret totum paene caelum humano genere conpletum, si uero inquit scrutari uetera et ex illis ea quae scriptores Graeciae prodiderunt eruere coner, ipsi illi maiorum gentium di qui habentur hinc a nobis profecti in caelum reperientur. quare quoniam demonstrantur sepulchra in Graecia, reminiscere, quoniam es initiatus, quae tradantur mysteriis: tum denique quam hoc late pateat intelleges. testatus est uidelicet Attici conscientiam, ex ipsis mysteriis intellegi posse quod omnes illi homines fuerint qui coluntur, et cum de Hercule Libero Aesculapio Castore Polluce incunctanter fateretur, de Apolline ac Ioue patribus eorum, item de Neptuno Uulcano Marte Mercurio, quos maiorum gentium deos appellauit, timuit aperte coner. et idcirco ait late hocpatere, ut idem de Ioue ceterisque antiquioribus diis intellegamus, quorum memoriam si eadem ratione ueteres consecrauerunt, qua se imaginem nomenque filiae consecraturum esse dicit, ignosci maerentibus potest, credentibus non potest. quis enim tam demens, qui consensu et plaCitO innumerabilium stultorum aperiri caelum mortuis arbitretur aut aliquem quod ipse non habeat dare alteri posse? apud Romanos deus Iulius, quia hoc scele- rato homini placuit Antonio, deus Quirinus, quia hoc pastoribus uisum est, cum alter gemini fratris extiterit, alter patriae parricida. quodsi non consul fuisset Antonius, Gaius Caesar pro suis in rem publicam meritis etiam defuncti hominis honore caruisset, et quidem consilio Pisonis soceri et Lucii Caesaris propinqui, qui uetabant funus ei fieri, et Dolabellae consulis, qui columnam in foro id est tumulum eius euertit ac forum expiauit. nam Romulum desiderio suis fuisse declarat Ennius, apud quem populus amissum regem dolens haec loquitur: o Romule, Romule die, qualem te patriae custodem di genuerunt! tu produxisti nos intra luminis oras, o pater, o genitor, o sanguen dis oriundum. ob hoc desiderium facilius creditum est Iulio Proculo mentienti, qui subornatus a patribus est, ut nuntiaret plebi uidisse se regem humano habitu augustiorem eumque mandasse ad populum, ut sibi delubrum fieret, se deum esse et Quirinum uocari. quo facto et ipsi populo persuasit Romulum ad deos abisse et senatum suspicione caedis regiae liberauit.
