english: Here I must also refute those who not only confess that gods originated from human beings, but actually boast of it in order to honor them—whether for their virtue, as with Hercules, for their gifts, as with Ceres and Liber, or for their discovery of arts, as with Aesculapius and Minerva. Such claims are utterly foolish and unworthy; they lead people to defile themselves with inexpiable guilt and make themselves enemies of God, since they despise the true God while devoting sacred rites to the dead. I will demonstrate the falsity of each point in turn. They claim that the virtue which elevates a human to heaven is not the moral excellence that philosophers discuss—the kind rooted in the goods of the soul—but merely physical strength. Because this bodily prowess was preeminent in Hercules, he is said to have earned immortality. Who could be so foolish as to judge divine or even human worth by bodily strength, when beasts possess it in greater measure, and a single illness or old age itself can break or diminish it? Hence, when Hercules saw his own flesh deformed by ulcers, he refused both healing and the prospect of growing old, lest he ever appear lesser or more deformed to himself. People imagined that he ascended to heaven from the pyre on which he burned himself alive, and they revered and consecrated the very things that are most absurd, preserving them in statues and images so that monuments to their vanity would endure forever—all because they believed gods could be made through the killing of beasts. Perhaps this is a Greek failing, since they have always treated the most trivial things as the greatest. But what of our own people? Are they any wiser? They scorn athletic virtue because it serves no practical purpose, yet they admire royal virtue precisely because it tends to cause widespread harm. Consequently, they assume that brave and warlike commanders gain a place among the gods, and they insist that the only road to immortality is to lead armies, ravage foreign lands, demolish cities, raze towns, and either slaughter or enslave free peoples. Clearly, the more men they afflict, plunder, and kill, the more noble and renowned they consider themselves; seduced by the illusion of empty glory, they attach the name of virtue to their own crimes. I would rather they invented gods from the slaughter of beasts than validate an immortality so drenched in blood. If someone kills a single human being, he is regarded as polluted and accursed, and it is deemed unlawful to admit him into this earthly dwelling of the gods. Yet the one who has slaughtered countless thousands, flooded fields with blood, and poisoned rivers is welcomed not only into the temple but into heaven itself. In Ennius, Africanus declares: "If it is permitted for anyone to ascend to the heavenly realms, the widest gate of heaven stands open to me alone" —precisely because he has wiped out and destroyed a great portion of the human race. Oh, what profound darkness you dwell in, Africanus—or rather, oh poet, who imagined that the ascent to heaven lies open to mortals through slaughter and bloodshed! Even Cicero gave his assent to this vanity. "It is true," he says, "Africanus; for that same gate was open to Hercules" —as if he himself had been the doorkeeper of heaven when it happened. I cannot decide whether to weep or laugh when I see serious, learned men, who regard themselves as wise, tossed about in such wretched waves of error. If this is the virtue that makes us immortal, I would rather die than become the cause of destruction for countless people. If immortality can be obtained only through bloodshed, what happens when all humanity agrees to live in harmony—something that can certainly occur if people renounce their ruinous and impious fury and choose to be innocent and just? Will no one then be worthy of heaven? Will virtue perish simply because men are no longer allowed to rage against one another? But those who count the overthrow of cities and peoples as the highest glory will never tolerate public peace; they will seize, rampage, and insolently inflict injuries, shattering the covenant of human society just so they can have an enemy to destroy more wickedly than they provoked. Now let us proceed to the remaining cases. Tradition assigned the title of gods to Ceres and Liber because of their gifts. I could prove from divine writings that grain and wine were already in human use before the offspring of Caelus and Saturn appeared, but let us suppose for argument's sake that these two discovered them. Can gathering grain and teaching people to bake bread from it, or pressing grapes from vines and making wine, really appear greater or more remarkable than creating the grain and the vines themselves and bringing them forth from the earth? Even if God left such discoveries to human ingenuity, it remains impossible that they are not His, since He gave human beings the wisdom to discover them and brought the discoverable things into existence. The arts, too, are said to have conferred immortality on their discoverers—medicine on Aesculapius, metalworking on Vulcan. Then let us also honor those who taught fulling or shoemaking. Why does the inventor of pottery receive no honor? Is it because the rich despise Samian ware? There are other arts whose discoverers have enormously benefited human life; why have temples not been dedicated to them as well? But perhaps Minerva is credited with discovering everything, and so craftsmen pray to her. Thus Minerva ascends to heaven from these lowly origins. Is it really plausible that anyone would abandon the One who created the earth with its living creatures and the heavens with their stars and lights, in order to venerate the one who merely taught how to weave a web? And what of the one who taught how to heal bodily wounds? Can he be more excellent than the One who formed the bodies themselves, gave them the capacity to feel and live, and originally devised and brought forth the herbs and all the other substances on which the art of healing depends?

latin: Hoc loco refellendi sunt etiam ii qui deos ex hominibus esse factos non tantum fatentur, sed ut eos laudent, etiam gloriantur, aut uirtutis gratia ut Herculem aut munerum ut Cererem ac Liberum aut artium repertarum ut Aesculapium ac Mineruam. haec uero quam inepta sint quamque non digna propter quae homines inexpiabili se scelere contaminent hostesque uero deo fiant, quo contempto mortuorum sacra suscipiunt, ex singulis rebus ostendam. uirtutem esse dicunt quae hominem tollat in caelum, non illam de qua philosophi disserunt, quae posita est in bonis animi, sed hanc corporalem quae dicitur fortitudo: quae quoniam praecipua in Hercule fuit, inmortalitatem meruisse creditur. quis tam stulte ineptus est, ut corporis uires diuinum uel etiam humanum bouum iudicet, cum sint et maiores pecudibus adtributae et uno morbo saepe frangantur uel senectute ipsa minuantur et corruant? itaque idem ille cum deformari ulceribus toros suos cerneret, nec sanari se uoluit nec senem fieri, ne quando se ipso minor aut deformior uideretur. hunc a rogo quo uiuum se ipse combusserat escendisse in caelum putauerunt eaque ipsa quae stultissime sunt admirati simulacris et imaginibus expressa et consecrata posuerunt, ut in perpetuum uanitatis illorum monumenta perstarent qui ob necem bestiarum deos fieri credidissent. sed haec fortasse Graecorum culpa sit, qui res leuissimas pro maximis semper habuerunt. quid nostri? num sapientiores? qui athleticam quidem uirtutem contemnunt, quia nihil obest, sed regiam, quia late solet nocere, sic admirantur, ut fortes ac bellicosos duces in deorum coetu locari arbitrentur; nec esse ullam aliam ad inmortalitatem uiam quam exercitus ducere, aliena uastare, delere urbes, oppida excindere, liberos populos aut trucidare aut subicere seruituti. uidelicet quo plures homines adflixerint spoliarint occiderint, eo se nobiliores et clariores putant et inanis gloriae specie capti sceleribus suis nomen uirtutis inponunt. iam mallem ut a ferarum caedibus deos sibi fingerent quam inmortalitatem tam cruentam probarent. si quis unum hominem iugulauerit, pro contaminato ac nefario habetur nec ad terrenum hoc domicilium deorum admitti eum fas putant. ille autem qui infinita hominum milia trucidarit, cruore campos inundauerit, flumina infecerit, non modo in templum, sed etiam in caelum admittitur. aput Ennium sic loquitur Africanus: 25 si fas endo plagas caelestum ascendere cuiquam est, mi soli caeli maxima porta patet, scilicet quia magnam partem generis humani extinxit ac perdidit. o in quantis tenebris, Africane, uersatus cs uel potius o poeta, qui per caedes et sanguinem patere hominibus ascensum in caelum putaueris! cui uanitati etiam Cicero adsensit. est uero inquit Africane: nam et Herculi eadem ista porta patuit; tamquam ipse plane, cum id fieret, ianitor fuerit in caelo. equidem statuere non possum dolendumne potius an ridendum putem, cum uideam graues et doctos et ut sibi uidentur sapientes uiros in tam miserandis errorum fluctibus uolutari. si haec est uirtus quae nos inmortales facit, mori equidem malim quam exitio esse quam plurimis. si aliter inmortalitas parari non potest nisi per sanguinem, quid fiet, si omnes in concordiam consenserint? quod certe fieri poterit, si pernicioso et impio furore proiecto innocentes esse ac iusti uelint. num igitur nemo erit caelo dignus? num peribit uirtus, quia hominibus in homines saeuire non dabitur? sed isti qui euersiones urbium populorumque summam gloriam conputant, otium publicum non ferent, rapient saeuient et iniuriis insolenter inlatis humanae societatis foedus inrumpent, ut habere hostem possint, quem (non) sceleratius deleant quam lacessierint. Nunc ad reliqua pergamus. nomen deorum Cereri ac Libero traditio munerum fecit. possum diuinis docere litteris uinum atque fruges ante progeniem Caeli atque Saturni fuisse in usu hominum, sed ab his sane inuenta esse fingamus. num potest plus aut maius uideri collegisse fruges iisque fractis panem facere docuisse aut uuas de uitibus lectas expressisse uinumque fecisse quam fruges ipsas aut uites generasse ac protulisse de terra? reliquerit haec sane deus humanis ingeniis eruenda, tamen fieri non potest quin ipsius sint omnia, qui et sapientiam tribuit homini ut inueniret et illa ipsa quae possent inueniri. artes quoque inuentoribus suis inmortalitatem peperisse dicuntur, ut Aesculapio medicina, Volcano fabrica. colamus igitur et illos qui fullonicam sutrinamue docuerunt. cur autem figulinae repertori honos non habetur? an quia isti diuites uasa Samia contemnunt? sunt et aliae artes quarum repertores humanae uitae plurimum profuerunt: cur non et illis adtributa sunt templa? sed nimirum Minerua est quae omnes repperit, ideoque illi opifices supplicant. ergo ab his sordibus Minerua ascendit in caelum. est uero cur quisquam derelinquat eum qui terram cum animantibus, caelum cum astris et luminibus exorsus est, ut eam ueneretur quae telam docuit ordiri. quid ille qui uulnera in corporibus sanare docuit? num potest esse praestantior quam qui corpora ipsa formauit, sentiendi ac uiuendi rationem dedit, herbas denique ipsas et cetera quibus medendi ars constat excogitauit ac protulit?

english: Among the Romans the author and founder of these empty rites was King Sabinus. He tangled the rough, unlearned minds of men with new superstitions, and to give his deception some authority he pretended to hold nocturnal meetings with the goddess Egeria. A pitch‑dark cave lay in the Aricinian forest, fed by a never‑failing spring. Sabinus used to slip there after dismissing his attendants, so he could claim the goddess had told him to hand the people those sacred rites most acceptable to the gods. He was clearly copying the cunning of Minos, who hid himself in the cave of Jupiter, stayed there a long time, then produced laws as if delivered by Jupiter himself, thereby binding men to obedience not only by command but by religion. Persuading shepherds was no great feat. Accordingly he created pontiffs, flamens, Salii, and augurs; he assigned the gods to families. Thus he softened the fierce temper of the new people and turned them from war to the pursuits of peace. Yet while he fooled others, he did not fool himself. Many years later, in the consulship of Cornelius and Baebius, diggers on the scribe Petilius' land beneath the Janiculum uncovered two stone chests. One held the body of Numa; the other held seven Latin books on pontifical law and seven Greek books on the discipline of wisdom. These writings dissolved not only the rites Numa had instituted but all the rest as well. The senate decreed that the books be destroyed, and the urban praetor Quintus Petilius burned them in a public assembly. That was a foolish act: what good did burning them do, when the very fact that they were burned because they undermined religion has been preserved in memory? No one in that senate escaped utter folly: they could have abolished the books and still kept the matter from ever coming to light. In trying to prove to posterity how devoutly they defended religion, they testified against the authority of religion itself.

Just as Pompilius founded foolish religions at Rome, so before him Faunus did the same in Latium. He established impious rites for his grandfather Saturn, honored his father Picus as a god, and consecrated his sister and wife Fenta Fauna. Gaius Bassus calls her Fata because she sang fates to women as Faunus did to men. Varro writes that her modesty was such that no man but her husband ever saw her or heard her name while she lived. Therefore women sacrifice to her with covered heads and call her the Good Goddess. Sextus Clodius, in his Greek book, says she was Faunus' wife. She secretly drank a jar of wine, became drunk, and was beaten to death with myrtle rods by her husband. Later, when he repented and could not bear his longing for her, he paid her divine honors; hence a covered jar of wine is placed in her rites. Faunus too left posterity no small error, though every prudent man sees through it. Lucilius mocks the folly of those who think statues are gods, writing: "He trembles at the terriculae, the Lamiae, which Faunus and Numa Pompilius established." As infant children believe every bronze statue lives and is a man, so these men take all fictions for truth, believing a heart beats inside the bronze. A painter's canvas — nothing true, all fiction! The poet compared foolish men to infants, but I say they are far more imprudent. The children think statues are men; these men think statues are gods. Age deceives the children; folly deceives these men. The children will soon stop being deceived; the vanity of these men endures and grows.

Orpheus first introduced the sacred rites of Father Liber into Greece and first celebrated them on Mount Cithaeron in Boeotian Thebes, where Liber was born. Because he often sang to the cithara, the mountain was named Cithaeron. Those rites are still called Orphic; in them Orpheus himself was later torn limb from limb. He lived at nearly the same time as Faunus. Which of them was older is doubtful, since Latinus and Priam reigned in the same years, as did their fathers Faunus and Laomedon; during Laomedon's reign Orpheus reached the Ilian shore with the Argonauts. Let us go further, then, and ask who was the very first author of the worship of the gods. Didymus, in his books of the Explanation of Pindar, says that Melisseus, king of the Cretans, first sacrificed to the gods and introduced new rites and solemn processions. He had two daughters, Amalthea and Melissa, who fed the child Jupiter with goat's milk and honey — whence the poetic fable arose that bees swarmed and filled the boy's mouth with honey. Melissa was appointed by her father as the first priestess of the Great Mother; therefore the priests of that Mother are still called Melissae. The Sacred History testifies that Jupiter himself, after gaining power, sank into such insolence that he founded temples to himself in many places. As he traveled the lands, he bound the kings and princes of each region to himself by hospitality and friendship; when he departed, he ordered a temple built in his host's name, as if to preserve the memory of the friendship and pact. Thus arose the temples of Jupiter Ataburius, Jupiter Labrandius — Ataburus and Labrandius had been his hosts and allies in war — and likewise Jupiter Laprius, Jupiter Molion, Jupiter Casius, and others of the same sort. He devised this cleverly, so as to win divine honor for himself and give his hosts a perpetual name linked with religion. They rejoiced, obeyed his command willingly, and celebrated annual rites and festivals for the sake of his name. Aeneas did something similar in Sicily: he founded the city of Acesta and gave it his host's name, so that Acestes would afterwards love, enlarge, and adorn it with joy. In this way Jupiter sowed the worship of himself throughout the world and set an example for others to imitate. Whether the rites of worship flowed from Melisseus, as Didymus reports, or from Jupiter himself, as Euhemerus says, the time when gods began to be worshiped is at least certain. Melisseus preceded Jupiter by a great span, having reared him as a grandson. It is therefore possible that he instituted the worship of the gods either before or while Jupiter was still a boy — that is, the worship of his foster‑child's mother Opis, his grandmother Tellus (wife of Uranus), and his father Saturn — and that by this example and institution he drove Jupiter to such pride that he afterward dared to assume divine honors for himself.

auctoritate, simulauit cum dea Egeria nocturnos se habere congressus. erat spelunca quaedam peropaca in nemore Aricino, unde riuus perenni fonte manabat. huc se remotis arbitris inferre consueuerat, ut mentiri posset monitu deae coniugis ea sacra populo se tradere, quae acceptissima diis essent. uidelicet astutiam Minois uoluit imitari, qui se in antrum Iouis recondebat et ibi diu moratus leges tamquam sibi a Ioue traditas adferebat, ut homines ad parendum non modo imperio, sed etiam religione constringeret. nec difficile sane fuit persuadere pastoribus. itaque pontifices flamines Salios augures creauit, deos per familias discripsit: sic noui populi feroces animos mitigauit et ad studia pacis a rebus bellicis auocauit. sed cum alios falleret, se ipsum tamen non fefellit. nam post annos plurimos Cornelio et Baebio consulibus in agro scribae Petili sub Ianiculo arcae duae lapideae sunt repertae a fossoribus, quarum in altera corpus Numae fuit, in altera septem Latini libri de religionibus derogabant, memoriae sit traditum? nemo ergo tunc in senatu non stultissimus: potuerunt enim et libri aboleri et tamen res in memoriam non exire. ita dum uolunt etiam posteris adprobare credunt signis cor inesse in aenis. pergula pictorum, ueri nihil, omnia ficta! poeta quidem stultos homines infantibus conparauit, at ego multo inprudentiores esse dico. illi enim simulacra homines excerpts.author: Origen
excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 1
english: To Celsus, who wants to slander Christianity, a major point is that Christians form secret agreements with each other, contrary to established laws, since some agreements are open—those made according to laws—while others are hidden, those made contrary to what is established. He also wants to slander the so-called love Christians have for one another, claiming it arises only from common danger and can overcome any obstacle. Since he accuses Christians of making agreements in violation of the common law, the response must be this: just as someone who has come to live among the Scythians, who have laws contrary to custom, and who has no chance to leave, would be forced to live among them, it would be reasonable for that person, because of the law of truth, as opposed to the Scythians' lawlessness, to make agreements with those who share his views, contrary to the Scythians' established laws. So too, when judged by the truth, the laws of the nations—laws concerning idols and the godless multitude of gods—are Scythian laws, and even more impious than the Scythians. It is therefore not unreasonable to make agreements contrary to established laws for the sake of truth. Just as, for example, if some people were to make secret agreements to overthrow a tyrant who had seized the city, they would be doing well; so also Christians, with the so-called devil tyrannizing among them along with falsehood, make agreements contrary to established laws against the devil and for the salvation of others, whom they may be able to persuade to turn away from the law of the Scythians and the tyrant.

greek: Πρῶτον τῷ Κέλσῳ κεφάλαιόν ἐστι βουλομένῳ διαβαλεῖν χριστιανισμὸν, ὡς συνθήκας κρύβδην πρὸς ἀλλήλους ποιουμένων Χριστιανῶν παρὰ τὰ νενομισμένα, ὅτι τῶν συνθηκῶν αἱ μέν εἰσι φανεραὶ, ὅσαι κατὰ νόμους γίνονται, αἱ δὲ ἀφανεῖς, οσαι παρὰ τὰ νενομισμένα συντελοῦνται. καὶ βούλεται διαβαλεῖν τὴν καλουμένην ἀγάπην Χριστιανῶν πρὸς ἀλλήλους, ἀπὸ τοῦ κοινοῦ κινδύνου ὑφισταμένην καὶ δυναμένην ὑπερόρκια. ἐπεὶ οὖν τὸν κοινὸν νόμον θρυλεῖ παρὰ τοῦτον λέγων Χριστιανοῖς τὰς συνθήκας, λεκτέον πρὸς τοῦτο ὅτι, ὥσπερ εἴ τις παρὰ Σκύθαις νόμους ἀθέσμους ἔχουσι γενόμενος ἀναχωρήσεως μὴ ἔχων καιρὸν βιοῦν παρ᾿ ἐκείνοις ἀναγκάζοιτο, εὐλόγως ἂν οὗτος διὰ τὸ τῆς ἀληθείας νόμον, ὡς πρὸς τοὺς Σκύθας παρανομίαν, καὶ συνθήκας πρὸς τοὺς τὰ αὐτὰ αὐτῷ φρονοῦντας ποιήσαι ἂν παρὰ τὰ ἐκείνοις νενομισμένα· οὕτως παρ᾿ ἀληθείᾳ δικαζούσῃ οἱ νόμοι τῶν ἐθνῶν, οἱ περὶ ἀγαλμάτων καὶ τῆς ἀθέου πολυθεότητος, νόμοι εἰσὶ Σκυθῶν καὶ εἴ τι Σκυθῶν ἀσεβέστερον. οὐκ ἄλογον οὖν συνθήκας παρὰ τὰ νενομισμένα ποιεῖν τὰς ὑπὲρ ἀληθείας. ὥσπερ γὰρ, εἰ ὑπὲρ τοῦ τύραννον προλαβόντα τὰ τῆς πόλεως ἀνελεῖν συνθήκας τινὲς κρύβδην ἐποιοῦντο, καλῶς ἂν ἐποίουν· οὕτω δὴ καὶ Χριστιανοὶ, τυραννοῦντος τοῦ παρ᾿ αὐτοῖς καλουμένου διαβόλου καὶ τοῦ ψεύδους, συνθήκας ποιοῦνται παρὰ τὰ νενομισμένα τῷ διαβόλῳ κατὰ τοῦ διαβόλου καὶ ὑπὲρ σωτηρίας ἑτέρων, οὓς ἂν πεῖσαι δυνηθῶσιν ἀποστῆναι τοῦ ὡσανεὶ Σκυθῶν καὶ τυράννου νόμου.

excerpts.author: Origen
excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 5
english: When the author turns to idolatry, he treats it as a subject that properly belongs to those who draw from the Word, and he builds his case by saying that people do not regard handmade objects as gods, because it is not reasonable that things fashioned by the most worthless craftsmen of evil character, often even by unjust men, should be considered divine. In what follows, wanting to show that this insight is not original to him, he cites Heraclitus: "It is like someone chattering in the houses, to treat the inanimate things that approach as gods." One must say, then, that just as with the other ethical topic, notions have been sown among human beings, and from these Heraclitus and any other Greek or barbarian who conceived of this idea drew their construction. He also presents the Persians as holding this view, citing Herodotus as his witness. We may add that Zeno of Citium says in the Republic: "There will be no need to build temples; for nothing must be considered sacred or worthy of much honor and holy, being the work of builders and craftsmen." It is clear, therefore, that concerning this doctrine as well it has been written "in the hearts" of men with the letters of God what must be done (Romans 2:15).

greek: Τὰ δὲ περὶ τῆς εἰδωλολατρείας ὡς ἴδια τῶν ἀπὸ τοῦ λόγου ἐκτιθέμενος καὶ ὑποκατασκευάζει λέγων αὐτοὺς διὰ τοῦτο μὴ νομίζειν αὐτοὺς χειροποιήτους θεοὺς, ἐπεὶ μὴ εὔλογόν ἐστι τὰ ὑπὸ φαυλοτάτων δημιουργῶν καὶ μοχθηρῶν τὸ ἦθος εἰργασμένα εἶναι θεοὺς, πολλάκις καὶ ὑπὸ ἀδίκων ἀνθρώπων κατασκευασθέντα. ἐν τοῖς ἑξῆς οὖν θέλων αὐτὸ κοινοποιῆσαι ὡς οὐ πρῶτον ὑπὸ τούτου εὑρεθὲν ἐκτίθεται Ἡρακλείτου λέξιν τὴν λέγουσαν· „ὅμοια, ὡς εἴ τις τοῖς δόμοις λεσχηνεύοιτο, ποιεῖν τοὺς προσιόντας ὡς θεοῖς τοῖς ἀψύχοις.“ οὐκοῦν καὶ περὶ τούτου λεκτέον ὅτι ὁμοίως τῷ ἄλλῳ ἠθικῷ τόπῳ ἐγκατεσπάρησαν τοῖς ἀνθρώποις ἔννοιαι, ἀφ᾿ ὧν καὶ ὁ Ἡράκλειτος καὶ εἴ τις ἄλλος Ἑλλήνων ἢ βαρβάρων τοῦτ᾿ ἐνενόησε κατασκευάσαι. ἐκτίθεται γὰρ καὶ Πέρσας τοῦτο φρονοῦντας, παρατιθέμενος Ἡρόδοτον ἱστοροῦντα αὐτό. προσθήσομεν δὲ καὶ ἡμεῖς ὅτι καὶ Ζήνων ὁ Κιτιεὺς ἐν τῇ Πολιτείᾳ φησίν· „ἱερά τε οἰκοδομεῖν οὐδὲν δεήσει· ἱερὸν γὰρ οὐδὲν χρὴ νομίζειν οὐδὲ πολλοῦ ἄξιον καὶ ἅγιον, οἰκοδόμων τε ἔργον καὶ βαναύσων.“ σαφὲς οὖν ὅτι καὶ περὶ τούτου τοῦ δόγματος γέγραπται „ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις“ τῶν ἀνθρώπων γράμμασι θεοῦ τὸ πρακτέον.

excerpts.author: Origen
excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 7
english: Since he repeatedly calls the Christian doctrine "secret," he deserves reproof, because almost the whole world has come to know the Christian proclamation far better than the teachings that appeal to philosophers. After all, what escapes notice? The birth of Jesus from a virgin, his crucifixion, his resurrection believed by many, and the coming judgment that punishes sinners as they deserve while honoring the righteous. Even the mystery of the resurrection, though not understood, is ridiculed by unbelievers. So to claim the doctrine is secret is quite absurd. The idea that there is an inner truth that does not reach the masses is not unique to Christian teaching; philosophers have the same practice. Among them some gave public lectures and others gave private ones. Some heard Pythagoras only through the saying "he himself said," while others were taught in secret doctrines deemed unworthy to reach profane and unpurified ears. And the mysteries celebrated everywhere, in Greece and among the barbarians, though secret, are not slandered. Therefore, without having accurately grasped what is secret about Christianity, he slanders it in vain.

greek: Εἶτ᾿ ἐπεὶ πολλάκις ὀνομάζει κρύφιον τὸ δόγμα, καὶ ἐν τούτῳ αὐτὸν ἐλεγκτέον, σχεδὸν παντὸς τοῦ κόσμου ἐγνωκότος τὸ κήρυγμα Χριστιανῶν μᾶλλον ἢ τὰ τοῖς φιλοσόφοις ἀρέσκοντα. τίνα γὰρ λανθάνει ἡ ἐκ παρθένου γέννησις Ἰησοῦ καὶ ὁ ἐσταυρωμένος καὶ ἡ παρὰ πολλοῖς πεπιστευμένη ἀνάστασις αὐτοῦ καὶ ἡ καταγγελλομένη κρίσις, κολάζουσα μὲν κατ᾿ ἀξίαν τοὺς ἁμαρτάνοντας γέρως δ᾿ ἀξιοῦσα τοὺς δικαίους; ἀλλὰ καὶ μὴ νοηθὲν τὸ περὶ τῆς ἀναστάσεως μυστήριον θρυλεῖται γελώμενον ὑπὸ τῶν ἀπίστων. ἐπὶ τούτοις οὖν λέγειν κρύφιον εἶναι τὸ δόγμα πάνυ ἐστὶν ἄτοπον· τὸ δ᾿ εἶναί τινα οἷον μετὰ τὰ ἐξωτερικὰ, μὴ εἰς τοὺς πολλοὺς φθάνοντα, οὐ μόνου ἴδιον τοῦ Χριστιανῶν λόγου ἀλλὰ γὰρ καὶ τοῦ φιλοσόφων, παρ᾿ οἷς τινες μὲν ἦσαν ἐξωτερικοὶ λόγοι ἕτεροι δὲ ἐσωτερικοί· καί τινες μὲν ἀκούοντες Πυθαγόρου, ὡς „αὐτὸς ἔφα,“ ἄλλοι δ᾿ ἐν ἀποῤῥήτῳ διδασκόμενοι μενοι τὰ μὴ ἄξια φθάνειν εἰς ἀκοὰς βεβήλους καὶ μηδέπω κεκαθαρμένας. καὶ πάντα δὲ τὰ πανταχοῦ μυστήρια κατὰ τὴν Ἑλλάδα καὶ τὴν βάρβαρον κρύφια ὄντα οὐ διαβέβληται· διόπερ μάτην μηδὲ νοήσας ἀκριβῶς τὸ κρύφιον τοῦ χριστιανισμοῦ διαβάλλει αὐτό.

excerpts.author: Origen
excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 7
english: Since Celsus repeatedly calls the Christian doctrine "secret," he deserves reproof on this point, because almost the whole world knows the Christian proclamation better than the teachings that please philosophers. After all, what escapes notice? The birth of Jesus from a virgin, his crucifixion, his resurrection believed by many, and the announced judgment that punishes sinners as they deserve while highly honoring the righteous? Even the mystery of the resurrection, though not understood, is ridiculed by unbelievers. So to claim the doctrine is secret is very absurd.

The idea that there is something like an inner truth that does not reach the many is not unique to Christian teaching; philosophers have it too. Among them some gave outer discourses and others inner ones: some heard Pythagoras only as "he himself said," while others were taught in secret things not worthy to reach the ears of the profane and not yet purified. And all the mysteries everywhere, in Greece and among barbarian lands, though secret, are not despised. Therefore, without accurately understanding the secret of Christianity, Celsus slanders it in vain.

excerpts.author: Origen
excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 20
english: And yet, against his will, Celsus is entangled into testifying that the world is comparatively modern, and not yet ten thousand years old, when he says that the Greeks consider those things as ancient, because, owing to the deluges and conflagrations, they have not beheld or received any memorials of older events. But let Celsus have, as his authorities for the myth regarding the conflagrations and inundations, those persons who, in his opinion, are the most learned of the Egyptians, traces of whose wisdom are to be found in the worship of irrational animals, and in arguments which prove that such a worship of God is in conformity with reason, and of a secret and mysterious character.

The Egyptians, then, when they boastfully give their own account of the divinity of animals, are to be considered wise; but if any Jew, who has signified his adherence to the law and the lawgiver, refer everything to the Creator of the universe, and the only God, he is, in the opinion of Celsus and those like him, deemed inferior to him who degrades the Divinity not only to the level of rational and mortal animals, but even to that of irrational also!— a view which goes far beyond the mythical doctrine of transmigration, according to which the soul falls down from the summit of heaven, and enters into the body of brute beasts, both tame and savage!

And if the Egyptians related fables of this kind, they are believed to convey a philosophical meaning by their enigmas and mysteries; but if Moses compose and leave behind him histories and laws for an entire nation, they are to be considered as empty fables, the language of which admits of no allegorical meaning!

excerpts.author: Origen
excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 25
english: The danger may well be no smaller for someone who drags the name of God, or the name of the Good, down onto things where it does not belong, than for someone who swaps the unspeakable names — shifting some from lesser realities up to greater ones, and others from greater realities down to lesser ones. I am not claiming that the moment the name Zeus is spoken, one immediately hears along with it the son of Cronus and Rhea, the husband of Hera, the brother of Poseidon, the father of Athena and Artemis, and the one who lay with his own daughter Persephone; nor that the name Apollo summons the son of Leto and Zeus, the brother of Artemis, the half-brother of Hermes, and whatever other titles the wise men of Celsus — fathers of doctrines and ancient theologians of the Greeks — attach to them. For what is the definition, if we speak literally of Zeus, that does not also include his father being Cronus and his mother Rhea? The same must be done for every other named god. Yet this charge does not touch at all those who assign the name Sabaoth to God, or Adonai, or any of the other names. When someone can philosophize about names as they exist in the unspeakable realm, they will discover many things also about the invocation of God's angels — one called Michael, another Gabriel, another Raphael — named in relation to the tasks they perform by the will of the God of all things throughout the universe. Our Jesus shares this same philosophy of names: his name has already been seen clearly to cast out myriads of demons from souls and bodies, and to work powerfully upon those from whom the demons were driven. Further, on the subject of names, it must be said that those skilled in the use of incantations report that the same incantation, when spoken in its own dialect, can accomplish what it promises; but when translated into any other language, it is seen to be feeble and unable to do anything. Thus it is not the meanings attached to things, but the qualities and properties of the sounds themselves, that possess some power for certain effects. So we will defend ourselves by such reasoning also concerning Christians who struggle to the death rather than proclaim Zeus as God or name him in any other tongue. For they either confess the common name God without qualification, or with the addition: "the creator of all things, the maker of heaven and earth, the one who sent to the race of men these certain wise men" — as if the name God, when invoked, accomplishes some power among human beings. Many other things could be said on the subject of names to those who think they should be indifferent to their use. And if Plato is admired for saying in the Philebus, "My fear, Protarchus, concerning the names of the gods is not small" — since Philebus had declared pleasure to be god, the one conversing with Socrates — how much more will we accept the reverence of Christians, who attach none of the names taken from myths to the creator of the universe? But enough of these things for now.

greek: Καὶ τάχα οὐκ ἐλάττων ὁ κίνδυνος τῷ τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ θεοῦ ἢ τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ ἐφ᾿ ἃ μὴ χρὴ κατάγοντι, ἤπερ τῷ τὰ κατά τινα ἀπόῤῥητον λόγον ὀνόματα ἐναλλάσσοντι καὶ τὰ μὲν κατὰ τῶν ἐλαττόνων φέροντι ἐπὶ τὰ κρείττονα τὰ δὲ κατὰ τῶν κρειττόνων ἐπὶ τὰ ἥττονα. καὶ οὐ λέγω ὅτι τῷ Διῒ εὐθέως συνεξακούεται ὁ Κρόνου καὶ Ῥέας υἱὸς καὶ Ἥρας ἀνὴρ καὶ Ποσειδῶνος ἀδελφὸς καὶ Ἀθηνᾶς καὶ Ἀρτέμιδος πατὴρ καὶ ὁ τῇ θυγατρὶ Περσεφόνῃ μιγεὶς, ἢ τῷ Ἀπόλλωνι συνεξακούεται ὁ Λητοῦς καὶ Διὸς υἱὸς καὶ Ἀρτέμιδος ἀδελφὸς καὶ Ἑρμοῦ ὁμοπάτριος ἀδελφὸς, καὶ ὅσα ἄλλα φέρουσιν οἱ σοφοὶ Κέλσου τῶν δογμάτων πατέρες καὶ ἀρχαῖοι θεολόγοι Ἑλλήνων. τίς γὰρ ἡ ἀποκλήρωσις, κυριολεκτεῖσθαι μὲν τὸν Δία οὐχὶ δὲ καὶ τὸν πατέρα μὲν αὐτοῦ εἶναι Κρόνον μητέρα δὲ Ῥέαν; τὸ δ᾿ ὅμοιον ποιητέον καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν ἄλλων ὀνομαζομένων θεῶν. τοῦτο δὲ τὸ ἔγκλημα οὐδαμῶς ἅπτεται τῶν κατά τινα ἀπόῤῥητον λόγον τὸ Σαβαὼθ τασσόντων ἐπὶ τοῦ θεοῦ ἢ τὸ Ἀδωναῒ ἤ τι τῶν λοιπῶν ὀνομάτων. ὅταν δὲ τὰ περὶ ὀνομάτων τις δύνηται τὰ ἐν ἀποῤῥήτοις φιλοσοφεῖν, πολλὰ ἂν εὕροι καὶ περὶ τῆς ἐπικλήσεως τῶν ἀγγέλων τοῦ θεοῦ· ὧν ὁ μέν τις Μιχαὴλ ἕτερος δὲ Γαβριὴλ καὶ ἄλλος Ῥαφαὴλ καλεῖται. φερωνύμως τοῖς πράγμασιν, ἃ διακονοῦνται κατὰ βούλημα τοῦ θεοῦ τῶν ὅλων ἐν τῷ παντί. τῆς δ᾿ ὁμοίας ἔχεται περὶ ὀνομάτων φιλοσοφίας καὶ ὁ ἡμέτερος Ἰησοῦς, οὗ τὸ ὄνομα μυρίους ἤδη ἐναργῶς ἑώραται δαίμονας ἐξελάσαν ψυχῶν καὶ σωμάτων, ἐνεργῆσαν εἰς ἐκείνους ἀφ᾿ ὧν ἀπηλάθησαν. ἔτι δ᾿ εἰς τὸν περὶ ὀνομάτων τόπον λεκτέον ὅτι οἱ περὶ τὴν χρῆσιν τῶν ἐπῳδῶν δεινοὶ ἱστοροῦσιν, ὅτι τὴν αὐτὴν ἐπῳδὴν εἰπόντα μὲν τῇ οἰκείᾳ διαλέκτῳ ἔστιν ἐνεργῆσαι ὅπερ ἐπαγγέλλεται ἡ ἐπῳδή· μεταλαβόντα δὲ εἰς ἄλλην οἱανδηποτοῦν φωνὴν ἔστιν ἰδεῖν ἄτονον καὶ οὐδὲν δυναμένην. οὕτως οὐ τὰ σημαινόμενα κατὰ τῶν πραγμάτων ἀλλ᾿ αἱ τῶν φωνῶν ποιότητες καὶ ἰδιότητες ἔχουσί τι δυνατὸν ἐν αὐταῖς πρὸς τάδε τινὰ ἢ τάδε. οὕτω δ᾿ ἀπολογησόμεθα διὰ τῶν τοιούτων καὶ περὶ τοῦ μέχρι θανάτου ἀγωνίζεσθαι Χριστιανοὺς, ἵνα μὴ τὸν Δία θεὸν ἀναγορεύσωσι μηδ᾿ ἄλλῃ διαλέκτῳ αὐτὸν ὀνομάσωσιν. ἢ γὰρ ἀορίστως ὁμολογοῦσι τὸ κοινὸν ὄνομα τὸ θεὸς ἢ καὶ μετὰ προσθήκης τῆς·“ ὁ δημιουργὸς τῶν ὅλων, ὁ ποιητὴς οὐρανοῦ καὶ γῆς, ὁ καταπέμψας τῷ γένει τῶν ἀνθρώπων τούσδε τινὰς τοὺς σοφούς“· ὡς τῷ ὀνόματι ἐφαρμοζόμενον τὸ θεὸς ὄνομα δύναμίν τινα παρὰ ἀνθρώποις ἐπιτελεῖ. πολλὰ δ᾿ ἂν καὶ ἄλλα λέγοιτο εἰς τὸν περὶ ὀνομάτων τόπον πρὸς τοὺς οἰομένους δεῖν ἀδιαφορεῖν περὶ τῆς χρήσεως αὐτῶν. καὶ εἴπερ θαυμάζεται Πλάτων εἰπὼν ἐν Φιλήβῳ· „τὸ δ᾿ ἐμὸν δέος, ὦ Πρώταρχε. περὶ τὰ ὀνόματα τῶν θεῶν οὐκ ὀλίγον.“ ἐπεὶ Φίληβος θεὸν τὴν ἡδονὴν εἶπεν ὁ προσδιαλεγόμενος τῷ Σωκράτει· πῶς οὐ μᾶλλον τῆς εὐλαβείας ἀποδεξόμεθα Χριστιανοὺς, μηδὲν τῶν ἐν ταῖς μυθοποιΐαις παραλαμβανομένων ὀνομάτων προσάπτοντας τῷ τοῦ παντὸς δημιουργῷ; ἀλλὰ γὰρ τούτων ἐπὶ τοῦ παρόντος ἅλις.

excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 31
english: You would also wonder where the disciples of Jesus got their resolve, if you listen to those who slander him. They claim the disciples never saw him risen from the dead, nor were they ever convinced that he was something divine. On top of that, they were not afraid to suffer the same fate as their teacher, to share his danger, and to leave their homelands behind in order to teach the message he had delivered to them, doing his will. I think anyone who examines the matter fairly would not say these men handed themselves over to a precarious life for the sake of Jesus' teaching without some powerful conviction. He instilled that conviction in them through his teaching, shaping them not only to live by his lessons themselves but to set others right as well — to correct them even if it meant stepping forward boldly as innovators before all people everywhere, and refusing to call anyone a friend who clung to the old doctrines and customs. Did Jesus’ disciples not see this, when they dared not only to prove to the Jews from the prophetic writings that he was the promised one, but also to declare to the other nations that the man crucified just the day before had willingly accepted that death for the sake of the whole human race? Their message was analogous to those who die for their homelands to stop a destructive plague, or a famine, or a peril at sea. For it is plausible that in the nature of things, according to certain unspeakable and hard-to-grasp truths, there is a principle such that one righteous person, dying voluntarily for the common good, can ward off the evil influences of wicked demons — demons that bring plagues, famines, perilous voyages, or similar disasters. So let those who refuse to believe that Jesus died for humanity on a cross answer this: will they not also accept the many Greek and barbarian histories that tell of individuals who died for the common good and delivered their cities and nations from evil? Or will they grant that those stories happened, yet insist that the man thought to have died to overthrow a great demon, the ruler of demons who had subjected all human souls on earth, has nothing persuasive about him? The disciples of Jesus saw all this, and more besides — things they likely learned from him in secret — and they were also filled with a certain power. He gave them strength and courage, not from some created maiden, but from the true prudence and wisdom of God. They hurried to make themselves known to everyone, not only to the Argives but to all Greeks and barbarians together, and to win a noble reputation.

greek: Πρὸς τούτοις δὲ θαυμάσαι ἄν τις, πόθεν ἐπῆλθε τοῖς μαθηταῖς αὐτοῦ, ὡς λέγουσιν οἱ κακολογοῦντες τὸν Ἰησοῦν, μὴ ἑωρακόσιν αὐτὸν ἀναστάντα ἀπὸ τῶν νεκρῶν μηδὲ πεισθεῖσιν ὅτι θειότερόν τι ἦν ἐκεῖνος, πρὸς τῷ μὴ φοβηθῆναι τὰ αὐτὰ τῷ διδασκάλῳ παθεῖν καὶ ὁμόσε χωρῆσαι τῷ κινδύνῳ καὶ καταλιπεῖν τὰς πατρίδας ὑπὲρ τοῦ διδάξαι κατὰ τὸ Ἰησοῦ βούλημα τὸν παραδοθέντα αὐτοῖς ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ λόγον. οἶμαι γὰρ ὅτι ὁ εὐγνωμόνως ἐξετάζων πράγματα οὐκ ἂν λέγοι τούτους ἑαυτοὺς παραδεδωκέναι περιστατικῷ βίῳ ἕνεκεν τῆς Ἰησοῦ διδασκαλίας χωρίς τινος μεγάλης πειθοῦς, ἣν ἐνεποίησεν αὐτοῖς διδάσκων οὐ μόνον διακεῖσθαι κατὰ τὰ μαθήματα αὐτοῦ ἀλλὰ καὶ ἄλλους διατιθέναι, καὶ διατιθέναι προὔπτου ὄντος ὡς πρὸς τὸν ἀνθρώπων βίον ὀλέθρου τῷ τολμῶντι πανταχοῦ καὶ πρὸς πάντας καινοτομεῖν καὶ μηδένα ἀνθρώπων, ἐμμένοντα τοῖς προτέροις δόγμασι καὶ ἔθεσι, φίλον ἑαυτῷ τηρεῖν. ἆρα γὰρ οὐχ ἑώρων οἱ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ μαθηταὶ, τολμῶντες οὐ μόνον Ἰουδαίοις ἐκ τῶν προφητικῶν λόγων παριστάνειν ὅτι οὗτος εἴη ὁ προφητευθεὶς, ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῖς λοιποῖς ἔθνεσιν ὅτι ὁ χθὲς καὶ πρώην σταυρωθεὶς ἑκὼν τοῦτον τὸν θάνατον ὑπὲρ τοῦ τῶν ἀνθρώπων γένους ἀνεδέξατο, ἀνάλογον τοῖς ἀποθανοῦσιν ὑπὲρ πατρίδων ἐπὶ τῷ σβέσαι λοιμικὰ κρατήσαντα καταστήματα ἢ ἀφορίας ἢ δυσπλοΐας; εἰκὸς γὰρ εἶναι ἐν τῇ φύσει τῶν πραγμάτων κατά τινας ἀποῤῥήτους καὶ δυσλήπτους τοῖς πολλοῖς λόγους φύσιν τοιαύτην, ὡς ἕνα δίκαιον ὑπὲρ τοῦ κοινοῦ ἀποθανόντα ἑκουσίως ἀποτροπιασμοὺς ἐμποιεῖν φαύλων δαιμονίων, ἐνεργούντων λοιμοὺς ἢ ἀφορίας ἢ δυσπλοΐας ἤ τι τῶν παραπλησίων. λεγέτωσαν οὖν οἱ βουλόμενοι ἀπιστεῖν τῷ Ἰησοῦν ὑπὲρ ἀνθρώπων ἀποτεθνηκέναι τρόπῳ σταυροῦ, πότερον οὐδὲ τὰς Ἑλληνικὰς παραδέξονται καὶ βαρβαρικὰς πολλὰς ἱστορίας περὶ τοῦ τινας ὑπὲρ τοῦ κοινοῦ τεθνηκέναι καθαιρετικῶς τῶν προκαταλαβόντων τὰς πόλεις καὶ τὰ ἔθνη κακῶν· ἢ ἐκεῖνα μὲν γεγένηται οὐδὲν δὲ πιθανὸν ἔχει ὁ νομιζόμενος ἄνθρωπος πρὸς τὸ ἀποθανεῖν ἐπὶ καθαιρέσει μεγάλου δαίμονος καὶ δαιμόνων ἄρχοντος, ὑποτάξαντος ὅλας τὰς ἐπὶ γῆν ἐληλυθυίας ἀνθρώπων ψυχάς; ὁρῶντες δὲ ταῦτα οἱ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ μαθηταὶ καὶ ἄλλα τούτων πλείονα, ἃ εἰκὸς αὐτοὺς ἐν ἀποῤῥήτῳ ἀπὸ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ μεμαθηκέναι, ἔτι δὲ καὶ δυνάμεώς τινος πληρωθέντες. ἐπεὶ ἔδωκεν αὐτοῖς μένος καὶ θάρσος οὐ ποιητική τις παρθένος ἀλλ᾿ ἡ ἀληθῶς φρόνησις καὶ σοφία τοῦ θεοῦ, (ἔσπευσαν,) ἵν᾿ ἔκδηλοι μετὰ πᾶσιν οὐ μόνοις Ἀργείοις γένοιντο ἀλλὰ καὶ πᾶσιν Ἕλλησιν ὁμοῦ καὶ βαρβάροις, καὶ κλέος ἐσθλὸν ἄροιντο.

excerpts.author: Origen
excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 34
english: Just as the prophets also foretold, the Messiah would come from a virgin. This came about in fulfillment of a promised sign: the one who would give birth to the child bearing the name that embodies the reality, showing that God would be with human beings at his birth. It also seems appropriate to me, in addressing the Jew’s persona, to set forth the prophecy of Isaiah, which declares that Emmanuel will be born of a virgin—a passage that Celsus omitted. He may have omitted it because he did not know it, despite his claim to know everything, or because he read it yet deliberately kept silent, so as not to appear to be constructing against his will an argument that ran counter to his own preference. The text reads as follows: ‘And the Lord spoke again to Ahaz, saying, “Ask a sign for yourself from the Lord your God, whether in the depths or in the heights.” But Ahaz replied, “I will not ask, and I will not test the Lord.” Then he said, “Hear now, O house of David: Is it too little for you to weary men, that you also weary my God? Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign: Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and you shall call his name Immanuel”’ (Isaiah 7:14), which is interpreted ‘God with us’. That Celsus acted maliciously in omitting this prophecy is clear to me from the fact that he passed over many things from the Gospel according to Matthew—such as the star that rose at the birth of Jesus and other remarkable events—and did not even mention the beginning of that account (Matthew 1:23). But if a Jew, seeking something to argue, claims that ‘Behold, the virgin’ is not written but rather ‘Behold, the young woman,’ we will reply that the Hebrew word ‘almah,’ which the Seventy translators rendered as ‘virgin’ and others as ‘young woman,’ is also found, they say, in Deuteronomy concerning a virgin. The passage reads: ‘If a virgin betrothed to a man is found in the city, and a man lies with her, you shall bring them both out to the gate of that city and stone them to death—the young woman because she did not cry out in the city, and the man because he violated his neighbor’s wife’ (Deuteronomy 22:23–24). And immediately afterward: ‘If a man finds a betrothed girl in the open country, and the man seizes her and lies with her, then only the man who lay with her shall die; but you shall do nothing to the girl, for the girl has committed no offense punishable by death.’

greek: ἀλλ᾿ ὡς καὶ προφῆται προεῖπον, ἀπὸ παρθένου. κατ᾿ ἐπαγγελίαν σημείου γεννώσης τὸν ἐπώνυμον πράγματος, δηλοῦντος ὅτι ἐπὶ τῇ γενέσει αὐτοῦ μετ᾿ ἀνθρώπων ἔσται θεός. Καὶ οἰκεῖόν γε φαίνεταί μοι πρὸς τὴν τοῦ Ἰουδαίου προσωποποιΐαν παραθέσθαι τὴν τοῦ Ἡσαΐου προφητείαν, λέγουσαν ἐκ παρθένου τεχθήσεσθαι τὸν Ἐμμανουήλ· ἣν οὐκ ἐξέθετο, εἴτε μὴ ἐπιστάμενος ὁ πάντ᾿ ἐπαγγελλόμενος εἰδέναι Κέλσος εἴτ᾿ ἀναγνοὺς μὲν ἑκὼν δὲ σιωπήσας, ἵνα μὴ δοκοίη κατασκευάζειν ἄκων τὸν λόγον ἐναντιούμενον αὐτοῦ τῇ προαιρέσει. ἔχει δ᾿ οὕτως ἡ λέξις· „καὶ προσέθετο κύριος τῷ Ἄχαζ λέγων· αἴτησαι σεαυτῷ σημεῖον παρὰ κυρίου θεοῦ σου εἰς βάθος ἢ εἰς ὕψος. καὶ εἶπεν Ἄχαζ· οὐ μὴ αἰτήσω οὐδ᾿ οὐ μὴ πειράσω τὸν κύριον. (καὶ εἶπεν·) ἀκούσατε δὴ, οἶκος Δαυὶδ, μὴ μικρὸν ὑμῖν ἀγῶνα παρέχειν ἀνθρώποις, καὶ πῶς κυρίῳ παρέχετε ἀγῶνα; διὰ τοῦτο δώσει κύριος αὐτὸς ὑμῖν σημεῖον· ἰδοὺ ἡ παρθένος ἐν γαστρὶ λήψεται καὶ τέξεται υἱὸν, καὶ καλέσεις τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ Ἐμμανουὴλ“, ὅπερ ἑρμηνεύεται „μεθ᾿ ἡμῶν ὁ θεός“. ὅτι δὲ κακουργῶν ὁ Κέλσος οὐκ ἐξέθετο τὴν προφητείαν, δῆλόν μοι γίνεται ἐκ τοῦ παραθέμενον αὐτὸν πολλὰ ἀπὸ τοῦ κατὰ Ματθαῖον εὐαγγελίου, ὥσπερ τὸν ἀνατείλαντα ἀστέρα ἐπὶ τῇ γενέσει τοῦ Ἰησοῦ καὶ ἄλλα τῶν παραδόξων, μηδὲ τὴν ἀρχὴν τούτου ἐμνημονευκέναι. ἐὰν δὲ Ἰουδαῖος εὑρεσιλογῶν τὸ „ἰδοὺ ἡ παρθένος“ μὴ γεγράφθαι λέγῃ ἀλλ᾿ ἀντ᾿ αὐτοῦ „ἰδοὺ ἡ νεᾶνις“, φήσομεν πρὸς αὐτὸν ὅτι ἡ μὲν λέξις ἡ ἀαλμὰ, ἣν οἱ μὲν ἑβδομήκοντα μετειλήφασι πρὸς τὴν παρθένον ἄλλοι δ᾿ εἰς τὴν νεᾶνιν, κεῖται, ὥς φασι, καὶ ἐν τᾷ Δευτερονομίῳ ἐπὶ παρθένου, οὕτως ἔχουσα·„ἐὰν δὲ γένηται παῖς παρθένος μεμνηστευμένη ἀνδρὶ, καὶ εὑρὼν αὐτὴν ἄνθρωπος ἐν πόλει κοιμηθῇ μετ᾿ αὐτῆς, καὶ ἐξάξετε ἀμφοτέρους ἐπὶ τὴν πύλην τῆς πόλεως αὐτῶν, καὶ λιθοβοληθήσονται λίθοις, καὶ ἀποθανοῦνται· τὴν νεᾶνιν ἐπὶ λόγου, διότι οὐκ ἐβόησεν ἐν τῇ πόλει, καὶ τὸν ἄνθρωπον ἐπὶ λόγου, διότι ἐταπείνωσε τὴν γυναῖκα τοῦ πλησίον αὐτοῦ·“ καὶ ἑξῆς· „ἐὰν δὲ ἐν πεδίῳ εὕρῃ ἄνθρωπος τὴν παῖδα τὴν μεμνηστευμένην καὶ βιασάμενος αὐτὴν ὁ ἄνθρωπος κοιμηθῇ μετ᾿ αὐτῆς, ἀποκτενεῖτε τὸν ἄνθρωπον τὸν κοιμώμενον μετ᾿ αὐτῆς μόνον, καὶ τῇ νεάνιδι οὐ ποιήσετε οὐδέν· οὐκ ἔστι τῇ νεάνιδι ἁμάρτημα θανάτου.“

excerpts.author: Origen
excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 35
english: Lest we appear to be offering consolation drawn from the Hebrew tongue to those who do not grasp it — whether they agree with it or not — let us instead find our comfort in the very wording of the prophecy: that the prophet said this one would be born of a virgin, and that on his birth the name 'God with us' is bestowed (Isaiah 7:14). Scripture records that the Lord said to Ahaz, 'Ask a sign for yourself from the Lord your God, whether in the depth or in the height' (Isaiah 7:11), and the sign given immediately follows: 'Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son.' What sort of sign would it be for a young woman, not a virgin, to give birth? And to whom does it more fittingly belong to bear 'Emmanuel' — that is, 'God with us' — a woman who has known intercourse and conceived through human passion, or one who remains pure, holy, and a virgin? For it is fitting for such a one to bear the offspring upon whose birth the words 'God with us' are declared. But if someone tries to rationalize by insisting the promise was spoken to Ahaz — 'Ask a sign for yourself from the Lord your God' — we will answer: in the days of Ahaz, who was born, upon whose birth the name 'Emmanuel, which is God with us,' is pronounced? If no one is found, then clearly what was said to Ahaz was addressed to the house of David, because the Savior is written to have been born 'according to the flesh' from the seed of David (Isaiah 7:14). Moreover, this 'sign' is said to reach 'into depth or into height,' since 'he who descended is also he who ascended above all the heavens, that he might fill all things' (Ephesians 4:10). I speak these things as one addressing a Jew who accepts the prophecy. Let Celsus, or anyone allied with him, declare: with what mind does the prophet speak of future things — whether these or others recorded in the prophecies? Is it a foreknowing mind, or not? For if it is a foreknowing mind, the prophets possessed a divine spirit; if not, let him explain the mind of the one who dares to speak of the future and is admired among the Jews for prophecy.

greek: Ἵνα δὲ μὴ δοκῶμεν ἀπὸ λέξεως Ἑβραϊκῆς τοῖς μὴ καταλαμβάνουσι, πότερον συγκαταθετέον αὐτῇ ἢ μὴ, φέρειν παραμυθίαν περὶ τοῦ προφήτην εἰρηκέναι ἐκ παρθένου τεχθήσεσθαι τοῦτον, ἐφ᾿ οὗ τῇ γενέσει λέλεκται τὸ „μεθ᾿ ἡμῶν ὁ θεὸς“, φέρε ἐπ᾿ αὐτῆς τῆς λέξεως παραμυθησώμεθα τὸ λεγόμενον. ὁ μὲν κύριος ἀναγέγραπται εἰρηκέναι τῷ Ἄχαζ· „αἴτησαι σεαυτῷ σημεῖον παρὰ κυρίου τοῦ θεοῦ σου εἰς βάθος ἢ εἰς ὕψος,“ ἑξῆς δὲ τὸ διδόμενον σημεῖον τὸ „ἰδοὺ ἡ παρθένος ἐν γαστρὶ ἕξει καὶ τέξεται υἱόν.“ ποῖον οὖν σημεῖον τὸ νεάνιδα, μὴ παρθένον τεκεῖν; καὶ τίνι μᾶλλον ἁρμόζει γεννῆσαι „Ἐμμανουὴλ,“ τουτέστι „μεθ᾿ ἡμῶν ὁ θεὸς,“ ἆρα γυναικὶ συνουσιασθείσῃ καὶ διὰ πάθους γυναικείου συλλαβούσῃ ἢ ἔτι καθαρᾷ καὶ ἁγνῇ καὶ παρθένῳ; ταύτῃ γὰρ πρέπει γεννᾶν γέννημα, ἐφ᾿ ᾧ τεχθέντι λέγεται τὸ „μεθ᾿ ἡμῶν ὁ θεός.“ ἐὰν δὲ καὶ οὕτως εὑρεσιλογῇ λέγων ὅτι τῷ Ἄχαζ εἴρηται· „αἴτησαι σεαυτῷ σημεῖον παρὰ κυρίου τοῦ θεοῦ σου,“ ἀπαντήσομεν· κατὰ τοὺς χρόνους τοῦ Ἄχαζ τίς ἐγεννήθη, ἐφ᾿ οἷ τῇ γενέσει λέγεται τὸ „Ἐμμανουὴλ, ὅ ἐστι μεθ᾿ ἡμῶν ὁ θεός,·“ εἰ γὰρ οὐδεὶς εὑρεθήσεται, δηλονότι τὸ τῷ Ἄχαζ εἰρημένον τῷ οἴκῳ εἴρηται Δαυὶδ διὰ τὸ „ἐκ σπέρματος Δαυὶδ“ ἀναγεγράφθαι τὸν σωτῆρα γεγονέναι „τὸ κατὰ σάρκα“· ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸ „σημεῖον“ τοῦτο „εἰς βάθος ἢ εἰς ὕψος“ λέγεται εἶναι, ἐπεὶ „ὁ καταβὰς οὗτός ἐστι καὶ ὁ ἀναβὰς ὑπεράνω πάντων τῶν οὐρανῶν, ἵνα πληρώσῃ τὰ πάντα.“ ταῦτα δὲ λέγω ὡς πρὸς τὸν Ἰουδαῖον συγκατατιθέμενον τῇ προφητείᾳ. λεγέτω δὲ καὶ Κέλσος ἤ τις τῶν σὺν αὐτῷ, ποίῳ νῷ ὁ προφήτης περὶ μελλόντων ἢ ταῦτα ἢ ἕτερα λέγει, ὁπόσα ἀναγέγραπται ἐν ταῖς προφητείαις· ἆρα γὰρ προγνωστικῷ μελλόντων ἢ οὔ; εἰ μὲν γὰρ προγνωστικῷ μελλόντων, θεῖον εἶχον πνεῦμα οἱ προφῆται· εἰ δ᾿ οὐ προγνωστικῷ μελλόντων, παραστησάτω τὸν νοῦν τοῦ ἀποτολμῶντος καὶ λέγοντος περὶ μελλόντων καὶ θαυμαζομένου παρὰ τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις ἐπὶ προφητείᾳ.

excerpts.author: Origen
excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 36
english: Since we have turned to the subject of the prophets, what follows will not be useless for the Jews, who believe the prophets spoke by the divine Spirit — and it will also serve the well-disposed among the Greeks. We will tell them that they must accept that the Jews had prophets too, if the Jews were indeed to remain bound together in the law given them, to believe in the Creator just as they had received him, and to have no opening to revolt into the polytheism of the nations. We will establish this necessity as follows. 'The nations,' as it is written even in the law of the Jews themselves, 'will listen to diviners and soothsayers'; but to that people it was said: 'The Lord your God has not given you such things' (Deuteronomy 18:14). And this is added to it: 'The Lord your God will raise up a prophet for you from among your brothers' (Deuteronomy 18:15). Now if the nations resort to divination — whether by omens, or by watching birds, or by reading entrails, or through ventriloquists, or through those who promise sacrificial rites, or through Chaldean astrologers — all of which were forbidden to the Jews — then, if the Jews had possessed no consolation of foreknowledge, they would have been driven by the same human craving to know the future. They would have despised their own heritage as having nothing divine in it; they would not have followed Moses as a prophet, nor recorded their words, but would have deserted to the divinations and oracles of the nations, or even tried to set up something similar among themselves. Therefore it is not absurd that the prophets among them spoke beforehand for the consolation of those who long for such knowledge — so that even Samuel prophesied about lost donkeys, and the prophet recorded in the third book of Kings spoke about the illness of a royal child (2 Kings 1:2–3). How else would the Jewish elders, who represent the law, have rebuked anyone who wanted to seek divination from idols? Just as Elijah is found rebuking Ahaziah and saying: 'Is it because there is no God in Israel that you are going to inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron?' (2 Kings 1:3).

greek: Ἐπεὶ δ᾿ ἅπαξ εἰς τὸν περὶ τῶν προφητῶν ἤλθομεν λόγον, Ἰουδαίοις μὲν, τοῖς πιστεύουσι θείῳ πνεύματι αὐτοὺς λελαληκέναι, οὐ μόνον οὐκ ἔσται ἀχρήσιμα τὰ ἐποισθησόμενα (ἀλλὰ) καὶ τοῖς εὐγνωμονοῦσι δὲ τῶν Ἑλλήνων. πρὸς οὓς ἐροῦμεν ὅτι ἀναγκαῖον παραδέξασθαι ὅτι καὶ Ἰουδαῖοι προφήτας εἶχον, εἴπερ ἔμελλον συνέχεσθαι ἐν τῇ δοθείσῃ αὐτοῖς νομοθεσίᾳ καὶ πιστεύειν τῷ δημιουργῷ, καθάπερ εἰλήφεισαν, καὶ ὅσον ἐπὶ τῷ νόμῳ μὴ ἔχειν ἀφορμὰς ἀποστῆναι εἰς τὴν τῶν ἐθνῶν πολυθεότητα. τὸ δ᾿ ἀναγκαῖον οὕτω παραστήσομεν. „τὰ ἔθνη,“ ὡς γέγραπται καὶ ἐν αὐτῷ τῷ τῶν Ἰουδαίων νόμῳ, „κληδόνων καὶ μαντειῶν ἀκούσονται“· τῷ δὲ λαῷ ἐκείνῳ εἴρηται· „σοὶ δὲ οὐχ οὕτως ἔδωκε κύριος ὁ θεός σου.“ καὶ ἐπιφέρεται τούτῳ τὸ „προφήτην ἐκ τῶν ἀδελφῶν σου ἀναστήσει σοι κύριος ὁ θεός σου.“ εἴπερ οὖν τῶν ἐθνῶν χρωμένων μαντείαις εἴτε διὰ „κληδόνων“ εἴτε δι᾿ οἰωνῶν εἴτε δι᾿ ὀρνίθων εἴτε δι᾿ ἐγγαστριμύθων εἴτε καὶ διὰ τῶν τὴν θυτικὴν ἐπαγγελλομένων εἴτε καὶ διὰ Χαλδαίων γενεθλιαλογούντων, ἅπερ πάντα Ἰουδαίοις ἀπείρητο. Ἰουδαῖοι εἰ μηδεμίαν εἶχον παραμυθίαν γνώσεως τῶν μελλόντων, ὑπ᾿ αὐτῆς ἂν τῆς ἀνθρωπίνης περὶ τὴν γνῶσιν λιχνείας τῶν ἐσομένων ἀγόμενοι κατεφρόνησαν μὲν ἂν τῶν ἰδίων ὡς οὐδὲν ἐχόντων θεῖον ἐν ἑαυτοῖς καὶ οὐκ ἂν μετὰ Μω(??)σέα προφήτην προσήκαντο οὐδ᾿ ἀνέγραψαν αὐτῶν τοὺς λόγους, αὐτόμολοι δὲ ἐπὶ τὸ τῶν ἐθνῶν μαντεῖα καὶ χρηστήρια μετέστησαν ἢ ἐπεχείρησαν ἂν ἱδρῦσαί τι τοιοῦτον καὶ παρ᾿ ἑαυτοῖς. ὥστ᾿ οὐδὲν ἄτοπόν ἐστι καὶ περὶ τῶν τυχόντων τοὺς παρ᾿ αὐτοῖς προφήτας εἰς παραμυθίαν τῶν τὰ τοιαῦτα ποθούντων προειρηκέναι, ὥστε καὶ „περὶ ὄνων ἀπολωλυιῶν“ προφητεύειν τὸν Σαμουὴλ καὶ περὶ νόσου παιδὸς βασιλικοῦ τὸν ἐν τῇ τρίτῃ τῶν Βασιλειῶν ἀναγεγραμμένον. πῶς δ᾿ ἂν τῷ βουλομένῳ ἀπὸ τῶν εἰδώλων μαντείαν λαβεῖν ἐπέπλησσον οἱ τὰ τοῦ νόμου Ἰουδαίων πρεσβεύοντες; ὥσπερ εὑρίσκεται Ἠλίας τῷ Ὀχοζίᾳ ἐπιπλήσσων καὶ λέγων· „εἰ παρὰ τὸ μὴ εἶναι θεὸν ἐν Ἰσραὴλ ὑμεῖς πορεύεσθε ἐκζητῆσαι ἐν τῇ Βαὰλ μυῖαν θεὸν Ἀκκαρῶν.“

excerpts.author: Origen
excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 37
english: It seems to me that the case has been reasonably established: not only will our Savior be born of a virgin, but there were also prophets among the Jews who foretold far more than just the broad outlines of the future. They spoke of Christ, of worldly kingdoms, of what would befall Israel, of the nations that would believe in the Savior, and of many other matters concerning him. Beyond these general predictions, they also foretold specific details—how Kish’s lost donkeys would be found, the illness that struck the son of Israel’s king, and anything else of that sort that stands recorded.

We must also address the Greeks, who refuse to believe in Jesus’ virgin birth. The Creator demonstrated in the generation of various animals that He could accomplish whatever He willed—not only for a single species, but for others and for human beings themselves. Certain female animals, as naturalists report, reproduce without any male partner; vultures, for instance, preserve their kind without mating. So what is so paradoxical if God, intending to send a divine teacher to humanity, caused the Logos of the one to be born to come into being by a different means instead of the seminal word that comes from the union of male and female?

Even according to the Greeks’ own accounts, not all humans originated from a man and a woman. If the world was generated, as many Greeks held, then the first human beings could not have come from sexual union; they had to arise from the earth, constituted by seminal logoi implanted in it. That strikes me as far more paradoxical than Jesus being born of a virgin in a manner essentially like that of other humans.

There is nothing out of place in appealing to Greek histories when speaking to Greeks, so that we do not appear to be the only ones relying on a paradoxical story. Some writers thought it worth recording not only ancient and heroic tales but also events of the very recent past—for example, that Plato was born of Amphictione after Ariston was prevented from lying with her until she gave birth to the child sown by Apollo. But these are plainly myths, invented to glorify a man they believed surpassed others in wisdom and power, crediting his bodily origin to superior, more divine seed—as if such a pedigree befitted those greater than ordinary mortals.

Now Celsus introduces a Jew who confronts Jesus and mocks, as he supposes, the claim of his virgin birth by dragging in the Greek myths about Danaë, Melanippe, Auge, and Antiope. The response must be that such talk suits a buffoon, not someone who is serious in his proclamation.

greek: Δοκεῖ μοι οὖν μετρίως κατεσκευάσθαι οὐ μόνον ὅτι γεννηθήσεται ἐκ παρθένου ὁ σωτὴρ ἡμῶν ἀλλ᾿ ὅτι καὶ προφῆται ἦσαν ἐν Ἰουδαίοις, προλέγοντες οὐ μόνον τὰ καθολικὰ περὶ μελλόντων, ὡς τὰ περὶ Χριστοῦ καὶ τὰ περὶ βασιλειῶν κοσμικῶν καὶ περὶ τῶν συμβησομένων τῷ Ἰσραὴλ καὶ περὶ τῶν πιστευόντων τῷ σωτῆρι ἐθνῶν καὶ πολλῶν ἄλλων τῶν περὶ αὐτοῦ λεχθέντων, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὰ καθ᾿ ἕνα, ὡς περὶ τῶν ὄνων Κὶς ἀπολομένων, πῶς εὑρεθήσονται, καὶ περὶ τῆς νόσου, ἧς ἐνόσησεν ὁ τοῦ βασιλέως Ἰσραὴλ υἱὸς, ἢ εἴ τι ἄλλο ἀναγέγραπται τοιοῦτον. ἔτι δὲ πρὸς Ἕλληνας λεκτέον, ἀπειθοῦντας τῇ ἐκ παρθένου γενέσει τοῦ Ἰησοῦ, ὅτι ὁ δημιουργὸς ἐν τῇ τῶν ποικίλων ζῴων γενέσει ἔδειξεν ὅτι ἦν αὐτῷ βουληθέντι δυνατὸν ποιῆσαι ὅπερ ἐφ᾿ ἑνὸς ζῴου καὶ ἐπ᾿ ἄλλων καὶ ἐπ᾿ αὐτῶν τῶν ἀνθρώπων. εὑρίσκεται δέ τινα τῶν ζῴων θήλεα, μὴ ἔχοντα ἄῤῥενος κοινωνίαν. ὡς οἱ περὶ ζῴων ἀναγράψαντες λέγουσι περὶ γυπῶν· καὶ τοῦτο τὸ ζῷον χωρὶς μίξεως σῴζει τὴν διαδοχὴν τῶν γενῶν. τί οὖν παράδοξον, εἰ βουληθεὶς ὁ θεὸς θεῖόν τινα διδάσκαλον πέμψαι τῷ γένει τῶν ἀνθρώπων πεποίηκεν ἀντὶ σπερματικοῦ λόγου, τοῦ· ἐκ μίξεως τῶν ἀῤῥένων ταῖς γυναιξὶ, [ποιῆσαι] ἄλλῳ τρόπῳ γενέσθαι τὸν λόγον τοῦ τεχθησομένου: καὶ κατ᾿ αὐτοὺς δὲ τοὺς Ἕλληνας οὐ πάντες ἄνθρωποι ἐξ ἀνδρὸς καὶ γυναικὸς ἐγένοντο. εἰ γὰρ γενητός ἐστιν ὁ κόσμος, ὡς καὶ πολλοῖς Ἑλλήνων ἤρεσεν, ἀνάγκη τοὺς πρώτους μὴ ἐκ συνουσίας γεγονέναι ἀλλ᾿ ἀπὸ γῆς, σπερματικῶν λόγων συστάντων ἐν τῇ γῇ· ὅπερ οἶμαι παραδοξότερον εἶναι τοῦ ἐξ ἡμίσους ὁμοίως τοῖς λοιποῖς ἀνθρώποις γενέσθαι τὸν Ἰησοῦν. οὐδὲν δ᾿ ἄτοπον πρὸς Ἕλληνας καὶ Ἑλληνικαῖς ἱστορίαις χρήσασθαι, ἵνα μὴ δοκῶμεν μόνοι τῇ παραδόξῳ ἱστορίᾳ ταύτῃ κεχρῆσθαι. Ἔδοξε γάρ τισιν οὐ περὶ ἀρχαίων τινῶν ἱστοριῶν καὶ ἡρωϊκῶν ἀλλὰ καὶ περί τινων χθὲς καὶ πρώην γενομένων ἀναγράψαι ὡς δυνατὸν ὅτι καὶ Πλάτων ἀπὸ τῆς Ἀμφικτιόνης γέγονε, κωλυθέντος τοῦ Ἀρίστωνος αὐτῇ συνελθεῖν, ἕως ἀποκυήσει τὸν ἐξ Ἀπόλλωνος σπαρέντα. ἀλλὰ ταῦτα μὲν ἀληθῶς μῦθοι, κινήσαντες εἰς τὸ ἀναπλάσαι τοιοῦτό τι περὶ ἀνδρὸς, ὃν ἐνόμιζον μείζονα τῶν πολλῶν ἔχοντα σοφίαν καὶ δύναμιν καὶ ἀπὸ κρειττόνων καὶ θειοτέρων σπερμάτων τὴν ἀρχὴν τῆς συστάσεως τοῦ σώματος εἰληφέναι, ὡς τοῦθ᾿ ἁρμόζον τοῖς μείζοσιν ἢ κατὰ ἄνθρωπον, ἐπεὶ δὲ τὸν Ἰουδαῖον ὁ Κέλσος εἰσήγαγε διαλεγόμενον τῷ Ἰησοῦ καὶ διασύροντα τὴν, ὡς οἴεται, προσποίησιν τῆς ἐκ παρθένου γενέσεως αὐτοῦ, φέροντα τοὺς Ἑλληνικοὺς μύθους περὶ Δανάης καὶ Μελανίππης καὶ Αὔγης καὶ Ἀντιόπης, λεκτέον ὅτι ταῦτα βωμολόχῳ ἔπρεπε τὰ ῥήματα καὶ οὐ σπουδάζοντι ἐν τῇ ἀπαγγελίᾳ.

excerpts.author: Origen
excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 41
english: We decided to address each of the objections he raises, to the best of our ability, so that we would not appear to be dodging an answer out of helplessness. In doing so, we paid attention not to the natural logic and sequence of the matters themselves, but to the order in which they appear in his book. Come, then, let us see what he says as he slanders the Holy Spirit, which the Savior saw in bodily form like a dove. A Jew is the one speaking these things to him — the very one to whom we acknowledge Jesus as our Lord. 'When you were being baptized by John,' the Jew says, 'you claim that a phantom bird descended on you from the air.' Then the Jew who is with him asks, 'Who is the credible witness who saw the phantom? Or who heard a voice from heaven declaring you to be the Son of God? — apart from the fact that you yourself say so and produce one of your own companions who was bribed.'

greek: Ἵνα δὲ μὴ δοκῶμεν ἑκόντες διὰ τὸ ἀπορεῖν ἀπαντήσεως ὑπερβαίνειν αὐτοῦ τὰ κεφάλαια, ἐκρίναμεν ἕκαστον κατὰ δύναμιν λῦσαι τῶν ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ προτιθεμένων. φροντίσαντες οὐ τοῦ ἐν τῇ φύσει τῶν πραγμάτων εἱρμοῦ καὶ ἀκολουθίας ἀλλὰ τῆς τάξεως τῶν ἐν τῇ βίβλῳ αὐτοῦ ἀναγεγραμμένων. φέρ᾿ οὖν ἴδωμεν, τί ποτε καὶ λέγει διαβάλλων τὸ οἷον σωματικῶς ἑωραμένον ὑπὸ τοῦ σωτῆρος πνεῦμα ἅγιον εἴδει περιστερᾶς· ἔστι δ᾿ ὁ Ἰουδαῖος αὐτῷ ἔτι ταῦτα λέγων, πρὸς ὃν ὁμολογοῦμεν εἶναι κύριον ἡμῶν τὸν Ἰησοῦν· λουομένῳ, φησὶ, σοὶ παρὰ τῷ Ἰωάννῃ φάσμα ὄρνιθος ἐξ ἀέρος λέγεις ἐπιπτῆναι. εἶτα πυνθανόμενος ὁ παρ᾿ αὐτῷ Ἰουδαῖός φησι· τίς τοῦτο εἶδεν ἀξιόχρεως μάρτυς τὸ φάσμα, ἢ τίς ἤκουσεν ἐξ οὐρανοῦ φωνῆς εἰσποιούσης σε υἱὸν τῷ θεῷ; πλὴν ὅτι σὺ φῂς καί τινα ἕνα ἐπάγῃ τῶν μετὰ σοῦ κεκολασμένων.

excerpts.author: Origen
excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 44
english: I address these words to the Jew, not because the Christian disbelieves Ezekiel and Isaiah, but out of reverence for what has been commonly entrusted to us: that this one is far more worthy of belief when he says he has seen such things and, as is likely, handed down to the disciples the vision he saw and the voice he heard (Matthew 3:16-17). Another might object that not all who heard Jesus recount these things were the ones who wrote down the account of the dove's appearance and the voice from heaven. Yet the same Spirit that taught Moses the earlier history — beginning from the creation of the world (Genesis 1:1) down to the time of Abraham his father — also taught the gospel writers the paradox that occurred at the time of Jesus' baptism. And the one adorned with the charism called 'word of wisdom' will recount the reason for the opening of the heavens and the appearance of the dove, and why the Holy Spirit appeared to Jesus in the form of this creature and not another. Our present discussion does not require us to recount that now; for the task at hand is to refute Celsus, who has improperly, like a Jew, thrown in unbelief about a matter that has more likely occurred than what he believed.

greek: Καὶ ταῦτα πρὸς τὸν Ἰουδαῖον λέγω, οὐκ ἀπιστῶν ὁ Χριστιανὸς τῷ Ἰεζεκιὴλ καὶ τῷ Ἡσαΐᾳ, ἀλλὰ δυσωπῶν ἐκ τῶν κοινῇ ἡμῖν πεπιστευμένων ὅτι πολλῷ οὗτος ἐκείνων ἄξιός ἐστι τοῦ πιστεύεσθαι τοιαῦτα λέγων ἑωρακέναι καὶ ὡς εἰκὸς παραδοὺς τοῖς μαθηταῖς ἣν εἶδεν ὄψιν καὶ τὴν φωνὴν ἧς ἤκουσεν. ἄλλος δ᾿ ἄν τις εἴποι ὅτι οὐ πάντες τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ἤκουσαν ταῦτα διηγουμένου οἱ ἀναγράψαντες τὰ περὶ τοῦ εἴδους τῆς περιστερᾶς καὶ τῆς ἐξ οὐρανοῦ φωνῆς· ἀλλὰ τὸ διδάξαν Μωϋσέα πνεῦμα τὴν πρεσβυτέραν αὐτοῦ ἱστορίαν, ἀρξαμένην ἀπὸ τῆς κοσμογενείας μέχρι τῆς κατὰ τὸν Ἀβραὰμ τὸν πατέρα αὐτοῦ, τοῦτ᾿ ἐδίδαξε καὶ τοὺς γράψαντας τὸ εὐαγγέλιον τὸ γενόμενον παράδοξον κατὰ τὸν χρόνον τοῦ βαπτίσματος Ἰησοῦ. ὁ δὲ κοσμηθεὶς χαρίσματι καλουμένῳ „λόγῳ σοφίας“ καὶ τὴν αἰτίαν διηγήσεται τῆς ἀνοίξεως τῶν οὐρανῶν καὶ τοῦ εἴδους τῆς περιστερᾶς, καὶ ὅτι οὐκ ἄλλου τινὸς ζῴου εἴδει ἢ τούτου ἐφάνη τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα τῷ Ἰησοῦ. περὶ τούτου δὲ οὐκ ἀπαιτεῖ νῦν ἡμᾶς ὁ λόγος διηγήσασθαι· τὸ γὰρ προκείμενόν ἐστιν ἐλέγξαι τὸν Κέλσον οὐχ ὑγιῶς Ἰουδαίῳ περιθέντα μετὰ τοιῶνδε λόγων ἀπιστίαν περὶ πράγματος, κατὰ τὸ εἰκὸς γενομένου μᾶλλον παρὰ τὰ πεπιστευμένα ὑπ᾿ ἐκείνου.

excerpts.author: Origen
excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 48
english: Even if the Jew refuses to defend Ezekiel and Isaiah, we ourselves claim the passages about the heavens opening for Jesus, the voice he heard, and the similar visions recorded in Ezekiel, Isaiah, or any other prophet. We will present our argument with all the force we can muster, arguing that just as many people believe they have experienced dreams — some more divine, some foretelling everyday future events, whether plainly or in riddles — and this is evident to everyone who accepts divine providence, so why should it seem absurd that the ruling faculty of the mind, while dreaming, can shape a vision that proves useful either to the dreamer or to those who hear his report? In the same way, we experience a dream as if we were hearing and seeing with physical ears and eyes, yet neither our bodily hearing nor our sight is actually engaged; rather, it is the ruling faculty that undergoes these impressions. Therefore it is not absurd that such things happened to the prophets, since Scripture records that they saw paradoxical visions, heard the Lord’s words, and beheld heavens opening. For I do not suppose that the physical heaven was literally torn open and Jesus’ body divided so that Ezekiel could write such things. Perhaps, then, we should accept a similar explanation for the Savior as well, even if it offends simpler people who, in their simplicity, disturb the world by tearing apart the unified body of the whole heaven. But the one who examines this more deeply will say that, since there exists a certain divine, generic faculty of perception — which only the blessed discover, as Solomon says, 'You will find divine sense' — and since this faculty has distinct modes: a vision capable of seeing realities superior to bodies, in which the cherubim and seraphim are revealed; a hearing that perceives voices not borne on air; a taste that partakes of living bread come down from heaven giving life to the world; a smell that discerns such things, as Paul says, 'the fragrance of Christ to God' (2 Cor 2:15); and a touch, as John says, 'we have touched with our hands concerning the word of life' (1 John 1:1) — the blessed prophets, having found this divine sense, saw divinely, heard divinely, tasted and smelled divinely, so to speak, and were touched by the Word through faith, so that its outflow came to them and healed them. Thus they saw what they wrote they saw, heard what they said they heard, and underwent similar experiences as they recorded, eating the 'scroll' given to them in a book (Ezek 2:8–3:3). Likewise Isaac 'smelled the smell of his son's garments' and pronounced a spiritual blessing: 'Behold, the smell of my son is like the smell of a field that the Lord has blessed' (Gen 27:27). In a parallel way, Jesus 'touched' the leper to cleanse him — as I think, in two ways: not only removing the sensory leprosy by sensory touch, but also the other leprosy by his truly divine touch. Thus John testified, saying, 'I saw the Spirit descending like a dove from heaven, and it remained on him. I did not know him, but the one who sent me to baptize with water said to me, "He on whom you see the Spirit descend and remain, this is he who baptizes with the Holy Spirit." And I have seen and have borne witness that this is the Son of God' (John 1:32–34). And the heavens were opened to Jesus; at that time no one except John is recorded as having seen the heavens opened. But Jesus, foretelling this future event to his disciples, said, 'Truly, truly, I say to you, you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man' (John 1:51). And thus Paul was caught up to the third heaven, having first seen it opened, since he was a disciple of Jesus. To explain now why Paul says, 'Whether in the body or out of the body I do not know; God knows' (2 Cor 12:2–3), is not the present task. I will also add the points that Celsus thinks Jesus himself spoke about the opening of the heavens and the Holy Spirit descending on him in the form of a dove by the Jordan; yet Scripture does not present Jesus as saying he saw this. Celsus did not notice that this does not accord with the command Jesus gave the disciples on the mountain of the vision: 'Tell no one the vision, until the Son of Man is raised from the dead' (Matt 17:9) — that the things seen and heard by John at the Jordan were told to the disciples. It is evident from Jesus' character everywhere that he avoided self-praise; for this reason he said, 'Even if I do bear witness about myself, my testimony is not true' (John 5:31). And he avoided self-praise in his works as well, preferring to demonstrate by deeds rather than words that he is the Christ; that is why the Jews said to him, 'If you are the Christ, tell us plainly' (John 10:24). Now since the speaker in Celsus' dialogue who addresses Jesus about the Spirit in the form of a dove is a Jew — saying, 'except that you say and bring along one of your followers' — it is necessary for Celsus to show that this language fits a Jewish character. For the Jews do not connect John with Jesus, nor John's punishment with Jesus' punishment. And so in this Celsus is refuted, he who boasted that he knew everything but did not know what words to put into the mouth of a Jewish character addressing Jesus.

greek: Εἰ καὶ μὴ ἀπολογήσεται οὖν ὁ Ἰουδαῖος περὶ Ἰεζεκιὴλ καὶ Ἡσαΐου, κοινοποιούντων ἡμῶν τὰ περὶ τῆς ἀνοίξεως τῶν οὐρανῶν ἐπὶ Ἰησοῦ καὶ τῆς ἀκουσθείσης αὐτῷ φωνῆς καὶ τὰ ὅμοια εὑρισκόντων ἐν τῷ Ἰεζεκιὴλ ἀναγεγραμμένα καὶ ἐν τῷ Ἡσαΐᾳ ἢ καί τινι ἄλλῳ προφήτῃ. ἡμεῖς γε τὸν λόγον ὅση δύναμις ἡμῖν παραστήσομεν λέγοντες ὅτι, ὥσπερ ὄναρ πεπίστευται πολλοὺς πεφαντασι ῶσθαι τινὰ μὲν θειότερα τινὰ δὲ περὶ μελλόντων βιωτικῶν ἀναγγέλλοντα εἴτε σαφῶς εἴτε καὶ δι᾿ αἰνιγμάτων, καὶ τοῦτ᾿ ἐναργές ἐστι παρὰ πᾶσι τοῖς παραδεξαμένοις πρόνοιαν, οὕτως τί ἄτοπον τὸ τυποῦν τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν ἐν ὀνείρῳ δύνασθαι αὐτὸ τυποῦν καὶ ὕπαρ πρὸς τὸ χρήσιμον τῷ ἐν ᾧ τυποῦται ἢ τοῖς παρ᾿ αὐτοῦ ἀκουσομένοις; καὶ ὥσπερ φαντασίαν λαμβάνομεν ὄναρ ἀκούειν καὶ πλήσσεσθαι τὴν αἰσθητὴν ἀκοὴν καὶ ὁρᾶν δι᾿ ὀφθαλμῶν, οὔτε τῶν τοῦ σώματος ὀφθαλμῶν οὔτε τῆς ἀκοῆς πλησσομένης ἀλλὰ τοῦ ἡγεμονικοῦ ταῦτα πάσχοντος, οὕτως οὐδὲν ἄτοπον τοιαῦτα γεγονέναι ἐπὶ τῶν προφητῶν, ὅτε ἀναγέγραπται ἑωρακέναι τινὰ αὐτοὺς παραδοξότερα ἢ ἀκηκοέναι λόγους κυρίου ἢ τεθεωρηκέναι οὐρανοὺς ἀνοιγομένους. ἐγὼ γὰρ οὐχ ὑπολαμβάνω τὸν αἰσθητὸν οὐρανὸν ἀνεῷχθαι καὶ τὸ σῶμα αὐτοῦ ἀνοιγνύμενον διῃρῆσθαι, ἵνα ἀναγράψῃ τὸ τοιοῦτον Ἰεζεκιήλ. μή ποτ᾿ οὖν καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ σωτῆρος τὸν φρονίμως ἀκούοντα τῶν εὐαγγελίων τὸ ὅμοιον ἐκδεκτέον, κἂν προσκόπτῃ τὸ τοιοῦτον τοῖς ἁπλουστέροις, οἳ διὰ πολλὴν ἁπλότητα κινοῦσι τὸν κόσμον, σχίζοντες τὸ τηλικοῦτον σῶμα ἡνωμένον τοῦ παντὸς οὐρανοῦ. ὁ δὲ βαθύτερον τὸ τοιοῦτον ἐξετάζων ἐρεῖ ὅτι οὔσης, ὡς ἡ γραφὴ ὠνόμασε, θείας τινὸς γενικῆς αἰσθήσεως, ἣν μόνος ὁ μακάριος εὑρίσκει ἤδη κατὰ τὸ λεγόμενον καὶ παρὰ τῷ Σολομῶντι· „ὅτι αἴσθησιν θείαν εὑρήσεις,“ καὶ ὄντων εἰδῶν ταύτης τῆς αἰσθήσεως, ὁράσεως πεφυκυίας βλέπειν τὰ κρείττονα σωμάτων πράγματα, ἐν οἷς δηλοῦται τὰ χερουβὶμ ἢ τὰ σεραφὶμ, καὶ ἀκοῆς ἀντιληπτικῆς φωνῶν οὐχὶ ἐν ἀέρι τὴν οὐσίαν ἐχουσῶν, καὶ γεύσεως χρωμένης ἄρτῳ ζῶντι καὶ ἐξ οὐρανοῦ καταβεβηκότι καὶ ζωὴν διδόντι τῷ κόσμῳ, οὕτω δὲ καὶ ὀσφρήσεως ὀσφραινομένης τοιῶνδε, καθὸ „Χριστοῦ εὐωδία“ λέγει εἶναι „τῷ θεῷ“ Παῦλος, καὶ ἁφῆς, καθ᾿ ἣν Ἰωάννης φησὶ ταῖς χερσὶν ἐψηλαφηκέναι „περὶ τοῦ λόγου τῆς ζωῆς“· οἱ μακάριοι προφῆται τὴν θείαν αἴσθησιν εὑρόντες καὶ βλέποντες θείως καὶ ἀκούοντες θείως καὶ γευόμενοι ὁμοίως καὶ ὀσφραινόμενοι, ἵν᾿ οὕτως ὀνομάσω, αἰσθήσει οὐκ αἰσθητῇ καὶ ἁπτόμενοι τοῦ λόγου μετὰ πίστεως, ὥστ᾿ ἀποῤῥοὴν αὐτοῦ ἥκειν εἰς αὐτοὺς θεραπεύσουσαν αὐτοὺς, οὕτως ἑώρων ἃ ἀναγράφουσιν ἑωρακέναι καὶ ἤκουον ἃ λέγουσιν ἀκηκοέναι καὶ τὰ παραπλήσια ἔπασχον, ὡς ἀνέγραφον, ἐσθίοντες „κεφαλίδα“ διδομένην αὐτοῖς βιβλίου. οὕτω δὲ καὶ Ἰσαὰκ „ὠσφράνθη τῆς ὀσμῆς τῶν“ τοῦ υἱοῦ θειοτέρων „ἱματίων“ καὶ ἐπεῖπε πνευματικῇ εὐλογίᾳ τό· „ἰδοὺ ὀσμὴ τοῦ υἱοῦ μου ὡς ὀσμὴ ἀγροῦ πλήρους, ὃν εὐλόγησεν ὁ κύριος.“ παραπλησίως δὲ τούτοις καὶ νοητῶς μᾶλλον ἢ αἰσθητῶς Ἰησοῦς „ηψατο“ τοῦ λεπροῦ, ἵν᾿ αὐτὸν καθαρίσῃ, ὡς ἐγὼ οἶμαι, διχῶς, ἀπαλλάττων αὐτὸν οὐ μόνον, ὡς οἱ πολλοὶ ἀκούουσι, λέπρας αἰσθητῆς δι᾿ αἰσθητῆς ἁφῆς ἀλλὰ καὶ τῆς ἄλλης διὰ τῆς ὡς ἀληθῶς θείας αὐτοῦ ἁφῆς, οὕτως οὖν „ἐμαρτύρησεν Ἰωάννης λέγων ὅτι τεθέαμαι τὸ πνεῦμα καταβαῖνον ὡς περιστερὰν ἐξ οὐρανοῦ, καὶ ἔμεινεν ἐπ᾿ αὐτόν. κἀγὼ οὐκ ᾔδειν αὐτὸν, ἀλλ᾿ ὁ πέμψας με βαπτίζειν ἐν τῷ ὕδατι, ἐκεῖνός μοι εἶπεν· ἐφ᾿ ὃν ἂν ἴδῃς τὸ πνεῦμα καταβαῖνον καὶ μένον ἐπ᾿ αὐτὸν, οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ βαπτίζων ἐν πνεύματι ἁγίῳ, κἀγὼ ἑώρακα, καὶ μεμαρτύρηκα ὅτι οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ.“ καὶ τῷ Ἰησοῦ γε ἠνοίχθησαν οἱ οὐρανοί· καὶ τότε μὲν πλὴν Ἰωάννου οὐδεὶς ἀναγέγραπται ἑωρακέναι ἀνοιχθέντας τοὺς οὐρανούς. τοῦτο δὲ τὸ ἀνοιχθῆναι τοὺς οὐρανοὺς προλέγων τοῖς μαθηταῖς ὁ σωτὴρ ἐσόμενον ὀψομένοις αὐτό φησιν· „ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν, ὄψεσθε τὸν οὐρανὸν ἀνεῳγότα καὶ τοὺς ἀγγέλους τοῦ θεοῦ ἀναβαίνοντας καὶ καταβαίνοντας ἐπὶ τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου.“ καὶ οὕτως Παῦλος ἡρπάγη εἰς τρίτον οὐρανὸν, πρότερον ἰδὼν αὐτὸν ἀνοιχθέντα, ἐπεὶ μαθητὴς ἦν Ἰησοῦ. διηγήσασθαι δὲ νῦν, διὰ τί ὁ Παῦλος λέγει τό· „εἴτε ἐν σώματι οὐκ οἶδα, εἴτε ἐκτὸς τοῦ σώματος οὐκ οἶδα, ὁ θεὸς οἶδεν,“ οὐ τοῦ παρόντος ἐστὶ καιροῦ. ἔτι δὲ προσθήσω τῷ λόγῳ καὶ αὐτὰ, ἃ οἴεται ὁ Κέλσος, ὅτι αὐτὸς Ἰησοῦς εἶπε τὰ περὶ τὴν ἄνοιξιν τῶν οὐρανῶν καὶ τὸ καταβὰν πνεῦμα ἅγιον ἐπ᾿ αὐτὸν (ἐν) εἴδει περιστερᾶς παρὰ τῷ Ἰορδάνῃ· τῆς γραφῆς τοῦτο οὐ παραστησάσης, ὅτι αὐτὸς εἶπε τοῦτο ἑωρακέναι. οὐ συνεῖδε δ᾿ ὁ γενναιότατος ὅτι οὐκ ἔστι κατὰ τὸν εἰπόντα τοῖς μαθηταῖς ἐπὶ τῇ ἐν τῷ ὄρει ὀπτασίᾳ· „μηδενὶ εἴπητε τὸ ὅραμα, ἕως ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἐκ νεκρῶν ἀναστῇ,“ εἰρηκέναι τοῖς μαθηταῖς τὸ παρὰ τῷ Ἰορδάνῃ ὀφθὲν ὑπὸ τοῦ Ἰωάννου καὶ ἀκουσθέν, ἐνιδεῖν δὲ ἔστι καὶ τῷ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ἤθει πανταχοῦ περιϊσταμένου τὴν περιαυτολογίαν καὶ διὰ τοῦτο λέγοντος „κἂν ἐγὼ εἴπω περὶ ἐμαυτοῦ, ἡ μαρτυρία μου οὐκ ἔστιν ἀληθής.“ καὶ ἐπὶ περιΐστατο τὴν περιαυτολογίαν καὶ τοῖς ἔργοις μᾶλλον ἐβούλετο δηλοῦν εἶναι Χριστὸς ἤπερ τῇ λέξει, διὰ τοῦτό φασιν οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι πρὸς αὐτόν· „εἰ σὺ εἶ ὁ Χριστὸς, εἰπὲ ἡμῖν παῤῥησίᾳ.“ ἐπεὶ δὲ Ἰουδαῖός ἐστιν ὁ παρὰ τῷ Κέλσῳ λέγων τῷ Ἰησοῦ περὶ τῶν κατὰ τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον ἐν εἴδει περιστρᾶς τό· πλὴν ὅτι σὺ φῂς καί τινα ἕνα ἐπάγῃ τῶν μετὰ σοῦ κεκολασμένων, ἀναγκαῖον αὐτῷ παραστῆσαι ὅτι καὶ τοῦτο οὐκ οἰκείως τῷ Ἰουδαϊκῷ προσώπῳ περιέθηκεν. οὐδὲ γὰρ συνάπτουσι τὸν Ἰωάννην οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι τῷ Ἰησοῦ καὶ τὴν Ἰωάννου τῇ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ κολάσει. καὶ ἐν τούτῳ οὖν ἐλέγχεται ὁ πάντ᾿ ἀλαζονευσάμενος εἰδέναι μὴ ἐγνωκὼς, τίνα προσάψῃ ῥήματα τῷ Ἰουδαϊκῷ πρὸς τὸν Ἰησοῦν προσώπῳ.

excerpts.anf_chapter_title: Chapter 57
english: The Jew still says to the Savior, "If you say that every human being, having come into existence by divine providence, is a son of God, how would you differ from anyone else?" We will reply that everyone whom Paul describes—those no longer driven by fear but choosing the good for its own sake—is a son of God. Yet this one differs vastly and profoundly from every son of God who owes that status to virtue; he is, as it were, the source and beginning of all such people. Paul's words are: "For you did not receive a spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you received a spirit of adoption, in which we cry, 'Abba, Father'" (Romans 8:15). Some will also object, as the Jew in Celsus puts it, that myriads claim Jesus spoke these things about himself, the very things prophesied concerning him. We do not know whether Celsus was unaware of certain people who had appeared in history and wanted to imitate Jesus, proclaiming themselves sons of God or a power of God.

Since, however, we are investigating the facts on the ground truthfully, we will say that before Jesus' birth a certain Theudas arose among the Jews, calling himself "someone great"; after his death, those deceived by him were scattered. After him, "in the days of the census," when Jesus appears to have been born, a certain Judas the Galilean drew many away from the Jewish people, presenting himself as wise and innovative; when he met his just end, his teaching was utterly destroyed, surviving only among a tiny handful. After Jesus' time, the Samaritan Dositheus also tried to convince the Samaritans that he was the Christ foretold by Moses, and some seemed to be won over by his teaching. But we must set forth the very wise statement of Gamaliel, recorded in the Acts of the Apostles, which shows that those men were strangers to the promise—neither sons of God nor his powers—while Jesus Christ truly was the Son of God. Gamaliel said there: "If this plan or this work is of human origin, it will be overthrown," as indeed theirs were when they died; "but if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow it—lest you even be found fighting against God" (Acts 5:38-39).

Simon the Samaritan magician also tried to use his magic to gain a following. For a time he succeeded in deceiving people, but now I doubt there are thirty Simonians to be found in the whole world; I may even have overstated the number. There are, however, very few of them around Palestine, and in the rest of the world his name is nowhere to be found—the very world in which he wished to spread his own glory. This account comes from those who transmit it, drawn from the Acts of the Apostles; Christians are the ones who say these things about him, and the evidence has testified that Simon was nothing divine.

greek: Ἔτι δὲ πρὸς τὸν σωτῆρα αὐτῷ ὁ Ἰουδαῖός φησιν ὅτι, εἰ τοῦτο λέγεις, ὅτι πᾶς ἄνθρωπος κατὰ θείαν πρόνοιαν γεγονὼς υἱός ἐστι θεοῦ, τί ἂν σὺ ἄλλου διαφέροις; πρὸς ὃν ἐροῦμεν ὅτι πᾶς μὲν ὁ, ὡς ὁ Παῦλος ὠνόμασε, μηκέτι ὑπὸ φόβου παιδαγωγούμενος ἀλλὰ δι᾿ αὑτὸ τὸ καλὸν αἱρούμενος υἱός ἐστι θεοῦ· οὗτος δὲ πολλῷ καὶ μακρῶ διαφέρει παντὸς τοῦ διὰ τὴν ἀρετὴν χρηματίζοντος υἱοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ, ὅστις ὡσπερεὶ πηγή τις καὶ ἀρχὴ τῶν τοιούτων τυγχάνει. ἡ δὲ τοῦ Παύλου λέξις οὕτως ἔχει· „οὐ γὰρ ἐλάβετε πνεῦμα δουλείας πάλιν εἰς φόβον, ἀλλ᾿ ἐλάβετε πνεῦμα υἱοθεσίας, ἐν ᾧ κράζομεν· Ἀββὰ ὁ πατήρ.“ τινὲς δὲ καὶ ἐλέγξουσιν, ὥς φησιν ὁ παρὰ Κέλσῳ Ἰουδαῖος, μυρίοι τὸν Ἰησοῦν φάσκοντες περὶ ἑαυτῶν ταῦτα εἰρῆσθαι, ἅπερ περὶ ἐκείνου ἐπροφητεύετο. οὐκ οἴδαμεν οὖν εἰ ὁ Κέλσος ἠπίστατό τινας ἐπιδημήσαντας τῷ βίῳ καὶ τὸ παραπλήσιον βουληθέντας ποιεῖν τῷ Ἰησοῦ καὶ θεοῦ υἱοὺς αὑτοὺς ἀναγορεύειν ἢ θεοῦ δύναμιν. ἐπεὶ δὲ φιλαλήθως τὰ κατὰ τοὺς τόπους ἐξετάζομεν, ἐροῦμεν ὅτι Θευδᾶς πρὸ τῆς γενέσεως Ἰησοῦ γέγονέ τις παρὰ Ἰουδαίοις „μέγαν“ „τινὰ ἑαυτὸν“ λέγων· οὗ ἀποθανόντος οἱ ἀπατηθέντες ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ διεσκεδάσθησαν. καὶ μετ᾿ ἐκεῖνον „ἐν ταῖς τῆς ἀπογραφῆς ἡμέραις,“ ὅτ᾿ ἔοικε γεγεννῆσθαι ὁ Ἰησοῦς, Ἰούδας τις Γαλιλαῖος πολλοὺς ἑαυτῷ συναπέστησεν ἀπὸ τοῦ λαοῦ τῶν Ἰουδαίων ὡς σοφὸς καὶ καινοτομῶν τινα· οὗ καὶ αὐτοῦ δίκας τίσαντος ἡ διδασκαλία καθῃρέθη πάνυ ἐν ὀλίγοις καὶ ἐλαχίστοις μείνασα. καὶ μετὰ τοὺς Ἰησοῦ δὲ χρόνους ἠθέλησε καὶ ὁ Σαμαρεὺς Δοσίθεος πεῖσαι Σαμαρεῖς ὅτι αὐτὸς εἴη ὁ προφητευόμενος ὑπὸ Μω(??)σέως Χριστὸς, καὶ ἔδοξέ τινων τῇ ἑαυτοῦ διδασκαλίᾳ κεκρατηκέναι. ἀλλὰ τὸ εἰρημένον πάνυ σοφῶς ὑπὸ τοῦ ἐν ταῖς Πράξεσι τῶν ἀποστόλων ἀναγεγραμμένου Γαμαλιὴλ οὐκ ἄλογον παραθέμενον δεῖξαι, πῶς ἐκεῖνοι μὲν ἀλλότριοι τῆς ἐπαγγελίας ησαν, οὔτε υἱοὶ θεοῦ οὔτε δυνάμεις ὄντες αὐτοῦ, ὁ δὲ Χριστὸς ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἀληθῶς ην υἱὸς θεοῦ. εἶπε δ᾿ ἐκεῖ ὁ Γαμαλιήλ· „ὅτι ἐὰν ᾖ ἐξ ἀνθρώπων ἡ βουλὴ αὕτη καὶ ὁ λόγος οὗτος, καταλυθήσεται,“ ὡς καὶ τὰ ἐκείνων κατελύθη ἀποθανόντων· „ἐὰν δὲ ᾖ ἐκ θεοῦ οὐ δυνήσεσθε καταλῦσαι τὴν τούτου διδασκαλίαν, μή ποτε καὶ θεομάχοι εὑρεθῆτε.“ ἠθέλησε δὲ καὶ Σίμων ὁ Σαμαρεὺς μάγος τῇ μαγείᾳ ὑφελέσθαι τινάς. καὶ τότε μὲν ἠπάτησε, νυνὶ δὲ τοὺς πάντας ἐν τῇ οἰκουμένῃ οὐκ ἔστι Σιμωνιανοὺς εὑρεῖν τὸν ἀριθμὸν οἶμαι τριάκοντα, καὶ τάχα πλείονας εἶπον τῶν ὄντων. εἰσὶ δὲ περὶ τὴν Παλαιστίνην σφόδρα ἐλάχιστοι· τῆς δὲ λοιπῆς οἰκουμένης οὐδαμοῦ τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ, καθ᾿ ἣν ἠθέλησε δόξαν περὶ ἑαυτοῦ διασκεδάσαι. παρὰ γὰρ οἷς φέρεται, ἐκ τῶν Πράξεων τῶν ἀποστόλων φέρεται· Χριστινανοὶ δ᾿ εἰσὶν οἱ ταῦτα περὶ αὐτοῦ λέγοντες, καὶ ἡ ἐνάργεια ἐμαρτύρησεν ὅτι οὐδὲν θεῖον ὁ Σίμων ἦν.
